question: Which of the following statements regarding parent-child relationships is incorrect? (In the event of a dispute, based on precedents)
A: Even if a conciliation or judicial settlement containing a statement confirming that there is no natural parent-child relationship between the parties is concluded, it has no effect.
B: Even a relative prescribed in Article 777 of the Civil Act is recognized as having standing as a plaintiff in an action to confirm the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only when that person qualifies as an interested party prescribed in Article 865 of the Civil Act.
C: Where, after co-heirs B and C of the decedent A (female) have already divided or disposed of the inherited property, it is clearly revealed by a final and conclusive judgment confirming the existence of a natural parent-child relationship that D is A’s child, the proviso to Article 860 of the Civil Act concerning the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment does not apply, and therefore D cannot deny the validity of the division or disposition made by B and C.
D: Where a child born through artificial insemination is born between a husband and wife who are living a normal marital life, the child born through artificial insemination is presumed to be the husband’s child, and if the husband later retracts his consent to the artificial insemination and files an action to disavow paternity, such action is not permitted.
E: A gender correction must not be denied merely on the ground that a transgender person has a minor child, without making a substantive determination by considering various circumstances for balancing legal interests so as to harmonize the protection of the transgender person’s fundamental rights with the protection and welfare of the minor child.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2015MEU0000]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the case and issues\\na. Summary of the case\\nNon-party 1 (deceased on August 10, 1909) was designated on August 15, 2010 as a recipient candidate for the Patriotic Medal, Grade 4, of the Order of Merit for National Foundation. After Non-party 3, a child of Non-party 1’s eldest daughter, Non-party 2 (deceased), was recognized through administrative litigation as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (the version before amendment by Act No. 11332 on February 17, 2012; hereinafter the “former Independence Merit Treatment Act”), the Plaintiff, who is the grandson of Non-party 1’s eldest son, Non-party 4 (deceased), filed this action against the Prosecutor seeking, among other things, a confirmation that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2.\\nThe lower court dismissed this action as inadmissible on the ground that even if the Plaintiff were to obtain a judgment confirming the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship as described above, he could not be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, and that there was no other legal interest in seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship. In response, the Plaintiff appealed, arguing that because he is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1 within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, he necessarily has an interest in filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, in accordance with prior Supreme Court precedents.\\n\\nb. Issue in this case\\nThe issue in this case is whether the Plaintiff, merely by virtue of the fact that he is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1, may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. In order to determine the issue, we shall first examine the scope of standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865, and then consider whether to maintain the prior Supreme Court precedents holding that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file such an action merely on the basis of being in such a status relationship.\\n\\n2. Standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865\\na. Persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship\\nA parent-child relationship, which is a parent-child relationship, is divided into a natural parent-child relationship based on blood ties and an adoptive parent-child relationship based on the parties’ intent. As to the natural parent-child relationship, the Civil Act provides several provisions for determining the existence or dissolution of the relationship, unlike the mother-child relationship, which is clearly determined by the natural facts of conception and birth. These include the provision on the presumption of legitimacy that a child conceived during marriage is presumed to be the child of the husband (Article 844, paragraph (1)); the provisions concerning an action for disavowal of paternity, which is the method for rebutting that presumption (Articles 846 through 851); the provisions concerning the determination by the court of paternity where a remarried woman gives birth (Article 845); the provisions concerning acknowledgment of a child born out of wedlock (Article 855, paragraph (1), and Article 863); and the provisions concerning revocation of acknowledgment and an action to object to acknowledgment (Articles 861 and 862). Accordingly, in litigation seeking the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it is in principle the person entitled to file the action as expressly specified in each of the above provisions who may file suit upon satisfying the requirements prescribed by those provisions.\\nCivil Act Article 865, paragraph (1) (hereinafter the “provision at issue”) provides: “A person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions of Article 845, Article 846, Article 848, Article 850, Article 851, Article 862, or Article 863 may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground.” This is intended to permit filing of an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship so as to correct a mismatch between the legal parent-child relationship and the parent-child relationship indicated in the family relations register.\\nConsidering that the provision at issue does not directly specify and regulate in concrete terms who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, but instead cites provisions concerning other litigation procedures with similar objectives and grants standing as Plaintiff to the person entitled to file each such action while only changing the grounds, the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under the provision at issue is supplementary to other litigation procedures concerning the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship.\\nIn light of the form, wording, and structure of the provision at issue, the characteristics of the litigation procedures prescribed by the above provisions, and the supplementary nature of the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, it is appropriate to view the persons who may file such an action as limited to the persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue.\\n\\nb. Specific scope of standing as Plaintiff\\n(1) Father, mother, and child as parties to a natural parent-child relationship\\nThe father, mother, and child, who are parties to a natural parent-child relationship, are persons who may file an action pursuant to Civil Act Articles 845, 846, 862, and 863, which are listed in the provision at issue, and may therefore file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the cause is another ground.\\n\\n(2) Lineal descendants of the child and their legal representatives\\nThe lineal descendants of the child, who is a party to a natural parent-child relationship, and their legal representatives are persons who may file an action pursuant to Civil Act Article 863, which is listed in the provision at issue, and may therefore file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the cause is another ground.\\n\\n(3) Adult guardians, testamentary executors, and lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife\\nCivil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are listed in the provision at issue, are all provisions that supplementarily expand standing as Plaintiff on the premise of Civil Act Article 846, which is the basic provision regarding standing as Plaintiff in an action for disavowal of paternity. Accordingly, adult guardians, testamentary executors, and the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife, who are persons entitled to sue under Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, should be regarded as having standing only when they satisfy the requirements for filing suit under those provisions. In other words, an adult guardian may newly file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the husband or wife has come under adult guardianship (Article 848); a testamentary executor may newly file such an action where the husband or wife has indicated by will an intent to deny the natural parent-child relationship (Article 850); and the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife may newly file such an action where the husband dies before the child’s birth or the husband or wife dies within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity (Article 851). If they do not satisfy the above requirements, it cannot be said that they necessarily have standing as Plaintiff to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under those provisions.\\n\\n(4) Interested persons\\nAn interested person may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground pursuant to Civil Act Article 862, which is listed in the provision at issue. Here, an interested person means a third party who has a legal interest, such as obtaining certain rights or being relieved from obligations, by a final judgment stating that a natural parent-child relationship exists or does not exist between other persons. Accordingly, only where the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between other persons will, by judicial determination, have a concrete impact on the interested person’s own rights or obligations concerning inheritance, support, or the like, or on his or her legal status, may such person file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as an interested person.\\nA person who files an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship while asserting that he or she is the natural father or natural mother of a child, even though no kinship relationship is indicated in the family relations register, is included among interested persons because, depending on the result of the judgment, that person will be directly affected with respect to the very existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship with the party.\\nIn the end, unless the Plaintiff who filed the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a person whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized as described in (1), (2), and (3) above, standing exists only where the Plaintiff falls within the category of interested persons referred to here. Whether a person falls within such an interested person category must be determined by individually examining, on the basis of the allegations made by the Plaintiff and the circumstances revealed in the pleadings, what concrete impact exists on the Plaintiff’s rights or obligations concerning inheritance, support, or the like, or on the Plaintiff’s legal status.\\n\\n3. Whether kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship\\na. Prior Supreme Court precedents\\nIn Supreme Court en banc Decision 80MEU60, rendered on October 13, 1981, the Court held that Article 35 of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation (enacted by Act No. 803 on December 6, 1961, effective as of January 1, 1962, and repealed by Act No. 4300 on December 31, 1990; hereinafter the same) applied mutatis mutandis Article 26, which provides that “the party, the legal representative, or the kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may file an action for nullity of marriage at any time,” to the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship prescribed in Civil Act Article 865, and thus held that standing as Plaintiff was necessarily recognized merely by the fact that one is in a kinship relationship prescribed in Civil Act Article 777.\\nThereafter, the Supreme Court reached the same conclusion not only in cases governed by the former Act on Personal Status Litigation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 81MEU77 rendered on March 8, 1983, and Supreme Court Decision 90MEU347 rendered on May 28, 1991), but also in cases governed by the Family Litigation Act newly enacted upon the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation (enacted by Act No. 4300 on December 31, 1990 and effective as of January 1, 1991; hereinafter the same) (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on October 20, 1998, and Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on February 12, 2004).\\n\\nb. Necessity of changing the precedent\\nHowever, in light of the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and other statutes, the enactment and implementation of the Family Litigation Act, changes in the family system such as the abolition of the head-of-family system, the special characteristics of status litigation, the diversification of family composition and the respect for the parties’ intent in that regard, and balance with other litigation procedures aimed at the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it must be concluded that the prior Supreme Court precedents holding that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may necessarily be filed merely on the ground that one is kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 can no longer be maintained. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n(1) The former Act on Personal Status Litigation, which set special provisions regarding litigation procedures concerning personal status in relation to the Civil Procedure Act, the basic Act governing ordinary civil litigation procedures, contained an express provision (Articles 35 and 26) stating that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. In fact, this became the core basis of the prior Supreme Court precedents. However, unlike the former Act on Personal Status Litigation, the Family Litigation Act, which integrated the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the former Family Affairs Adjudication Act (enacted by Act No. 1375 on July 31, 1963, effective as of October 1, 1963, and repealed by Act No. 4300 on December 31, 1990), contains no provision at all concerning who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The Family Litigation Act merely applies mutatis mutandis the provisions concerning the opposing party in an action for nullity of marriage, etc. (Article 24) to an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, while not applying the provision concerning the person entitled to file suit (Article 23). Accordingly, with the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the implementation of the Family Litigation Act, the legal basis of the prior Supreme Court precedents disappeared.\\n(2) As legal norms surrounding family relations and social circumstances changed, social perceptions regarding natural parent-child relationships, which together with marital relations form the foundation of family relations, also changed.\\nAt the time of the enactment of the Civil Act and even after the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the enactment of the Family Litigation Act, for a considerable period of time Korean civil law maintained the household head system, under which family relations were publicly recorded in the family register organized by household unit based on the head of family. At that time, most persons in a kinship relationship, such as the lineal ascendants and lineal descendants of the head of family, collateral relatives, and their spouses, were entered in the family register as members of the household centered on the head of family. However, with the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act, the household head system was completely abolished and reorganized into a family system centered on spouses and children, and as of January 1, 2008, when the Act on the Registration, etc. of Family Relations (enacted by Act No. 8435 on May 17, 2007; hereinafter the “Family Relations Registration Act”) came into force, the family relations registration register replacing the family register has recorded, centered on the individual, the occurrence and changes of family relations through marriage, birth, and the like. In addition, in our society, the nuclear family consisting of parents and unmarried children has already become the norm, rather than the traditional extended family, and with the progress of urbanization and industrialization, individualism and liberalism have become widely prevalent in family life as well.\\nIn light of these legal and social changes concerning the family system and the like, unlike the period when the household head system was maintained, the legal and social basis for viewing kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 as having a close status-related legal interest has weakened today.\\n(3) The action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a litigation procedure designed to correct entries in the family relations registration register that do not correspond to the true blood relationship (Family Relations Registration Act Article 107). However, today family relations are formed not only on the basis of blood relations but also diversely on the basis of the parties’ intent. The Supreme Court has held that the presumption of legitimacy also applies to a child born through artificial insemination during marriage, and that even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by a wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, it cannot be said that the presumption of legitimacy does not apply (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016MEU2510 rendered on October 23, 2019). The Supreme Court has also held that where a party registers a child as born of the party’s own biological child with the intent to create an adoptive parent-child relationship, the effect of adoption is recognized if the requirements for adoption are satisfied (however, the Civil Act amended by Act No. 11300 on February 10, 2012 and effective as of July 1, 2013 requires approval from the Family Court as a requirement for adoption of a minor), and that a claim for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted in relation thereto (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2000MEU1493 rendered on May 24, 2001). This is because legal protection is needed not only where the presumption of legitimacy applies to a parent-child relationship formed without a blood relationship, but also where, even if the presumption of legitimacy does not apply, that parent-child relationship has been substantially formed on the basis of the parties’ intent. Accordingly, while respecting the free intent of the parties regarding the formation of the legal parent-child relationship that underlies marriage and family relations, it is necessary to impose certain limitations so that third parties do not improperly intervene in that regard.\\n(4) An action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship falls under a “Category A family litigation case” under the Family Litigation Act (Article 2, paragraph (1), subparagraph 1(a) of the Family Litigation Act). The effect of a judgment granting such an action extends to third parties as well (Article 21 of the same Act), and the court must investigate facts and take necessary evidence ex officio and may examine the parties at any time (Article 17 of the same Act). In particular, considering the reality that blood relationship can now be proved relatively easily through DNA testing and the like, broadly viewing the scope of third parties who may contest the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship in the name of finding the truth of blood ties and allowing the case to proceed to the merits is highly likely to inevitably undermine the stability of status order and infringe the parties’ autonomous decision-making regarding marriage and family life. Accordingly, it is not desirable to expand arbitrarily, by interpretation and without an express statutory basis, the scope of third parties who may bring an action contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\nAlthough the Family Litigation Act provides in Article 24, paragraph (2), and Article 28 for cases in which a third party files an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, these are provisions concerning the opposing party (defendant capacity), not the person entitled to sue, and therefore cannot serve as a basis for expanding the scope of persons entitled to file suit.\\n(5) Since an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is supplementary to other litigation procedures aimed at the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it is clear that where such an action may be filed under another litigation procedure, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted.\\nMeanwhile, where there is a dispute concerning a legal natural parent-child relationship, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is often used in place of other litigation procedures whose filing requirements are relatively strict, and current practice also shows such a tendency. The Supreme Court has extended the legal principles concerning an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship to adoptive parent-child relationships as well (see Supreme Court Decision 92MEU372 rendered on July 16, 1993), and moreover, the filing period for an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not prescribed except where one or both parties to the natural parent-child relationship have died (Civil Act Article 865, paragraph (2)).\\nIn this way, the filing requirements for an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship have already been relaxed in several respects, and further expanding the scope of standing as Plaintiff to kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 is not balanced even when compared with the other litigation procedures described above. This is even more so because of the risk that the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may be distorted into a means of circumventing the requirements or restrictions established by statutory provisions concerning other litigation procedures.\\n(6) The natural parent-child relationship, which forms the basis of status relationships, does not end merely as a matter between the parties, but may affect inheritance issues among relatives and various other legal relationships based on kinship, such as parental authority and support (see Supreme Court Decision 2004MEU405 rendered on June 24, 2004). It is therefore of course necessary that certain third parties also be given the opportunity to contest the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through a proper judicial procedure. Since the Civil Act, in the provision at issue, allows a third party who is not a party to the natural parent-child relationship to contest its existence or nonexistence if that third party qualifies as an interested person, a third party who is kin also has standing if that person qualifies as an interested person. Accordingly, even if not all kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 are uniformly granted standing as Plaintiff, it cannot be said that the rights or right to a judicial remedy of third parties who have a legal interest in the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship are unjustly restricted.\\n\\nc. Change in precedent\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on October 20, 1998, which held in relation to cases governed by the Family Litigation Act that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, absent special circumstances, have a litigation interest in filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship merely by reason of being in such a status relationship, and Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on February 12, 2004, and other judgments to the same effect, are changed to the extent they are inconsistent with the view of this judgment.\\n\\n4. Determination in this case\\na. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts may be found.\\n(1) Non-party 1 was designated on August 15, 2010 as a recipient candidate for the Patriotic Medal, Grade 4, of the Order of Merit for National Foundation, and Non-party 1’s children were the eldest son, Non-party 4, the eldest daughter, Non-party 2, and the second daughter, Non-party 5. Non-party 4 and his spouse and children, as well as Non-party 5 and her spouse, all died before the date on which the recipient candidate was designated, and the only surviving child of Non-party 5 was Non-party 6 (date of birth omitted, male). The Plaintiff is the grandson of Non-party 4.\\n(2) On August 30, 2010, Non-party 6 applied to the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs for registration as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under Article 6 of the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, on the ground that he is a grandson of Non-party 1, and was registered on November 24, 2011 as the first-priority bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence.\\n(3) Meanwhile, Non-party 3 (date of birth omitted, female) applied on November 25, 2011 to the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs for registration as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, asserting that she is a child of Non-party 1’s eldest daughter, Non-party 2, and thus the first in priority among Non-party 1’s grandchildren, but the head of the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs rejected the application on November 30, 2011. Thereafter, Non-party 3 filed an action for cancellation of the refusal to register her as a person of distinguished service to independence against the head of the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs (Gwangju District Court Case No. 2011GUHAP4510), obtained a judgment in her favor on all claims, and that judgment later became final and conclusive after appeal and further appeal.\\n\\nb. Examining the above factual relations in light of the legal principles discussed above leads to the following conclusion.\\n(1) The Plaintiff is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1 as Non-party 1’s lineal descendant (great-grandchild), but does not fall within the category of persons whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized under the provision at issue.\\n(2) According to Article 5, paragraph (1), and Article 12, paragraph (2), paragraph (4), subparagraph 1 of the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, compensation is paid only to one first-priority bereaved family member among the person of distinguished service to independence and his or her bereaved family members, and the scope of bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation is limited in the order of spouse, child, grandchild, and daughter-in-law of the person of distinguished service to independence, with the older person receiving priority if there are two or more persons of the same rank. Therefore, under the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, the Plaintiff, who is merely the great-grandchild of Non-party 1, cannot be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, and since Non-party 6 in addition to Non-party 3 (child of the eldest daughter, Non-party 2) appears to be alive as a grandchild of Non-party 1, the Plaintiff cannot be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence even if he obtains a judgment confirming the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2. Nor does the question whether the Plaintiff may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence depend on whether Non-party 2 is the child of Non-party 7, the wife of Non-party 1.\\n(3) Even if a judgment confirming that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2, and between Non-party 7 and Non-party 2, respectively, becomes final and conclusive, the Plaintiff cannot be said to have a legal interest therein. Accordingly, this action must be regarded as unlawful because it was filed by a person lacking standing as Plaintiff.\\n\\nc. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper as it follows the legal principles discussed above. The lower court did not err, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by misapprehending the law on standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, by failing to conduct the necessary examination, or by exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the principles of logic and experience.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang and Justice Min Yoo-sook, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are supplementary opinions by Justice Park Jeong-hwa, Justice Kim Seon-su, and Justice Roh Jeong-hee regarding the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang and Justice Min Yoo-sook\\nWe agree with the majority opinion regarding the change in Supreme Court precedent. However, we differ from the majority opinion as to the scope of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship and whether the Plaintiff in this case falls within that category.\\n\\na. First, our view regarding the change in precedent.\\n(1) The provision at issue states, “A person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions of Article 845, Article 846, Article 848, Article 850, Article 851, Article 862, or Article 863 may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground.” Accordingly, it is clear from the wording of the provision at issue that the person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is limited to the persons specified therein.\\nHowever, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation provided that “kin under Civil Act Article 777” may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship (Articles 26 and 35). Yet, since the provision at issue in the Civil Act had already expressly specified the person entitled to sue with respect to an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation’s inclusion of a separate provision concerning the person entitled to sue created systemic confusion. On December 31, 1990, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the former Family Affairs Adjudication Act were both repealed and the integrated Family Litigation Act came into force, and the Family Litigation Act deleted the provision from the former Act on Personal Status Litigation concerning the person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. With the implementation of the Family Litigation Act, the overlapping provisions were eliminated, and the persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship became governed solely by the provision at issue in the Civil Act.\\n(2) Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on October 20, 1998, which the majority opinion cites as a precedent to be changed, held that if a person is kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, that person may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship merely by reason of being in such a status relationship, and thus failed properly to reflect the changes brought about by the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the implementation of the Family Litigation Act. However, Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on February 12, 2004, also cited as a precedent to be changed, unlike Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585, held that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as an “interested person” who is a person entitled to sue under the provision at issue. Accordingly, if one takes the later Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 as the benchmark, the current Supreme Court precedent is not that kin under Civil Act Article 777 “become persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship even though there is no longer any legal basis” (the premise of the majority opinion), but rather that they “become persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as interested persons under the provision at issue.”\\n(3) Although the Civil Act as amended by Act No. 4199 on January 13, 1990 reduced the scope of kin, Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503, which held that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 necessarily fall within the category of “interested persons,” may still be evaluated as merely following the repealed provisions of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation, and it is therefore appropriate to change it. Accordingly, the change in precedent should target the holding that “kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 fall within the category of interested persons under the provision at issue merely by virtue of their status relationship,” and we agree with the majority opinion as to such change in precedent.\\n\\nb. In this case, the issue is whether the Plaintiff, as the great-grandchild of Non-party 1, falls within the persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue, namely “lineal descendants of the husband or wife” or “interested persons.” Since we differ from the majority opinion on this point, we set forth our view in detail below.\\n(1) Before addressing the issue, we first consider the majority opinion concerning the necessity of changing precedent.\\n(a) According to the majority opinion, because family relations today are formed diversely not only on the basis of blood relations but also on the basis of the parties’ intent, the free intent of the parties should also be respected as to the existence or nonexistence of a legal natural parent-child relationship. However, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a judicial procedure for confirming the existence or nonexistence of a true blood relationship, and the existence or nonexistence of the legal natural parent-child relationship that is the subject matter of the litigation is not of a nature that can be determined by the free intent of the parties.\\nUnder the Civil Act, the chapter on kin (Part IV) is broadly structured around Chapter 3, “Marriage,” and Chapter 4, “Parents and Child,” and Chapter 4, “Parents and Child,” is again divided into provisions concerning Section 1, “Natural Child,” and Section 2, “Adopted Child.” This shows that the relationship between parents and children is formed on the basis of blood ties and the parties’ intent, but that among them the natural parent-child relationship is based on blood ties (the Supreme Court en banc Decision 2000MEU1493 rendered on May 24, 2001, cited by the majority opinion, concerns the legal doctrine of adoption, under which the parent-child relationship is formed by the parties’ intent).\\nIn addition, in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, admission of the claim and confession are not permitted (Article 12 of the Family Litigation Act), and the prior mediation principle also does not apply (Article 50, paragraph (1) of the same Act), so it is impossible in such proceedings to determine the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by the parties’ intent. Disposition by the parties’ free will concerning the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted.\\n(b) The majority opinion takes the view that the scope of persons entitled to sue should be limited so that third parties do not improperly intervene in family relations. We fully agree that private life and domestic peace should be protected against threats by third parties. Indeed, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016MEU2510 rendered on October 23, 2019, held, in substance, that in a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy applies, third parties must be prevented from intervening indirectly in another person’s family matters by allowing only an action for disavowal of paternity, which strictly limits the persons entitled to sue and the filing period.\\nHowever, the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship in this case is fundamentally different from an action for disavowal of paternity in this respect. Because a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy applies can be denied only by a judgment in an action for disavowal of paternity, there is practical benefit in limiting the persons entitled to sue in order to achieve that purpose. By contrast, a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy does not apply may not only be contested through an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, but when it becomes a preliminary issue in other litigation procedures such as civil litigation, anyone may allege and prove its nonexistence in that litigation procedure (see Supreme Court Decision 78DA71 rendered on April 11, 1978). Therefore, even if the scope of third parties who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is limited, such limitation cannot prevent them from contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through civil litigation, etc. Limiting the scope of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, as in the majority opinion, has little practical effect in preventing third parties from intervening in another person’s family matters and cannot be said to be an appropriate method. Rather, permitting certain third parties to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship makes it possible to finally resolve disputes surrounding status relationships and thereby also ensure the accuracy and authenticity of the family relations registration register. This is because only when the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is determined in the “disposition” of a judgment by filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship can the family relations registration register be corrected, the effect of a judgment granting the claim extends to third parties as well, and special provisions such as orders to undergo testing are more helpful in ascertaining the true blood relationship.\\nEven in this case, Non-party 3, a relative whose interests are opposed to those of the Plaintiff, had already, through administrative litigation, asserted that there is a natural parent-child relationship between her mother and Non-party 1, obtained a final and conclusive judgment in her favor, and the reasons for that judgment include a determination regarding blood relationship. It does not appear easy to preserve the peace of these families merely by blocking the Plaintiff’s filing of this subsequent action.\\n(c) Looking at the statistics on “litigation relating to parent-child relationships” in the Judicial Yearbook published annually by the courts over the past five years, actions for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship account for 75 to 80 percent of all litigation relating to parent-child relationships, occupying an overwhelming share. In actions for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the rate at which the Plaintiff’s claim is granted at first instance exceeds 75 percent, and the appeal rate is only around 1 percent. Unlike the fact that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is prescribed under the Civil Act as a supplementary form of litigation, in practice it has become the principal form of litigation relating to parent-child relationships, and although the Family Litigation Act is structured to have an adversarial-party framework, in practice there are mostly not serious disputes between the relevant parties concerning the very “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship.”\\nEven today, as in the past when public registers, etc. for publicizing status relationships were not adequately established, birth registrations and the like are often made contrary to the actual blood relationship due to legal restrictions or personal circumstances. Under the Supreme Court precedents that a family relations registration register cannot be corrected absent a final and conclusive judgment concerning matters that have a significant impact under the law of kinship or inheritance, as prescribed in Article 2, paragraphs (1) and (2) of the Family Litigation Act (see the Supreme Court en banc Decision on correction of family registers, 93SEU14, 15, 16 rendered on May 22, 1993), even if there is no substantive dispute between the parties regarding the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, which is a family litigation with an adversarial structure, must nonetheless be filed in order to correct the family relations registration register (see the above statistics on the rate at which claims are granted and the appeal rate).\\nFurthermore, whether a person falls within the category of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a matter of standing as Plaintiff, which is a litigation requirement, and thus a matter to be examined ex officio. The more strictly the scope of standing as Plaintiff is limited or the more complex the criteria for judgment are set, the more likely it is, as noted above, that even where there is no substantive dispute between the parties regarding the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, the court will ex officio examine standing as Plaintiff and dismiss the action, resulting in an increased number of such cases.\\n(d) The majority opinion is concerned that if the scope of persons entitled to sue is broadened, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may be distorted into a means of evading legal restrictions. However, that is a matter for the family court handling the case to faithfully examine the relevant issues and distinguish the genuine from the spurious; it is not a matter to be resolved by limiting standing as Plaintiff and thereby blocking the filing of the action itself.\\n(2) We now consider the first issue, namely the part of the majority opinion that limited the filing requirements for “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife.”\\n(a) The majority opinion states that “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only where the husband dies before the child’s birth or the husband or wife dies within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity.\\nHowever, because an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a litigation procedure entirely different from an action for disavowal of paternity in terms of litigation structure and legal nature, it is not appropriate to require separate conditions, as in an action for disavowal of paternity, even when lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n(b) An action for disavowal of paternity may be filed only by one of the spouses, and therefore it is necessary to make provision for the case where the person entitled to file it has died. Civil Act Article 851 provides that in such a case, the “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants” of the husband or wife may file the action. However, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship expressly contemplates, from the outset, filing not only by the parties to the natural parent-child relationship but also by third parties (Article 24, paragraph (2), and Article 28 of the Family Litigation Act). Therefore, the structure in which, if the party entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity dies, his or her lineal ascendants or lineal descendants become supplementary persons entitled to sue does not fit an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\nAn example will clarify this. Since the mother-child relationship arises from the natural facts of conception and birth, the wife (hereinafter “A”) may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against a person recorded in the family relations register as her biological child (hereinafter “B”), alleging the nonexistence of a blood relationship without any time limit, and if A dies, A’s lineal descendants may file such an action against B. In such a case, the majority opinion says that A’s lineal descendants may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only if A died within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity (two years from the date on which the cause for disavowal was known). However, since there is no room for the presumption of legitimacy itself to arise between A and B, it is impossible to assume a date on which the cause for disavowal became known, and the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity cannot run either. According to the majority opinion, it is difficult to tell how one is to determine whether the requirement of the filing-period limitation has been met. Moreover, while A could have filed the action at any time during her lifetime, once A dies, one arrives at the strange conclusion that, retroactively to some specific point in the past, the filing period had already expired.\\n(c) The parties to a natural parent-child relationship are the parent and the child. The lineal descendants of the child may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship pursuant to the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 863 without satisfying any other filing requirements, and the majority opinion does not differ on this point.\\nIf the lineal descendants of the child are allowed to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship without any further restriction, it is balanced and natural in terms of textual interpretation to regard the lineal descendants of the parent as likewise being able to file such an action without any time limit. In practice, there is much greater possibility or necessity for the lineal descendants of the parent to file an action contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship after the parent’s death than there is for the lineal descendants of the child to do so after the child’s death.\\n(d) In addition, where the parent, who is a party to the natural parent-child relationship, dies without filing an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, and only a testamentary executor is appointed, or where adult guardianship has commenced while the parent had not filed such an action, the adult guardian and testamentary executor, as persons entitled to sue, will have the question of whether filing is permitted separately determined under the Civil Act provisions concerning the scope of their duties even if standing as Plaintiff is recognized under the provision at issue, and thus the issue differs from the present case.\\n(e) The reasons why descendants file an action after the parent has not, during the parent’s lifetime, resolved the family relations registration register so that it matches the blood relationship vary depending on individual circumstances and family relations. There may be cases in which a child files an action against the parent’s wishes during the parent’s lifetime, but as in the Judicial Yearbook statistics mentioned above, in most cases the first-instance judgment in favor of the Plaintiff is accepted by both sides and becomes final and conclusive as rendered. There are even cases where a person who, because there was no blood relationship and thus no substantive status as a child during the parent’s lifetime, claims inheritance rights on the basis of the family relations registration register after the parent’s death, causing other heirs to bring litigation.\\n(3) We now consider the second issue, namely the part of the majority opinion that explained the requirements for an “interested person.”\\n(a) The majority opinion states that an “interested person,” as a person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, is a third party having a legal interest, such as obtaining certain rights or being relieved from obligations, by a final judgment confirming the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between other persons. The majority opinion’s view on this point is almost identical to the holdings in Supreme Court Decision 4293MINSANG314 rendered on September 29, 1960, and Supreme Court Decision 90MEU88 rendered on July 13, 1990, so it is in effect understood as relying on those decisions. However, because all of those Supreme Court decisions were holdings in cases governed by the already repealed former Act on Personal Status Litigation, it is not appropriate for the majority opinion to continue to rely on them.\\n(b) The primary criterion for determining the scope of an interested person should be whether the person suffers detriment in his or her legal status based on a status relationship due to the registration of a natural parent-child relationship different from the true blood relationship in the current family relations registration register, and whether there exists a legally protectable interest worth correcting through a judgment confirming the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The criterion presented by the majority opinion, namely whether the person “obtains certain rights or is relieved from obligations,” is not an appropriate criterion because it may be extended to cases where there is no effect on status relationships but only a property interest (for example, an insurance beneficiary or a creditor of an heir).\\n(c) If whether a person qualifies as an interested person is to be determined case by case on the basis of the circumstances shown in the Plaintiff’s allegations or pleadings, there is a risk of a side effect whereby the focus of the family court’s examination and determination shifts from the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” which is the subject matter of the litigation, to the “impact on rights, obligations, or legal status.” This is because, in litigation procedures in which the court must determine the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the Plaintiff’s order of succession or order of support must first be alleged and examined in order to determine standing as Plaintiff.\\nSuch side effects are more pronounced where the legal interest is related to public law status. The “impact on the rights and obligations of third parties” may appear, as in this case, in the form of public-law legal relationships where special statutes, including the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, provide for payment of compensation or benefits to a certain range of “bereaved family members,” etc. In such cases, if the above principle is applied in determining whether a person qualifies as an interested person, the family court will bear the burden of ex officio examining and determining the compensation standards, the beneficiaries of benefits, and the scope of bereaved family members prescribed by various administrative statutes. It cannot be said to be appropriate to compel interpretation and determination of administrative statutes, which are not within the family court’s area of expertise, in a family litigation case.\\nIn fact, before determining the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” which was the cause of action, the lower court in this case examined in detail the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act and whether the Plaintiff could be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence. It is not desirable for such examination and determination of administrative statutes to become the center of an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, which is a family litigation case.\\nc. In conclusion, we consider this case.\\n(1) Since the Plaintiff is a lineal descendant of Non-party 1 and Non-party 7, namely a great-grandchild, he falls under “lineal descendants of the husband or wife,” which is a person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 851. Moreover, whether the Plaintiff may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Independence Merit Treatment Act is not something to be strictly examined and determined ex officio, and once it is shown that the result of this case is likely to affect whether he may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, he should be included among the persons entitled to sue as an interested person. Nevertheless, the lower court erred in its legal interpretation concerning standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by failing to determine at all whether the Plaintiff, as a lineal descendant of Non-party 1, falls within the category of persons entitled to sue, and by holding that he lacked standing because he could not be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Independence Merit Treatment Act.\\n(2) However, the lower court, as an alternative determination, found that the evidence was insufficient to conclude that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 and between Non-party 7 and Non-party 2, and instead recognized that such natural parent-child relationships exist in light of the various circumstances. This falls within the exclusive province of the lower court as the trier of fact, and it does not appear to contain any error exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence. If so, even if this action is deemed lawful, the Plaintiff’s claim cannot be granted. Moreover, in this case, where only the Plaintiff appealed, setting aside the lower court judgment and dismissing the claim would result in a disadvantage to the Plaintiff; therefore, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, the appeal has no choice but to be dismissed.\\nAs stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of the case, because the reasons differ, we state this in a separate opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplementary opinion of Justice Park Jeong-hwa, Justice Kim Seon-su, and Justice Roh Jeong-hee regarding the majority opinion\\nWe offer supplementary reasoning to the majority opinion on several points.\\n\\na. The majority opinion stated that among the “adult guardian, testamentary executor, or lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” listed in Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are cited in the provision at issue, only those who satisfy the requirements for filing suit under those provisions have standing as Plaintiff, and that standing as Plaintiff is not necessarily recognized where those requirements are not met. This is reasonable for the following reasons.\\n(1) The provision at issue does not directly regulate who the persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship are. The provision at issue merely states that “a person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions” listed therein may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground. Accordingly, in light of the form, wording, and structure of the provision at issue, it is natural to interpret the persons who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as “persons who may file suit by satisfying the requirements under each provision” listed in the provision at issue.\\n(2) The requirements set forth in Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851 all pertain not to the grounds of an action for disavowal of paternity but to the “person entitled to sue.” Accordingly, the requirements concerning the “person entitled to sue” under those provisions should also apply to the persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n(3) Since Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are cited in the provision at issue, are all supplementary provisions concerning the person entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity, the interpretive standard for determining “persons who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship pursuant to those provisions” must be consistent. In other words, in the case of a testamentary executor under Civil Act Article 850, it should be interpreted that the executor may file an action for disavowal of paternity only when the husband or wife expresses by will an intent of denial, and that, pursuant to the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 850, the testamentary executor may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only when the husband or wife has indicated by will an intent to deny the natural parent-child relationship. There is neither need nor reason to recognize standing as Plaintiff for a testamentary executor where there was no such will by the husband or wife.\\n(4) The separate opinion states that “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” under the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 851 may, without needing to satisfy the requirements set forth in those provisions, file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship without restriction. Civil Act Article 851 does not automatically allow the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife to file an action for disavowal of paternity merely because the husband or wife has died; rather, it limits the filing period to cases where the husband dies before the child’s birth or where the husband or wife dies within the period for exercising the right of disavowal of paternity. This reflects the purpose of respecting the lifetime intent of the parties regarding the natural parent-child relationship and promoting stability in status order by permitting, exceptionally, persons other than the party entitled to disavow paternity (lineal ascendants or lineal descendants) to file an action for disavowal of paternity where the husband or wife had no opportunity during life even to file such an action or died before the period for exercising the right of disavowal expired and thus could not realize that intent.\\nHowever, if, as in the separate opinion, “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship without any restriction under the provision at issue, the result may be to undermine the purpose of Civil Act Article 851, which exceptionally allows persons who are not entitled to disavow paternity to file an action for disavowal of paternity only in limited cases. As the majority opinion explains, a natural parent-child relationship can be formed diversely not only on the basis of blood relations but also on the basis of the parties’ intent, and the presumption of legitimacy may also apply to a parent-child relationship formed without a blood relationship. However, where the parties to such a parent-child relationship formed without blood relation (especially the parent) die and a considerable amount of time passes, it may become difficult to objectively determine whether the person recorded as a child in the family relations registration register is a person to whom the presumption of legitimacy applies. In such cases, “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife,” who originally could not file an action for disavowal of paternity due to the restrictions in Civil Act Article 851, may nonetheless contest the existence or nonexistence of the blood relationship against the intent of the parties by filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. Furthermore, where a parent-child relationship formed without blood relation is substantially formed on the basis of the parties’ intent, as in cases where a child born through artificial insemination is registered as a biological child even though the presumption of legitimacy does not apply, or where a child born out of wedlock of a spouse is registered as a biological child while satisfying the requirements and intent to adopt (the Civil Act as amended in 2012 and effective as of July 1, 2013 requires approval from the Family Court when adopting a minor, but the supplementary provisions limit retroactive effect), legal protection should not be excluded merely because the presumption of legitimacy does not apply. Even where the parent did not raise any issue during his or her lifetime regarding the existence or nonexistence of blood relation with the child, allowing the parent’s lineal ascendants or other lineal descendants to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against the child on the ground that there was no blood relation after the parent’s death may infringe the personality rights or right to pursue happiness of the parties concerning the formation of family relations. Accordingly, the separate opinion’s view that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may be filed without restriction merely because one is a lineal ascendant or lineal descendant of the husband or wife is not appropriate.\\n(5) The majority opinion’s interpretation, which narrows as much as possible the scope of persons whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized under the provision at issue, is not unrelated to the fact that the provision at issue designates interested persons as persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. Even if standing as Plaintiff is not necessarily recognized under the provision at issue, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may still be filed where the person qualifies as an interested person; therefore, it is appropriate to interpret the scope of automatic persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue as above.\\n\\nb. We now consider the standard for determining the scope of an interested person.\\n(1) The persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under the provision at issue include interested persons. Because an interested person is a broad concept meaning a third party with a legal interest in the existence or nonexistence of another person’s natural parent-child relationship, it is important in practice to determine its specific scope. The majority opinion limits interested persons to those whose rights, obligations, or legal status concerning inheritance, support, or the like are concretely affected by the final and conclusive judgment on the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. By contrast, the separate opinion states that in order to have standing as Plaintiff as an interested person, the person must have an interest worthy of legal protection to correct the record in the family relations registration register, and that this should be based on whether the person suffers detriment in legal status grounded in a status relationship due to a record in the family relations registration register contrary to the true blood relationship. However, the respective standards proposed by the majority opinion and the separate opinion do not in practice create a significant difference in determining whether a person is an interested person. This is because, even under the majority opinion, one examines what concrete effect exists on the person’s rights, obligations, or legal status concerning inheritance, support, or the like, and therefore, contrary to the concern expressed in the separate opinion, a third party who has no effect on status relationships and only a property interest will not be included among interested persons. In fact, it is difficult to find cases in prior Supreme Court precedents or lower court practice in which such a person was recognized as an interested person.\\n(2) The separate opinion points out that if the issue of whether a person qualifies as an interested person is to be determined individually in each case, there is a side effect whereby the focus of the family court’s examination and determination shifts from the subject matter of the litigation, namely the “existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship,” to the Plaintiff’s “rights, obligations, or impact on legal status,” or that the family court will bear the burden of having to interpret and determine administrative statutes.\\nHowever, since the provision at issue expressly designates interested persons as persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, where the Plaintiff asserts that he or she filed such an action as an interested person, a stage must be gone through to determine whether the Plaintiff actually qualifies as such. Such review of party capacity also has practical value in harmoniously realizing the two ideas governing parent-child relationships, namely securing the legal stability of parent-child relationships and the principle of blood truth. Moreover, the need to reasonably adjust the scope of party capacity and establish criteria for such determination before proceeding to the merits is not a problem unique to family litigation cases. Today, family litigation cases often raise legal issues from other areas, including public law relations, but this is an unavoidable result of the very diverse and complex manner in which legal interests surrounding status relationships are manifested. Accordingly, the side effects pointed out by the separate opinion are not matters that must essentially be considered in determining the scope of interested persons and the principles for examining and deciding that issue.\\n\\nAs stated above, we present this supplementary opinion regarding the majority opinion."}

{"[2016MEU2510]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Judgment on the grounds for appeal as to Defendant 1\\n\\nA. Parent-child relationship of a child conceived and born through artificial insemination during marriage by the wife\\n\\n(1) Whether the presumption of paternity provision applies to a child conceived through artificial insemination\\n\\nThe Civil Act classifies the parent-child relationship between parents and children into a natural parent-child relationship based on blood ties (the Civil Act has provisions on natural children in Article 844 et seq.) and an adoptive relationship based on the parties’ intent (the Civil Act has provisions on adoption in Article 866 et seq.). Among these, the natural parent-child relationship is a parent-child relationship arising by birth; since it presupposes the case where parents give birth to a child conceived through natural sexual intercourse, in principle there exists a biological blood relationship between the parents and the born child.\\n\\nEven in a natural parent-child relationship, the mother-child relationship and the father-child relationship appear differently. Unlike the mother-child relationship, which is clearly determined by the natural fact of conception and birth, the father-child relationship requires separate requisites for establishing the relationship. The Civil Act has a presumption of paternity provision that presumes a child conceived by the wife during marriage to be the husband’s child (Article 844(1); hereinafter referred to as the “presumption of paternity provision”). In the case of a child born out of wedlock, legal parent-child relationship may be created by having the biological father acknowledge the child (Article 855(1)) or by the child filing an action for acknowledgment against the father (Article 863) and thereby establishing the existence of a natural parent-child relationship; here, whether there exists a blood relationship between the father and the child constitutes the principal fact to be proved (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 14, 2002, 2001MEU1537; Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 11, 2015, 2014MEU8217).\\n\\nThe issue in the present case against Defendant 1 is by what standard the parent-child relationship of a born child should be recognized where the wife, during marriage, receives sperm from a third party other than her husband and becomes pregnant by artificial insemination rather than natural means and gives birth to a child (hereinafter referred to as an “artificial insemination child”). (There are various forms of artificial insemination. Here, matters other than the above-mentioned “third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination” are not addressed.) Under the current Civil Act, there is no express provision regarding the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child. At the time of the enactment of the Civil Act on February 22, 1958, the possibility that a wife could conceive a child through artificial insemination was not contemplated, and therefore no provision on this matter could be made.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the text and structure of the Civil Act provisions relating to natural children, particularly the presumption of paternity provision; the basic legislative purpose and history of the Civil Act in providing the presumption of paternity provision with respect to the legal status of children born during marriage; and the marriage and family system guaranteed by the Constitution, it is reasonable to regard the presumption of paternity provision as applying even where the wife, during marriage, receives sperm from a third party other than her husband and gives birth through artificial insemination, and to understand that a child born through artificial insemination is presumed to be the husband’s child. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(a) First, the meaning of the presumption of paternity provision shall be considered.\\n\\nThe mother-child relationship is the so-called natural parent-child relationship, in which the parent-child relationship is established by the fact of birth, whereas the father-child relationship is a legal parent-child relationship in the sense that it is established only when recognized by law because the existence of a natural fact cannot be ascertained. The presumption of paternity provision provides that, where the wife gives birth to a child conceived during marriage, the child shall be presumed to be the husband’s natural child. Furthermore, considering that direct proof of conception during marriage is not easy, the Civil Act provides that a child born within 200 days from the day marriage is formed or within 300 days from the day the marital relationship ends shall be presumed to have been conceived during marriage (Article 844(2), (3)), thereby enabling the determination of whether conception occurred during marriage according to uniform criteria. Such a presumption of paternity provision is premised on the fact that scientific verification of parent-child relationships is practically impossible and that, based on the social and legal background that a wife in a legal marital relationship will conceive a child of her husband, there is a high probability that a child born during marriage has a blood relationship with the husband.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision by itself contains the possibility of creating a legal parent-child relationship that does not correspond to a true blood relationship. Since it may be regarded as a principle of the marriage and family system guaranteed by the Constitution that the legal parent-child relationship should conform to the true blood relationship (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA14, 96HEONGA7, etc.), the Civil Act, for this purpose, recognizes in the husband and wife a right to deny paternity as a means to remove the father-child relationship formed pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision (Article 847; hereinafter referred to as the “provision on the action for disavowal of paternity”). However, if the period during which the right to disavow paternity may be exercised is recognized as too long or is not limited, the need to promptly determine a child’s status and the stability of legal relations surrounding status may be impaired; therefore, the Civil Act sets a filing period by providing that an action for disavowal of paternity must be filed within 2 years from the day the husband or wife became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity (Article 847(1)). Thus, under the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, which limits standing and the filing period, the effect of the presumption of paternity has stronger force than other presumptions recognized by law. Unless paternity is disavowed and the child remains presumed to be a natural child, the biological father cannot acknowledge the child as a child born out of wedlock, nor can the child file an action for acknowledgment against the biological father; and after the filing period has expired, the presumption cannot be overturned even if it is later revealed to be contrary to the truth.\\n\\nThe Civil Act strictly provides for the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity as the method of rebutting it, and where paternity cannot be disavowed, the child’s legal status is finally determined. Accordingly, the father-child relationship of a child born during marriage is uniformly determined pursuant to the Civil Act provisions, and is not determined by individually and specifically examining the blood relationship. In other words, the Civil Act normatively forms a family relationship called parent-child relationship based on the fact that the child was born in a marital relationship and affords strong legal protection to the family relationship so formed.
