While protecting the child’s welfare in such general and institutional respects, the basic attitude of the Civil Act is to coordinate the conflicting interests surrounding the establishment of parent-child relationships by allowing those who seek to deny the status relationship formed under the presumption of paternity provision to escape that status relationship through reasonable methods and within a reasonable period.\\n\\nThe question of how to set the standard for the presumption of paternity regarding a child born during marriage concerns the legal status and relationship of spouses and children, and is a matter of how to harmonize, in accordance with social reality or traditional conceptions, the “interests of spouses and children in aligning the legal parent-child relationship with the truth” and the “child’s interest in securing legal stability through prompt determination of the parent-child relationship.” This is a matter to be decided in consideration of the basic rights of the interested parties and the constitutional decisions regarding marriage and family life, and in principle is left to the legislature’s discretion (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623). It can be said that the Civil Act has made a legislative decision regarding the standard for establishing a parent-child relationship for children conceived and born during marriage through the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\n(b) Next, the reason why the presumption of paternity provision should be applied equally to artificial insemination children shall be considered.\\n\\nThe objective of interpretation of law is to seek concrete appropriateness within the bounds that do not impair legal stability. For this purpose, while it is a principle to interpret the law as faithfully as possible to the ordinary meaning of the words used in the statute, within the limits of not departing from the ordinary meaning of the text, a reasonable interpretation in accordance with the goal of legal interpretation may be achieved by additionally employing systematic and logical methods of interpretation that take into account the legislative purpose and object of the law, the history of enactment and amendment, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other laws and regulations (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 23, 2009, 2006DA81035; Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 11, 2014, 2013MEU4591; Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 25, 2016, 2015DU37815). Moreover, even phenomena not contemplated at the time of legislation must, if not resolved legislatively, be incorporated into the structure of the existing legal system so as to seek a more reasonable solution.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision merely provides that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. As a matter of text, the presumption of paternity provision does not limit the application of the presumption based on the specific circumstances by which conception occurred, nor exclude from its application a child conceived through artificial insemination rather than natural means. Such a form of the presumption of paternity provision was maintained unchanged even when amended by Act No. 14965 on October 31, 2017. Nor do other provisions of the Civil Act exclude or limit the application of the presumption of paternity provision to artificial insemination children. Accordingly, applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child falls within the scope of interpretation permitted by the statutory text.\\n\\nArticle 36(1) of the Constitution provides, “Marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.” Thus, it protects marriage based on individuals’ autonomous intent and equality of the sexes, and family life formed on that basis. On the basis of these constitutional principles, the presumption of paternity provision contributes to maintaining domestic peace by affording a stable legal status to family relationships formed on the basis of the spouses’ normal married life. The marital relationship that forms the background for the birth of an artificial insemination child, and the family relationships such as the parent-child relationship that arise as a result of the artificial insemination child’s birth during marriage, are likewise formed on the basis of the individual and family autonomy that should be respected, and therefore should not be treated differently from other children born during marriage. The need to protect family life formed on the basis of marriage does not change merely because a child born during marriage is an artificial insemination child. There is no legal basis for concluding that the legal status of a child born during marriage differs depending on the specific circumstances of conception. Nor is there any reasonable basis to exclude the application of the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child born while the marital relationship remains normal, merely because the child was not born through sexual intercourse.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision was intended to eliminate the legal protection gap by affording children born during marriage a stable legal status from the moment of birth. The same applies to children born through artificial insemination during marriage.\\n\\nTaking sexual intercourse or biological blood relationship alone as the basis for the establishment of a parent-child relationship, or regarding the artificial insemination child as incapable of being presumed to be the husband’s child on that basis, would result in a situation where paternity cannot be determined for an artificial insemination child born during marriage. This would destabilize the legal status of the artificial insemination child and directly run counter to the purpose of the system that led the Civil Act to adopt the presumption of paternity provision, and is therefore unjust. If the presumption of paternity provision is not applied to an artificial insemination child and biological blood relationship alone is prioritized, even more unjust results would follow. If the sperm donor is anonymous, it is difficult to identify the donor. The sperm donor cannot reasonably expect to act as a father because he cannot anticipate that he must bear paternal responsibility for a child born from his sperm, and apart from anonymously donating sperm, he plays no other role that would warrant attributing to him the status of father with respect to conception and birth of the child. Therefore, it is not reasonable to immediately treat the sperm donor as the legal father or to hold him responsible as such merely because of the blood relationship. If the father-child relationship of an artificial insemination child is not determined pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision, absurd results will follow, such as making it impossible in practice to determine paternity or causing a father-child relationship not contemplated by the Civil Act to come into existence.\\n\\nIn short, the presumption of paternity provision applies to children born during marriage; and in light of the text and legislative purpose of the presumption of paternity provision, as well as the constitutional guarantee of marriage and family life, it must be understood that artificial insemination children born during marriage are included among children born during marriage.\\n\\n(c) Since the child’s welfare is the foremost factor to be considered in the establishment and maintenance of the parent-child relationship, even when considering whether the presumption of paternity provision applies to an artificial insemination child, emphasis must be placed on the child’s welfare. The child’s welfare is not limited merely to providing the substance of a parent-child relationship in the form of protection and upbringing for the child; rather, it must enable the child to function in a parental role by forming a corresponding legal parent-child relationship, and accordingly the system must ensure that parents can sufficiently support the child’s development. It is beneficial to the child’s welfare to attribute the status relationship with the child to the parent who continuously bears responsibility for the child’s welfare. Concluding that no natural parent-child relationship arises with respect to an artificial insemination child would be a significant shock not only to the married couple who have been raising the artificial insemination child but also an irreparable risk to the child who has formed family relationships on that basis.\\n\\n(d) Even in light of the birth process of an artificial insemination child and the actual form of the family relationship surrounding it, social appropriateness may be recognized in applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child.\\n\\nIn the case of artificial insemination, instead of the element of natural sexual intercourse, there exists the auxiliary act of artificial insemination or embryo transfer. Where the husband consents to the wife conceiving a child by artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm, the spouses would have anticipated that they would jointly bear responsibility for the child even if the child has no blood relationship with the husband, and it should be understood that a parent-child relationship with the child born pursuant to that consent is formed. The husband participates by consenting to the wife’s process of conception and childbirth through artificial insemination, and the child born in that process may be regarded, like a child conceived and born through the spouses’ natural sexual intercourse, as a child born during marriage between the spouses. Based on such a parent-child relationship, the artificial insemination child forms and maintains a substantive parent-child relationship with the spouses as their child. Socially as well, such a formed parent-child relationship is accepted as the spouses’ child, just as in the case of a child born through natural sexual intercourse.\\n\\nNevertheless, if the application of the presumption of paternity provision were excluded or if it were said that no legal parent-child relationship is established between the spouses and the artificial insemination child, it would destroy legal stability and peace and place the artificial insemination child in a vacuum with no legal protection, which is difficult to accept in our society.\\n\\n(2) Whether disavowal of paternity should be permitted as to an artificial insemination child\\n\\n(a) As seen above, the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity was established for the benefit of aligning legal parent-child relationships with the truth. However, where it becomes clear that a child not having a blood relationship was born, the premise for applying the presumption of paternity provision may be regarded as having disappeared. In such a case, the Civil Act allows the husband and wife to file an action for disavowal of paternity within a reasonable period in order to protect their personality rights, rights to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes, which they should enjoy in family life and status relations (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA14, 96HEONGA7).\\n\\nThe reason the presumption of paternity provision presumes an artificial insemination child to be the husband’s child is that applying the presumption of paternity provision to a child born between spouses who participated in the conception and childbirth process by giving “consent” is justified in light of the entire family law system, including the Constitution and the Civil Act. Applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child is intended to guarantee the family life and status relationship of spouses in marriage, and to legally secure, in accordance with their free will, family relationships and the substance of family relationships socially recognized.\\n\\nIn light of the process of conceiving and giving birth to an artificial insemination child, the fact that the child was not conceived through sexual intercourse between husband and wife and, accordingly, has no blood relationship with the husband are all matters already taken into account when applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child, and are not different from the facts known to the husband at the time the artificial insemination child is born. Presuming an artificial insemination child to be the husband’s child through the presumption of paternity provision, based on such premise facts, is intended to guarantee and realize the husband’s personality rights, rights to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes, which he should enjoy in family life and status relations. Conversely, it cannot be said that allowing the husband to file an action for disavowal of paternity is a fundamental right of the husband.\\n\\nAn action for disavowal of paternity may be filed on the ground that, as to a child conceived and born through natural sexual intercourse, there was no sexual intercourse process and, accordingly, there is no biological blood relationship. If an action for disavowal of paternity may also be filed as to an artificial insemination child on the same grounds, this presupposes that the natural parent-child relationship is determined by biological blood ties, resulting in the denial of the formation of parent-child relationships through artificial insemination. This does not accord with the purpose or object of the Civil Act, which, by providing the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, sought to determine natural parent-child relationships while also considering factors other than blood ties.\\n\\n(b) Where an artificial insemination child is born between spouses who are normally maintaining their married life, the husband participates in the child’s conception and birth by way of consent, and this may be said to be the basis on which the presumption of paternity provision applies. A husband who consented to artificial insemination cannot later reverse that consent and file an action for disavowal of paternity. Furthermore, in light of the current legal system’s deficiencies regarding consent to artificial insemination, the medical realities of artificial insemination, and the purpose of Article 852 of the Civil Act, which restricts disavowal of paternity by a person who has acknowledged paternity, it should not immediately be concluded that the parent-child relationship is denied or that an action for disavowal of paternity may be filed merely because circumstances exist in which such consent was not clearly established.\\n\\nThe current law does not have an adequately developed system regarding consent to artificial insemination and therefore lacks express provisions on the preparation of consent forms or their retention period. The Bioethics and Safety Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Bioethics Act”) requires medical institutions to provide necessary explanations and obtain written consent from the person undergoing in vitro fertilization and his or her spouse (Article 24(1)); however, because the explanation and consent content primarily concerns matters related to the procedure, such as the purpose of embryo creation, if a dispute arises over whether consent regarding the establishment of a parent-child relationship existed, it may be difficult to clearly prove the presence or absence of consent. In addition, even if a consent form under the Bioethics Act or medical records clearly confirming whether the husband consented in relation to the determination of legal parentage were prepared, there is also concern that such materials may disappear because the retention period is limited to about 10 years (according to Article 20(4) of the Enforcement Rule of the Bioethics and Safety Act, the retention period for consent forms is also set at 10 years). In such a situation, to regard the existence of a parent-child relationship as differing depending on whether a consent form was prepared or retained is not an appropriate solution in light of the nature of status relations, which require clarity and stability. Therefore, as to whether disavowal of paternity is possible for an artificial insemination child, it should be interpreted according to the following standards, while in any case carefully determining the matter so as not to contravene the child’s welfare or to nullify the legislative purpose for which the Civil Act established the presumption of paternity provision.\\n\\nWhere spouses are normally maintaining their married life, there is a high probability that the husband consented as to an artificial insemination child born during marriage. Therefore, with respect to an artificial insemination child born during marriage, the husband’s consent should be deemed to have existed unless other clear circumstances are proven.\\n\\nAccording to the Ethical Guidelines for Assisted Reproductive Technology of the Korean Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology (hereinafter referred to as the “Ethical Guidelines”), sperm donation procedures using a third party’s sperm are in principle to be conducted only for legally married couples, and, in order to receive another person’s sperm, it must be confirmed that the husband cannot otherwise conceive naturally, such as where he is determined to have irreversible azoospermia. The Ethical Guidelines further provide that the couple subject to the procedure must be fully informed of the Ethical Guidelines and relevant laws and regulations, and that the procedure must be carried out after both spouses accept and consent thereto; they also provide that the couple subject to the procedure must be able to normally raise the child born through sperm donation and that the child born shall, in all cases, be regarded as identical to a child by blood. In light of this medical reality of sperm donation procedures, it is practically very difficult for a married wife to conceive and give birth to an artificial insemination child without the husband’s consent.\\n\\nEven if the preparation of a consent form or its retention is not clearly established, where, after the birth of the artificial insemination child, the husband performs an act that publicly represents the artificial insemination child as his own child, such as filing a birth registration while knowing that the child is an artificial insemination child, or where, after the birth of the artificial insemination child, he has maintained a substantive parent-child relationship for a considerable period and has informed society that the artificial insemination child is his own child, it should be treated the same as where consent existed.\\n\\nArticle 852 of the Civil Act limits the opportunity to disavow paternity by providing that a person who, after a child’s birth, acknowledges the child as his or her natural child may not thereafter file an action for disavowal of paternity. In this way, if the person who may file an action for disavowal of paternity acknowledges the child as his or her natural child, the parent-child relationship is thereafter fixed, thereby promptly stabilizing the status relationship of parent and child and producing results consistent with the child’s welfare. Where the husband performs acts that publicly represent or accept the parent-child relationship, such as filing a birth registration for the artificial insemination child or maintaining a substantive parent-child relationship for a considerable period after the child’s birth, this may be evaluated as an act by which the husband, who can be deemed to know the entire birth process of the artificial insemination child, acknowledges the child as his own child on the premise of such facts. Thereafter, the husband’s assertion of disavowal of paternity must be regarded as contrary not only to the purpose of Article 852 of the Civil Act, but also as conduct inconsistent with prior acts and thus impermissible in light of the principle of good faith.\\n\\nB. Factual background\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the lower court and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff and the non-party were a married couple who completed their marriage registration on August 2, 1985. After marrying the non-party, the Plaintiff was diagnosed with azoospermia at ○○○ Hospital around 1992. Accordingly, with the Plaintiff’s consent, the non-party received sperm from a third party and conceived a child through artificial insemination by in vitro fertilization, and then gave birth to Defendant 1 at the above hospital on (date 1 omitted).\\n\\n(2) In the portion indicating personal details among the photographs taken immediately after the birth of Defendant 1 that are attached to Defendant 1’s birth record, the acronym “IVF” for in vitro fertilization is written in the upper right corner.\\n\\n(3) On March 29, 1993, the Plaintiff completed the birth registration of Defendant 1 as his and the non-party’s child without raising any issue regarding Defendant 1’s birth.\\n\\n(4) Due to marital discord, the Plaintiff and the non-party filed an application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement with the Seoul Eastern District Court on June 28, 2013. Defendant 1, having lived without knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, learned of this when, around the time of the above application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, he heard the Plaintiff say during an argument with the non-party that Defendant 1 was not his own biological child.\\n\\n(5) The Plaintiff and the non-party lived together with Defendant 1 from after their marriage until around the time of filing the present action. Until then, there are no circumstances suggesting that the Plaintiff raised any particular objection to the parent-child relationship with Defendant 1.\\n\\n(6) The court of first instance and the lower court in this case made a factual inquiry to the above hospital in order to confirm whether Defendant 1 was born at ○○○ Hospital through in vitro fertilization using a third party’s sperm donation and whether the Plaintiff consented at that time; however, the hospital replied that no medical records existed because the retention period for medical records had expired.\\n\\n(7) According to the transcript of the conversation recorded on July 28, 2013, after the Plaintiff filed the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement (Exhibit 4), it can be seen that, at the time of the artificial insemination of Defendant 1, the Plaintiff knew that he was azoospermic and had consented to giving birth to Defendant 1 at the above hospital, and accordingly he had stated an intention to treat Defendant 1 as his daughter and to take responsibility until Defendant 1’s marriage.\\n\\nC. Existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to Defendant 1\\n\\n(1) Examining the above factual circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, Defendant 1, the child born through artificial insemination during the Plaintiff’s marriage to the non-party, should be presumed, pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision, to be the Plaintiff’s natural child. Moreover, since the Plaintiff acknowledged Defendant 1 as his own child, it should be understood that the Plaintiff cannot seek to disavow paternity as to Defendant 1. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(a) After marrying the non-party, the Plaintiff underwent hospital testing and was diagnosed with azoospermia, and, recognizing that he could not have a child through natural sexual intercourse, consented to the non-party conceiving and giving birth to Defendant 1 using a third party’s sperm. Although the medical record retention period has expired and it is not possible to specifically verify in what form the Plaintiff gave consent, the Plaintiff consented to the non-party conceiving and giving birth to Defendant 1 using a third party’s sperm not long after receiving the diagnosis of azoospermia after having been unable to have a child for a long period after marriage. The Plaintiff’s consent may be viewed not merely as consent to a medical procedure, but as consent given with the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1.\\n\\n(b) The Plaintiff completed the birth registration of Defendant 1 as the child of the Plaintiff and the non-party without raising any issue regarding Defendant 1’s birth on (omitted date) which was 9 days after (date 1 omitted) when Defendant 1 was born. The Plaintiff filed the birth registration regarding Defendant 1 while clearly recognizing that he could not have a child due to azoospermia and that, with his consent, the non-party had conceived and given birth to Defendant 1 using a third party’s sperm. Through this, it may be seen not only that the Plaintiff consented with the intent to form a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, but also that the Plaintiff acknowledged Defendant 1 as his own child and publicly represented this through the birth registration.\\n\\n(c) After Defendant 1 was born, the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 1 for more than 20 years until he and the non-party applied for divorce by agreement around 2013, forming a substantive parent-child relationship, and he had never acted inconsistently with that relationship. Even until shortly after the application for divorce by agreement, he expressed an intention to fulfill the role of a father to Defendant 1. Thus, by protecting and educating Defendant 1 for a long period while Defendant 1 was registered as his own child and by forming a substantive parent-child relationship, the Plaintiff may be evaluated as having acknowledged Defendant 1 as his own natural child.\\n\\n(2) In the same vein, the lower court’s determination that the Plaintiff’s action seeking, against Defendant 1, who is presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child under the presumption of paternity provision, a confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship provided in Article 865 of the Civil Act is unlawful, is proper as it is based on the legal principles discussed above. The lower court made no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the legal principles on presumption of paternity as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the grounds for appeal as to Defendant 2\\n\\nA. Whether the fact that there is no blood relationship may be a reason for the presumption of paternity not to apply\\n\\nIn order to rebut the presumption of paternity under Article 844(1) of the Civil Act, one spouse must file an action for disavowal of paternity as provided in Articles 846 and 847 of the Civil Act and obtain a final judgment. It is unlawful for one spouse to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Article 865 of the Civil Act rather than an action for disavowal of paternity (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 25, 1984, 84MEU84; Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 22, 2000, 2000MEU292).\\n\\nTaking together the text and structure of the presumption of paternity provision discussed above, the basic legislative purpose and history of the Civil Act in providing the presumption of paternity provision regarding the legal status of children born during marriage, the marriage and family system guaranteed by the Constitution, the secrecy and freedom of private life, and the concrete balancing of interests related to the legal status of spouses and children, even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, it cannot be said that the presumption of paternity does not apply. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Determining the scope to which the presumption of paternity provision applies based on the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship is not only contrary to the text of the Civil Act provisions, but would in effect render the presumption of paternity provision dead letter, thereby contravening the purpose and structure of the Civil Act, which treats the presumption of paternity provision as a basic rule concerning the establishment of parent-child relationships.\\n\\n(a) The presumption of paternity provision does not distinguish the scope of its application based on the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship. To regard the presumption of paternity as not applying where it is later revealed that the child has no blood relationship with the husband is not consistent with the text of the Civil Act provisions.\\n\\n(b) As seen in 1.A.(1)(b) above, the presumption of paternity provision is intended to recognize a parent-child relationship based on the fact that the child was born during marriage so as to afford the child a stable legal status from birth and eliminate the legal protection gap at the time of the child’s birth. It also recognizes an action for disavowal of paternity so that a legal parent-child relationship that does not correspond to the true blood relationship can be aligned with the true blood relationship, while setting a filing period to promptly determine the child’s status and seek stability in legal relations.\\n\\nIn light of such legislative purpose and the form of the provisions, it should not be concluded that the presumption of paternity does not apply or falls under an exception merely because it is confirmed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, or that anyone may at any time dispute the father-child relationship presumed to be a natural parent-child relationship under the presumption of paternity provision. This is because it is contrary to the original legislative purpose of the presumption of paternity provision, which is to maintain family peace on the premise that the spouses are living a normal married life and to promptly stabilize the child’s legal status to prevent a vacuum in legal status. Where the legal relationship formed through the presumption of paternity provision has persisted for a long time and become solid, there is also a social need to ensure the child’s status is stably guaranteed by making it difficult for anyone to easily infringe upon the status so formed.\\n\\nExcluding the application of the presumption of paternity provision on the ground that there is no blood relationship destabilizes at once the parent-child relationship formed over a long period on the basis of the presumption of paternity provision, as well as the family relationships underlying social life, including the marital relationship closely connected thereto. Leaving the parent-child relationship in a state of long-term instability cannot be said to conform to the form of parent-child relationship that the Civil Act sought to establish by providing the presumption of paternity provision, and it is inconsistent with the inherent nature of a status order that requires stability.\\n\\n(c) How to determine the standard for the presumption of paternity regarding a child born during marriage is a matter concerning the fundamental rights of interested parties such as spouses and children and the constitutional decision concerning marriage and family life, and in principle is left to the legislature’s discretion (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623). Ultimately, the parent-child relationship should be understood as something the legislature may specifically determine within the bounds of the Constitution, taking into account social reality and traditional conceptions.\\n\\nWith the recent development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing has become possible. Social perceptions regarding divorce and remarriage have changed, and there is a greater possibility that, when the marital relationship has broken down, the wife may conceive and give birth to a child of another man rather than her husband. Thus, the social and legal circumstances have changed from the time when the presumption of paternity provision was introduced in the enacted Civil Act. However, such changes do not render the presumption of paternity provision itself, which is the fundamental rule regarding the presumption of paternity between father and child, meaningless, nor can it be said that the presumption of paternity provision has become unconstitutional.\\n\\nFamily relationships, including status relations, basically begin from the biological relationship of blood ties, but they are not necessarily composed only of blood relationships. Just as there are family relationships formed through social relations such as marriage, even when limited to parent-child relationships, in modern society not only blood ties but also parent-child relationships substantially formed while living as a family together have important value, so the need to protect them has increased. This does not change merely because scientific testing techniques have developed so that blood relationships can be easily confirmed.\\n\\nToday, in most countries, the principle of presuming natural children pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision is universally accepted, and the presumption of paternity provision continues to be maintained even in the course of amending laws relating to parent-child relationships. There are countries that allow the right to disavow paternity without limitation where there is no blood relationship, but even in such cases the persons entitled to exercise the right to disavow paternity in litigation are limited to the spouses, the child, and the biological father who have direct legal interests in the parent-child relationship. It is difficult to find a comparable example in comparative law where anyone may, without restriction, dispute the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship merely because the absence of a blood relationship between father and child has been revealed.\\n\\n(d) Presuming, under the presumption of paternity provision, that the wife’s conceived child is the husband’s child is premised not only on the high probability that a child born during marriage is the husband’s child, but also on the high probability that a substantive family relationship will actually be formed on that basis. However, family relationships formed without blood ties also constitute family relationships that the Constitution and the Civil Act seek to protect. If such a family relationship has matured socially and become solid over a long period, for example by continuing until the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity has expired, the need to protect such family relationship and the trust placed in it becomes even greater, and it should not be allowed for anyone to easily overturn it (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 26, 2015, 2012HEONBA357).\\n\\n(2) If the scope of the effect of the presumption of paternity provision is determined based on the existence or nonexistence of blood ties, it is unavoidable that a third party who is not a party to the family relationship will become deeply involved in the private sphere inside the home, such as the marital relationship and family relationship. In order to make the presumption of paternity not apply to a child who is presumed to be a natural child, or to obtain a public confirmation thereof, a judicial determination must ultimately be obtained, and in such a case state agencies, including the courts, become deeply involved in the parent-child relationship. Marriage and the family relationship based thereon are guaranteed by the Constitution against state interference, and if such involvement is broadly permitted, it may instead result in the State or a third party infringing on the marriage and family relationship that the State should guarantee, which also runs counter to the constitutional purpose.\\n\\nDetermining a natural parent-child relationship based on the existence or nonexistence of blood ties requires, for a child born between spouses who were living a normal married life, proof individually that the child was conceived by the husband during marriage, or otherwise prevents the parent-child relationship from being finally established until such proof is made. In such a state, anyone may recklessly dispute the child’s legal status, and family peace is also destabilized. If the natural parent-child relationship is determined based on the existence or nonexistence of blood ties, then in a case where a suit related to the parent-child relationship is filed, it would be necessary to conduct a paternity test or investigate even the confidential aspects between spouses in order to objectively and scientifically prove that the parent-child relationship does not exist, and the spouses’ intimate private life may be infringed in the process. If a third party were allowed to intrude into another person’s family and, claiming to be the parent of a child born to another person’s wife, demand paternity testing and the like, family peace would be difficult to maintain. Broadly allowing third-party involvement in matters belonging to the spouses’ and family’s private life in the name of blood truth is contrary to the purpose of the presumption of paternity provision, which takes the maintenance of family peace as one of its important legislative objectives.\\n\\nThe harm caused by such invasion of privacy is not limited to the relationship between spouses alone. Privacy formed in the parent-child relationship under the presumption of paternity provision is also infringed. All of these persons have the right to privacy, and the child’s privacy in particular is directly related to the child’s welfare and requires greater protection. Such privacy deserving protection does not change in the extent of its protection merely because it is a matter of the past or because the marital relationship currently has been dissolved. In other words, such invasion of privacy cannot be justified on the ground that the spouses are no longer forming a family, for example because they have divorced.\\n\\nEven if the spouses’ marital relationship ends and the family is dissolved, it cannot be said that the need to maintain the legal stability of the child’s status relationship naturally disappears. The presumption of paternity provision does not merely protect the married couple or the child individually, but also functions to protect the parent-child relationship itself. Even after the dissolution of the family, the former family members have a legal interest in continuing to conduct their social life fully and stably based on the existing legal relationships.\\n\\nArticle 36(1) of the Constitution clearly states that marriage and family life must be formed and maintained while respecting individual dignity. Marriage and family life are the most fundamental and private spheres of human life. In marriage and family life, the individual must be respected as an independent person, and the individual and family’s autonomous decision-making regarding how to organize marriage and family life must be respected. It is desirable for the State to respect family life formed on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes and not to intervene in family relations based on personal and affectionate human relationships (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 27, 2000, 98HEONGA16, 98HEONMA429; Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on February 3, 2005, 2001HEONGA9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 2004HEONGA5, etc.). Unless marriage and family relations infringe upon another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest, state interference in marriage and family life should be restrained.\\n\\n(3) Even as a matter of legal theory, the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship may constitute a ground for rebutting the presumption of paternity, but it cannot be a ground for determining the scope within which the presumption of paternity does not apply.\\n\\nWhile providing for the presumption of paternity, the Civil Act also allows the husband to file an action for disavowal of paternity within 2 years from the day he became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity; thus, unless the husband knows of the cause for disavowal of paternity, the filing period for the action for disavowal of paternity does not run. This gives the husband, who seeks to align the legal parent-child relationship with the truth based on awareness of the true blood relationship, a practical opportunity to deny the presumption of paternity. Once an action for disavowal of paternity is lawfully filed, whether there exists a biological blood relationship between the parents and the born child becomes the principal fact to be proved. Ultimately, when one learns that there is no blood relationship, the filing period for bringing an action for disavowal of paternity begins to run, and the actual absence of a biological blood relationship is a ground on which the presumption of paternity may be rebutted by action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThus, the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship, or awareness thereof, is a ground that allows the presumption of paternity to be rebutted through an action for disavowal of paternity, serving as the basis for whether such action is well-founded or as the starting point for the filing period. It cannot, however, be a factor that causes the presumption of paternity not to apply at the outset so as to eliminate even the need to file an action for disavowal of paternity. Treating the absence of a blood relationship as a premise fact causing the presumption of paternity not to apply would make the existence of the action for disavowal of paternity, which imposes limitations on standing and filing period, meaningless, and is difficult to accept as a matter of interpreting the current Civil Act. Even if a practical opportunity to exercise the right to disavow paternity has been afforded, if it is not exercised within the filing period and can no longer be contested, such a state cannot be regarded as infringing the husband’s personality rights, rights to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 26, 2015, 2012HEONBA357). It is also difficult to recognize any special necessity that would warrant granting the husband a renewed opportunity to disavow paternity by resorting to an interpretation contrary to the Civil Act provisions.\\n\\nB. Factual background\\n\\nThe factual circumstances found by the lower court are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The non-party conceived Defendant 2 through an extramarital relationship and gave birth to Defendant 2 on (date 2 omitted). On August 6, 1997, the Plaintiff completed the birth registration of Defendant 2 as the child of the Plaintiff and the non-party.\\n\\n(2) By no later than around 2008, when Defendant 2 was in fifth grade of elementary school, the Plaintiff appears to have already known through a hospital examination that Defendant 2 was not his biological child.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, for a long period until around the time of filing this action, the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 2 without raising any issue regarding the fact that Defendant 2 had been registered as a natural child at birth, and protected and educated Defendant 2 as a father.\\n\\n(4) During the process of divorcing by agreement with the non-party around 2013, the Plaintiff notarized a memorandum stating that he “waives parental authority and custody over the minor Defendant 2, and will pay 500,000 won per month as child support for Defendant 2 until high school graduation.”\\n\\n(5) Defendant 2 grew up not knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, and learned of this when, around the time of the above application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, he heard the Plaintiff say during an argument with the non-party that Defendant 2 was not his own biological child.\\n\\n(6) The Plaintiff and the non-party eventually reached a mediation in the divorce action, and on October 30, 2015, a mediation was established to the effect that they would divorce.\\n\\nC. Existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to Defendant 2\\n\\n(1) The lower court determined that the Plaintiff’s action as to Defendant 2 was unlawful for the following reasons.\\n\\nEven in the case of genotype incompatibility, the effect of the presumption of paternity should be regarded as not applying, and it is clear that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2. However, at least before the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied, and an adoptive parent-child relationship was validly established between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2. There are no special circumstances such as the need to terminate the adoptive relationship between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2 by dissolution of adoption. Accordingly, the present action by the Plaintiff seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to Defendant 2 lacks a legal interest in confirmation.\\n\\n(2) However, according to the legal principles discussed above, since the non-party conceived and gave birth to Defendant 2 during marriage to the Plaintiff, Defendant 2 is presumed, pursuant to Article 844(1) of the Civil Act, to be the Plaintiff’s natural child, and even where the fact of genotype incompatibility is revealed afterward, the presumption of paternity still applies. Accordingly, unless the Plaintiff filed an action for disavowal of paternity within 2 years from the day he became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity as to Defendant 2, who is subject to the presumption of paternity, and obtained a judgment denying paternity, it is unlawful to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n\\nAlthough there are inappropriate aspects in the lower court’s determination, its conclusion, which dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s action as to Defendant 2, is proper. The lower court committed no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the relevant legal principles as alleged in the grounds for appeal or exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of logic and experience.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAs the Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit, all of it is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged. Except for the separate opinions of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Noh Jeong-hee, and Kim Sang-hwan, and the separate opinion (as to Defendant 1) and dissenting opinion (as to Defendant 2) of Justice Min Yoo-sook, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and Justice Kim Jae-hyeong filed a concurring opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n4. Separate Opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Noh Jeong-hee, and Kim Sang-hwan\\n\\nA. As to the grounds for appeal concerning Defendant 1\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion states that where the wife, during marriage, receives sperm from a third party other than her husband and gives birth to a child conceived through artificial insemination, it is reasonable, when determining the parent-child relationship of the born child, to apply the presumption of paternity provision under the current Civil Act and regard the child born through artificial insemination as presumed to be the husband’s child, in the absence of a provision on this matter in the current Civil Act. However, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion that a child born through artificial insemination during marriage should be regarded as the husband’s child, we differ as to the reasons therefor, and therefore clarify this point.\\n\\nThe Civil Act presupposes that the natural parent-child relationship between parents and children is based on the existence of a biological blood relationship between the parents and the born child. Thus, since the mother-child relationship can be clearly ascertained externally by the natural facts of conception and birth regardless of whether the woman is married, there is no need for the Civil Act to have a provision on this. By contrast, because it was practically nearly impossible to verify blood ties in the father-child relationship, the Civil Act established the presumption of paternity provision that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. This presumption of paternity provision is based above all on the high probability that a child born during marriage will have blood ties with the husband under the social background that it is naturally expected that a wife in a marital relationship will conceive the husband’s child.\\n\\nHowever, with the recent rapid development of medical technology concerning assisted reproduction, including artificial insemination, the social and cultural background underlying the Civil Act provisions on natural children has itself changed in the area of family law, and ethical issues and legal tasks that cannot be resolved by the existing Civil Act provisions and the traditional legal doctrine have newly arisen. Representative examples include the fact that persons who previously could not have children due to infertility or sterility are now able to become parents with the help of assisted reproductive technology, and how to regulate the parent-child relationship of a child born through such technology. What was once a so-called “problem of fate” has today become a “problem of choice,” and public discussion of the accompanying ethical and social responsibility is urgently needed. Due to the development of genetic testing technology, the uncertainty of blood ties in the father-child relationship, which is the premise for applying the presumption of paternity provision, can no longer exist. As the majority opinion does, it should not be said that a separate legal requirement such as presumption of paternity or acknowledgment is necessary for determining the father-child relationship, unlike in the mother-child relationship. It is now time to seriously discuss the legal evaluation of the “intent” of the husband and wife who wished to have a child through artificial insemination and the limits of their responsibility.\\n\\n(2) As a principle, legal regulation of newly arising social phenomena should be made through legislation, that is, enactment or amendment of statutes. However, even though legal disputes arising from a new social phenomenon are actually occurring, if legislation of the law to be applied in adjudication has not yet been enacted, the courts vested with judicial power by the Constitution cannot refuse to adjudicate. Therefore, courts must discover and declare the legal principles that a reasonable legislator would naturally have taken as a standard norm in such situations. Such judge-made law must be understood as properly included in judicial power as an effort to bridge the gap between social reality and the legal order when a “vacuum in law” arises due to the legislature’s failure to exercise its legislative power despite changing social reality. This judicial process of identifying the law is distinct from analogical application or analogical interpretation of statutes. Analogical application of statutes means applying legal norms concerning a similar matter, to the extent deemed justified in light of the legal system, legislative intent and purpose, etc., to matters for which there is a gap in regulation that the legislature did not intend despite the legislation (see the concurring opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyeong to the majority opinion in the en banc judgment rendered on March 22, 2018, 2012DA74236). Even only for the case of the birth of an artificial insemination child through assisted reproduction technology, there are various types, including not only cases such as this one where sperm donation procedures using a third party’s sperm other than the husband are performed, but also cases where an egg from a third party other than the wife is provided or a child is born through a surrogate mother agreement. Whether such matters should be permitted from the standpoint of the legal order as a whole, and if so, how the establishment of their parent-child relationship should be regulated from the standpoint of family law, are matters to be resolved by legislation, not matters to be solved by applying existing presumption of paternity provisions, as the majority opinion argues. The courts must exercise judicial power by going through the process of forming the most appropriate dispute-resolution standard for resolving the matter at hand, that is, a “concrete and historical law,” by comprehensively considering the constitutional provisions relating thereto and their relationship with other statutes, the fundamental values pursued by the law, and the generally shared legal consciousness of society.\\n\\nComparatively speaking, many legal systems have resolved this issue by separately enacting legislation. In Korea as well, although legislative efforts have been made several times, they have not borne fruit. As the majority opinion also points out, at the time of the enactment of the Civil Act in 1958, it could not be envisaged that a wife could conceive and give birth to a child through artificial insemination, and therefore there was of course no need to have a provision on this matter.\\n\\n(3) The parent-child relationship between parents and children, together with the marital relationship, belongs to the most fundamental and private sphere of human life and at the same time becomes the basis of family relations under the Civil Act as the foundation for forming our community. The Constitution declares in Article 10 that “All citizens shall be assured of human dignity and worth and have the right to pursue happiness,” in Article 17 that “All citizens shall not be infringed upon in their privacy,” and in Article 36(1) that “Marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.” Therefore, parents’ efforts to have children constitute an exercise of the right to pursue happiness and of the autonomous decision-making right concerning the formation of family relations, and must be respected to the fullest extent unless they infringe upon another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest; their secrecy must also be guaranteed.\\n\\nThe Civil Act provides procedures such as an action for disavowal of paternity or an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship so that the parent-child relationship and the true blood relationship may be aligned on the premise that natural parent-child relationships between parents and children require a blood relationship between parents and the born child. Nevertheless, on the other hand, where the legal interest of the child’s welfare and prompt determination of the parent-child relationship is deemed to take precedence, it prevents the arbitrary denial of an already formed parent-child relationship from a social perspective. The imposition of limitations such as standing and filing periods on the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity is an example. In this way, the Civil Act normatively first forms a family relationship called parent-child relationship on the basis of the fact that the child was born in a marital relationship and grants strong legal protection to the family relationship so formed; as the majority opinion aptly points out, this is a legislative decision left to the legislature’s discretion and should be understood as reflecting the basic values pursued by the law and the generally shared legal consciousness of society. Such values pursued by the Civil Act regulating family relations, and the social sentiment or legal consciousness generally discernible therefrom, should also be respected in setting the standard for the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child born through assisted reproductive procedures.\\n\\nIf the husband and wife, in the course of the artificial insemination child’s birth, consented to the implementation of assisted reproductive procedures through a true concurrence of intent, this carries the meaning that, both privately and socially, they assume parental responsibility for the child with the intent of becoming the child’s parents. At this point, the husband is not merely consenting to the wife’s artificial insemination procedure. It is more consistent with reality to understand that the husband participates in the artificial insemination procedure from an equal position with the wife, by the unified intent of the spouses, and thereby actualizes the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with the child born therefrom.\\n\\nAs discussed above, where a husband and wife who are in a marriage have a concurrence of intent regarding the birth of an artificial insemination child and, on that basis, consent to the assisted reproductive procedure of artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm, the child should be regarded as the spouses’ natural child. This best accords with the Constitution’s principles of the people’s right to pursue happiness, the secrecy and freedom of private life, and the guarantee of family life; harmonizes with the Civil Act provisions concerning family relations; and accords with the basic values pursued by law as well as society’s generally shared legal sentiment and consciousness. Furthermore, the husband and wife’s concurrence of intent and consent to the procedure cannot be reversed retroactively. This is because doing so would contravene the constitutional decision on human dignity and value, the basic order of the Civil Act concerning parent-child relationships, and good morals and social order.\\n\\n(4) The lower court did not accept the Plaintiff’s appeal against the first-instance judgment dismissing this part of the Plaintiff’s action, and gave the following circumstances as reasons. The non-party, with the consent of the Plaintiff, who was the spouse, received sperm from a third party and conceived and gave birth to Defendant 1 through artificial insemination, and therefore Defendant 1 is presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child pursuant to Article 844(1) of the Civil Act. It is unlawful for the Plaintiff to seek, against Defendant 1, who is subject to the presumption of paternity, confirmation of the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as provided in Article 865 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nAs described in detail by the majority opinion, according to the factual circumstances discernible from the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff agreed with the non-party, his then wife, with the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, that is, with the intent to become Defendant 1’s parent, and that Defendant 1 was born through artificial insemination on that basis. Therefore, Defendant 1 constitutes the Plaintiff’s natural child, and the action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship filed by the Plaintiff against Defendant 1 should be dismissed as without merit. However, in this case, where only the Plaintiff has appealed, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, the Court cannot render a judgment more unfavorable to the Plaintiff than the lower court’s judgment deeming this part of the action unlawful and accordingly dismissing it. Ultimately, the Plaintiff’s appeal as to Defendant 1 is dismissed.\\n\\nB. As to the grounds for appeal concerning Defendant 2\\n\\n(1) Under the existing Supreme Court precedents, as to the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision, the Supreme Court in the en banc judgment rendered on July 12, 1983, 82MEU59, stated: “Article 844 applies where the spouses are cohabiting and in a state where the wife can conceive a child of the husband, and where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption does not apply.” Since then, through a number of decisions, the Court has consistently maintained the position of recognizing “exceptions to the presumption of paternity” under certain requirements (hereinafter referred to as the “limitation theory regarding the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision”) (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered on April 25, 1988, 87MEU73; May 10, 1988, 88MEU85; July 24, 1992, 91MEU566; January 28, 2000, 99MEU1817; August 22, 2000, 2000MEU292, etc.).\\n\\nIn the present case, however, the majority opinion states, “Even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, the presumption of paternity still applies,” and gives the “detailed reasons” therefor. Examining these reasons, first, determining the scope to which the presumption of paternity provision applies based on the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship is not only contrary to the text of the Civil Act provisions but also effectively renders the presumption of paternity provision dead letter; second, if the scope of the effect of the presumption of paternity provision is determined based on the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, it is unavoidable that a third party who is not a party to the family relationship will become deeply involved in private areas inside the home such as the marital relationship and family relationship; and third, even as a matter of legal theory, the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship may constitute a ground for rebutting the presumption of paternity, but cannot be a ground for determining the scope within which the presumption of paternity does not apply.\\n\\nConsidering the majority opinion in light of its reasons, it may appear to suggest changing the existing “limitation theory regarding the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision” that the precedents have taken, by holding that no exception to the presumption of paternity may be recognized even where the absence of blood relationship is confirmed. On the other hand, it may also be read as maintaining the precedents by not expressing a view on this issue on the ground that this case is, in any event, not one to which the existing precedents concerning exceptions to the presumption of paternity apply. Although it is necessary to avoid unnecessary legal confusion on this point, the majority opinion is not clear as to its position. Accordingly, while we agree with the majority opinion that it cannot be said that the presumption of paternity does not apply merely because it has been revealed that the child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, we wish to state our own separate opinion regarding whether there should be limits on the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision and the standards for such determination.\\n\\n(2) The above en banc judgment in 82MEU59 changed the prior unlimited theory regarding the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision to the limitation theory, and stated the reason as follows: “Article 844, together with the provisions on the action for disavowal of paternity in Article 846 et seq., was established for the peace of the family on the premise that the spouses are carrying on normal married life; therefore, applying it even where the factual premise is not satisfied and causing the matter to be resolved by the action for disavowal of paternity, whose requirements are strict, would rather run counter to the purpose of the system and may produce unjust results, such as promoting the establishment of father-child relationships contrary to true blood relations.” This was an effort, under the historical background of a time when it was practically difficult to scientifically prove blood ties and when the old Civil Act (before amendment by Act No. 7427 on March 31, 2005) limited the standing of the plaintiff in the action for disavowal of paternity to the “husband” and the filing period to “within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known,” to harmoniously interpret the legal interest of domestic peace protected by family law and the principle of truth in blood relationships. The Constitutional Court also understands the issue of the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision as a matter of how to harmonize, according to social realities and traditional conceptions, the “interests of the mother, child, biological father, and father in aligning the legal parent-child relationship with the truth” and the “interest of the party in seeking legal stability through prompt determination of the parent-child relationship.” Thus, the matter is in principle left to the legislature’s discretion; however, if the standard for the presumption of paternity is excessively unreasonable or the means of escaping from it are excessively limited so that it compels a parent-child relationship contrary to the true blood relationship, then it exceeds the limits of legislative formation and is unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623).\\n\\nHowever, compared with the time of the above en banc judgment in 82MEU59, which first recognized an exception to the presumption of paternity in 1983, today’s circumstances have greatly changed in social, technological, and legal respects; therefore, the existing precedents that adopt the outward appearance theory as the criterion for recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity need to be comprehensively reconsidered.\\n\\nFirst, divorce and remarriage have increased sharply, and social perceptions of divorce and remarriage have also changed significantly. Accordingly, relevant laws and institutions have also changed, and the Civil Act provision that prohibited remarriage of women for a certain period was abolished, while the period from the breakdown of the marital relationship to the effectuation of divorce has become longer, increasing the possibility that a woman may conceive and give birth to a child of a man other than her husband. There are also many cases in which one spouse resides for a long period in a remote place or abroad, or both spouses reside in different foreign countries while maintaining married life. Above all, with the development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing is no longer difficult. In today’s circumstances, where the absence of blood ties can be directly proven through scientific paternity testing, it is not an exaggeration to say that the need to restrict the application of the presumption of paternity provision by indirectly proving the absence of blood ties through the outward appearance or formality of “lack of cohabitation” has almost disappeared.\\n\\nFurthermore, through the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act, the person entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity was changed from the “husband” to the “spouses,” and the filing period was changed from “within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known” to “within 2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known.” A sufficient period was thereby granted for the spouses to carefully deliberate, based on awareness of the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, whether to maintain a parent-child relationship with no blood ties. Nevertheless, if the spouses raise no objection during that period, it may be regarded as an implied intent to accept the already presumed parent-child relationship as the legal parent-child relationship or not to exercise their right to disavow paternity. In such a case, there is a need to limit the spouses’ interest in being able to disprove the presumption of paternity in order to align the legal parent-child relationship with the blood relationship (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 26, 2015, 2012HEONBA357). Therefore, it should be understood that a parent-child relationship cannot be denied by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship simply because the spouses and child lack a blood relationship, and moreover by proving outward appearance or formality such as “lack of cohabitation,” which is only an indirect means of proving blood relationship.\\n\\n(3) On the other hand, as already noted above, under Articles 10, 17, and 36(1) of the Constitution, all citizens have the right to pursue happiness and the autonomous decision-making right concerning the formation of family relations, and these rights should be respected to the fullest extent unless they infringe upon another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest. Further, although legal parent-child relationships or family relationships in our society are generally based on blood ties, legal parent-child relationships or family relationships are not composed solely of blood ties or necessarily coincide with them. Under our Civil Act, the adoption system, although distinguished from the natural child system, was early on transformed from an adoption system for the household head or adoptive parents to an adoption system for the child, and an adopted child without blood ties to the adoptive parents has the same status as the adoptive parents’ natural child from the time of adoption (Article 882-2(1)). A special adopted child under the special adoption system introduced by the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act is regarded as born during the married life of the spouses (Article 908-3(1)), is also indicated in the family relation register as the adoptive parents’ natural child, and takes the surname and family origin of the adoptive parents. Since a parent-child relationship subject to the presumption of paternity provision may be dissolved only by an action for disavowal of paternity, this necessarily presupposes the formation and maintenance of a legal parent-child relationship without blood ties. As seen above, even in cases where a child is born after receiving sperm from a third party through assisted reproduction technology, a social parent-child relationship different from biological blood ties is formed. Thus, while legal parent-child relationships or family relationships may still be said to start from biological blood ties, social parent-child relationships or family relationships unrelated to biological blood ties already exist in our society’s traditions and are accepted and recognized in more diverse ways within today’s social system.\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of today’s heightened consciousness of rights among the people, the concept of equality between the sexes, and the highly diversified forms of family in social reality, status-law regulation of children should above all be aimed at improving the child’s welfare, and the constitutional demand that the autonomous decisions of the parties to a parent-child relationship should be respected as much as possible must also be heeded (see Supreme Court Order rendered on January 31, 2019, 2018SEU566; Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on February 3, 2005, 2001HEONGA9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 2004HEONGA5; Constitutional Court en banc decision in 2012HEONBA357, etc.). In light of the ideals of family law and the purpose of the presumption of paternity and disavowal provisions—namely, prompt determination of the child’s status and legal stability—the need to recognize exceptions to the presumption of paternity should be examined from the standpoint of the child’s welfare. As discussed above, since the parent-child relationship has important value not only in blood ties themselves but also in the substance of social life as parents and children, if a social parent-child relationship has been formed and matured between legally recognized parent and child, it cannot be denied that there is a need to limit the trust in that social parent-child relationship so that it cannot be arbitrarily destroyed by one party or a third party (see the above Constitutional Court en banc decision in 2012HEONBA357). On the other hand, there are also cases where, beyond scientific proof that there is no blood relationship between the husband and child, no social parent-child relationship has been formed between them, or such social parent-child relationship has broken down irretrievably so that no interest exists to be protected by the presumption of paternity system. Moreover, the Civil Act does not provide a provision recognizing the right of disavowal of paternity for the child or biological father, who are the direct parties in interest to the legal parent-child relationship formed by the presumption of paternity provision. Although the mother’s right to disavow paternity is recognized, it cannot be said to necessarily coincide with the child’s interests. Where the mother and the legal father do not raise the child and, due to indifference toward the child, do not file an action for disavowal of paternity or let the filing period lapse, while the biological father has in fact formed a parent-child relationship by raising the child or there is a high probability that such a relationship could be formed, it is difficult to find a justifiable reason to restrict the personality rights and rights to pursue happiness of the interested party seeking the truth of the blood relationship, absent special circumstances. In such cases, limiting the application of the presumption of paternity provision may better accord with the child’s welfare that the presumption of paternity system seeks to protect.\\n\\nAccordingly, the traditional limitation theory that has recognized exceptions to the presumption of paternity only on the criterion of whether there are “outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband” can no longer be maintained as is. Considering the aforementioned constitutional demands, where scientific proof establishes that there is no blood relationship between the husband and child and no social parent-child relationship has been formed or it has broken down, it should be understood that the parent-child relationship may be denied without an action for disavowal of paternity as an exception to the presumption of paternity; however, even if the absence of blood relationship is scientifically proven, it is reasonable to understand that the parent-child relationship may not be casually denied by the law of exception to the presumption of paternity where a social parent-child relationship exists. Here, a social parent-child relationship may be understood to mean a state in which an emotional bond as father and child has been formed between father and child and the actual circumstances of life have been formed, such as the father’s intent to play the role of a father and to protect and educate the child. In determining this, various circumstances surrounding the family relationship should be comprehensively considered, such as whether the spouses’ marriage continues, whether and for how long there has been a living arrangement that may be regarded as a former family community, whether an emotional bond has been formed between father and child, the cause of the breakdown of the parent-child relationship and the parties’ responsibility therefor, the child’s age, the possibility of restoring the social parent-child relationship, and the effect that recognizing the breakdown of the parent-child relationship has on the child’s personality formation and emotions.\\n\\n(4) Examining the factual circumstances discernible from the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record in light of the legal principles discussed above, as the majority opinion states. In this case, the Plaintiff has maintained the parent-child relationship for a long period after Defendant 2’s birth while knowing that he had no biological blood relationship with Defendant 2. Defendant 2, knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, has the intent to maintain a parent-child relationship with the Plaintiff and does not yet know who his biological father is. Although Defendant 2 learned of this when, while the Plaintiff and the non-party were divorcing, he heard the Plaintiff say that Defendant 2 was not his biological child, having lived without knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, he still regards the Plaintiff as his father and is litigating the present claim while hoping that the Plaintiff will remain his father.\\n\\nIf such are the circumstances, it cannot be said that the social parent-child relationship between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2 has been extinguished, nor can it be said that there is no interest to be protected through the presumption of paternity provision. Therefore, Defendant 2 is still presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child pursuant to Article 844(1) of the Civil Act, and it is not permissible for the Plaintiff to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against Defendant 2, who is subject to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nAlthough there are inappropriate aspects in the lower court’s determination, its conclusion, which dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment dismissing this part of the Plaintiff’s action, is proper. The lower court made no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the relevant legal principles as alleged in the grounds for appeal or exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of logic and experience.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nAs stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of the case, we differ as to the reasons, and therefore state this in our separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Separate opinion of Justice Min Yoo-sook (as to Defendant 1) and dissenting opinion (as to Defendant 2)\\n\\nA.
