Premise for discussion\\n\\nThe parts concerning Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 share many issues. Both Defendants were born while the lawful marriage relationship between the Plaintiff and the non-party remained in force and while they were cohabiting as spouses, but genetic testing revealed that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff. However, Defendant 1 was born through artificial insemination using sperm from a third party with the Plaintiff’s consent, while Defendant 2 was born from the non-party’s extramarital relationship. The Plaintiff filed this action seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to the Defendants, and argued that the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act did not apply because there was no blood relationship and because the Plaintiff had azoospermia, among other circumstances.\\n\\nThe lower court, as to Defendant 2, held that the effect of the presumption of paternity does not apply where the genotype is incompatible, but as to Defendant 1, it took a somewhat inconsistent stance by holding that, even though the genotype incompatibility was apparent in the third-party-sperm artificial insemination, the child is presumed to be the husband’s natural child if the husband consented.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Supreme Court is now in a situation where it must make a clear determination as to the scope of the effect of the presumption of paternity and the permissibility and, if permitted, the scope of any exception thereto.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, in its determination as to Defendant 2, states that even if it is revealed that there is no blood relationship between the child and the father, the child is still presumed to be a natural child, and it devotes the entire majority opinion to explaining the basis therefor, pointing out, inter alia, that because the presumption of paternity provision under the Civil Act is strictly framed, the father-child relationship of a child is uniformly determined according to the Civil Act provisions and cannot be determined through individual and concrete examination. The majority opinion then concludes that since Defendant 2 was born during the marriage of the Plaintiff and the non-party, the effect of the presumption of paternity applies even though genotype incompatibility was revealed, and therefore the lower court’s contrary determination is improper.\\n\\nIn other words, the majority opinion takes the position that even where there is no blood relationship, no exception to the presumption of paternity is allowed, and then immediately concludes that the presumption of paternity applies without further examining whether there are any other exceptions to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nHowever, Supreme Court precedents have adopted the so-called outward appearance theory and have allowed exceptions to the presumption of paternity in certain cases. Because the lower court held, as to Defendant 2, that “the effect of the presumption of paternity does not apply,” if the majority opinion had held that “the absence of blood relationship does not fall under an exception to the presumption of paternity,” it would then have had to determine, as the next step, whether there are cases in which an exception to the presumption of paternity is recognized by Supreme Court precedent or interpretation, and whether this case falls within that scope, before reaching the conclusion as to whether the presumption of paternity applies to Defendant 2.\\n\\nConsidering the logical stages of such determination, the majority opinion appears to mean not only that the absence of blood relationship does not fall under an exception to the presumption of paternity, but also that no exception grounds to the presumption of paternity are allowed at all as a matter of interpretation. This is not only contrary to the position of prior Supreme Court precedents, but this opinion rather takes the position that the Supreme Court precedents should be expansively interpreted; therefore, we dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the concurring opinion to the majority opinion states that “the majority opinion did not address whether exceptions to the presumption of paternity may be recognized as a matter of interpretation because it did not mention prior Supreme Court precedents.” Although we find this difficult to accept, if the majority opinion’s intention is indeed not to express a view on the “interpretation and application of the Supreme Court precedents concerning exceptions to the presumption of paternity,” we wish to state our opinion in the sense that, in future cases where this issue arises, the matter should be interpreted as set out below.\\n\\nFor convenience of discussion below, we shall first address the part concerning Defendant 2, to which the general legal doctrine of presumption of paternity applies, and then address the part concerning Defendant 1, where the unique legal doctrine of artificial insemination is at issue.\\n\\nB. Dissenting opinion as to Defendant 2\\n\\n(1) Summary of the dissenting opinion\\n\\nThe lower court held that the presumption of paternity under Article 844(1) of the Civil Act does not apply to Defendant 2, but that all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied between the Plaintiff and the above Defendant, and therefore a valid adoptive parent-child relationship was established. The majority opinion and the separate opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Noh Jeong-hee, and Kim Sang-hwan (hereinafter referred to as the “First Separate Opinion”) both conclude that the presumption of paternity applies to Defendant 2 without even proceeding to a determination on the effect of adoption.\\n\\nHowever, Defendant 2 should be regarded as not subject to the presumption of paternity, and the lower court’s determination as to whether the effect of adoption is recognized is erroneous in that it misunderstood the legal principles concerning the effect of adoption and implied ratification and failed to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\nFirst, the majority opinion, on the premise that the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act is to be strictly applied and that no exception is allowed in any case except for the action for disavowal of paternity provided in the Civil Act, denies even the area where existing Supreme Court precedents had allowed exceptions to the presumption of paternity in certain cases.\\n\\nAlthough the majority opinion may present a legally superior interpretation, it cannot derive a reasonable conclusion in many cases where “there is no parent-child relationship, but the family relation register has erroneously registered such relationship and the parties seek to correct it.” It is for this reason that, together with two successive improvement legislations easing the requirements for disavowal of paternity, existing Supreme Court precedents recognized exceptions to the presumption of paternity under the so-called “outward appearance theory.”\\n\\nWe agree with the First Separate Opinion to the extent that it pointed out the problems in the majority opinion regarding the permissibility of exceptions to the presumption of paternity and concluded that exceptions to the presumption of paternity should be allowed within a certain scope as a matter of interpretation. However, we differ as to the First Separate Opinion’s presentation of the so-called “social parent-child relationship theory,” which the Supreme Court had not previously adopted, and as to its view that the presumption of paternity applies to Defendant 2.\\n\\n(2) Whether the presumption of paternity applies\\n\\n(a) The majority opinion says that the presumption of paternity still applies even though the absence of blood relationship has been revealed. However, the nonexistence of blood relationship is a basic element in allowing exceptions to the presumption of paternity. Rather, the issue here concerns whether the existing “exception where the presumption of paternity does not apply,” which Supreme Court precedents have formed over time, should be maintained and, if so, to what extent; in other words, whether the legal doctrine that, by departing from the rigidity of the action for disavowal of paternity provided in the Civil Act, recognizes cases in which the presumption of paternity does not apply under certain requirements, should be maintained and what its scope should be.\\n\\n(b) Supreme Court precedents and their application in practice\\n\\nThe established Supreme Court precedents have held that where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband, due to “lack of cohabitation,” such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption of paternity does not apply (see Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on July 12, 1983, 82MEU59; Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 22, 2000, 2000MEU292, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the Supreme Court precedents, even in cases where the child is born during marriage and the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act should apply, if the absence of blood relationship is proven by showing outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child due to “lack of cohabitation” during the period in which the wife could have conceived the child, one may exceptionally escape the presumption of paternity and correct the status relationship in the family relation register to conform to the truth through an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The reason Supreme Court precedents have allowed exceptions to the presumption of paternity is, needless to say, that in the reality of our society there are diverse circumstances and reasons by which persons lacking true blood ties are registered as parent and child in the family relation register, and there is a need to correct the registration afterward to conform to the facts, while the interests surrounding this are diverse and complex, and the rigidity of the presumption of paternity provision in the Civil Act and the strict filing requirements for the action for disavowal of paternity cannot resolve this.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision, combined with the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, bars a person subject to the presumption of paternity from disputing the child’s status relationship if the person with standing under the action for disavowal of paternity does not file suit within the filing period, and thereby causes unreasonable results by requiring that even where the substance of marital and family cohabitation has already disappeared and the parties also seek to escape the legal regulation of the parent-child relationship, and there is little legal interest that the presumption of paternity provision was intended to protect, the matter can be rebutted only by the strict action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe previous Supreme Court decisions held that it is not in all cases where it is outwardly apparent that the wife cannot conceive the husband’s child, but rather where there are outwardly apparent circumstances due to “lack of cohabitation,” that the exception to the presumption of paternity is to be recognized.\\n\\nAccordingly, through the interpretation and application of the standard of the “outward appearance theory,” it was intended to harmonize, in concrete cases, the legislative purpose of protecting privacy and domestic peace and ensuring the child’s stable status, with the fundamental rights of the parties seeking to align the legal parent-child relationship with the truth.\\n\\nHowever, because using only “lack of cohabitation” as the criterion for recognizing an exception to the presumption of paternity poses the following problems, it is necessary to expansively interpret, in line with current circumstances, the meaning of “outwardly apparent circumstances” that the previous Supreme Court precedents use as the standard for determination.\\n\\n(3) Exception to the presumption of paternity\\n\\n(a) Reflection of social change\\n\\nLimiting “outwardly apparent reasons making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child” solely to lack of cohabitation would make it impossible to reflect changes in the surrounding conditions of adjudication in concrete cases.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity have existed since the enacted Civil Act, and the first Supreme Court precedent recognizing an exception to the presumption of paternity was rendered in 1983. At that time, it was normal for spouses to cohabit in one place after marriage, so “lack of cohabitation” became an outwardly apparent circumstance showing that the wife could not conceive the husband’s child, as a means of clearly proving the absence of blood relationship without infringing on the secrecy and freedom of private life, which is the intimate sphere between spouses.\\n\\nHowever, at present, together with the rise in divorce rates and a general shift in social perceptions regarding gender relations, several circumstances have changed from the time when the presumption of paternity provision was introduced, including stricter regulation of divorce (introduction of the property division system upon divorce and reinforcement of the noncustodial parent’s duty to pay child support after divorce), which has lengthened the period from breakdown of the marital relationship to divorce. Forms of marriage in which women work while residing in different regions or countries from their spouses have also increased. With the development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing has become possible at low cost and with remarkable accuracy without infringing privacy. In such circumstances, using only “lack of cohabitation” as an indicator of whether normal married life is maintained or whether the wife had the possibility of conceiving the husband’s child does not fit the current form of married life or the dispute situations arising therefrom. Thus, under the changed current circumstances, the “lack of cohabitation” formerly emphasized by the Supreme Court has become difficult to function as a reasonable criterion for recognizing an exception to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nWhile recognizing the presumption of paternity principle, the courts must, through legal interpretation of the presumption of paternity provision, determine who may, until when, and on what grounds assert an exception where the presumption of paternity does not apply, and by what standards such a claim will be accepted, in order to decide whether to permit the parties to escape the situation where the presumption of paternity applies. This does not negate the significance of the existence of the presumption of paternity provision; rather, it is to determine through interpretation the permissible scope of escape from the unjust results that may arise from the uniform application of the presumption of paternity provision, which was already contemplated when the provision was created.\\n\\n(b) Amendment to the Civil Act and its limits\\n\\nAmendments to the Civil Act regarding the presumption of paternity have proceeded in the direction of easing the requirements for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe enacted Civil Act set the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity as a short period of “1 year from the day the child’s birth became known” and limited the person entitled to file the action to the husband, but this was held to be unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in its decision of March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA14, 96HEONGA7, on the ground that it infringed the husband’s fundamental rights to deny the parent-child relationship according to free will. As an improvement legislation, Article 847(1) of the Civil Act, amended by Act No. 7427 on March 31, 2005, set the filing period for the action for disavowal of paternity as “within 2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known” and added the wife to the persons entitled to file. What is notable is that the above improvement legislation not only eased the requirements beyond the amendment recommendation then presented by the Constitutional Court, thereby recognizing a longer filing period, but also did not provide a rule limiting the filing period to within a certain period after the child’s birth.\\n\\nSubsequently, the Constitutional Court also rendered an unconstitutional decision in Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623, holding that the portion of Article 844(2) of the enacted Civil Act that presumes a child born within 300 days after the termination of marriage to be the natural child of the former husband infringed the mother’s fundamental rights. As an improvement legislation in response, the Civil Act amended by Act No. 14965 on October 31, 2017 maintained the principle of presumption of paternity while newly introducing a system for a permission request for disavowal of paternity and a permission request for acknowledgment, so that, for a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, the presumption of paternity could be excluded by a simpler method than an action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nIn particular, Articles 854-2 and 855-2 of the Civil Act provide that, for a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, the presumption of paternity in principle applies, but if the family court grants a permission request for disavowal of paternity filed by the mother or the mother’s former husband, or a permission request for acknowledgment filed by the biological father, taking into account the results of examinations by scientific methods such as blood typing tests by blood sampling and genetic testing, or other circumstances such as long-term separation, the presumption of paternity shall not apply. Although limited to a specific period, this may be assessed as reflecting the legal doctrine that the scope of non-application of the presumption of paternity can be reasonably set through judicial determination by a court taking into account the surrounding circumstances.\\n\\nThe two rounds of improvement legislation demonstrate that, in response to social change, the need to allow exceptions to the presumption of paternity has become increasingly high. In areas not resolved by the improvement legislation, the need to expand the existing Supreme Court precedents is raised.\\n\\nAlthough the scope of relief has been broadened by the improvement legislation, in light of the reality of disputes surrounding the family system and the changed system, the filing period of “2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known” is still not sufficient for the person entitled to file in some cases.\\n\\nIn actual family relationships, a party seeking to file an action for disavowal of paternity inevitably must prepare for the termination of the marriage. Accordingly, an action for disavowal of paternity is filed on the premise of a divorce suit or a divorce by agreement procedure. Where a husband learns that a child has no blood relationship with him and decides to divorce, and then chooses between divorce by agreement and judicial divorce procedures, the period of 2 years may be insufficient before filing an action for disavowal of paternity. The reason is that the family court’s protective role in divorce procedures has been strengthened.\\n\\nIn the case of divorce by agreement, the divorce cooling-off period system was introduced on December 21, 2007 (Civil Act Article 836-2), so where there is a child to be raised, the time required to obtain confirmation of the intent to divorce is extended by 3 more months. Whether by divorce by agreement or judicial divorce, matters concerning the upbringing of minor children, including the custodian and child support costs, must be determined pursuant to Civil Act Articles 843 and 837.\\n\\nFurthermore, even after divorce procedures have commenced, there are cases where the spouses seek to maintain the family again. If the 2-year filing period is uniformly applied, the person entitled to file is forced into a dilemma of either, instead of attempting to maintain the family, filing an action for disavowal of paternity within a short period and thereby extinguishing not only the parent-child relationship but also the family relationship, or forever losing the opportunity to disavow paternity by renouncing the right to do so. Such a result is undesirable because it runs counter to the purpose for which the Civil Act established the marriage and family system by legally regulating the child’s status through the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe more efforts are made to improve divorce procedures and prevent indiscriminate divorces and family dissolution, the greater the need becomes to allow exceptions to the presumption of paternity proportionately.\\n\\nThe child and the biological father, who are the direct interested parties, are still denied standing (the concurring opinion to the majority opinion argues that the child may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship even if there are grounds for disavowal of paternity, but this directly contradicts the established Supreme Court precedents, which held that as long as the presumption of paternity applies, “no one” may deny the parent-child relationship and an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not allowed). In a large number of lower-court cases in which the presumption of paternity provision appears to apply, it is not difficult to find cases where judgments granting claims for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship filed by a child or biological father have become final without objection. The Korea Legal Aid Center for Family Relations, which provides legal consultation and litigation support regarding legal issues arising in family relations, submitted an opinion in this case (Civil Procedure Rules Article 134-2), stating that the presumption of paternity provision is excessively strict in light of social changes, and that in counseling practice it sees many people who suffer because they cannot register births, and that for this reason the scope of recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity should be expanded so that parent-child relationships based on true blood ties may be formed, while giving priority to the child’s welfare. This shows that, depending on the concrete case, applying the presumption of paternity provision may instead produce results contrary to the original legislative purpose for which the presumption of paternity provision was established.\\n\\n(c) Intermediate conclusion\\n\\nThe existing Supreme Court precedents recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity under certain requirements should be maintained, and indeed need to be interpreted expansively. The “outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child,” which the existing Supreme Court precedents used as the criterion for recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity, should be interpreted as including not only “lack of cohabitation” but also, in light of the various changes in the circumstances surrounding the presumption of paternity provision and the purpose of the amended Civil Act discussed above, “other circumstances that may be outwardly apparent as making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child.” Which cases fall under “outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child” cannot be stated uniformly. The family court hearing each case will reasonably determine the matter so as to seek concrete appropriateness by considering various circumstances. In the process, it may comprehensively consider not only the results of tests by scientific methods such as blood typing tests and genetic testing, but also the existence and duration of separation, whether one spouse had a separate residence or frequently traveled to distant places or abroad, and other surrounding circumstances. Furthermore, the court will be able to determine “outwardly apparent circumstances” by hearing and evaluating various circumstances, such as whether the spouses’ marital relationship has ended or broken down to such an extent that the former cohabitation surrounding the child cannot be maintained, the circumstances and process thereof, the attitudes and intent of the persons concerned, whether the person asserting the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship is a direct interested party in that relationship such as the parent or child, whether the biological father has the intent to acknowledge and raise the child if he is the claimant, and whether, in the case of a third-party claimant, there are signs of intentions other than the original purpose of establishing true status relationships, such as property interests.\\n\\n(d) Propriety of the lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe part of the lower court’s determination that, if a child conceived and born by the wife has a genotype incompatible with that of the husband, the presumption of paternity does not apply, is not appropriate. However, the lower court’s determination as a whole appears not to have recognized an exception to the presumption of paternity merely on the basis of the absence of blood relationship, but rather to have judged that the presumption of paternity did not apply by comprehensively considering all the surrounding circumstances revealed in the proceedings, including the substance of the marital relationship, the circumstances by which Defendant 1, who is four years older than Defendant 2, was obtained through artificial insemination, the fact that the Plaintiff learned that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, and the circumstances leading to the divorce from the non-party, who is the mother of the Defendants. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination denying the presumption of paternity as to Defendant 2 is proper.\\n\\n(4) Effect of adoption by birth registration\\n\\n(a) The lower court held that all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2, and that an adoptive parent-child relationship had been established.\\n\\n(b) Even where a false birth registration of a natural child is filed, the legal doctrine that gives effect to adoption where the substantive requisites for adoption are satisfied has been established and maintained since the Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on July 26, 1977, 77DA492.\\n\\nDespite criticism that the above precedent lacks a theoretical basis or does not fit the adoption-registration system, it has remained firmly in place to date. This is because adoption had substituted for the system of raising a blood-unrelated child as if he or she were a natural child under legal constraints that made it impossible for an adopted child to take the adoptive father’s surname in a reality that negatively viewed adoption. This not only produced results consistent with the welfare of minor children, but also played an important role in stabilizing status relations by preventing third parties from disputing the effect of adoption. The fact that the existing Supreme Court precedents sought to ensure the welfare of children, especially minor children, by protecting the substance of parent-child relationships such as upbringing and support and by seeking stability in the child’s status relationship continues to have value today.\\n\\n(c) However, even if one respects the value of the Supreme Court precedents, if the adoption system and legal regulations have changed, one must follow accordingly. The 2005 amendment to the Civil Act introduced the special adoption system, reflecting the adoptive parents’ intent to raise the adopted child as their own natural child while requiring strict requisites and procedures. Furthermore, under the Civil Act amended by Act No. 11300 on February 10, 2012, it was provided as a requisite for adopting a minor that permission from the family court must be obtained, and adoption of a minor without permission from the family court was made a ground of invalidity (Articles 867 and 883(2)). The existing precedents also require as a requisite that there be no ground for invalidity of adoption between the parties; therefore, in cases to which the amended Civil Act applies, even if a false birth registration was made with intent to adopt, it would, absent permission from the family court, fail to satisfy the requisites for adoption and fall within the case of a ground for invalidity of adoption. Accordingly, where the amended Civil Act applies, the existing Supreme Court decisions granting effect of adoption to birth registration as to minors will no longer be sustainable. However, the amended Civil Act provisions have been in force since July 1, 2013, and in order to ensure stability in status relationships formed previously, they provide that they do not affect the effects arising under the prior provisions even after the amended Civil Act enters into force (Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions to the above amended Civil Act). Therefore, if all substantive requisites for adoption were already satisfied before the amended Civil Act took effect in a concrete case, the above legal doctrine would not apply.\\n\\n(d) Even where the amended Civil Act does not apply, the fact that the adoption system and legal regulations have changed as above is a factor to be considered when applying the purpose of the existing Supreme Court precedents to a concrete case.\\n\\nFor adoption to be effected, the adoptive father, adoptive mother, and adoptee must each express an intention to adopt. Supreme Court precedents have eased the requirements by recognizing adoption retrospectively where, even absent the consent of a statutory agent to substitute for the adoptee in giving consent to adoption, the adoptee can be regarded as having implicitly ratified the adoption after acquiring capacity to be adopted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 9, 1990, 89MEU389). Meanwhile, where the effect of adoption by birth registration is at issue concerning a child born out of wedlock by one spouse, the consent of the blood-related spouse is not an issue and the biological father is excluded from the person entitled to consent (see, e.g., Supreme Court Order rendered on April 25, 2011, 2011SEU62; Supreme Court Decision rendered on May 24, 2012, 2011MEU3389). Ultimately, the “intent to adopt by the remaining spouse,” who has no blood relationship, becomes the sole factor determining the agreement to adopt. In such cases, when the spouse himself denies the intent to adopt and asserts the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship, careful attention must be paid in determining the existence of an intent to adopt, particularly an implied intent to adopt by ratification, after thorough examination.\\n\\nEven in the area of property law, in order to recognize implied ratification, there must be circumstances from which it can be seen that the person fully understood the legal status arising from the act and, based on true intent, acknowledged that the consequences of the act would be attributable to him or her (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 27, 2014, 2012DA106607), and merely allowing matters to stand without objection for a long period while knowing of the defect is insufficient to recognize implied ratification (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 11, 2007, 2006DA50055). Even without invoking the above legal principles, it is necessary to exercise caution in recognizing implied ratification solely on the basis that the person knew of the invalid adoption and “did not object.”\\n\\n(e) Propriety of the lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court held that the Plaintiff appears to have already known through a hospital examination by no later than around 2008, when Defendant 2 was in fifth grade of elementary school, that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, and that, for a considerably long period until around the time of filing the present action, the Plaintiff had lived together with Defendant 2 without raising any issue regarding the fact that Defendant 2 had been registered as a natural child at birth, while protecting and educating Defendant 2 as a father and continuously maintaining an adoptive parent-child relationship, and on that basis determined that at least until before the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, all requisites for adoption were satisfied and a valid adoptive parent-child relationship had been established.\\n\\nAccording to the lower court’s findings of fact and determination, the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement was made before the amended Civil Act took effect, so the amended Civil Act does not appear to apply.\\n\\nHowever, the lower court’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nAccording to the facts found by the lower court, the Plaintiff clearly learned in 2008 that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, so it is difficult to see that the Plaintiff had an intent to adopt from the time of the birth registration concerning Defendant 2 until that time. The lower court only found that the Plaintiff did not object to the fact that Defendant 2 had been registered as a natural child until around 2013 when the present action was filed, or that the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 2; it cannot readily be concluded that the Plaintiff thereby implicitly ratified an invalid adoption.\\n\\nFurthermore, according to the record, during that period the Plaintiff appears to have repeatedly pressed his wife as to who Defendant 2’s biological father was, and conflict appears to have continued until the present action was filed. The Plaintiff applied for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement on June 28, 2013, and after the application was withdrawn, he filed an application for mediation seeking divorce on October 8, 2013, and a mediation was established on October 30, 2015, resulting in divorce. In the process, he alleges that the fact that Defendant 2 was a child born of an extramarital relationship became known to those around them, including the wife’s family, and to the Defendants, and that conflict with the spouses as well as with the children intensified, so that normal family life could not be maintained.\\n\\nIf so, the Plaintiff’s argument is that, at the time of Defendant 2’s birth registration, he was not certain that Defendant 2 was not his own natural child, and thus registered him as a natural child because he thought so, but by 2008 he clearly knew he was not, and yet spent about 5 years in a situation where he had to choose whether to end the marital relationship—which would also affect his relationship with Defendant 2, his spouse, and the other children—or to maintain the marital relationship as is. The lower court should have carefully examined the circumstances at the time and all surrounding circumstances, including the Plaintiff’s attitude, in addition to the fact that he did not object, and then determined the existence of an intent to adopt and whether there was ratification. The ground of appeal alleging that the lower court misunderstood the legal principles concerning the effect of adoption and implied ratification and failed to conduct the necessary examination is well-founded.\\n\\nC. Separate opinion as to Defendant 1\\n\\n(1) Summary of the separate opinion\\n\\nAlthough we agree with the majority opinion and the First Separate Opinion as to the conclusion that the Plaintiff cannot deny the parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, we differ as to the reasons. First, we agree with the majority opinion that, in the absence of legislation concerning the parent-child relationship of children born through artificial insemination, the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act applies. However, we differ from the majority opinion regarding the scope to which this legal doctrine applies, whether disavowal of paternity is permitted, and its requirements. Next, the First Separate Opinion is an entirely different view in that it does not find the basis for recognizing the parent-child relationship in the Civil Act.\\n\\n(2) Application of the presumption of paternity provision\\n\\n(a) In Korea, there is no legislation governing artificial insemination and parent-child relationships. In countries that have legislation on this matter, they generally recognize the establishment of the parent-child relationship between the husband and the child born through artificial insemination on the basis that the husband of the mother consented to the artificial insemination. However, because there are differences regarding whether an action for disavowal of paternity is allowed, and regarding the requirements and manner of consent, it is difficult to find a uniform standard.\\n\\n(b) In the absence of legislation, there is an aspect in which it is difficult to apply as is the presumption of paternity provision that was established on the premise of a child conceived through sexual intercourse.\\n\\nHowever, the legislative purpose of eliminating the legal protection gap at birth is also valid in the case of artificial insemination, and taking into account that the presumption of paternity system for determining the father-child relationship has a structure similar to this case, where the husband and the sperm donor are separate, and further that if the sperm donor is anonymous it is not only difficult to identify the donor but also impossible to expect an acknowledgment procedure, it is appropriate, in third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination, to apply the presumption of paternity provision in Article 844 of the Civil Act between the husband and the born child.\\n\\nMeanwhile, third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination presupposes from the outset, prior to conception, that the child born to the spouses will have no biological blood relationship with the husband. In artificial insemination conducted with the husband’s consent, this is a circumstance already known to and accepted by the spouses, and the auxiliary acts of “the husband’s consent” and “artificial insemination or embryo transfer” substitute for sexual intercourse. Therefore, in such cases, it is difficult to find the necessity or justification for applying the outward appearance theory as an exception to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\n(c) However, this legal doctrine applies only where the wife, during marriage, gives birth to a child through artificial insemination using “third-party-donated sperm” with the “husband’s consent.” In this point, we differ from the majority opinion.\\n\\nAlthough the majority opinion expressly stated at the outset that it was dealing only with the case of “third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination,” in its actual reasoning it concludes otherwise that “the presumption of paternity applies to a child born through artificial insemination during marriage,” and thus says that the Civil Act presumption of paternity provision applies uniformly to all artificial inseminations.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states, “The legal status of the child does not differ depending on the specific circumstances by which conception occurred. Nor is there any reasonable basis to exclude the application of the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child on the ground that the child was not born through sexual intercourse.” Whether the conception occurred through sexual intercourse or artificial insemination is a factor entirely unrelated to the recognition of a natural parent-child relationship. There is no doubt that the presumption of paternity provision under the Civil Act applies where the wife, for medical reasons or other circumstances, receives the husband’s sperm during marriage and gives birth through artificial insemination; such a case is entirely different from “third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination.” The reason the presumption of paternity issue arises in this case is also not that “Defendant 1 was not born through sexual intercourse,” but that “Defendant 1 has no blood relationship with the Plaintiff.”\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that “it is unjust to take biological blood relationship alone as the basis for establishing a parent-child relationship.” However, it is questionable whether the core of the parent-child relationship can be divorced from biological blood relationship. Cases where the existence of a blood relationship is clear and cases where the nonexistence of a blood relationship is clear cannot be regulated in the same way.\\n\\nNext, this discussion does not apply even to cases in which assisted reproductive methods are used on the “wife” side. Generally, the mother-child relationship is interpreted as a natural parent-child relationship established by childbirth, but with medical advances, if all or some of the following differ: the “woman who provided the egg,” the “woman who actually gave birth by implanting the in vitro fertilized embryo into her uterus,” and the “woman who requested childbirth through surrogacy with the intent to become a parent,” then the scope of “wife” in “a child conceived by the wife during marriage” under Article 844(1) of the Civil Act and the scope of “husband” in “presumed to be the husband’s child” must be interpreted and determined under separate legal principles.\\n\\n(3) Whether disavowal of paternity should be permitted as to an artificial insemination child\\n\\n(a) Since the application of the presumption of paternity provision is affirmed regarding the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child, the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity must also apply, and accordingly an action for disavowal of paternity may be filed.\\n\\nHowever, where the husband has consented to artificial insemination, it is interpreted that the natural parent-child relationship cannot be denied by analogical application of Article 852 of the Civil Act. This is because the husband’s consent is given to the medical act of artificial insemination, but since artificial insemination is carried out pursuant to that consent and is inevitably connected to conceiving, giving birth to, and raising the child, the consent should, absent other special circumstances, be regarded as intended to recognize the parent-child relationship of the child to be born in the future.\\n\\n(b) However, the majority opinion goes further and says that “in the absence of other proof, consent should be deemed to have existed,” and in that part regarding the requirements for recognizing consent, we differ from the majority opinion.\\n\\nSince consent has an important legal significance, whether consent was given must of course be recognized by evidence, and neither where the fact of consent is not recognized nor where the existence of consent is unclear and thus the fact of consent is difficult to recognize can consent be presumed or deemed. Also, unless the husband knew of the fact of artificial insemination birth, even if he registered the child’s birth and raised the child believing him or her to be his own child, this cannot be taken as consent. As long as there remains the probability that artificial insemination was carried out on the basis of a consent form prepared without consent or against the spouse’s will, the requirements for recognizing consent must be strengthened, not relaxed.\\n\\n(4) The First Separate Opinion says that if a husband and wife who are in a marriage had a concurrence of intent regarding the birth of an artificial insemination child and, on that basis, consented to an artificial insemination procedure using a third party’s sperm, the child should be regarded as the spouses’ natural child. It also excludes an action for disavowal of paternity in such a case by saying that the husband and wife’s concurrence of intent and consent to the procedure cannot be reversed after the fact. The legal doctrine proposed by the First Separate Opinion creates, by interpretation, a parent-child relationship so firm that it cannot be reversed after the fact where there is “concurrence of intent between spouses” and “the act of giving birth pursuant to artificial insemination procedures.”\\n\\nThe Civil Act does not provide that the effect of establishing a natural parent-child relationship arises solely on the basis of the “intent” to become a parent. Parent-child relationships form the basis of family relationships and have important status-law effects that serve as the basis for various related legal effects. It is difficult to agree with the First Separate Opinion, which excludes the related provisions of the Civil Act that can be applied in the absence of legislation and, through interpretation, seeks to achieve greater legal effects than the Civil Act anticipates.\\n\\nD. For the above reasons, although we agree with the majority opinion and the First Separate Opinion as to the conclusion concerning Defendant 1, we differ as to the reasons, and state this in our separate opinion; as to Defendant 2, we cannot agree with the majority opinion or the First Separate Opinion.\\n\\n6. Concurring Opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyeong to the Majority Opinion\\n\\nI would like to present an opinion supplementing the majority opinion concerning several questions raised about the majority opinion.\\n\\nA. Can the presumption of paternity provision be applied to an artificial insemination child?\\n\\n(1) When new circumstances not anticipated by the legislature arise due to changes in society, how the law should be interpreted or applied often raises difficult problems.\\n\\nDue to the limits of human cognitive and predictive ability, the legislature cannot enact laws while anticipating all concrete cases to which the laws will apply. Nor can it preliminarily determine the contents of laws to fit a wide variety of cases in response to ever-changing social reality and various problem situations. Therefore, the law must continue to maintain vitality as a norm regulating real life not only for cases specifically contemplated by the legislature at the time of enactment, but also for cases not so contemplated. If the law were applied only to the specific cases anticipated by the legislature, then as society changes and science and technology develop, the law would easily lose vitality and require constant new legislation.\\n\\nEven where a case arises that the legislature had not anticipated at all at the time of enactment, the courts cannot refuse to adjudicate. Where neither written law nor custom serving as the standard for adjudication in a civil case exists, the judge must adjudicate according to reason and logic (Civil Act Article 1). The courts, in order to determine whether existing laws can be applied to new cases not anticipated by the legislature, must utilize various methods of legal interpretation to ascertain the meaning of the law and carefully examine whether it can be applied to the new case.\\n\\nGenerally speaking, unless contrary to the ordinary meaning of the statutory text, the courts must respond to changes and developments in the times by interpreting and determining the meaning of the law as concretely applicable through systematic and logical interpretive methods that consider the legislative purpose and object, the history of enactment and amendment, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other laws and regulations. It is not desirable to simply conclude that a case requires judge-made law and attempt to solve it by new legal doctrine merely because it is a case the legislature had not anticipated at all at the time of enactment, without carefully examining whether existing law can be applied or applied by analogy.\\n\\n(2) As the majority opinion notes, at the time the Civil Act was enacted, it was not conceivable that a child could be born through artificial insemination, and therefore no express provision could be established concerning the attribution of the parent-child relationship of a child conceived through artificial insemination. Even after the phenomenon of children being born through artificial insemination emerged, no legislation was enacted to determine the attribution of the parent-child relationship of such children. Thus, it may be said that there is a legal vacuum with respect to the issue of attribution of the parent-child relationship of children conceived through artificial insemination.\\n\\nHowever, to resolve this issue, one must begin from the Civil Act’s provisions determining parent-child relationships. The Civil Act does not have an express provision excluding the application of the presumption of paternity to an artificial insemination child. The presumption of paternity provision in the Civil Act is framed very broadly, providing that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. Therefore, interpreting this provision as generally applying to the father-child relationship of a child conceived by the wife during marriage is consistent with textual interpretation.\\n\\nThe Civil Act legislator anticipated that a child conceived by the wife during marriage might not have blood ties with the husband, and contemplated the application of the presumption of paternity provision even in such a case. Even if a child born through artificial insemination by receiving a third party’s sperm has no blood relationship with the husband, applying the presumption of paternity provision to such a child cannot be regarded as contrary not only to the statutory text but also to the legislature’s intent and purpose. Accordingly, the fact that the Civil Act legislator did not anticipate conception and birth of an artificial insemination child when establishing the presumption of paternity provision cannot, by itself, exclude the application of the presumption of paternity provision.\\n\\nThe meaning of statutory text is not fixed. It may change according to socioeconomic changes and the development of science and technology. Objects that were not previously expected to fall within the scope of the statutory text may, with the passage of time and social change, be included within the subject matter regulated by the law. Even where the wife conceives through a new method such as artificial insemination by receiving a third party’s sperm, it is reasonable, from today’s perspective, to regard this as included in the concept of “conception,” which is a requirement for the application of the presumption of paternity provision. Because the presumption of paternity provision does not specify a particular regulated subject such as natural conception, but instead sets forth the rule in a broad manner, it can be seen as flexibly responding to the new phenomenon of artificial insemination.\\n\\nIf the presumption of paternity provision does not apply to artificial insemination, at minimum analogical application should be affirmed. This is because there are similarities between the case contemplated by the legislature when establishing the presumption of paternity provision and the case of an artificial insemination child, and in light of the system of legal norms and the legislative intent and purpose, applying the presumption of paternity provision by analogy can be assessed as justified. However, the legal effect does not differ depending on whether the presumption of paternity provision is applied or applied by analogy to an artificial insemination child. It is not the case that analogical application must always be considered merely because a case was not anticipated by the legislature; as noted above, in light of the textual form of the presumption of paternity provision, applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child is a reasonable method of interpretation and application of law.\\n\\nB. Can parent-child relationships be determined according to social parent-child relationships?\\n\\n(1) The separate opinion states that where no social parent-child relationship has been formed between legally recognized parent and child, or where a social parent-child relationship has broken down and there is no interest to be protected by the presumption of paternity system, and where scientific proof establishes that there is no blood relationship between the mother’s husband and the child due to genotype incompatibility, an exception to the presumption of paternity should be recognized. Through this, the separate opinion takes the existence or nonexistence of the so-called “social parent-child relationship” as the standard for determining parent-child relationships. However, this standard lacks legal basis and cannot serve as a standard for determining parent-child relationships.\\n\\n(2) Legal interpretation should, as a principle, faithfully follow the ordinary meaning of the text, and furthermore should aim to produce the most reasonable interpretation for the concrete case by additionally employing systematic and logical methods of interpretation that consider the legislative purpose and object of the law, the history of enactment and amendment, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other laws and regulations. However, if the statutory text itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, other methods of interpretation are in principle unnecessary or may be used only in limited fashion (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 23, 2009, 2006DA81035, etc.).\\n\\nAs the majority opinion notes, the presumption of paternity provision determines whether the presumption of paternity applies solely by reference to conception during marriage, and does not distinguish application on other grounds. The factors determining whether the presumption of paternity provision applies are marriage, conception, and birth. Since all of these are determined at the time of birth, it cannot be said that whether the presumption of paternity applies changes according to circumstances arising after birth. Treating the existence or nonexistence of a “social parent-child relationship,” which is a circumstance after birth, as a ground for exception to the presumption of paternity is not consistent with the Civil Act’s approach of determining the application of the presumption of paternity provision based on the time of birth.\\n\\n(3) Circumstances that a social parent-child relationship was not formed or has broken down after birth are not only difficult to function as a consistent standard, but interpreting them as grounds on which the presumption of paternity does not apply also runs counter to the purpose and object of the presumption of paternity provision.\\n\\nThe “social parent-child relationship” proposed by the separate opinion as a standard of determination contains many evaluative elements and is difficult to operate as a consistent standard. Also, the breakdown of a social parent-child relationship may be intentionally created by the parties and is mutable. Even if the relationship appears broken down at the time of trial, it may be restored. The separate opinion views that where a child has formed a social parent-child relationship with the biological father, an exception to the presumption of paternity should be recognized so that a legal parent-child relationship with the biological father can be secured; however, it should not be overlooked that the social parent-child relationship between child and biological father may also be mutable.\\n\\nFurthermore, it is not reasonable to treat such criteria as grounds for exception to the presumption of paternity so as to deny the legally presumed parent-child relationship. The presumption of paternity provision has the legislative purpose of maintaining family peace and promptly stabilizing the child’s legal status. Moreover, the fact that the Civil Act limits standing and the filing period in the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, thereby giving the presumption of paternity stronger force than other presumptions recognized by law, was also intended to protect the legal interests of the persons concerned through the stability of status relations. Since there is no express exception provision in the statute and interpretation contrary to the statutory text in a direction opposed to legislative intent and purpose should be restrained.\\n\\nGermany’s recognition of the biological father’s right to disavow paternity even with respect to a child presumed to be his and its limitation of the biological father’s right to disavow paternity where there exists a “social family relationship” between the legally formed father and child can also be understood from this perspective. German Civil Code laws prescribe the procedure for disavowal of paternity by statute and limit the eligible applicants and the application period for the stability of the child’s legal status (Sections 1600 and 1600b). In particular, although it allows not only the father (where recognized by marriage or acknowledgment, etc.), the mother, and the child, but also the biological father to exercise the right to disavow paternity, it further limits the biological father’s right by providing that, unlike the other applicants, the biological father may exercise the right only on the premise that no “social family relationship” exists between the legally formed father and child. It permits the biological father’s disavowal of paternity only where no social family relationship exists between father and child. Thus, in Germany, the concept of “social family relationship” is introduced for the purpose of protecting the social family relationship formed pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision and maintaining the legal stability of status relations. This results in social family relationships being placed above blood relationships by protecting the legal relationship under the presumption of paternity provision. Conversely, allowing, regardless of who seeks to deny the natural parent-child relationship, denial of the legally presumed parent-child relationship on the basis of the “breakdown of the social parent-child relationship” may rather result in emphasizing clearly established biological parent-child relationships or blood relationships, and therefore cannot be accepted as a theory of interpretation of our Civil Act.\\n\\nC. Why the majority opinion did not change the existing precedent\\n\\nThe Civil Act presumes that a child conceived during marriage is the husband’s natural child, and recognizes an action for disavowal of paternity as a means to rebut this presumption, while strictly limiting standing and the filing period.\\n\\nThe enacted Civil Act provided that only the husband could file an action for disavowal of paternity within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known. Since the husband often cannot know within that period whether the child is his natural child, it was necessary to ease the requirements for filing an action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court, in cases governed by the enacted Civil Act, held that where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption of paternity does not apply (see the above Supreme Court en banc judgment in 82MEU59; Supreme Court Decision in 2000MEU292, etc.). The reason given was that the presumption of paternity provision was established for the peace of the family on the premise that the spouses are carrying on normal married life, and that applying it even where that factual premise is not satisfied and allowing it to be denied only by the action for disavowal of paternity, whose requirements are strict, would run counter to the purpose of the system and could produce unjust results, such as causing the establishment of a father-child relationship contrary to the true blood relationship. The precedents can be understood as recognizing the above problems and developing a theory of interpretation that preserves the purpose of the presumption of paternity provision while preventing unjust results from its application.\\n\\nThere are arguments both for and against these precedents. Some argue that not only in cases of lack of cohabitation but also where genotype incompatibility is present, the presumption of paternity should not apply, while others argue that the precedents should be changed so that the presumption of paternity provision applies without limitation to children born during marriage. The majority opinion does not mention these precedents and does not address this issue.\\n\\nThe issues in this case are: ① whether the presumption of paternity provision can be applied to an artificial insemination child, and ② whether an exception to the presumption of paternity can be recognized on grounds other than the exceptions recognized by existing Supreme Court precedents.\\n\\nAs stated above, the presumption of paternity still applies even in the case of genotype incompatibility. Whether the existing exceptions to the presumption of paternity, recognized by Supreme Court precedents under the outward appearance theory, should be maintained, or whether the precedent should be changed so that the presumption of paternity provision applies without limitation to children born during marriage, are matters not directly related to the concrete resolution of this case, and such arguments are not included in the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to the Defendants. The majority opinion, without addressing whether to change the above precedents, limited its determination to whether the presumption of paternity applies to the Defendants under the issues discussed above.\\n\\nD. How should the problems arising from limiting standing in the action for disavowal of paternity be resolved?\\n\\nThe Civil Act has eased the strictness of the action for disavowal of paternity through the following amendment process. Article 847(1) of the Civil Act, amended by Act No. 7427 on March 31, 2005, set the filing period for the action for disavowal of paternity as “within 2 years from the day the husband or wife became aware of the cause,” so that the filing period does not run until the husband or wife becomes aware of the truth of the blood relationship with the child, and grants a practical opportunity to deny the presumption of paternity by providing a period for careful deliberation on whether to maintain the parent-child relationship based on awareness of the true blood relationship. Articles 854-2 and 855-2 of the Civil Act, newly established by the amendment Act No. 14965 on October 31, 2017, while in principle allowing the presumption of paternity to apply to a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, allow the mother and the mother’s former husband to file a permission request for disavowal of paternity, and the biological father to file a permission request for acknowledgment, thereby allowing the presumption of paternity to be excluded by a simpler method than an action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nNevertheless, arguments continue to be made that the scope within which the presumption of paternity does not apply should still be expanded. The most important reason is that the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity does not contain a provision allowing the child or biological father, who are direct interested parties in the parent-child relationship (as to the child, the need for allowing the right to disavow paternity is even greater than for the biological father, and there is much controversy as to whether the biological father should be granted the right to disavow paternity and, if so, what restrictions should be imposed; therefore, below we limit our discussion to the child), to exercise the right to disavow paternity. If disavowal of paternity is not allowed for the child without exception, the child’s personality rights may be seriously infringed, or there may be a marked discrepancy between the legally presumed father-child relationship and the socially recognized father-child relationship, and yet the opportunity to correct this may be blocked from the outset.\\n\\nAs a matter of legislative policy, it is desirable to amend the Civil Act and grant the right to disavow paternity to interested parties including the child, provided certain requirements are met. Before such legislation is enacted, it is necessary to seek a solution at the level of interpretation. To solve this problem, opinions are being presented that the scope of exceptions where the presumption of paternity provision does not apply should be further expanded; however, this risks damaging the form of the parent-child relationship that the Civil Act sought to create by providing the presumption of paternity and the action for disavowal of paternity, and is also difficult to accept as a matter of legal doctrine. Here, we wish to propose a solution whereby, for husbands or wives who are recognized as having standing under the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, the parent-child relationship is determined according to that provision, and for children and others who are not recognized as having standing under that provision, the parent-child relationship is determined by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through a systematic and rational interpretation of the current Civil Act.\\n\\nInterpretation and application of statutes in adjudicating concrete cases is an inherent authority and mission entrusted to the courts, and if a reasonable method of interpretation that considers both the connotation and extension of the statutory text can be achieved within that range, the courts should adopt such a constitutionally conforming interpretation.\\n\\nUnder the current Civil Act, which recognizes standing to file an action for disavowal of paternity in the husband or wife, the husband or wife may, upon learning that the child is not a natural child, file an action for disavowal of paternity within 2 years from that day and thereby remove the legal parent-child relationship with the child. However, unless paternity is disavowed, the child cannot escape the legal parent-child relationship under the presumption of paternity provision by means of an action for disavowal of paternity even if he or she learns that he or she is not a natural child. Meanwhile, the Civil Act provides, in addition to the action for disavowal of paternity, a provision on an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship (Article 865) as a means to correct discrepancies when the substantive legal parent-child relationship and the legal parent-child relationship in the family relation register do not match. According to Article 865 of the Civil Act, a person having an interest in the natural parent-child relationship may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on the ground of “other reasons.”\\n\\nSince the husband or wife may file an action for disavowal of paternity pursuant to the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity where there are grounds for disavowal of paternity, seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on such grounds is not permitted as it violates Article 865 of the Civil Act. However, although the child is the direct party in interest subject to the effect of the presumption of paternity under the presumption of paternity provision, standing is not recognized for the action for disavowal of paternity. Yet, if the Civil Act is interpreted in a direction that completely excludes the opportunity for the child, the direct party in interest, to align the legally presumed parent-child relationship with biological truth merely on this ground, it would seriously restrict the child’s personality rights, right of self-determination, right to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family relations based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes. This is not the proper method of interpretation that the Supreme Court, which takes as a principle of statutory interpretation the interpretation of statutes in harmony with constitutional norms, should adopt. Accordingly, it is necessary to examine whether the unreasonable result above may be removed through the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship recognized by the Civil Act. If, even according to the ordinary meaning of the statutory text, it is possible to interpret that the child subject to the presumption of paternity may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, and such a result does not run counter to the legislative purpose of providing the presumption of paternity provision and the action for disavowal of paternity, then through such interpretation it may be a reasonable method to realize the child’s constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights by allowing the child an opportunity to escape the consequences of the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nFirst, in the child’s case, although grounds for disavowal of paternity exist, the child cannot file an action for disavowal of paternity, so seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on such grounds is not, in light of the text of Article 865 of the Civil Act, naturally prohibited. That said, it should not be understood that anyone with an interest in the parent-child relationship of a child presumed to be a natural child may seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Article 865 of the Civil Act in relation to the child’s status. As seen above, the legislative purpose of restricting the action for disavowal of paternity in the Civil Act can be found in the early stabilization of status relations, the child’s welfare, and prevention of third-party interference in the marital family; through this, it protects the privacy of the child and spouses subject to the presumption of paternity and the peace of the marital family. Considering the legislative purpose of the presumption of paternity provision and the purpose of strictly prescribing the procedure and period for seeking disavowal of paternity in the action for disavowal of paternity, interested parties who may dispute the status of a child born during marriage and subject to the presumption of paternity should be recognized only within the extent that does not undermine such legislative purpose. Therefore, the child subject to the effect of the presumption of paternity should be understood as able to file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship because the child has a direct interest, but in addition, a person with a status-related or property-related interest should not, absent special circumstances, be understood as being able to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n\\nEven if the child may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, it cannot be said to be allowed without any limitation. The provision on the action for disavowal of paternity sets a filing period, requiring the husband or wife to file the action within 2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known. Even where a child subject to the presumption of paternity files an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, absent special circumstances, the filing period should be limited by analogically applying the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, and the starting point should be understood as when the child became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity (if the child learned of the cause while still a minor, the day the child reached majority).\\n\\nIn this way, if a child subject to the presumption of paternity receives a final judgment declaring the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the res judicata effect of that judgment extends to third parties as well pursuant to Article 21 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Registration, etc. of Family Relationships, so that no one may assert, in or out of litigation, any claim contrary to the effect of such disavowal of paternity, and the effect of the presumption of paternity disappears. However, even a child who can file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship with the effect of disavowal of paternity cannot immediately assert an exception to the presumption of paternity or deny the effect of the presumption of paternity in the absence of such a judgment. In other words, unless there is a final judgment granting such a claim for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, a child subject to the presumption of paternity cannot file an action for acknowledgment against the biological father, nor can the biological father acknowledge such a child.\\n\\nIt is desirable to resolve the problems arising from the strict limitation of standing in the action for disavowal of paternity by allowing the effect of the presumption of paternity under the presumption of paternity provision to be rebutted within the extent that the purpose of the presumption of paternity provision or the action for disavowal of paternity is not nullified.\\n\\nI present the above supplemental opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2018DA1049]": "We consider the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Civil Act Article 860 provides in its main text that “acknowledgment shall have effect retroactively from the time of the child’s birth,” while its proviso states that “however, it shall not prejudice rights acquired by a third party,” thereby limiting the retroactive effect of acknowledgment; and Civil Act Article 1014 provides that “if a person who became a co-heir by acknowledgment or by a final and conclusive judgment after the opening of succession claims partition of the inherited property, and another co-heir has already partitioned or otherwise disposed of it, such person has the right to claim payment of an amount equivalent to his/her share of the inheritance.”\\nHowever, between a child born out of wedlock and the birth mother, a legal parent-child relationship arises automatically by the child’s birth without waiting for the birth mother’s acknowledgment or birth registration (see Supreme Court Judgment 67DA1791, rendered October 4, 1967), and it is not the case that such relationship may be recognized only where there is an entry in the family relation register or a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship by a court (see Supreme Court Judgment 92NU3199, rendered July 10, 1992). Therefore, the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 concerning the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment does not apply, nor is it applied by analogy, to a mother-child relationship that does not require acknowledgment, and it cannot be said on the basis of Civil Act Article 1014, which prescribes the right of a person who became a co-heir by acknowledgment or by a final and conclusive judgment after the opening of succession to claim payment of value, that such person may not deny the effect of the division or disposition of inherited property made by the mother’s other co-heir. The same applies even if the mother-child relationship was only later made clear through the finality of a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship, etc., after another co-heir had already partitioned or disposed of the inherited property.\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below determined as follows. Inherited property that was partitioned or disposed of by co-heirs before acknowledgment definitively vests in the co-heir who received the partition or the transferee, pursuant to the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment prescribed in the proviso to Civil Act Article 860, and this legal principle also applies where a person who was later determined to be an heir by the finality of an action for confirmation of the existence of a parent-child relationship after the opening of succession comes into existence. The judgment that a biological parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiff (selected party) and the designated parties (hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiffs, etc.”) and Non-party 1 became final after Defendant 1 disposed of the real property listed in Attached List 1 of the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as “the Real Property”) to Defendant 2 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership. Ultimately, the Plaintiffs, etc. fall under “a person who became a co-heir by the finality of a judgment after the opening of succession” under Civil Act Article 1014, and therefore may exercise only the right to claim payment of value equivalent to the purchase price against Defendant 1, and may not deny the effect of the disposition of the Real Property, whose ownership was definitively vested in Defendant 2.\\nb. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n1) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\na) Non-party 1 married Non-party 2 and gave birth to Defendant 1, and thereafter divorced, while maintaining a de facto marital relationship with Non-party 3 and giving birth to the Plaintiffs, etc.\\nb) Non-party 1 owned the Real Property and died on January 27, 2015.
