Therefore, the lower court’s determination that the investigative agency executing the warrant at issue violated the seizure procedure is proper, and there is no illegality in the lower court’s above determination that violated no rules of logic or experience, did not exceed the limits of free evaluation of evidence, and did not misapprehend the legal principles regarding the nature of the defense counsel’s right to participate.\\n\\nc. 1) However, when all of the following circumstances ascertainable through the above factual relationship and the record are comprehensively considered, the above procedural violation by the investigative agency does not amount to an infringement of the substantive content of due process, and rather there is ample room to view this as an exceptional case in which excluding the admissibility of evidence collected through the execution of the warrant at issue would produce a result contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act in establishing procedural provisions regarding criminal procedure so as to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby realize criminal justice.\\n\\na) On 2019. 10. 25., the investigative agency, after confirming from the Defendant, who was then the only person entitled to participate as the person from whom items were seized, that he did not wish to participate in the process of searching, duplicating, and printing the computer at issue, began the search of the computer at issue. At the time of the search, the Defendant had already stated that “illegal filming videos are stored on the hard disk of the computer at issue.”\\n\\nb) By the time the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel was appointed, it appears that the investigative agency had already carried out the search of the computer at issue to some extent and had identified at least the location of the folder where the seized electronic information was stored.\\n\\nc) The Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel had not inquired of the investigative agency about the status of execution of the warrant at issue, nor had he requested participation in the process.\\n\\nd) At the time of execution of the warrant at issue, there was no established precedent or internal guideline of the investigative agency that the defense counsel appointed or selected after the commencement of the seizure and search procedure had to be separately notified in advance notwithstanding the person from whom items were seized having waived or refused participation.\\n\\ne) In the course of executing the warrant at issue, the investigative agency seized videos that the Defendant had recorded, through hidden cameras installed in restrooms of PC rooms, singing rooms, etc. since around 2011, of the bodies of hundreds of victims, and indicted him for 296 of those acts (the charged facts at issue in this case). The Defendant confessed to all of those offenses in the investigative agency and in court.\\n\\n2) If so, the lower court should have carefully determined, by comprehensively considering the circumstances of the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue, the provisions relating to seizure procedures for electronic information in force at the time of execution of the warrant at issue, the probative purpose of the seized evidence, the circumstances that led to the procedural violation and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent regarding it, and the content and nature of the offense in this case, whether this case falls under an exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, based solely on the reasons stated in its opinion, concluded that the evidence collected through the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue could not be used as evidence of guilt and found the charged facts at issue in this case not guilty. In this respect, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The Prosecutor’s ground for appeal pointing out this error is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment finding not guilty is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for retrial and reconsideration of this portion, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO14654]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the charges at issue\\n\\nThe Defendant, ① from around 2018. 1. 2. to around 2018. 12. 10., committed sexual abuse acts such as sexual harassment causing sexual humiliation against each of the 14 child and juvenile victims in the Attached Sheet of the judgment of the court below, “Amended Crime List I,” and at the same time produced obscene materials by using them; ② on 2019. 3. 1., distributed obscene materials using children and juveniles by transmitting photographs taken of the victim’s genital area, etc.; and ③ from around 2018. 6. 14. to around 2019. 1. 5., possessed a total of 229 items of obscene materials using children and juveniles.\\n\\n2. Judgment concerning the seizure pursuant to the warrant in this case\\n\\nA. The judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below, based on the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the procedure by which the mobile phone in this case, etc., owned by the Defendant, was seized from the Defendant’s residence pursuant to the warrant in this case was not unlawful, such as by violating the warrant principle or infringing the Defendant’s right to participate in the seizure and search proceedings.\\n\\nB. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\n(1) Article 215(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “When necessary for a criminal investigation, the prosecutor may conduct seizure, search, or inspection by a warrant issued upon application to a judge of a district court, limited to property for which there are circumstances sufficient to suspect that the suspect committed the offense and which may be recognized as related to the case concerned.” Accordingly, if separate evidence unrelated to the criminal facts that formed the ground for issuance of the warrant is seized, such evidence cannot, in principle, be used as evidence of guilt. However, in the case of an offense that was the object of the seizure and search, or an offense related thereto, the results of such seizure and search may be used as evidence of guilt. A “crime related to the criminal suspicion stated in a seizure and search warrant” means a crime that has an objective connection with the suspected facts stated in the seizure and search warrant and a personal connection between the person subject to the warrant and the suspect. Among such crimes, “objective connection” with the suspected facts means a case directly related to the suspected facts themselves stated in the seizure and search warrant or to an offense having the same basic factual relationship as such facts; however, it may also be recognized where the evidence can be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and background of the offense, the means and method of the offense, the time and place of the offense, etc. At this time, objective connection should be recognized only where, taking into comprehensive consideration the content of the suspected facts stated in the seizure and search warrant, the object of the investigation, and the course of the investigation, there is a concrete and individual relationship, and such connection should not be deemed to exist merely because the suspected facts and the offense are of the same kind or similar. And the personal connection with the suspect refers to the offense of the person stated in the seizure and search warrant, but it may also be recognized in criminal cases against accomplices such as co-principals, instigators, and indirect principals, as well as necessary accomplices (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO13489, decided 2017. 1. 25.; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO13458, decided 2017. 12. 5., etc.).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(a) The police, based on the results of seizure and search regarding the Defendant’s Facebook account through which the victim communicated, confirmed that the subscriber to the access IP address of the account through which the offender conversed with the victim via Facebook Messenger was Non-Indicted Person 1 (the Defendant’s mother). The police further confirmed that Non-Indicted Person 2 (the Defendant’s father) and Non-Indicted Person 3 (the Defendant’s younger brother) were residing together on the resident registration record of Non-Indicted Person 1. At the time, the Defendant was residing at the above Facebook access location, but because his resident registration address was different, he did not appear on Non-Indicted Person 1’s resident registration record. The police, after identifying Non-Indicted Person 3 as the suspect, applied for a seizure and search warrant, and the judge of the district court issued the instant warrant as requested by the police.\\n\\n(b) In the instant warrant, the Defendant’s younger brother, “Non-Indicted Person 3,” is specified and stated as the suspect of the crime; “a. Jeollabuk-do, Jeonju-si (address omitted), b. the body of the suspect Non-Indicted Person 3 and the property possessed, owned, or held by the suspect” are specified and stated as the places, persons, or things to be searched and inspected; and “smartphones, etc., digital devices and storage media owned, possessed, held, managed, or used by the suspect Non-Indicted Person 3” are specified and stated as the items to be seized.\\n\\n(c) When the police arrived at the Defendant’s residence to execute the instant warrant, the Defendant was absent because he had gone to work, and the police heard from Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 3 that the person who committed the instant charged facts was not Non-Indicted Person 3 but the Defendant.\\n\\n(d) Accordingly, the police presented the instant warrant to Non-Indicted Person 1 and searched the above residence pursuant to the instant warrant and seized the instant mobile phone, etc. owned by the Defendant. At that site, the police prepared a seizure record for each of the seized items, and in the “seizure circumstances” section, they wrote: “Although Non-Indicted Person 3, residing at the Facebook access IP installation location, was identified as the suspect, upon on-site visit, the older brother, the Defendant, was residing there together in a separately divided household status, and after hearing the statements of the mother and Non-Indicted Person 3, it was confirmed that the actual suspect was the Defendant. However, because he was at work and absent at the time of execution of the warrant, the instant warrant was executed with the participation of the mother, Non-Indicted Person 1.”\\n\\n(3) Examining the above facts together with the following circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, the seizure of the Defendant’s mobile phone, etc. by executing the instant warrant issued against a person other than the Defendant as the suspect was unlawful.\\n\\n(a) In light of the spirit of due process and the warrant principle that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, the words used by a judge when issuing a seizure and search warrant to specify the “items to be seized” must be strictly construed and must not be expansively or analogically construed to the disadvantage of the person subject to seizure, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO763, decided 2009. 3. 12., etc.).\\n\\n(b) The police applied for the instant warrant in order to seize items owned or possessed by Non-Indicted Person 3, by identifying Non-Indicted Person 3 as the suspect in this case, and the judge issued the instant warrant to permit seizure of items owned or possessed by Non-Indicted Person 3 in accordance with the purpose of that application. Therefore, according to the wording of the instant warrant, the person subject to the seizure and search is Non-Indicted Person 3, and the items to be seized are limited to those owned, possessed, held, managed, or used by Non-Indicted Person 3.\\n\\n(c) Even if the police heard at the seizure and search site from another person that the true offender in this case was the Defendant, they cannot seize items owned by the Defendant contrary to the wording stated in the instant warrant. Even if there may be a recognized difference between coercive measures against property and coercive measures against persons in terms such as the degree of substantiation of the criminal facts, once a warrant has been issued identifying the suspect and the person subject to seizure, it cannot be regarded as lawful and valid to execute the warrant by construing another person as the person subject to seizure.\\n\\n(4) Nevertheless, the court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the execution of the instant warrant was lawful; thus, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the unlawfulness of seizure procedures pursuant to a warrant issued against a person other than the Defendant as the suspect.\\n\\n(5) However, among the instant mobile phone, etc. seized by executing the instant warrant, the file discovered in the E310K mobile phone cannot be regarded as relating to a crime connected with the suspected facts stated in the instant warrant, and thus lacks admissibility of evidence; and because no evidence that could be used as evidence of a crime was discovered in the remainder, the court below did not use as evidence of guilt the evidence obtained from the instant mobile phone, etc. that were unlawfully seized as above.\\n\\nAccordingly, since the above error by the court below did not affect the outcome of the judgment, the Defendant’s argument in this part of the grounds for final appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Judgment concerning seizure by voluntary submission\\n\\nA. The seizure and search by an investigative agency of electronic information such as e-mails stored in a suspect’s information processing device, such as a computer, against an internet service user who is the suspect is permitted by the interpretation of the Criminal Procedure Act as a coercive measure in rem against the owner or possessor of the electronic information. Even where the electronic information to be seized and searched is not contained in an information processing device, such as a computer, at the search location stated in the seizure and search warrant, but is stored in a storage medium such as a remote server managed by a third party, connected to the information processing device through an information and communications network, if the investigative agency, pursuant to a warrant issued in lieu of the access authority to the suspect’s email account, enters the suspect’s email account ID and password lawfully obtained by using the information processing device, such as a computer, at the search location stated in the warrant, thereby accessing the remote storage medium in the ordinary manner by which the suspect would access it and downloading or displaying on the screen of the information processing device at the search location the suspect’s email-related electronic information stored there, this also concerns electronic information belonging to or possessed by the suspect, and therefore the seizure and search of that electronic information need not be viewed differently (see Supreme Court Decision 2017DO9747, decided 2017. 11. 29.). If, when voluntarily submitting a mobile phone, the suspect voluntarily provided the investigative agency with the ID and password for accessing cloud storage, etc., with the intent to submit to the investigative agency electronic information stored not in the mobile phone but in remote locations such as the cloud, managed by a third party, then the electronic information stored in the cloud, etc. may be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted.\\n\\nB. Judgment\\n\\nThe court below determined, for the reasons stated in its holding, that the Defendant, based on his voluntary intent, submitted the Samsung mobile phone Galaxy Note8 in his possession to the investigative agency, and voluntarily submitted to the investigative agency the SDCard stored files, Naver Cloud files, and Galaxy Note gallery files connected to the Galaxy Note8.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles discussed above, the court below’s above determination is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the unlawfulness of seizure procedures by voluntary submission, the admissibility of evidence voluntarily submitted, or the specification of the source of evidence, nor is there any error exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2021DO11170]": "The grounds of appeal (the contents of the supplemental appellate brief submitted after the period for submitting the appellate brief are considered only to the extent that they supplement valid grounds of appeal) are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Regarding the grounds of appeal challenging the admissibility of evidence\\n\\n1) Admissibility of the electronic information stored in the two PCs in the lecturer break room of OO University (hereinafter referred to as “the PCs at issue”)\\n\\na) Relevant legal principles\\n\\n(1) Standards for determining the scope of seizure of electronic information and relevance when an information storage medium containing electronic information is voluntarily submitted\\n\\nIn light of the importance of electronic information stored in an information storage medium from the perspective of, in addition to due process, the warrant requirement, and the principle of proportionality that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, the protection of the secrecy and freedom of private life, the right to informational self-determination, and property rights, a declaration of intent by a person voluntarily submitting an information storage medium to designate the electronic information contained therein or to limit the scope of submission must be strictly construed, and it is impermissible for an investigative agency to carelessly infer the unidentified submitter’s intent. Therefore, where an investigative agency can readily confirm the submitter’s intent but, without doing so, voluntarily receives an information storage medium containing both electronic information related to a specific criminal suspicion and electronic information unrelated thereto, it cannot be treated as though all electronic information stored in that information storage medium was voluntarily submitted and seized.\\n\\nWhen an investigative agency seeking to seize electronic information seizes an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein by the method of voluntary submission, if, due to reasons such as failing to properly confirm the submitter’s intent regarding the specific scope of submission, the object and scope of the seizure of electronic information according to the voluntary submission are unclear or cannot be ascertained, only electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that motivated the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission and having at least minimal value capable of proving it shall be subject to seizure. Here, electronic information related to the criminal suspicion may include not only the criminal suspicion itself or conduct directly related to an offense based on the same basic factual relationship, but also information that may be used as indirect or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and background of the offense, the means and method of the offense, the time and place of the offense, and the like. However, such relevance is recognized only where, taken comprehensively in light of the content of the criminal suspicion that motivated the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission, the object of the investigation, the course of the investigation, the process of voluntary submission, and the like, there exists a concrete and individual nexus; mere similarity to the criminal suspicion or the fact that the offense is of the same kind is not sufficient to establish relevance (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DO348, decided November 18, 2021).\\n\\n(2) Guarantee of the right to participate in the search, copying, and printing of electronic information\\n\\nWhere an investigative agency that has voluntarily received an information storage medium or a copy thereof containing both electronic information subject to seizure and electronic information not subject to seizure transfers the information storage medium, etc. to the prosecutor’s office or the like and searches, copies, and prints it, in such a series of processes it must, in principle, comply with the warrant requirement and due process by guaranteeing the opportunity to participate to the party subject to seizure/search under Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as “the person subject to seizure”) or his or her defense counsel, by preparing and delivering a seizure inventory specifying the file details of the seized electronic information, and by taking appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the criminal suspicion. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as where the person subject to seizure expressly indicated an intent not to participate or where, in light of the purpose and course of the voluntary submission or the nature and content of the process in which the act violating the procedure occurred, it cannot be deemed that the purpose of guaranteeing the opportunity to participate in the procedure to the person subject to seizure was substantially infringed, the seizure/search cannot be regarded as lawful, and this is not altered by the fact that the investigative agency copied or printed only electronic information related to the criminal suspicion from the information storage medium or its copy.\\n\\nFurthermore, where a third party such as a victim voluntarily submits, without a warrant, an information storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, it is difficult to deem that the suspect, who is the person substantially subject to seizure, consented to the investigative agency’s unrestricted search of all electronic information therein; moreover, even when the suspect himself or herself voluntarily submits the information, in view also of the fact that the suspect’s right to participate, etc. must be guaranteed, unless there are special circumstances, appropriate measures must be taken under Articles 219, 121, and 129 of the Criminal Procedure Act to guarantee the suspect’s procedural rights, such as guaranteeing the suspect the right to participate and delivering a list of the seized electronic information (see the above en banc decision in 2016DO348, etc.).\\n\\nIn this way, in addition to the person subject to seizure who voluntarily submitted the information storage medium, the “information storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect” as to which the right to participate must also be guaranteed to a suspect who is not the submitter refers to a case where the suspect, at the time of seizure/search or until a time temporally proximate thereto, actually dominated and managed the information storage medium, possessed and exercised exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein, and did not otherwise transfer or waive it to a third party according to his or her own intent, and thereby may be evaluated as the person substantially subject to seizure with respect to the electronic information stored in that information storage medium. Whether this applies must be determined not by a legal or ex post facto judgment based on the attribution of rights under civil law, but on the basis of the externally and objectively recognizable factual condition at the time of the seizure/search. Apart from such externally and objectively dominant and managerial conditions concerning the information storage medium, persons who merely had prior involvement in the use of the information storage medium or the creation/use of individual electronic information, or persons identified as the data subject by electronic information created in that process, are not to be treated as parties actually subjected to seizure/search.\\n\\nb) Facts found\\n\\nThe reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted show the following facts.\\n\\n(1) By around September 10, 2019, the prosecution had conducted investigative measures, including execution of search-and-seizure warrants for the Defendant’s professor’s research room at OO University and for ◇◇◇ High School, with criminal suspicion facts including forgery of a private document concerning a commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University dated September 7, 2012 against the Defendant (the facts charged in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP738), uttering of a forged private document arising from Person 1’s submission of the above commendation certificate in the application process to the Graduate School of Medicine of △△ University and □□ University, obstruction of the performance of official duties by deception concerning the admissions screening work of the Graduate School of Medicine of □□ University arising from the above commendation certificate and other false career entries, and other offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school.\\n\\n(2) Person 2 had served as an assistant to the ☆☆ College of OO University from March 1, 2019, and had been responsible for taking over and managing the lecturer break room at OO University and the items therein from his or her predecessor. The PCs at issue were stored in the lecturer break room without any separate marking as to ownership or legal relations.\\n\\n(3) The basic purport of Person 2’s statement regarding the ownership and management status of the PCs at issue was that, having been told by his or her predecessor that they were “items left behind by retirees, so return them to the school authorities or handle them as appropriate,” he or she understood them in that way. Furthermore, according to Person 2’s statement, if there were a professor who wished to use the PCs at issue, he or she intended to provide them.\\n\\n(4) The Defendant’s side also argued, at the first hearing date in the first instance, that the Defendant had never used the PCs at issue and that they had been used only as shared PCs at OO University; although their arguments changed several times up to the lower court, their basic position was that the PCs at issue had been used as shared PCs at OO University, then taken by the Defendant to his or her residence, etc. for use for a certain period, and then returned to OO University around December 2016 so that they could again be used as shared PCs at the OO University English camp and the like. This is consistent with the state at the time of the search and seizure in this case, in which the objective and actual dominion, custody, and attribution of the authority to manage and dispose of the PCs at issue were with OO University.\\n\\n(5) While cooperating in the investigation by guiding the prosecutorial investigators through the interior of the ☆☆ College building at OO University on September 10, 2019 based on the cooperation instructions of OO University, Person 2, at the request of the prosecutorial investigator, enabled the prosecutorial investigator to operate one of the PCs at issue and to inspect the electronic information stored therein. In the course of the prosecutorial investigator’s search of the electronic information stored in that PC in Person 2’s presence, a folder related to Person 3 was discovered, and while the search continued, a situation occurred in which the PC emitted a “pop” sound and powered off. Thereupon, the prosecutorial investigator asked Person 2 and Person 4, the Director of the Administrative Support Office who oversaw the management of OO University’s property, whether they could discontinue the search at the scene and submit the PCs at issue to the prosecution.\\n\\n(6) In response, Person 2 and Person 4 voluntarily submitted the PCs at issue in response to the prosecutorial investigator’s request, and in that process they entered their personal details, signed, and affixed their seals/thumbprints on the “Consent to Voluntary Submission” form, which stated that they were voluntarily submitting the PCs at issue and listed the PCs at issue in the section for voluntarily submitted items.\\n\\n(7) At that time, the prosecutorial investigator asked Person 2 and Person 4 whether they wished to attend the imaging and search of the PCs at issue, extraction of electronic information, and the like, but Person 2 and Person 4 replied that they would not attend. Thereafter, Person 2 and Person 4 entered their personal details, signed, and affixed their seals/thumbprints in the section for “the person subject to seizure (voluntary submitter)” of the “Confirmation of Whether to Attend the Submission and Imaging, etc. of an Information Storage Medium” form (hereinafter referred to as the “Confirmation of Whether to Attend”), which stated in substance that they would not attend the hard copy/imaging of the voluntarily submitted information storage medium, search and copying (printing) of electronic information, and the like.\\n\\n(8) The prosecutorial investigator received the above “Consent to Voluntary Submission” and “Confirmation of Whether to Attend” from Person 2 and Person 4, delivered to them a “Seizure Inventory Receipt” concerning the PCs at issue, and then took the PCs at issue to the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office. In that process, the prosecutorial investigator did not additionally reconfirm with Person 2 and Person 4 their intent regarding the specific scope of submission of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue.\\n\\n(9) Thereafter, the prosecution carried out imaging and forensic work on the PCs at issue to extract electronic information, and as a result, evidence was discovered indicating that the forgery of the private document concerning the commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University had been carried out around June 16, 2013 using one of the PCs at issue.\\n\\n(10) Accordingly, on November 27, 2019, in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP738, the prosecution filed a motion for amendment of the indictment, changing the existing charged facts that “the Defendant forged a commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University by arbitrarily affixing the President’s official seal of OO University on September 7, 2012 at OO University” to the effect that “the Defendant forged a commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University in electronic file form using a PC at his or her residence on June 16, 2013.” However, upon being denied leave on the ground that the identity of the charged facts was not recognized, the prosecution additionally indicted the Defendant on December 17, 2019 in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP1050 on charged facts identical to those in the motion for amendment of the indictment.\\n\\n(11) On February 11, 2020, the prosecution delivered to Person 2 and Person 4 a list specifying the file details of the electronic information extracted from and seized from the PCs at issue.\\n\\n(12) The electronic information stored in the PCs at issue was used as evidence of the offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school among the facts charged in this case, including forgery of a private document dated June 16, 2013 (the facts charged in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2019GOHAP1050).\\n\\nc) Holding\\n\\n(1) Voluntary submission of the PCs at issue\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, examination of the above facts found shows that, as of September 10, 2019, the PCs at issue were not being used exclusively by a specific person for a specific purpose, but were being kept in the lecturer break room for nearly three years on the premise that OO University personnel would use them as shared PCs at OO University or otherwise dispose of them at their discretion, and the assistant responsible for the management and custody of the PCs at issue at the ☆☆ College of OO University, Person 2, was carrying out the custody and management duties concerning the PCs at issue. It is therefore recognized that Person 2, the assistant in charge of the custody and management duties at the time, and Person 4, the Director of the Administrative Support Office overseeing the management of OO University’s property, submitted the PCs at issue to the prosecution according to a voluntary intent reflecting OO University’s position.\\n\\n(2) Necessity and relevance of the seizure of electronic information stored in the PCs at issue\\n\\n(a) In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court erred in presuming that, in the case of a voluntary submission of an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein, the object of seizure is not limited to the extent that necessity and relevance are recognized, and in concluding that, even though the investigative agency did not confirm with Person 2 and Person 4 their intent regarding the specific scope of submission of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, all of the PCs at issue and all electronic information stored therein could be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted. The PCs at issue were an information storage medium in which electronic information related to the criminal suspicion concerning the Defendant and electronic information unrelated thereto were commingled, and in such a case, it is in principle impermissible to arbitrarily infer the unidentified submitter’s intent and treat all electronic information stored in the PCs as having been voluntarily submitted and seized.\\n\\n(b) Where, as such, the object and scope of seizure of electronic information according to the voluntary submitter’s intent cannot be clearly ascertained, only electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that motivated the seizure pursuant to the voluntary submission and having at least minimal value capable of proving it should be deemed subject to seizure.\\n\\nAt the time of the voluntary submission of the PCs at issue, the Defendant was already under investigation for the offense of uttering a forged private document to the effect that a forged commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University had been submitted in the application process to the Graduate School of Medicine of △△ University and □□ University by Person 1, as well as for obstruction of the performance of official duties by deception concerning the admissions screening work of the Graduate School of Medicine of □□ University arising from the above commendation certificate and other false career entries.\\n\\nAccordingly, electronic information created by using the PCs at issue in the process of Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school, such as the Defendant’s use of one of the PCs at issue on June 16, 2013 to forge the above commendation certificate, can be regarded as evidence having a concrete and individual nexus to proving the motive and background, means and method, and the like, of the offense concerning the above criminal suspicion, and even comprehensively considering the object and course of this investigation and the process of voluntary submission, it is sufficient to recognize necessity and relevance.\\n\\n(c) Ultimately, among the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, the portions used as evidence of the offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school among the facts charged in this case have both necessity and relevance for seizure pursuant to voluntary submission; thus, the lower court’s legal error as noted above does not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\n(3) Guarantee of the right to participate in the process of search and extraction of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue\\n\\n(a) In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court erred in stating, in substance, that when an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein are voluntarily submitted and seized, there is in principle no room to recognize the right to participate on the part of the person subject to seizure or the suspect during the process of searching the electronic information.\\n\\nThe PCs at issue were an information storage medium in which electronic information related to the criminal suspicion concerning the Defendant and electronic information unrelated thereto were commingled, and after the prosecution voluntarily received them from Person 2 and Person 4 and seized them, the prosecution moved them to the National Digital Forensics Center of the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office and, in the process of searching and extracting the electronic information stored therein, had, in principle, to guarantee the opportunity to participate to OO University, the person subject to seizure.\\n\\n(b) However, as seen in the facts found above, in light of the course of the search and extraction of the electronic information related to the criminal suspicion from the PCs at issue, it is recognized that the prosecution confirmed the intent to participate and afforded an opportunity to Person 2 and Person 4, who were the persons subject to seizure, but that the persons subject to seizure waived that opportunity. Therefore, it cannot be said that there was a defect in the seizure/search procedure for the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue in that the right to participate of the persons subject to seizure was not guaranteed.\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of the purpose of guaranteeing the opportunity for the persons subject to seizure to participate as one of the appropriate measures to prevent distortion of electronic information in an information storage medium subject to seizure/search or arbitrary copying of electronic information unrelated to the suspected facts (see Supreme Court Order 2009MO1190, dated May 26, 2011, Supreme Court en banc Order 2011MO1839, dated July 16, 2015, etc.), examining the entire process of the seizure/search in this case, the reasons asserted by the Defendant alone, such as that no additional measure such as detailed notification of the criminal suspicion facts was taken with respect to Person 2 at the time of seizure pursuant to voluntary submission of the PCs at issue, cannot establish that the purpose of guaranteeing procedural participation to the persons subject to seizure was substantially infringed.\\n\\n(c) Also, examining the above facts found on the basis of the foregoing legal principles, when viewed according to the objectively and externally recognizable factual condition at the time of the seizure/search pursuant to voluntary submission of the PCs at issue, it cannot be recognized that the PCs at issue or the electronic information stored therein belonged to or were under the Defendant’s ownership or control. Rather, in light of objective circumstances such as OO University’s actual domination and management of the PCs at issue by keeping them in the lecturer break room for nearly three years from around December 2016 while also seeming to be able to use them as shared PCs or take other measures such as discretionary disposal, it is recognized that OO University was, at that time, in a state of actually possessing and exercising comprehensive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored in the PCs at issue.\\n\\nEven considering all the circumstances asserted by the Defendant, such as that the Defendant had, before around December 2016, taken the PCs at issue to the Defendant’s residence, etc. and used them exclusively, or that after around December 2016 the lecturer break room where the PCs at issue were stored was near the Defendant’s professor’s research room, it cannot be said that the Defendant’s actual domination and management of the PCs at issue and the authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein continued until the time of the seizure/search in this case. Accordingly, this case does not fall within a situation in which the Defendant can be evaluated as the person substantially subject to seizure/search in relation to the seizure/search in this case.\\n\\nTherefore, even under the legal principles set forth in the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DO348, the seizure/search of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue does not fall within a case in which the suspect’s right to participate must be guaranteed.\\n\\n(d) Meanwhile, the Defendant also argues that, during the seizure/search process of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, the Defendant’s side should have been guaranteed the right to participate on the ground that the Defendant’s side was the “data subject” of the electronic information. As noted above, in order for a suspect to assert a right to participate in the course of searching electronic information in an information storage medium voluntarily submitted without the suspect’s involvement, the premise is the suspect’s actual domination and control over the information storage medium and possession of exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information therein. Therefore, this argument cannot be accepted, as it is not intended to recognize the right to participate even to those who merely participated in the creation/use, etc. of individual electronic information, or to persons who are the data subjects identified by the electronic information created in that process, irrespective of such domination and control.\\n\\n(e) Ultimately, the right to participate was guaranteed to the persons subject to seizure in the course of the search and extraction of the electronic information stored in the PCs at issue, and the case does not fall within a situation where the Defendant’s side also had to be guaranteed a right to participate; accordingly, the lower court’s error in this part also does not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\n(4) Admissibility of the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the prosecution’s voluntary receipt and seizure of the PCs at issue from OO University, the possessor and custodian of those PCs, did not constitute an unlawful investigation after indictment, that it could not be said that the admissibility of the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue was recognized only if the Defendant’s side consented thereto, and that the electronic information extracted from the PCs at issue could be used as evidence because the identity and integrity between that electronic information, the documents printed therefrom, and the originals were proven.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the facts found above, although there are some inappropriate parts in the lower court’s statement of reasons, the conclusion of the lower court recognizing the admissibility of the evidence extracted from the PCs at issue is proper, and there is no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning compulsory investigation after indictment, the necessity of consent of the data subject in the seizure/search of voluntarily submitted items by a third party’s consent, the status and voluntariness of the custodian in seizure of voluntarily submitted items, the scope of the provisions mutatis mutandis of Article 219 of the Criminal Procedure Act in the seizure of voluntarily submitted items from an information storage medium, identity and integrity with the original, and the warrant requirement, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2) Admissibility of the results of execution of the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts\\n\\na) The lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that, in executing the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts, the prosecution’s series of execution methods—sending, through the Criminal Justice Information Network, requests for provision of financial transaction information, copies of the warrants, and copies of the investigators’ identification cards to several financial institutions by electronic fax, receiving financial transaction data by e-mail or fax from the financial institutions, analyzing the received financial transaction data, then finally preparing a list of selected data related to the case, and thereafter directly visiting the financial institutions to present the original warrants, storing the selected data in a storage medium, while also delivering a seizure inventory and preparing a seizure protocol—did not violate the seizure/search procedures prescribed by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, and that the financial transaction data collected and submitted as evidence by such method in this case were admissible.\\n\\nb) However, as a matter of principle, investigative agencies’ seizure and search must be based on a search-and-seizure warrant issued by a judge, and the original warrant must be presented to the person receiving the disposition (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2015DO10648, decided September 7, 2017; Supreme Court Decision 2018DO2841, decided March 14, 2019). Accordingly, even in executing a search-and-seizure warrant for tracing financial accounts, if the investigative agency did not present the original warrant in advance to the financial institution before receiving financial transaction data from it, such method cannot in principle be regarded as a lawful method of execution.\\n\\nHowever, where, as a result of the investigative agency’s request to the financial institution for provision of financial transaction information under Article 4(2) of the Act on Real Name Financial Transactions and Guarantee of Secrecy (hereinafter referred to as the “Financial Real Name Act”), accompanied by a copy of the warrant, the financial transaction data received in reply from the financial institution fall within the objects and scope of execution of the warrant; and where the entire process of requesting provision of financial transaction information and receiving the data by facsimile transmission or electronic transmission is based on the financial institution’s voluntary willingness to cooperate; and where, after going through the procedure of selecting from among the data those financial transactions related to the criminal suspicion facts, the original warrant is finally presented and the seizure procedure is executed for the financial transaction data thus selected; and where the process is carried out in the manner prescribed by the Financial Real Name Act and there are no circumstances suggesting that it was otherwise conducted with the intent to circumvent due process and the warrant requirement—only in such a case may it exceptionally be regarded as a lawful method of execution of the warrant, on the basis that the entire series of procedures can be evaluated as “presenting the original warrant in a timely manner based on one warrant and seizing/searching on that basis.”\\n\\nc) In light of such legal principles, examining the process of execution of each of the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts in this case, even if the original warrant was not presented in advance to the financial institution before the investigative agency received financial transaction data from it, this case falls within a situation where the subsequent series of procedures—after going through the selection process for data related to the criminal suspicion facts, ultimately presenting the original warrant and directly seizing the selected data—can, viewed as a whole, be evaluated as presenting the original warrant in a timely manner based on one warrant and seizing/searching within the original objects and scope of execution of the warrant on that basis. Nor are there circumstances sufficient to recognize that the investigative agency executed the warrant in the above manner with the intent to circumvent due process and the warrant requirement.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s conclusion that the admissibility of the financial transaction data secured in the execution process of the search-and-seizure warrants for tracing financial accounts in this case is recognized is proper, and there is no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the method of presenting the warrant and the lawfulness of the seizure/search procedure, the admissibility of the seized items and secondary evidence in this part, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3) 120,000 physical shares of [Company Name 1 omitted]\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the search-and-seizure warrant concerning 120,000 physical shares of [Company Name 1 omitted] was lawfully presented to the person subject to seizure, and that admissibility of evidence was recognized because the necessity of seizure and relevance to the criminal suspicion facts were also recognized.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the admissibility of evidence of this seized item and secondary evidence, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4) Admissibility of the audio recording file of a telephone conversation kept by [Company Name 2 omitted]\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the necessity of seizure and the relevance to the criminal suspicion facts were recognized with respect to the audio recording file of the telephone conversation kept by [Company Name 2 omitted], and thus the evidence was admissible.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the admissibility of evidence of this seized item and secondary evidence, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the offenses related to Person 1’s fraudulent application to the medical graduate school\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court found that the Defendant forged the commendation certificate in the name of the President of OO University as alleged in the facts charged in this part (obstruction of business, obstruction of performance of official duties by deception, uttering of a forged official document concerning the experiential activity confirmation issued in the name of the head of the ◎◎◎◎ Research Institute of ▽▽ University, uttering of a forged official document as an alternative charge concerning the internship confirmation issued in the name of the head of the ▷▷▷▷▷ Center of ◁ University at △△ University, forgery of a private document dated June 16, 2013, and uttering of a forged private document), and that all other supporting documents were also false; that submitting them in the application process to the Graduate School of Medicine of △△ University and □□ University by Person 1, or entering them in the career history, constituted deception for the offenses of obstruction of business and obstruction of performance of official duties by deception; that the Defendant’s intent and the conspiracy with Person 1, etc. were recognized in that process; and that this constituted an act obstructing the admissions screening work of each medical graduate school and could not be regarded as merely due to inadequate review by the persons in charge. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, misapprehension of legal principles concerning the establishment of co-principal liability, the “deception” and “intent” elements of obstruction of business and obstruction of performance of official duties by deception, or danger of obstruction, or omission of judgment or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the fraud and violation of the former Subsidy Management Act (the Act before amendment by Act No. 13931 on January 28, 2016; hereinafter referred to as the “former Subsidy Act”)\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court held that the special grant money stated in the facts charged in this part constituted a subsidy under the former Subsidy Act, and that the Defendant fraudulently applied for and received research assistant allowances, thereby finding that this constituted a deceptive act for the offense of fraud. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the interpretation of Article 2(1) and Article 9 of the former Subsidy Act, Article 4(1) [Appended Table 1] of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, or deception in the offense of fraud, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nD. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the part violating the Capital Markets and Financial Investment Services Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Capital Markets Act”) due to the use of undisclosed material information (excluding the part acquitted on grounds)\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that, as alleged in the facts charged in this part, the Defendant purchased shares of [Company Name 1 omitted] using undisclosed material information. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the establishment of the act of using undisclosed material information, the presumption of innocence, insufficient judicial examination, or lack of reasons, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nE. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the “purpose of evading the law” in the offense of violating the Financial Real Name Act, or insufficient judicial examination, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nF. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning instigation of destruction of evidence\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court held that the Defendant, as alleged in the facts charged in this part, with the intent to destroy materials related to Person 3 or materials related to Person 5, who were evidence in the Defendant’s criminal case, conspired with Person 6 and Person 7 to cause instigation of destruction of evidence against employees of [Company Name 3 omitted], and that common intent to act jointly and functional control over the act were recognized, and that such conduct by the Defendant constituted an abuse of the right of defense. On that basis, the lower court found this part of the charges guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the establishment of co-principal liability for instigation of destruction of evidence, the “intent to instigate” and “common intent to act jointly regarding the instigation,” the “evidence relating to a criminal case or disciplinary case” under the offense of destruction of evidence, or abuse of the right of defense, or contradiction in reasons, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nG. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning instigation of concealment of evidence\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court found that the Defendant instructed Person 8 to conceal evidence concerning the storage medium of the PC at the Defendant’s residence and the main unit of the PC in the Defendant’s professor’s research room at OO University, as alleged in the facts charged in this part; that such conduct by the Defendant constituted instigation, not co-principal liability for concealment of evidence; and that Person 8 merely resolved to conceal evidence in accordance with the Defendant’s instructions and common intent to act jointly could not be recognized. On that basis, the lower court reversed the first-instance judgment, which had found this part of the charges not guilty, and found the Defendant guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning recognition of “consummation” and “principal offender” in the offense of concealment of evidence, the “functional control over the act” that serves as the criterion for distinguishing co-principal liability from instigation liability, the “commencement of execution” of concealment of evidence, or Person 8’s “common intent to act jointly,” as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court maintained the first-instance judgment insofar as it found not proven or declared not guilty, with respect to the principal charges concerning uttering of a forged official document, embezzlement in the course of duties, violation of the Capital Markets Act due to the use of undisclosed material information in connection with over-the-counter purchase of 120,000 physical shares of [Company Name 1 omitted], and violation of the Act on the Regulation and Punishment of Criminal Proceeds Concealment, violation of the Capital Markets Act due to a false report of change, violation of the Financial Real Name Act by using the account of [Company Name 2 omitted] (account number omitted), and instigation of evidence forgery, among the facts charged in this case, concerning the internship confirmation issued in the name of the head of the ▷▷▷▷▷ Center of ◁ University at △△ University.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the intent for the offense of uttering a forged official document, the intent of unlawful appropriation for the offense of embezzlement in the course of duties, the establishment of the offense of violating the Capital Markets Act due to the use of undisclosed material information, the establishment of co-principal liability, the “purpose of evading the law” in the offense of violating the Financial Real Name Act, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning instigating conduct, or omission of judgment, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the order."}

{"[2022DO7453]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination of the argument that the legal doctrine concerning the right to participate in the voluntary submission procedure for a digital storage medium was misunderstood\\n\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) The importance of electronic information stored in a digital storage medium derives, along with the due process of law, the principle of warrant requirement, and the principle of proportionality that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, from the perspectives of the secrecy and freedom of private life and the right to informational self-determination.\\n\\nWhere a law-enforcement agency that has received on a voluntary basis a digital storage medium, or a duplicate thereof, in which electronic information subject to seizure and electronic information not subject to seizure are intermingled, transports the digital storage medium, etc. to the agency office and searches, copies, and prints it, the agency must, in that series of processes, guarantee the opportunity to participate to the party upon whom the execution of a seizure and search warrant prescribed in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act is carried out (hereinafter referred to as the “person subject to seizure”) or to that person’s defense counsel, prepare and deliver a seizure inventory specifying the file details of the seized electronic information, and take appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the facts suspected of crime, thereby complying with the principle of warrant requirement and due process of law. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as the party subject to seizure side having expressly indicated an intention not to participate, or such that, in light of the purport and course of the voluntary submission or the nature and content of the process in which the violation occurred, it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing participation to the party subject to seizure side was substantially infringed, the seizure and search cannot be assessed as lawful; nor does it matter even if the law-enforcement agency copied and printed only electronic information related to the facts suspected of crime from the digital storage medium or its duplicate.\\n\\nWhere a victim or other third party voluntarily submits a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, it is difficult to regard the substantive person subject to seizure, i.e. the suspect, as having consented to the law-enforcement agency’s unrestricted search of all of the electronic information, and even when compared with the case where the suspect himself or herself makes the voluntary submission, in which the suspect’s participation right, etc. must be guaranteed, unless special circumstances exist, appropriate measures to ensure the suspect’s procedural rights, such as guaranteeing the suspect’s participation right and delivering an inventory of the seized electronic information, must be taken (see Supreme Court en banc decision of November 18, 2021, 2016DO348, etc.).\\n\\n2) The “digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect,” to which the participation right must be guaranteed not only for the person subject to seizure who voluntarily submitted the digital storage medium but also for the suspect who is not the person making the voluntary submission, means a case in which the suspect, at the time of seizure and search or at a temporally close point thereto, actually dominates and controls the digital storage medium while retaining and exercising exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored in that digital storage medium, and has not otherwise transferred or abandoned it to a third party according to his or her own will, so that the suspect can be evaluated as a substantive party to the seizure and search as to all electronic information stored in the digital storage medium. Whether this applies shall be determined not on the basis of a legal judgment following the attribution of rights under civil law, but on the basis of the factual condition outwardly and objectively recognizable at the time of seizure and search. Apart from such outward and objective state of domination and control over the digital storage medium, etc., it is not the case that they must be treated as substantive parties subject to seizure and search merely because the suspect or another third party had in the past been involved in the use of the digital storage medium or in the creation or use of individual electronic information, or because they correspond to the data subject identified by electronic information created in that process (see Supreme Court decision of January 27, 2022, 2021DO11170, etc.).\\n\\nb. Facts found\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower-court judgment and the evidence duly admitted, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n1) The law-enforcement agency, starting with the seizure and search conducted around August 27, 2019, on (Name 2 omitted) University, (Name 3 omitted) office, and (Name 1 omitted) academy, etc. in connection with suspicions of admissions and academic irregularities involving the children of Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2, suspicions of improprieties in private equity fund investments, suspicions of irregularities at the (Name 1 omitted) academy, and the like, began a full-scale investigation into the various allegations.\\n\\n2) In preparation for the investigation such as seizure and search, Non-Indicted Person 1, in order to conceal computers, etc. storing electronic information related to the suspected facts, around August 31, 2019, handed over to Non-Indicted Person 3 three digital storage media used by Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. at their residence (hereinafter referred to as “the instant hard disk drive”), namely one of two digital storage media detached from a computer in the study (one HDD), two digital storage media detached from the computer of his son, Non-Indicted Person 4 (one HDD and one SSD), and instructed him to hide them “until the investigation is over.” Non-Indicted Person 3 concealed the instant hard disk drive in places such as a personal locker at a gym on the basement level 1 of a commercial building located in Yangcheon-gu, Seoul.\\n\\n3) The instant hard disk drive stored evidence that Non-Indicted Person 1 intended to conceal, namely internship certificates used in his children’s university and graduate school admissions and text messages of Non-Indicted Person 4, the Defendant, and other related persons.\\n\\n4) The law-enforcement agency, around September 10, 2019, took Non-Indicted Person 3 into custody as a suspect on charges of concealment of evidence. Non-Indicted Person 3 voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive to the law-enforcement agency on September 11, 2019.\\n\\n5) In the process of the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive and the search, copying, and printing of the electronic information stored therein, the law-enforcement agency guaranteed the participation right by confirming with Non-Indicted Person 3 and his defense counsel whether they wished to participate and by affording them the opportunity to participate, but Non-Indicted Person 3’s side indicated an intention not to participate in the search, copying, and printing process. The law-enforcement agency did not confirm such intention to participate with Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. nor afford them an opportunity to participate.\\n\\nc. Determination\\n\\nTaking into account the legal principles examined above and the following circumstances discernible from the above facts found, it cannot be said that participation rights must be guaranteed also to Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., who were not the persons making the voluntary submission, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3, who voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence. In the same purport, the lower court’s determination recognizing the admissibility of the electronic information stored in the instant hard disk drive is justified and can be accepted.\\n\\n1) Non-Indicted Person 3, as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, which was the criminal facts giving rise to the voluntary submission, voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive during the investigation against him. The instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein are evidence not only concerning the suspected facts of Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., who are the principal offenders, but also the direct object of the concealment act, and thus constitute evidence concerning Non-Indicted Person 3’s suspicion of concealment of evidence. Accordingly, Non-Indicted Person 3 is a person with a substantive interest in the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein. Throughout the entire process, including the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive itself and the searching, copying, and printing of the electronic information related to the suspicion of concealment of evidence, Non-Indicted Person 3 has an interest in participation.\\n\\n2) As the investigation into himself and Non-Indicted Persons 2, etc. became full-scale, Non-Indicted Person 1 delivered the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 while instructing him to hide it. Non-Indicted Person 3 voluntarily concealed the instant hard disk drive in a place known only to himself so that it would not be discovered. Thereafter, when Non-Indicted Person 3 was taken into custody as a suspect on suspicion of concealment of evidence, he disclosed the concealment to the law-enforcement agency and voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive. In light of the circumstances surrounding the concealment and voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, and the extent of involvement of Non-Indicted Person 3 and Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. in that process, it may be said that the person who actually possessed the instant hard disk drive at the time of seizure and search or at a time close thereto was Non-Indicted Person 3. Further, insofar as Non-Indicted Person 3 actually possessed the instant hard disk drive around that time by the foregoing circumstances, it may be regarded, absent other special circumstances, that he was also in a position to de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of the stored electronic information.\\n\\n3) Non-Indicted Person 1 was not the suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, which was the criminal facts giving rise to the voluntary submission, and moreover, he delivered the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3, requesting vaguely that it be hidden “until the investigation into himself is over,” with the purpose of concealing the very existence of the instant hard disk drive. This can be regarded as an expression of an intention, under the purpose of concealing and severing the outward connection between himself and the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein, to abandon or wholly transfer to Non-Indicted Person 3 the exclusive right of domination and control over the instant hard disk drive until the indefinite time of “completion of the investigation,” if necessary for achieving that purpose. As a result, Non-Indicted Person 3 came to be in a state where he could de facto retain and exercise actual and factual domination over the instant hard disk drive and exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein, and he actually exercised that authority by concealing the instant hard disk drive at a place of his own choosing and thereafter voluntarily submitting it to the law-enforcement agency.\\n\\n2. Determination of the remaining arguments for final appeal\\n\\nThe lower court maintained the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case guilty for the reasons stated in the opinion. Examining the reasons of the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence duly admitted, there is no error affecting the judgment in that the lower court either exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, without fully conducting the necessary examination, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning relevance between the seized items and the facts charged, abuse of prosecutorial authority, the presumption of innocence and the principle of trial based on evidence concerning the falsity of the instant certificate, deception and risk of result in the crime of obstruction of business, intent and co-principal liability, and the admissibility of derivative evidence, etc.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the main text. In this judgment, except for the dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justices Min Yu-sook, Lee Heung-gu, and Oh Kyung-mi, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are the concurring opinions of Supreme Court Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion, as well as the concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justice Oh Kyung-mi on the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n4. Dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justices Min Yu-sook, Lee Heung-gu, and Oh Kyung-mi\\n\\na. Summary of the dissenting opinion\\n\\n1) The majority opinion held that Non-Indicted Person 3, who voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive, had a substantive interest in the electronic information stored therein as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, and could de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of that electronic information by actually possessing it; therefore, it was sufficient that participation rights were guaranteed to him in the seizure and search procedure, and since Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., who handed over the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 to conceal evidence concerning their own suspected facts, had abandoned or transferred the exclusive authority to manage and dispose of it, they did not correspond to the substantive persons subject to seizure who were the objects of the guarantee of participation rights.\\n\\n2) However, we cannot agree. The majority opinion understands the “substantive person subject to seizure,” the subject to whom the participation right is guaranteed, narrowly with a focus on the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search, and this does not accord with the purport and direction of the precedents. In addition, according to the majority opinion, by disregarding the constitutional demand to realize due process and the principle of warrant requirement in the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning electronic information, which is increasingly important to individuals and businesses in modern society, it allows an anti-constitutional result in which the fundamental rights concerning the secrecy and freedom of private life of the electronic-information manager and disposer, who is the substantive person subject to seizure, are infringed.\\n\\n3) In the above Supreme Court en banc decision 2016DO348 (hereinafter referred to as the “2016DO348 en banc decision”) and Supreme Court decision 2021DO11170, etc., the Supreme Court stated that the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the subject to whom participation rights are guaranteed in the seizure and search of electronic information, is a person who actually dominates and controls the digital storage medium concerned, retains and exercises exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in that digital storage medium, and can be evaluated as a person who is a substantive party to the seizure and search thereof. According to the legal principles and purport of such precedents, where, in addition to the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium, who is the direct party to the coercive disposition and the formal person subject to seizure, there separately exists an owner/manager, and there is a risk that his or her privacy and freedom, the right to informational self-determination, property rights, etc. concerning the electronic information may be infringed by the coercive disposition, that owner/manager must be regarded as the substantive person subject to seizure who is the object of the guarantee of participation rights. At this time, it is not required that the substantive person subject to seizure be the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search.\\n\\n4) Therefore, where a person who concealed evidence received instruction from the principal offender to conceal evidence and voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency, in the status of a suspect, the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender that the evidence concealer had possessed and kept, and where the principal offender can be assessed as having a substantive interest not to have his privacy and freedom, etc. infringed during the search, copying, and printing of the electronic information stored in that digital storage medium, participation rights must also be guaranteed to the principal offender, who has such substantive interest together with the evidence concealer as both the voluntary submitter and the suspect.\\n\\nOn that point, we differ from the majority opinion. The detailed grounds are as follows.\\n\\nb.
