From the perspective of participation rights, are the investigative procedure against the principal offender and the investigative procedure against the evidence concealer truly and substantively completely independent separate procedures, or is the latter substantially subsumed as part of the former? Since the principal offender and the evidence concealer each occupy the status of suspect while simultaneously and overlap-wise occupying the status of a third party with respect to the other party’s criminal suspicion, can each not become a subject to whom participation rights belong?\\n\\nThe structure of the principal offender and the evidence concealer contains a variety of issues for debate in determining the subject to whom participation rights belong. Focusing on these many special features, the dissenting opinion is the result of an effort to find answers to the above questions and, based on the precedents concerning the guarantee of participation rights, to determine the essence of participation rights and the core indicia of the subject to whom they belong. Based on the discussion developed by the dissenting opinion, I hope that this will provide an opportunity for active additional discussion on the scope and direction of participation-right guarantees in seizure and search procedures concerning digital storage media in an increasingly advanced information society.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I supplement the dissenting opinion."}

question: Among the explanations concerning personal liberty, which of the following are all incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents) (a) A statutory provision that allows the reduction or exemption of a sentence for a person who has served all or part of the sentence in a foreign country does not infringe personal liberty because it falls within the scope of the legislator's legislative discretion. (b) Unlike punishment, a security measure is based on the actor's future risk of recidivism, and since whether to pronounce a security measure is determined by assessing the risk of recidivism at the time of trial rather than at the time of the act, even if a certain security measure has a strong penal character and restricts personal liberty to a degree equivalent to deprivation of personal liberty, the principle of non-retroactivity of punishment does not apply. (c) Excluding foreigners detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act from the scope of detainees who may file a petition for relief under the Habeas Corpus Act deprives them of the opportunity to contest the legality of their detention under the Habeas Corpus Act and thus infringes personal liberty. (d) A statutory provision that states that a person who has received a deportation order may be detained in a detention facility until deportation becomes possible if the person cannot be immediately deported outside the Republic of Korea infringes personal liberty because it emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity. (e) The right to meet and communicate with counsel, in light of the constitutional provisions, is a fundamental right concerning personal liberty limited only to suspects or accused persons who have been arrested or detained, and it cannot be said that those provisions derive a right of counsel to meet and communicate with an arrested or detained suspect or accused person.

supporting_precedents: {"[2010HEONGA82]": "[Appendix] Related Provisions\\n\\nFormer Act on the Attachment, etc. of Electronic Devices for Location Tracking of Specific Criminal Offenders (as amended by Act No. 10257 on April 15, 2010, and before amendment by Act No. 11558 on December 18, 2012)\\n\\nArticle 1 (Purpose) The purpose of this Act is to protect the people from specific crimes by taking the additional measure of attaching to the body an electronic device that can track the offender’s movements and determine his or her location, for the prevention of recidivism by specific offenders and for their resocialization through the correction of their conduct.\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The definitions of terms used in this Act are as follows:\\n4. “Location-tracking electronic device (hereinafter referred to as ‘electronic device’)” means a series of mechanical equipment, as determined by Presidential Decree, that identifies location or detects a movement route by using the principle of emitting and tracking electromagnetic waves.\\n\\nArticle 4 (Scope of Application) When an attachment order is sentenced against a person under 19 years of age, an electronic device under this Act may not be attached until the person reaches 19 years of age.\\n\\nArticle 5 (Petition for an Attachment Order) ① A prosecutor may file with the court a petition for an order to attach an electronic device (hereinafter referred to as an “attachment order”) against a person who falls under any of the following subparagraphs and is deemed likely to commit a sexual violence offense again.\\n1. Where a person who has been sentenced to an actual term of imprisonment with labor for a sexual violence offense commits a sexual violence offense within 10 years after the execution thereof has been completed or exempted\\n2. Where a person who has previously been attached with an electronic device under this Act for a sexual violence offense again commits a sexual violence offense\\n3. Where a person has committed a sexual violence offense two or more times (including cases where a final and conclusive judgment of conviction has been rendered) and thus a habitual pattern is recognized\\n4. Where a sexual violence offense is committed against a person under 16 years of age\\n④ A petition for an attachment order under paragraphs 1 through 3 shall be filed by the time the appellate proceedings of a specific crime case in which an indictment has been instituted are concluded.\\n⑤ When the court deems it necessary to sentence an attachment order as a result of hearing a specific crime case in which an indictment has been instituted, it may require the prosecutor to file a petition for an attachment order.\\n⑥ No petition for an attachment order may be filed if 15 years have elapsed from the institution of an indictment without a final judgment in a specific crime case under paragraphs 1 through 3.\\n\\nArticle 6 (Investigation) ① When deemed necessary in order to file a petition for an attachment order, a prosecutor may request the head of the probation office (including its branch office; hereinafter the same shall apply) having jurisdiction over the residence of the suspect or the location of the prosecutor’s office to which the suspect belongs (including its branch office; hereinafter the same shall apply) to investigate matters necessary regarding the suspect, such as the motive for the crime, the relationship with the victim, mental state, and the risk of recidivism.\\n④ In filing a petition for an attachment order, the prosecutor shall, if necessary, refer to the results of a psychiatric evaluation of the suspect or other expert diagnosis.\\n\\nArticle 9 (Judgment on Attachment Order, etc.) ① When the court deems a petition for an attachment order to be well-founded, it shall sentence an attachment order by judgment, setting the attachment period within the following periods. Provided, however, that where a specific crime is committed against a person under 13 years of age, the lower limit of the attachment period shall be twice the lower limit of the attachment period under the following subparagraphs.\\n1. Specific crimes for which the upper limit of the statutory punishment is death or life imprisonment: not less than 10 years and not more than 30 years\\n2. Specific crimes for which the lower limit of the term of imprisonment among the statutory punishments is fixed-term imprisonment of not less than 3 years (excluding specific crimes falling under subparagraph 1): not less than 3 years and not more than 20 years\\n3. Specific crimes for which the lower limit of the term of imprisonment among the statutory punishments is fixed-term imprisonment of less than 3 years (excluding specific crimes falling under subparagraph 1 or 2): not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years\\n③ A person sentenced to an attachment order shall be subject to probation under the Act on Probation, etc. during the attachment period.\\n④ The court shall dismiss a petition for an attachment order by judgment when it falls under any of the following subparagraphs:\\n1. When the petition for an attachment order is deemed to be without merit\\n2. When a judgment or decision of acquittal (excluding cases where medical treatment and custody is sentenced on the ground of mental incapacity), extinguishment of prosecution, or dismissal of prosecution is rendered in a specific crime case\\n3. When a fine is imposed in a specific crime case\\n4. When a suspended sentence or suspension of execution is imposed in a specific crime case (excluding cases where attachment of an electronic device is ordered pursuant to Article 28(1))\\n⑤ A judgment in a case involving a petition for an attachment order shall be rendered simultaneously with the judgment in the specific crime case.\\n⑦ The pronouncement of an attachment order shall not be considered favorably in sentencing for the specific crime case.\\n\\nArticle 9-2 (Compliance Requirements) ① When sentencing an attachment order pursuant to Article 9(1), the court may, within the scope of the attachment period, set a compliance period and impose one or more of the following compliance requirements. Provided, however, that the compliance requirement under subparagraph 4 shall have its period set within the scope of 500 hours.\\n1. Restriction on going out during nighttime or at specific times\\n2. Prohibition of entry into specific areas or places\\n2-2. Restriction on residential areas\\n3. Prohibition of approach to specific persons, such as victims\\n4. Completion of a specific crime treatment program\\n5. Other matters necessary for the prevention of recidivism and the correction of conduct of a person sentenced to an attachment order\\n\\nArticle 14-2 (Extension, etc. of Attachment Period) ① If a person subject to attachment falls under any of the following subparagraphs, the court may, upon a petition by a prosecutor filed at the request of the head of the probation office, extend the attachment period within the limit of 1 year or make a decision to add or modify the compliance requirements under Article 9-2(1).\\n1. Where a compliance requirement under Article 32 of the Act on Probation, etc. has been violated without justifiable grounds\\n2. Where the report has not been made in violation of Article 14(2) without justifiable grounds\\n3. Where, in violation of Article 14(3), the person moved residence, traveled within the country, or departed from the country without permission, or obtained permission by false means, without justifiable grounds\\n② Even where there is a change in circumstances other than those prescribed in the subparagraphs of paragraph 1, the court may, if it deems there to be reasonable grounds, make a decision to add, modify, or delete the compliance requirements under Article 9-2(1) upon a petition by a prosecutor filed at the request of the head of the probation office.\\n\\nArticle 16 (Preservation, Use, Destruction, etc. of Received Data) ① The head of the probation office shall receive the electromagnetic waves emitted from the electronic device of a person subject to attachment and preserve the data therefrom (hereinafter referred to as “received data”).\\n② The received data may not be inspected, queried, or disclosed except in the following cases:\\n1. Where used as investigation or trial materials concerning a suspicion of a specific crime committed by the person subject to attachment\\n2. Where used by a probation officer for the purpose of guidance and assistance\\n3. Where used for the review of the provisional suspension of an attachment order and its revocation by the Probation Review Committee under Article 5 of the Act on Probation, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Review Committee”)\\n④ When a prosecutor or judicial police officer inspects or queries the received data, they shall present a warrant of seizure and search issued by a judge.\\n⑤ The head of the probation office shall destroy the received data when it falls under any of the following subparagraphs:\\n1. {"[2012HEONMA686]": "[Annex] Relevant Provisions\\n\\nAct on the Protection of Personal Liberty (Enacted by Act No. 8724 on 2007. 12. 21.)\\nArticle 1 (Purpose) The purpose of this Act is to protect the fundamental rights of the people guaranteed by the Constitution by establishing relief procedures for individuals whose personal liberty is unjustly restricted due to an unlawful administrative disposition or commitment to a facility by a private person.\\n\\nAct on the Protection of Personal Liberty (Amended by Act No. 10364 on 2010. 6. 10.)\\nArticle 3 (Petition for Relief) When detention of a detainee has commenced unlawfully or, after lawful detention, the ground therefor has ceased to exist but the person is still being detained, the detainee, his or her statutory representative, guardian, spouse, lineal relative, sibling, cohabitant, employer, or person working at the detention facility (hereinafter referred to as “petitioner for relief”) may petition the court for relief as prescribed by this Act. Provided, that where another Act provides a relief procedure, it must be clearly impossible to obtain relief under that Act within a reasonable period.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (Amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)\\nArticle 46 (Persons Subject to Deportation) ① The head of a local immigration office or foreigners' office may deport from the Republic of Korea any foreigner who falls under any of the following items in accordance with the procedures prescribed in this Chapter.\\n(Items omitted)\\nArticle 51 (Detention) ① An immigration control officer may detain a foreigner by obtaining a detention order from the head of a local immigration office or foreigners' office if there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the foreigner falls under any of the items of paragraph 1 of Article 46 and if there is a risk of flight.\\n③ In an urgent case where there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the foreigner falls under any of the items of paragraph 1 of Article 46 and there is a risk of flight or a possibility of flight, and there is no time to obtain a detention order from the head of a local immigration office or foreigners' office, the immigration control officer may detain the foreigner urgently by informing the person of the reason therefor.\\nArticle 52 (Period and Place of Detention) ① The period of detention for examining and determining whether a foreigner detained under Article 51 is subject to deportation shall be within 10 days. Provided, that where there is an unavoidable reason, the period may be extended only once within the extent not exceeding 10 days with the permission of the head of a local immigration office or foreigners' office.\\nArticle 55 (Objection to Detention) ① A person detained pursuant to a detention order or his or her statutory representative, etc. may file an objection to detention with the Minister of Justice through the head of a local immigration office or foreigners' office.\\n② Upon receiving an objection under paragraph 1, the Minister of Justice shall, without delay, examine the relevant documents and, if the objection is found to be without merit, dismiss it by decision, and if it is found to be well-founded, order, by decision, release from detention of the detained person.\\n③ Before making a decision under paragraph 2, the Minister of Justice may, if necessary, hear the statements of persons concerned.\\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release from Detention of a Person Who Has Received a Deportation Order) ① If the head of a local immigration office or foreigners' office cannot immediately repatriate a person who has received a deportation order outside the {"[2013HEONMA129]": "The Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint case seeking revocation of the non-prosecution disposition of suspension of indictment, which the Respondent determined on 2012. 11. 30. in relation to the assault case No. 2012HYEONGJE15580 at the Pohang Branch Office of the Daegu District Prosecutors’ Office, alleging that it infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights, including the constitutionally guaranteed right to equality.\\n\\nHowever, even upon close examination of the record of this case, it does not appear that the Respondent conducted an investigation with respect to the above case that was manifestly contrary to equity, or that there was any serious error in the interpretation of the Constitution, application of law, or evaluation of evidence that affected the decision to issue the non-prosecution disposition, and there is otherwise no material from which to conclude that the Respondent’s disposition in this case is an arbitrary disposition to such an extent that the Constitutional Court would be concerned; therefore, it cannot be said that the fundamental rights asserted by the Petitioner were infringed thereby.\\n\\nAccordingly, since the petition for adjudication in this case is without merit, it is decided to dismiss it, and the decision is made as stated in the Order, by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating.\\n\\n2013. 7. 25."}

{"[2015HEONMA1204]": "1. Summary of the Case  \\nA. Suspect Yun XX-hyeon was arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant at around 19:00 on 2015. 10. 5., and a detention warrant was sought. The Claimant, an attorney, was entrusted by the family of the above suspect and, after inquiring by telephone at around 17:00 on 2015. 10. 6. to the Respondent prosecutor of the XX District Prosecutors’ Office who was investigating the case (hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent Prosecutor”) whether a counsel visitation was possible, visited the prosecutor’s office room No. XX at the XX District Prosecutors’ Office at around 19:00 on the same day, carrying a visitation application, and applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for a counsel visitation.  \\nB. The Respondent correctional officer of the XX Detention Center who was in charge of escorting the above suspect (hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent Correctional Officer”) received custody of the above suspect from the Respondent Prosecutor’s office at around 17:00 on the same day and kept him waiting in the detention room within the Prosecutors’ Office, and then, at around 19:10 on the same day, upon receiving a request from the Respondent Prosecutor to summon the suspect for night questioning, brought the above suspect into the prosecutor’s office.  \\nC. The Respondent Prosecutor informed the Respondent Correctional Officer that the Claimant had made an application for visitation, and the Respondent Correctional Officer, after inquiring with the official in charge of counsel visitation at the XX Detention Center regarding the procedures for handling it, informed the Claimant that, pursuant to Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, counsel visitation could not be permitted because the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials (“09:00 to 18:00”) had elapsed.  \\nD. Thereafter, the Respondent Prosecutor took no further action regarding the Claimant’s application for visitation, and the Claimant remained in the prosecutor’s office but ultimately left without having visited the above suspect. After the Claimant left, the Respondent Prosecutor continued questioning the above suspect, and the Claimant was not retained as counsel for the above suspect.  \\nE. The Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint on 2015. 12. 28., alleging that the acts of the Respondents in denying the application for counsel visitation, and Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, which the Respondent Correctional Officer relied upon as the legal basis therefor, infringed his fundamental rights.  \\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\nThe subject matter of this case is whether: ① the acts of the Respondents in failing to take measures to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect Yun XX-hyeon at prosecutor’s office room No. XX of the XX District Prosecutors’ Office at around 19:00 on 2015. 10. 6. (hereinafter, the Respondent Prosecutor’s denial of visitation shall be referred to as the “Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case,” the Respondent Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation shall be referred to as the “Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case,” and these acts collectively as the “denial of visitation in this case”), and ② Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (wholly amended by Presidential Decree No. 21095 on 2008. 10. 29.; hereinafter referred to as the “Visitation Hours Provision in this case”) infringe the Claimant’s fundamental rights (hereinafter, the “Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners” shall be referred to as the “Execution of Sentences Act”).  \\nThe provision subject to adjudication and related provisions are as follows:  \\n\\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]  \\nEnforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (wholly amended by Presidential Decree No. 21095 on 2008. 10. 29.)  \\nArticle 58 (Visitation) (1) Visitation by a prisoner shall take place every day (excluding public holidays and days designated by the Minister of Justice) within working hours pursuant to Article 9 of the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials.  \\n\\n[Related Provisions]  \\nCriminal Procedure Act (enacted by Act No. 341 on 1954. 9. 23.)  \\nArticle 34 (Visitation, Communication, and Medical Treatment with Defendant or Suspect) A defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint and may exchange documents or articles with him or her, and may have a physician provide treatment.  \\n\\nCriminal Procedure Act (amended by Act No. 8496 on 2007. 6. 1.)  \\nArticle 243-2 (Participation of Defense Counsel, etc.) (1) A prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground.  \\n(2) to (5) Omitted  \\n\\nAct on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (wholly amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21.)  \\nArticle 3 (Scope of Application) This Act applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required.  \\n\\nEnforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (amended by Presidential Decree No. 25397 on 2014. 6. 25.)  \\nArticle 58 (Visitation) (1) Omitted  \\n(2) Except for untried prisoners who visit with defense counsel (including persons intending to become defense counsel; the same shall apply hereinafter), the visitation time for prisoners shall be limited to not more than 30 minutes per visit.  \\n(3) The number of visits by prisoners shall be four times per month.  \\n(4) Visitation by prisoners shall take place in a place equipped with contact-blocking facilities; provided, however, that this shall not apply in any of the following cases:  \\n1. Where an untried prisoner (including a convicted prisoner under investigation or trial in a criminal case and a person sentenced to death whose sentence has become final and conclusive) visits with defense counsel  \\n2. Where a prisoner visits with an attorney who is a representative in a litigation case, and where there is no risk of undermining the safety or order of the correctional institution  \\n(5) Except for the matters prescribed in the Act and this Decree, necessary matters concerning the number, time, place, etc. of visits by prisoners other than convicted prisoners, persons sentenced to death, and untried prisoners shall be determined by the Minister of Justice.  \\n(6) If necessary in order to perform affairs concerning the visitation of prisoners by persons outside the correctional institution, the warden may process data containing a resident registration number, passport number, driver’s license number, or alien registration number pursuant to Article 19 of the Enforcement Decree of the Personal Information Protection Act.  \\n\\nRegulations on the Service of National Public Officials (amended by Presidential Decree No. 23010 on 2011. 7. 4.)  \\nArticle 9 (Working Hours, etc.) (1) The weekly working hours of public officials shall be 40 hours excluding lunch time, and Saturdays shall, in principle, be days off.  \\n(2) The daily working hours of public officials shall be from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and lunch time shall be from 12:00 noon to 1:00 p.m.; provided, however, that if the head of an administrative agency deems it necessary in consideration of the nature of the duties, the region, or the special characteristics of the institution, he or she may set lunch time differently within the range of one hour.  \\n(3), (4) Omitted  \\n\\n3. The Claimant’s Arguments  \\nA. The Claimant was unable to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon due to the Respondents’ denial of visitation in this case, and as a result, lost the opportunity to assist the above suspect, and direct disadvantage was caused to the exercise of the above suspect’s right of defense. The denial of visitation in this case infringed not only the above suspect’s right of access and communication with counsel, but also the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right of access and communication with counsel.  \\nB. Since a detention warrant is sought within 48 hours after a suspect is arrested, the right of a suspect to immediately receive assistance from counsel must be guaranteed during that period as well, and considering that the period immediately before the warrant review hearing is the time when the assistance of counsel is most needed, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which limits counsel visitation hours to public officials’ working hours, violates the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction and infringes the Claimant’s right of access and communication with counsel.  \\nMoreover, where an arrested suspect is housed in a police detention cell, Article 7(1) of the Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc. and Article 37(1) of the Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects apply, so that counsel visitation is permitted even outside the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials. Accordingly, because an unreasonable discrimination arises in the exercise of defense counsel’s right of access and communication depending on whether the suspect is confined in a detention center or housed in a detention cell, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case infringes the Claimant’s right to equality.  \\n\\n4. The Visitation and Communication System between Suspects/Defendants and Defense Counsel  \\nA. Constitutional Basis  \\nThe main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that “any person who is arrested or detained shall have the right to prompt assistance of counsel.” The Constitutional Court has held: “Even in the case of a suspect who is not detained, the right to the assistance of counsel is a natural content recognized under the constitutional principles of a rule-of-law state and due process contained in our Constitution, and Article 12(4) of the Constitution also separately and expressly provides for this in order to particularly emphasize the importance of the right to the assistance of counsel for persons under physical restraint.” (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138). In this manner, a suspect or defendant (hereinafter, “suspect or defendant” shall be referred to as “suspect, etc.”) is recognized as having the right to the assistance of counsel regardless of whether he or she is arrested or detained.  \\nIn order for a suspect, etc. to sufficiently exercise the right of defense, he or she must be able to consult sufficiently on all factual and legal issues through visitation and communication with defense counsel or a “person who intends to become defense counsel” (hereinafter, defense counsel or a “person who intends to become defense counsel” shall be referred to as “defense counsel, etc.”). With respect to visitation and communication between a suspect, etc. and defense counsel, etc., matters are provided in Article 34 and Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 84(1) and (2), and Article 85 of the Execution of Sentences Act, etc., and these provisions concretize the right to the assistance of counsel guaranteed by the Constitution as above. Among them, Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that a “person who intends to become defense counsel” also has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc.  \\n\\nB. Meaning of “Under Physical Restraint” and “Person Who Intends to Become Defense Counsel”  \\n(1) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint.” Here, “a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint” means not only a suspect, etc. detained pursuant to a detention warrant, but also a suspect, etc. arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant or arrested by emergency arrest or as a person caught in flagrante delicto, and it should be understood to presuppose deprivation of physical liberty in whatever form.  \\n(2) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that not only defense counsel but also a “person who intends to become defense counsel” has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc. Here, “a person who intends to become defense counsel” should be understood to include not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment of defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own. It is difficult to say that, in a state where physical liberty is suppressed and communication with the outside is severed, a suspect, etc. can decide and carry through his or her own intention without being conscious of investigative authorities, and if the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” were permitted only when the suspect, etc. expressly indicates an intention to receive the assistance of counsel, this could result in the existence of the right of visitation and communication being substantially determined by the will of the investigative authorities.  \\nThe Supreme Court, in a case where an attorney not appointed as defense counsel expressed an intention to exercise the right of visitation and communication with respect to a suspect arrested, but it was not confirmed what the suspect’s intention was, held that “even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a ‘defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel’ as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act” (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.).  \\n\\nC. Subject Authorized to Determine Whether to Permit Visitation  \\nThe Execution of Sentences Act aims to promote the correction and rehabilitation of convicted prisoners and their sound return to society, and to prescribe matters necessary concerning the treatment and rights of prisoners and the operation of correctional institutions (Article 1). Accordingly, Part II of the Execution of Sentences Act regulates the treatment of prisoners, and matters concerning the treatment of prisoners, such as confinement of prisoners, visitation, exchange of correspondence and telephone communication, maintenance of safety and order, discipline and rewards/punishments, and special protection for female prisoners and pregnant women, are vested in the authority of the heads of prisons and detention centers. Meanwhile, the Execution of Sentences Act is a statute that applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required (Article 3). In light of the legislative purpose, regulatory content, scope of application, etc. of the Execution of Sentences Act, when there is an application for visitation by a prisoner, this concerns a matter of treatment of prisoners; therefore, if the place is a space where the guarding and control of prisoners by correctional officers is required, it is in principle the warden of the prison or detention center, or the correctional officer entrusted by such warden, who determines whether to permit it.  \\nHowever, Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground,” thereby establishing a special provision to the above principle and making the prosecutor or judicial police officer determine whether to permit such visitation when there is an application for visitation by defense counsel during the interrogation of a suspect.  \\nArticle 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act, however, regulates the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel and the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” without making any distinction between them; therefore, even where a “person who intends to become defense counsel” applies for visitation pursuant to Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act during the interrogation of a suspect, the subject who determines whether to permit it should also be the prosecutor or judicial police officer, and such interpretation is consistent with the content of Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act.  \\n\\n5. Determination on Whether the Requirements for Adjudication Are Satisfied  \\nA. Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case  \\n(1) Existence of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case  \\nA constitutional complaint may be filed when fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution are infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power (Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act); therefore, in order to file a constitutional complaint, there must first be a fact of “exercise or non-exercise of public power” that caused the infringement of fundamental rights, and where there is no fact at all of exercise or non-exercise of public power that is subject to constitutional complaint, the petition is unlawful (see Constitutional Court 2004. 11. 25. 2004HEONMA178; Constitutional Court 2014. 3. 31. 2014HEONMA239).  \\nHere, as seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor merely informed the correctional officer of the fact that the Claimant had applied for visitation, and even though the Claimant continued to stay in the prosecutor’s office in order to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon after the correctional officer in charge denied visitation between the Claimant and the suspect, the Respondent Prosecutor did not take measures such as allowing the visitation to take place in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room.  \\nSince the Respondent Prosecutor’s failure to take any further measures after the correctional officer’s notice of denial of visitation can be assessed as substantially equivalent to denying the Claimant’s application for visitation (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181; Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.), the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case exists as an exercise of public power subject to a constitutional complaint.  \\n(2) Whether the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized - Whether the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” can be regarded as a constitutional fundamental right  \\n(a) Organization of the issue  \\nBecause the Claimant was not appointed as defense counsel for suspect Yun XX-hyeon, with respect to the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, only whether the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” was infringed is at issue.  \\nA constitutional complaint is a system by which a “person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed” petitions the Constitutional Court for adjudication in order to obtain relief from that infringement; therefore, for the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case to be lawful, the right allegedly infringed by the Claimant, namely the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” must not only be recognized as a statutory right but must further be recognized as a constitutional fundamental right.  \\n(b) Constitutional Court precedents  \\nThe Constitutional Court, in its decision rendered on 2003. 3. 27., 2000HEONMA474, for the first time recognized the core part of the right to assistance of counsel as a constitutional fundamental right, and also took the same position in its decision 2016HEONMA503 rendered on 2017. 11. 30.; the gist of the decision 2016HEONMA503 is as follows:  \\n“[T]he right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can be concretely realized in the mutual relationship between them and defense counsel. The right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can become solid through the guarantee of the right of defense counsel to assist them, whereas if the right of defense counsel is not guaranteed, it may become a mere empty shell. The core part of the right of defense counsel to assist a suspect or defendant, without which it becomes a dead letter for them to receive the assistance of counsel, stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel. Therefore, in order to practically secure the right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect and defendant must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.”  \\n(c) Determination  \\n1) Article 27(4) of the Constitution provides that “a criminal defendant shall be presumed innocent until a conviction becomes final and conclusive,” thereby declaring the principle of presumption of innocence. This principle of presumption of innocence originates from the constitutional ideal that has the respect for human dignity as its ultimate goal and seeks to protect the status of suspects, etc., who are in an unfavorable position, so that their disadvantages in criminal proceedings are limited to the minimum necessary. Detention is a system recognized only when there are especially unavoidable reasons with respect to suspects, etc., but the detention system is susceptible to abuse by investigative or trial authorities merely for the convenience of investigation or trial, and while in a detained state, the right to remain silent prescribed in Article 12(2) of the Constitution may not be effectively guaranteed. Accordingly, in order to remove the various harms arising from the situation of physical restraint with respect to suspects, etc. who are presumed innocent and to ensure that detention is not improperly used beyond its original purpose, the main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution guarantees as a fundamental right the right of a person under physical restraint to receive the assistance of counsel as stated above (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21. 92HEONMA144).  \\nThe reason for and necessity of recognizing, as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a detained suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel applies equally to arrested suspects, etc.  \\n2) The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution clearly provides that, upon being arrested or detained, a person has the right to prompt assistance of counsel, thereby making clear that suspects, etc. have the right to receive the assistance of counsel even before counsel is appointed. The right of a suspect, etc. who has not yet appointed defense counsel to receive the assistance of counsel is concretized through the appointment of defense counsel; the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel is the starting point and the most basic component of the right to receive the assistance of counsel, and is a right that cannot even be limited by law (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138). Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication with a “person who intends to become defense counsel” that a suspect, etc. has for purposes of appointing defense counsel must also be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.  \\n3) In order for a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel, a relationship of trust must be formed between the suspect, etc. and the “person who intends to become defense counsel,” and for this purpose, sufficient consultation must be conducted through visitation and communication with the “person who intends to become defense counsel.” In this way, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is intended to solidify the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel and receive assistance from that counsel; if it is not guaranteed, the right of the suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from defense counsel through the appointment of counsel will inevitably become meaningless. Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is a core part for assisting a suspect, etc., and stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect, etc. to visit and communicate with a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”  \\n4) Therefore, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” as a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., must also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right in order to practically secure the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of a “person who intends to become defense counsel.” Accordingly, this part of the petition seeking a constitutional determination on the ground that the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case infringed the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right, namely the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” also satisfies the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.  \\n(3) Whether an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is recognized  \\nA constitutional complaint must be filed only after all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act); however, where the claimant failed to take a prior remedy procedure due to a mistake based on justifiable grounds not attributable to his or her disadvantage, or where there is little possibility that the right will be remedied through the prior remedy procedure, or where it is objectively uncertain whether the right-concretization procedure is permitted, making it impossible to expect performance of the prior remedy procedure, it is recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity (see Constitutional Court 1989. 9. 4. 88HEONMA22; Constitutional Court 2008. 5. 29. 2007HEONMA712, etc.).  \\nHowever, since the subject who finally determines the Claimant’s application for visitation with suspect Yun XX-hyeon is the Respondent Prosecutor, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case falls under “dispositions concerning detention by a prosecutor and dispositions concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2” that are subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without first filing a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act.  \\nThe Supreme Court, however, has held that even a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of a denial of visitation by an investigative agency must have a legal interest, and that where the purpose sought to be achieved through the quasi-appeal during the pendency of the case has already been achieved or where the interest has been lost due to the lapse of time or other circumstances, the quasi-appeal becomes unlawful for lack of interest (see Supreme Court Decision 98MO121 dated 1999. 6. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2014MO686 dated 2014. 4. 15.), yet has not presented specific criteria therefor. Accordingly, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, which ended on the day of the incident, it is objectively uncertain whether the court would deem legal interest to be lacking or would proceed to a merits determination, and thus this is a case where it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure.  \\nAccordingly, this part of the petition should be recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity.  \\n(4) Sub-conclusion  \\nAs above, the petition concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case targets an exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint, the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized, an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is also recognized, and all other requirements for lawfulness are satisfied; thus, it is lawful.  \\n\\nB. The Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case  \\nArticle 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act limits the subject matter of constitutional complaints to acts of public power by providing that a person whose fundamental rights have been infringed by the “exercise or non-exercise of public power” may file a constitutional complaint.  \\nAccording to the record, at the time of the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case, the Respondent Prosecutor handed over the physical custody of suspect Yun XX-hyeon to the Respondent Correctional Officer so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but it is recognized that an interrogation of the suspect was scheduled even at night, and thus it may be said that the interrogation of the above suspect was ongoing. In addition, the Claimant at that time applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for counsel visitation.  \\nAs seen above, where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect, the prosecutor or judicial police officer must determine whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that a correctional officer who escorted the suspect to the investigative agency is not vested with the authority to permit or restrict such visitation.  \\nArticle 118 of the “Operational Guidelines on the Management of Prisoners” (Ministerial Instruction of the Ministry of Justice No. 1077, 2015. 1. 13.), which was in force at the time of this case, provided that where there is an application for defense counsel visitation with a prisoner outside the institution who is being escorted out, the escorting correctional officer is to conduct the visitation between the escorted prisoner and defense counsel through certain procedures, such as obtaining permission from the warden. However, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center, or a correctional officer delegated by them, determines whether to permit it, and cannot be said to apply to cases, such as this one, where an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. is made during the interrogation of a suspect, and the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it.  \\nUltimately, in this case, because it cannot be said that the Respondent Correctional Officer had the authority to determine whether to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect Yun XX-hyeon, the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case does not constitute an “exercise of public power” that is made subject to constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act.  \\n\\nC. The Visitation Hours Provision in this case  \\nThe main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that “a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may ... file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court,” which means that only a person whose own fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been currently and directly infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint. Therefore, if the exercise of public power has no effect whatsoever on the legal status of the person seeking to file a constitutional complaint, then there is no possibility or danger of infringement of fundamental rights in the first place, and filing a constitutional complaint against such exercise of public power is not permitted (see Constitutional Court 1999. 5. 27. 97HEONMA368; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2012HEONMA630, etc.).  \\nThe Visitation Hours Provision in this case is a provision that applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and it cannot be said to apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that the denial or restriction of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect cannot be based on that provision. In practice as well, the police and prosecutors impose no time restrictions whatsoever on visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect [see Article 7 of the “Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc.” (Korean National Police Agency Instruction No. 882, 2018. 8. 13.), Article 37(2) of the “Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects” (Korean National Police Agency Instruction No. 883, 2018. 8. 13.), Article 2(6) and Article 8 of the “Guidelines on the Operation of Defense Counsel Participation in Suspect Interrogation” (Korean Supreme Prosecutors’ Office guidelines, amended 2017. 12. 4.), and Article 230 of the “Guidelines on Defense Counsel Visitation and Communication with Suspects” (Seoul Central District Prosecutors’ Office Rule No. 230, 2017. 8. 30.)].  \\nAs seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation with suspect Yun XX-hyeon, against whom interrogation was continuing, and therefore the Visitation Hours Provision in this case does not apply here, nor did the Respondent Prosecutor at the time deny the above visitation application by applying that provision. Accordingly, this part of the petition lacks self-relatedness for purposes of the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.  \\n\\n6. Determination on Whether the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in this Case Infringed Fundamental Rights  \\nA. Whether the Claimant’s right of access and communication was restricted  \\nAs seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation and remained in the prosecutor’s office, but due to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ultimately could not visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon and left the prosecutor’s office; accordingly, it is reasonable to view the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as having restricted the Claimant’s right of access and communication with the above suspect.  \\nHowever, according to the record, suspect Yun XX-hyeon did not raise an objection to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, visited with another attorney twice the following day, and that attorney personally appeared and responded at the pre-detention suspect interrogation hearing. Nevertheless, even if the suspect did not indicate an intention to visit and communicate with a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” if a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, visitation with the suspect must be permitted (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.); moreover, the Claimant had even been entrusted by suspect Yun XX-hyeon’s family and intended to visit the suspect, so at the time of the visitation application there was sufficient possibility that the Claimant would become defense counsel for the above suspect; and the person claiming infringement of fundamental rights caused by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is not suspect Yun XX-hyeon but the Claimant. In light of these circumstances, the facts recognized above are not factors to be considered in determining whether the Claimant’s fundamental rights were infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case.  \\n\\nB. Whether the Claimant’s visitation application was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication  \\nBecause the right of access and communication of defense counsel, etc. must be exercised within the limits that do not infringe the original purpose of the physical restraint system, attempts by defense counsel, etc. to visit a suspect, etc. beyond the limits that can realistically be guaranteed in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances do not constitute a proper exercise of the right of access and communication and cannot be permitted (see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO657 dated 2007. 1. 31.; Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.).  \\nHowever, in this case, since suspect Yun XX-hyeon was scheduled to continue being interrogated at night on that day, it appears that measures could have been taken to permit visitation and communication between the Claimant and the above suspect in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room before the interrogation, and thus in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances at the time of the visitation application, no specific circumstances are discernible showing that the Claimant, who intended to become defense counsel, attempted to abuse the exercise of visitation and communication with the suspect beyond the limits realistically guaranteeable or beyond the original purpose of the physical restraint system.  \\nAccordingly, the Claimant’s visitation application must be deemed to have been exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”  \\n\\nC. Whether it was based on the Constitution or statutes  \\n(1) In the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc., “free visitation,” that is, “visitation in which confidentiality regarding the content of the conversation is fully guaranteed and the parties may converse freely without any restriction, influence, pressure, or improper interference,” is not of a nature that can be restricted under any pretext (see Constitutional Court 1992. 1. 28. 91HEONMA111). However, this means only that such is the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc.; it does not mean that no restriction whatsoever may be imposed on visitation itself with defense counsel, etc. The right to the assistance of counsel and the right of visitation and communication with counsel, which is one component thereof, may, like all other constitutional fundamental rights, be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare (see Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26. 2009HEONMA341; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2015HEONMA243), and the same shall apply to the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”  \\n(2) As seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor temporarily handed over the physical custody of suspect Yun XX-hyeon to the correctional officer in charge so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but since a night interrogation of the above suspect was planned, it may be said that the investigation or interrogation of the above suspect was continuing.  \\nAlthough the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel, etc. may be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law, neither the Constitution nor laws such as the Criminal Procedure Act contain a provision allowing restriction or refusal where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect. This is to ensure, in light of the importance of the right of access and communication held by a suspect, etc., that the right of access and communication held by defense counsel, etc. is also guaranteed to the maximum extent.  \\nThe Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which is delegated by Article 41(4) of the Execution of Sentences Act, restricts visitation and communication between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. by limiting visitation by prisoners to working hours pursuant to the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials; however, as seen above, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and does not apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it, and thus it must be said that visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. cannot be denied or restricted on the basis of that provision.  \\nAccordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes.  \\n\\nD. Sub-conclusion  \\nUltimately, the Claimant’s visitation application concerning suspect Yun XX-hyeon was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” and furthermore the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes; therefore, it infringed the Claimant’s right of access and communication.  \\n\\n7. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case should be found unconstitutional and revoked; however, since the denial of visitation has already ended, we shall, for declaratory purposes and to prevent repetition of the same or similar infringement of fundamental rights, make a determination that it is unconstitutional. The petition regarding the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case and the Visitation Hours Provision in this case is unlawful in its entirety and shall therefore be dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the order. The concurrence of the remaining participating Justices was reached, except for the dissenting opinion by Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as stated in Section 8 below.  \\n\\n8. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok on the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in this Case  \\nWe are of the view that the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is also unlawful and should be dismissed, and we state our opinion as follows.  \\n\\nA. Possibility of Infringement of Fundamental Rights  \\n(1) A constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only by a person whose “fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution” have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power. Therefore, a constitutional complaint alleging infringement of a right based merely on statute, rather than on a constitutional fundamental right, is unlawful.  \\n(2) In the Constitutional Court’s decision 2012HEONMA610 rendered on 2015. 7. 30., three Justices presented the following separate opinion:  \\n“Guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel means sufficiently and substantively guaranteeing the activities of defense counsel aimed at assisting the person arrested, etc. Thus, the Criminal Procedure Act recognizes, as concrete means for substantively guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel, the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel (Article 34), defense counsel’s right to inspect and copy investigative and litigation records (Articles 35 and 266-3), and defense counsel’s right to participate in various procedures such as investigation and trial (Articles 121, 163, 243-2, etc.).  \\nThe reason special rights such as the right to inspect and copy records or the right of visitation and communication are recognized for defense counsel is that they all originate from the purpose of faithfully guaranteeing the right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel, and it cannot be viewed as a right recognized in order to guarantee defense counsel’s own fundamental rights. Defense counsel exercises the ‘right to assist as defense counsel’ recognized in the Criminal Procedure Act for the benefit of the person arrested, etc. as an assistant to the person arrested, etc., not for the protection of his or her own fundamental rights. Therefore, the ‘right to assist as defense counsel’ should be viewed as a statutory right recognized as a result of the legislator concretely shaping it through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act in order to faithfully guarantee the constitutional fundamental right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel.  \\nFrom this perspective, the Constitutional Court has long held that the constitutional right of visitation and communication with defense counsel is a fundamental right concerning personal liberty limited only to suspects and defendants, and that defense counsel’s own right of visitation and communication with a suspect or defendant cannot be regarded as a constitutional right, but is merely a right guaranteed only by Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act; accordingly, it dismissed a constitutional complaint filed by defense counsel on the ground that there was no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181).”  \\nFor the reasons stated in the above separate opinion, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is also merely a statutory right specifically formed through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act as an indirect and incidental effect arising from recognizing the “right to receive the assistance of counsel” of a person arrested, etc. as a fundamental right, and cannot be viewed as an “independent fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.”  \\n(3) The majority opinion relies on the Court’s majority opinions in Constitutional Court 2000HEONMA474 decided on 2003. 3. 27. and Constitutional Court 2016HEONMA503 decided on 2017. 11. 30., which held that “in order for the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel to be practically secured, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right,” and reasons that the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” should also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right because it is a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., and if it is not guaranteed, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless.  \\nIt is true that through visitation counsel can grasp the status of a detained suspect, etc. and devise appropriate responses accordingly, explain the meaning of the facts of suspicion or the charges, consult about countermeasures by hearing the opinions of the suspect, etc. thereon, and provide comfort to a suspect, etc. who is in a legally and psychologically anxious state, thereby restoring psychological stability and enabling the suspect, etc. to effectively exercise the right of defense within the criminal procedure (see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992). It is also true that through visitation and communication between a “person who intends to become defense counsel” and a suspect, etc., such advice, consultation, and comfort to the suspect, etc. are possible to some extent. However, when a “person who intends to become defense counsel” visits and communicates with a suspect, etc., because the point at which it is confirmed whether the suspect, etc. will actually retain the attorney and receive assistance from him or her has not yet been reached, the main purpose may be seen as the person’s own retention activities rather than assistance to the suspect, etc.; and the disadvantage suffered by the “person who intends to become defense counsel” due to inability to visit the suspect, etc., namely the disadvantage resulting from failure to obtain a criminal case retention, is merely an indirect, factual, and economic interest (see Constitutional Court 2004. 4. 29. 2002HEONMA756).  \\nMeanwhile, as stated by the majority opinion, it is reasonable to view not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment as defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own, as falling within the meaning of “a person who intends to become defense counsel,” and the Supreme Court has also held that “even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a ‘defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel’ as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act” (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.). If the meaning of “a person who intends to become defense counsel” is interpreted as above, the right of visitation and communication of such a person should be viewed as a right recognized to that person regardless of the suspect’s or defendant’s will, at the stage before assisting the suspect, etc.  \\nIn light of the above circumstances, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” cannot be viewed as standing in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the right of a suspect, etc. to receive assistance, and it cannot be concluded that, unless it is elevated and guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless. Therefore, even if one adopts the view that the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist a suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right, there is no need, as in the majority opinion, to understand the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” as well as a constitutional fundamental right.  \\n(4) Ultimately, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be regarded as a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution; accordingly, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint against the denial of visitation is unlawful because there is no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.  \\n\\nB. Subsidiarity  \\n(1) Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “if there is an objection to a disposition concerning detention, seizure, or the return of seized articles made by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, or to a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2, a petition may be filed with the court having jurisdiction over the place where the duties are performed, or with the court corresponding to the prosecutor’s public prosecutors’ office to which the prosecutor belongs, for revocation or alteration of the disposition.”  \\nAn act by an investigative agency denying visitation between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. falls under a “disposition concerning detention” or a “disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc.” subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore not only the suspect or defense counsel but also a “person who intends to become defense counsel” may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal pursuant to that provision (see Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO656 dated 2007. 1. 31., etc.).  \\nA constitutional complaint may not be filed unless all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act), and the Constitutional Court has held that where a constitutional complaint is filed without going through such a procedure despite the availability of a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is unlawful for failure to exhaust the lawful remedy procedure prescribed by other laws (see Constitutional Court 2007. 5. 31. 2006HEONMA1131).  \\n(2) The Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case constitutes a “disposition concerning detention” or a “disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc.” subject to a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without seeking revocation or alteration of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case through the quasi-appeal procedure.  \\nThe majority opinion held that, because the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ended on the day of the incident, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation thereof, it would be objectively uncertain whether the court would proceed to a merits determination, and thus it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure; on that basis, it concluded that the constitutional complaint concerning the denial of visitation was lawful as an exception to subsidiarity.  \\nHowever, after the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, the Claimant was unable to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon or participate in the interrogation of the suspect, and ultimately was not retained as defense counsel for the above suspect. In addition, with respect to the above suspect, a detention warrant was issued and he was prosecuted while in custody. There is nothing in the record to suggest any circumstance that would lead a court to find legal interest to be lacking or extinguished if the Claimant filed a quasi-appeal against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case. The Supreme Court has decided on the merits on the premise that legal interest exists even when a defense counsel’s participation was denied during the interrogation of a suspect and the interrogation procedure had ended (see Supreme Court Decision 2008MO793 dated 2008. 9. 12.); the same should apply where visitation is denied during the interrogation of a suspect.  \\nAccordingly, even if the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case has already ended, the Claimant may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act; thus, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint regarding the denial of visitation in this case fails to satisfy the subsidiarity requirement and is unlawful.  \\n\\nC. Conclusion  \\nThe right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be said to be a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, and therefore the Claimant’s petition regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case lacks the possibility of infringement of a fundamental right. Moreover, because the Claimant did not go through the quasi-appeal procedure under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the subsidiarity requirement is also not satisfied.  \\nAccordingly, the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is unlawful in any event and must be dismissed."}

{"[2020HEONGA1]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\nA. 2020HEONGA1\\n\\nThe petitioner for referral, Park ○○ (a foreigner), is a foreign national of the Arab Republic of Egypt who entered the Republic of Korea on 2018. 7. 21. with tourist/transit (B-2) status and remained in the Republic of Korea after the period of stay granted to him had expired.\\n\\nThe Head of the Suwon Immigration and Foreigners Office, on 2018. 10. 17., pursuant to Article 51(3) of the Immigration Control Act, placed the above petitioner for referral under emergency protection, and on 2018. 10. 18., pursuant to Article 46(1) No. 3, No. 8, Article 11(1) No. 8, and Article 17(1) of the same Act, issued a deportation order against the above petitioner for referral and, at the same time, pursuant to Article 63(1) of the same Act, issued a detention order.\\n\\nAccordingly, the above petitioner for referral filed an action seeking cancellation of the above deportation order and detention order (Suwon District Court 2019GU-DAN6240), and during the pendency of that case applied for a request to refer the matter for adjudication on the constitutionality of Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, etc. (Suwon District Court 2019A4057). The referring court, having granted the application insofar as it concerned Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, referred the constitutional review of this case on 2020. 1. 23.\\n\\nB. 2021HEONGA10\\n\\nThe petitioner for referral, Jha ○○ (a foreigner), is a foreign national of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh who entered the Republic of Korea on 2017. 5. 13. with short-term business (C-3-4) status and, after applying for refugee status recognition on 2017. 8. 7., was additionally granted other (G-1-5) status.\\n\\nThe Head of the Seoul Immigration and Foreigners Office, on 2017. 11. 22., on the ground that the above petitioner for referral had entered the country by fraudulent invitation, issued a deportation order against the above petitioner for referral pursuant to Article 46(1) No. 2 and No. 3, Article 7-2 No. 2, and Article 11(1) No. 3 and No. 4 of the Immigration Control Act and, at the same time, pursuant to Article 63(1) of the same Act, issued a detention order.\\n\\nAccordingly, the above petitioner for referral filed an action seeking cancellation of the above deportation order and detention order (Seoul Administrative Court 2018GU-DAN54708), and during the pendency of that case applied for a request to refer the matter for adjudication on the constitutionality of Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, etc. (Seoul Administrative Court 2018A12518). The referring court, having granted the application insofar as it concerned Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, referred the constitutional review of this case on 2021. 2. 9.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of this case is whether Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.) (hereinafter referred to as the “provision subject to review”) violates the Constitution. The provision subject to review and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)\\n\\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release from Detention of a Person Subject to a Deportation Order) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain in a detention facility a person subject to a deportation order until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation.\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10282 on 2010. 5. 14.)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The meanings of the terms used in this Act are as follows:\\n\\n11. The term “detention” means enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under any item of Article 46(1) in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)\\n\\nArticle 46 (Persons Subject to Deportation) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may deport outside the Republic of Korea an alien falling under any of the following items in accordance with the procedures prescribed in this Chapter.\\n\\n2. An alien who has violated Article 7-2 or an alien who entered the Republic of Korea through acts such as fraudulent invitation prescribed in that Article\\n\\n3. A person whose ground for denial of entry, falling under any item of Article 11(1), is discovered or arises after entry\\n\\n8.
