Thus, the relevant rules have been amended, and in practice the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office actively grants applications for temporary release from detention by foreigners with no criminal record or minors, so the effectiveness of the temporary release from detention system is also expanding.\\n\\n(d) As seen above, considering that since the precedent decision, positive institutional and practical improvements have been made to supplement the absence of an upper limit on the detention period, it cannot be said that there has been a change in normative or factual circumstances sufficient to justify changing the precedent.\\n\\n(5) The constitutional opinions state that, in light of many foreign examples establishing an upper limit on the detention period, it is possible to set a reasonable upper limit on detention. However, in the case of the United States, the law merely provides that if a foreigner does not leave within the 90-day removal period, detention of the foreigner may continue after the removal period, and does not expressly specify a legal upper limit; and the federal regulations on detention after the removal period, enacted after the U.S. Supreme Court held in Zadvydas v. Davis that the reasonable period during which detention is possible after expiration of the 90-day removal period is presumed to be 6 months, provide only that in certain cases, such as detention for security or terrorism reasons, continued detention is possible even if deportation execution is impossible, without otherwise placing any special restriction on the detention period, as already explained in the precedent. Neighboring countries of the Republic of Korea, such as Japan and China, still do not prescribe an upper limit on the period of custody for persons subject to deportation; this circumstance is the same as at the time of the precedent decision, namely that if the Republic of Korea were to set an upper limit on the detention period, the possibility of a sharp increase in the number of foreigners staying unlawfully in the Republic of Korea cannot be ruled out.\\n\\n(6) The matter of setting an upper limit on the detention period of persons subject to deportation is tied to whether there are measures to secure execution of deportation, whether there is a system to manage persons subject to deportation who are released from detention, and whether support measures for their livelihood, employment, housing, and medical care are in place. This shall be examined.\\n\\n(a) Difficulty in executing deportation against persons refusing departure\\n\\nDetention under the provision subject to review is intended to secure execution of deportation, so in order to set an upper limit on the detention period, repatriation or deportation of persons subject to deportation must first be possible within a fixed period. However, in the case of persons subject to deportation whose actions to cancel the deportation order and detention order or actions to cancel the decision of non-recognition of refugee status have all been dismissed and whose judgments have become final and conclusive, and who thereafter are refusing departure without particular reason, there is no means of forcibly deporting them other than inducing departure through interviews, persuasion through family members or acquaintances, requests to their home-country consulates for support and cooperation in deportation, and efforts to execute deportation at national expense; and even by the method of escorting the foreigner abroad together with immigration control officials, airlines may refuse boarding for security reasons, making execution difficult. Thus, if a person subject to deportation refuses departure, it is in practice impossible to execute deportation within a certain period. In fact, according to the record of this case, it is recognized that many of the persons subject to deportation who have been under long-term detention for more than one year are people refusing departure, intentionally damaging passports or even refusing a proposal that deportation be executed at national expense. In such a situation, if an upper limit on the detention period is set and detention is to be released after a certain period, there is a concern that this may greatly undermine the will of persons subject to deportation to depart voluntarily.\\n\\n(b) Difficulty in managing the stay of persons subject to deportation released from detention\\n\\nIn order to set an upper limit on the detention period, a system capable of systematically managing persons subject to deportation who have been released from detention must be established as a premise. In order for measures such as restricting residence or requiring reporting while releasing detention due to expiration of the detention period, designating a guarantor, or requiring payment of a security deposit, to have effectiveness, the costs and material and human resources necessary for managing them must all be secured. However, it can be confirmed that, from 2018 to 2020, a total of 394 temporary releases from detention occurred, and in 60 of those cases the temporary release was revoked due to unknown whereabouts and flight. Thus, it is difficult to say that the management of foreigners temporarily released from detention is currently being carried out thoroughly. In light of this, if the number of persons subject to deportation who are released from detention increases beyond the current level by setting an upper limit on the detention period, it is doubtful whether their stay in the Republic of Korea can be managed efficiently.\\n\\nFurthermore, whether to release persons subject to deportation after the upper limit on the detention period has been exceeded and whether to permit their stay in the country are closely related to national policies on employment, wages, housing, medical care, and livelihood support. For example, in Germany, where an upper limit on detention exists, a foreigner who has an obligation to depart but whose deportation is difficult for factual or legal reasons is granted Duldung, a temporary suspension of deportation execution; a foreigner granted Duldung may receive permission to work after a three-month waiting period, except in exceptional cases such as where the foreigner is at fault for the non-deportable reason, thereby establishing a system that can ease the conditions of stay for foreigners released from detention. By contrast, in the Republic of Korea, concrete support measures for housing, medical care, and livelihood for persons who have not obtained domestic stay status or whose domestic stay status has been revoked are not specifically in place; rather, in the case of temporary release from detention, conditions are sometimes attached prohibiting profit-making activities such as employment during the release period (Article 13(3) No. 4 of the Regulations on Handling Temporary Release from Detention). Thus, no system exists to ease the conditions of stay for foreigners released from detention. In such a situation, if an upper limit is set on the detention period and persons subject to deportation whose detention period has exceeded that limit are allowed to stay in the Republic of Korea, the livelihood and health of such persons may be threatened, they may become more exposed to crime, and difficulties may arise in public safety and maintenance of order.\\n\\n(c) Thus, the issue of imposing an upper limit on the detention period of persons subject to deportation should be discussed on a policy basis grounded in social consensus regarding how much administrative cost arising from the management of persons subject to deportation released from detention can be borne, what employment opportunities should be granted to foreigners subject to deportation, and what level of humanitarian support should be provided. In the precedent, while noting the need to carefully examine whether a reasonable upper limit on detention suited to the circumstances of the Republic of Korea can be established, it was held that there are unavoidable aspects to not setting an upper limit on detention, taking into account that setting such a limit is not merely a matter of immigration control administration but is closely related to overall national policy. It is difficult to say that there have been policy changes or other changed circumstances that would justify altering that judgment.\\n\\n(7) Whether to have a third independent neutral institution or a judicial body intervene at the stage of commencement or extension of detention is a matter of legislative policy in each country. The provision subject to review cannot be held to violate the principle of due process merely because the legislature excluded court involvement at the stage of commencement or extension of detention of persons subject to deportation in order to expand administrative expertise, ensure prompt response, and promote appropriate and efficient immigration control taking into account diplomatic relations and international situations. As a matter of principle, execution of a deportation order should be carried out without delay (Article 62(3) of the Immigration Control Act), and detention under the provision subject to review is a temporary and provisional measure taken to achieve the objective of prompt execution of a deportation order by detaining a person who cannot be repatriated immediately outside the Republic of Korea. In light of the purpose and spirit of detention under the provision subject to review—“prompt and efficient execution of a deportation order”—it is doubtful whether making an independent and neutral third institution review and control the validity of detention at the commencement stage would be a practical measure. In addition, the Minister of Justice has established within the Ministry of Justice the “Deliberation Committee on Long-Term Detention of Foreigners,” which includes private members such as lawyers, professors, religious figures, and members of organizations related to international organizations or civic groups, to deliberate on matters concerning release from detention or temporary release from detention of foreigners detained for more than one year [Article 2(1) and (4), Article 3(1) of the Guidelines for the Operation of the Deliberation Committee on Long-Term Detention of Foreigners (as amended by Ministry of Justice Regulation No. 1250 on 2020. 4. 14.)], thereby also establishing procedures to reflect the opinions of neutral third parties in matters such as release from long-term detention.\\n\\nFurthermore, because a deportation order is the premise for a detention order and detention is carried out to execute the deportation order, in determining whether the person subject to deportation was afforded a procedural opportunity to submit opinions and materials, the series of procedures from the deportation order through detention must be examined organically and comprehensively. The United States also guarantees opportunities for hearings, presentation of evidence, and examination of witnesses in deportation order proceedings conducted by immigration judges under the Department of Justice [Immigration and National Act, Sections 239 and 240], but does not grant an essential opportunity to state opinions at the stages of commencement of detention, requests to review release from detention, or applications for release from detention based on habeas corpus. Thus, at what stage and in what manner procedural rights are guaranteed from deportation order through commencement, extension, and release from detention are matters each country may determine within the scope of legislative policy. Therefore, whether the provision subject to review complies with the principle of due process should be determined not by whether a separate opportunity to state opinions or submit materials is granted at each stage of commencement, extension, and release of detention, but by whether an opportunity to submit opinions and materials regarding the deportation order, detention order, and release from detention is guaranteed in the overall procedure.\\n\\nFirst, at the stage where a deportation order, which is the premise of a detention order, is made, if procedural opportunities to state opinions and submit materials are guaranteed in the investigation of a foreigner suspected of being subject to deportation, namely the suspect (Article 47 of the Immigration Control Act), and in requests to appear and interrogation (Article 48), it cannot be said that the principle of due process is violated merely because an opportunity to submit opinions and materials is not separately granted before the detention order is issued. In addition, a person detained pursuant to a detention order is immediately guaranteed an opportunity to contest the detention order through an objection to detention. In particular, because materials substantiating the grounds for the objection must be attached to the objection petition (Article 69 of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), and because the Minister of Justice may hear the statement of the person concerned if necessary before deciding on the objection (Article 55(3) of the Immigration Control Act), it cannot be categorically said that the stage of objection completely excludes the opportunity for the party to submit opinions and materials. Furthermore, the detainee may also apply for temporary release from detention by submitting a request for temporary release accompanied by materials substantiating the grounds for the request and the ability to pay a security deposit at any time during detention (Article 65(1) of the Immigration Control Act, Article 79(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), thereby being able to submit opinions and substantiating materials concerning temporary release from detention in writing.\\n\\nIn addition, the Immigration Control Act and its Enforcement Decree require that the detention order be presented upon execution (Article 53 of the Immigration Control Act); that within 3 days from the date of detention, a detention notice stating the reasons, date, and place of detention and the fact that an objection may be filed be notified to the legal representative (Article 54(1)); that if the detained person so desires, the date, place, and reasons for detention be notified to the consul of the country of nationality or citizenship stationed in the Republic of Korea, unless there are urgent circumstances or other unavoidable reasons (Article 54(2)); that a decision on an objection must be prepared in the form of a decision document stating the order, reasons, applicable provisions, etc., and sent to the applicant (Article 70(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act); and that where approval for extension of detention period is sought pursuant to Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office must directly substantiate the necessity of extending the detention period (Article 78(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), thereby sufficiently preparing procedures to guarantee the party’s procedural rights within the bounds that do not undermine the efficiency of immigration control administration. Therefore, the provision subject to review cannot be deemed to violate due process merely because it does not expressly afford the detainee a procedural opportunity to submit opinions and materials at the stages of commencement or extension of detention.\\n\\n(8) Meanwhile, detention under the provision subject to review is an administrative disposition by which a person subject to deportation is temporarily taken and confined as part of immigration control administration to secure execution of a deportation order, and the strict warrant principle under Article 12(3) of the Constitution does not apply. In addition, although Article 12(6) of the Constitution requires that a procedure be established so that not only arrest or detention in criminal procedure but also arrest or detention in administrative proceedings can be reviewed by a court as to legality, the legislature is afforded legislative discretion in shaping the concrete contents of such procedure (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104). In particular, detention under the provision subject to review is carried out to ensure the administrative purpose of securing execution of a deportation order and to execute it efficiently, and its purpose and nature differ from physical restraint in criminal procedure or other administrative restraint whose very purpose is to restrict freedom of the person; thus, matters concerning its concrete procedure lie within the domain of policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONMA474 et al.). Therefore, as already stated by the Constitutional Court in its 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686 decision, a person subject to deportation may not only contest the causal relationship by filing a cancellation action against the deportation order that gave rise to the detention, but may also file an administrative action seeking cancellation of the detention order itself or apply for a stay of execution thereof; and, as noted above, strict prior procedures such as presentation of the detention order upon execution, written notice of the date, place, and reasons for detention, as well as ex post relief measures such as objections to the detention order in addition to objections to the deportation order, are in place, effectively supplementing the limitations of remedies through administrative litigation procedures. Since the legislature’s judgment cannot be said to exceed the scope of legislative discretion, the provision subject to review does not violate Article 12(6) of the Constitution. In addition, for the same reason, we dissent from Justice Lee Mi-seon’s constitutional opinion in the form of a supplementary opinion, which held that the provision subject to review violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, in addition to the five Justices’ constitutional opinion of incompatibility with the Constitution.\\n\\n(9) Taking the foregoing into account, the points raised in the constitutional opinions cannot be said to constitute changed circumstances sufficient to alter the precedent, and no other necessity for changing the Constitutional Court’s precedent is recognized.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the Constitutional Court stated in its 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29 decision that the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, the normative or factual circumstances surrounding the provision subject to review do not appear to have changed so drastically as to require a stricter determination than before regarding whether the provision is unconstitutional, and no other new necessity for reinterpretation can be found. Rather, the Ministry of Justice, the competent ministry, has continuously improved the relevant systems and practices since the above 2017HEONGA29 decision was rendered. Considering that immigration control administration is an area in which legislative policy is determined to a certain extent, there remains doubt whether it is desirable, after only about 5 years, to change the precedent and thereby eliminate through a Constitutional Court decision the room for voluntary and gradual institutional improvement by the legislative and executive branches.\\n\\nThe precedent’s position that the provision subject to review, which is established to conduct immigration control administration as a sovereign state, does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction or the principle of due process remains valid even at this time, there is no error in that judgment, and no necessary and sufficient changed circumstances justifying a change of precedent can otherwise be recognized.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Mi-seon to the Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon\\n\\nIn addition to the constitutional opinion of the five Justices that the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process, I wish to state as follows that it also violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, which provides for the right to request judicial review of the legality of arrest or detention.\\n\\nArticle 12(6) of the Constitution provides: “Any person arrested or detained shall have the right to request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention.” Thus, it establishes the system of judicial review of arrest or detention. This is an ex post remedial procedure intended to promote prompt and effective relief by allowing a person whose freedom of the person has been restricted by arrest or detention by public power to request judicial review by a court, and to obtain immediate release not only where the physical restraint was unlawfully commenced but also where continuation of the restraint is unlawful.\\n\\nBecause the freedom of the person guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution may be directly restricted not only by investigative agencies but also by other state institutions, including general administrative agencies, “arrest or detention” in Article 12(6) of the Constitution must also be interpreted broadly. Therefore, Article 12(6) applies to all cases in which any public power exercising agency restricts freedom of the person by means of arrest or detention. Furthermore, Article 12(6) is a provision that guarantees at the constitutional level a procedure by which the person concerned may request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention itself, separate from the final judicial determination procedure regarding the causal relationship that led to the arrest or detention. Because this right to request judicial review of arrest or detention has an independent status at the constitutional level, the legislature has an obligation to provide persons concerned, through the overall legal system, with at least one opportunity to properly exercise the concrete procedural right (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686). Furthermore, Article 12(6) of the Constitution states that “any person” has the right to request a court to review the legality of arrest or detention, thereby recognizing that right also for foreigners.\\n\\nAccordingly, with respect to a foreigner detained pursuant to the provision subject to review, there must be provided at least one opportunity to request judicial review of the legality of the detention itself (see Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686).\\n\\nHowever, the provision subject to review and the Immigration Control Act, including the provision subject to review, do not establish a procedure by which, in the event of detention pursuant to the provision subject to review, the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention may be requested to a court for review. In addition, the Habeas Corpus Act, which provides for court remedies concerning bodily liberty, excludes “persons detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act” from the scope of its application (see Article 2 and Article 3 of the Habeas Corpus Act), so foreigners detained pursuant to the provision subject to review cannot, unlike other forms of administrative physical restraint, file a petition for relief under the Habeas Corpus Act.\\n\\nIn shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power and may make various choices regarding the concrete contents and nomenclature of the law in the course of legislation (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104), and the detainee may file an administrative action seeking cancellation of the detention order or a motion for a stay of execution thereof. However, the purpose of guaranteeing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention separately from the right to file a judicial action under Article 27(1) of the Constitution is to enable a person who has been physically restrained by public power to request judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of the physical restraint, thereby establishing a prompt and effective remedy. Yet, in the current situation where no court involvement whatsoever exists at the stage of commencement or extension of detention under the Immigration Control Act, it is difficult to say that such ordinary administrative litigation procedures alone guarantee a swift and effective judicial remedy. Also, even where detention was lawfully commenced but continuation of detention became unlawful due to the disappearance of the necessity for detention, it cannot be said with certainty whether proper and effective relief can be provided in an action to cancel the detention order or in a motion for a stay of execution. The Immigration Control Act provides an ex post remedy by allowing an objection to detention to be filed with the Minister of Justice; however, it is obvious that such an objection system cannot constitute part of the system of judicial review of arrest or detention under Article 12(6) of the Constitution, the core element of which is court review. Furthermore, ex post control by the Minister of Justice, who is merely a supervisory authority rather than a neutral and objective institution, or other procedures prescribed by the Immigration Control Act, such as prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention, presentation of the detention order to the person concerned, and detention notices, cannot be regarded as supplementing the system of judicial review of arrest or detention.\\n\\nAs noted above, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power in shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, but considering the purpose of Article 12(6) of the Constitution in guaranteeing that right, a procedure must be secured whereby the legality of the state of detention itself under the provision subject to review may be requested to a court for review; and this is equally true even if detention under the provision subject to review is carried out as part of immigration control administration, because the detention causes a serious restriction on freedom of the person.\\n\\nTaken together, the provision subject to review, which does not establish a procedure for requesting judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention from a court in the event of detention under the provision subject to review, violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning administration under the rule of law is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Where a statute delegates matters of autonomous legislation to the articles of association of a public-law entity, the constitutional prohibition of blanket delegation legislation under Article 75 of the Constitution applies in principle, and even where delegation is made, if the matter relates to the rights and duties of the people, at least the basic and essential matters concerning the rights and duties of the people must be determined by the National Assembly.
B: The modern principle of legal reservation is understood as embodying not only the requirement that administrative action merely have a statutory basis, but also the requirement that, in areas of fundamental and important significance to the national community and its members, the legislator, as the representative of the people, must itself decide the essential matters.
C: A notice of exclusion from lawful union status is a grave infringing disposition that deprives a duly established labor union of its legal status, and as a matter that in principle must be prescribed by the legislator, the representative of the people, in a formal statute, legislation; to prescribe it by administrative legislation, there must necessarily be an explicit and specific delegation by statute.
D: Where, as with corporate income tax and comprehensive income tax, the taxpayer is imposed not only the duty to pay tax but also the duty to calculate and report the tax base and tax amount on its own, the basic matters necessary to fulfill the reporting duty, and the disadvantages the taxpayer will suffer in the event of non-performance of the reporting duty, etc., as the basic and essential content constituting the tax liability, must be prescribed by statute.
E: Cadets of the Army 3rd Military Academy may have their fundamental rights restricted more than ordinary citizens, but even in such a case, the constitutional principles governing restrictions on fundamental rights, such as the principle of legal reservation and the principle of proportionality, must be observed.

supporting_precedents: {"[2006DU14476]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the appeal\\n\\nA. Portion alleging a misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of quasi-retroactive legislation\\n\\nIn amending a statute, if the parties’ reliance on the continued existence of the former statute is reasonable and justified, and if the harm to, or infringement of the interests of the parties caused by the amendment of the statute is so grave that the public-interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new statute cannot justify the destruction of such reliance, the legislature must take appropriate measures to protect the parties’ reliance, such as by providing transitional provisions, and it would be impermissible to enact or apply the new statute as it is without such appropriate measures, because doing so would violate the principle of protection of reliance derived from the rule-of-law principle, which is a fundamental principle of the Constitution. In determining whether such a violation of the principle of protection of reliance exists, one must comprehensively compare and balance, on the one hand, the protected value of the infringed interest, the degree of severity of the infringement, the degree to which reliance has been impaired, and the manner of the infringement of reliance, and, on the other hand, the public-interest purpose sought to be realized through the new statute (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DU12899 rendered on 2006. 11. 16.).\\n\\nArticle 28(4) of the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act, as enacted by Act No. 6852 on 2002. 12. 30. and before amendment by Act No. 7392 on 2005. 3. 18. (hereinafter the “former Urban Improvement Act”), provided that, before applying for approval of project implementation, the project implementer (excluding the Mayor, County Governor, or housing corporation, etc.; hereinafter the same) was required to obtain in advance the consent of at least two-thirds of the landowners within the area of the rearrangement zone based on the area of land, and the consent of at least four-fifths of the owners of land, etc., with respect to the contents of the project implementation plan. However, Article 28(4) of the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act as amended by Act No. 7392 on 2005. 3. 18. (hereinafter the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act as amended as above is referred to as the “Amended Urban Improvement Act,” and when the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act is referred to simply regardless of the above amendment, it is referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”) was amended to provide in its main clause that the project implementer must, before applying for approval of project implementation, obtain the consent of the owners of land, etc. in accordance with the articles of association, etc. Meanwhile, according to the reasons of the judgment below, the Defendant-intervenor, a redevelopment association established before the Amended Urban Improvement Act came into force (hereinafter the “Intervenor Association”), upon the amendment of the Urban Improvement Act as above, obtained the consent of at least one-half of its members and newly established an articles-of-association provision stating that “when applying for approval of project implementation, consent to project implementation shall be sought from the landowners of at least one-half of the area of land within the rearrangement zone and from at least two-thirds of the owners of land, etc.”; and the Plaintiffs, as members of the Intervenor Association, owned land comprising at least one-third of the total area of the redevelopment project site.\\n\\nIn light of the above factual circumstances and the contents of the relevant statutes, the Intervenor Association, while Article 28(4) of the former Urban Improvement Act was applicable, could apply for approval of project implementation only if it obtained the consent of landowners holding at least two-thirds of the area of land within the redevelopment zone, and thus the applicants, who owned land comprising at least one-third of that area, could, by exercising their right of consent at the time of application for approval of project implementation, restrict the implementation of the redevelopment project by the association in this case. However, after the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act came into force, depending on how the redevelopment association in this case prescribed in its articles of association the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation, the applicants could also lose the above existing status.\\n\\nNevertheless, the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act merely requires owners of land, etc., such as the applicants, to exercise their right of consent in accordance with what is prescribed in the articles of association of the association, which is the project implementer, in relation to the application for approval of project implementation; it does not deprive them of the right of consent itself. Even if the applicants’ existing status concerning the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation became unstable due to the enforcement of the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act, it is difficult to view this as a direct or serious infringement of the Plaintiffs’ property rights. Meanwhile, Article 16 of the Urban Improvement Act requires, in establishing an association for the purpose of a housing redevelopment project or an urban environment improvement project, the consent of at least four-fifths of the owners of land, etc., thereby imposing strict consent requirements for the very establishment of an association for the purpose of a housing redevelopment project, etc., which may affect the property rights of the owners of land, etc. However, once the association has been established through such strict consent requirements, there is a need, in the implementation of the project, to set consent requirements in a manner suited to the circumstances of the relevant association so as to enable prompt and efficient project implementation in accordance with the autonomous and democratic will of the members, and it appears that Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act was enacted to meet such public-interest requirements. In light of these circumstances, it is difficult to say that the necessity of protecting the Plaintiffs’ reliance on the continued existence of Article 28(4) of the former Urban Improvement Act is greater than the public interest sought to be achieved through the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act violated the principle of protection of reliance in quasi-retroactive legislation.\\n\\nThe judgment below, which reached the same conclusion on this point, is proper, and there is no illegality affecting the outcome of the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of quasi-retroactive legislation, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Portion alleging a misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of delegated legislation and whether such limits were exceeded\\n\\nWhere a statute delegates matters of autonomous regulation to the articles of association of a public-law entity, etc., it is appropriate to view that the prohibition against blanket delegation legislation under Article 75 of the Constitution does not, in principle, apply. Meanwhile, even where a statute delegates autonomous matters to the articles of association, if the matter relates to the rights and obligations of the people, at least the basic and essential matters concerning the rights and obligations of the people must be determined by the National Assembly (see Constitutional Court Decision 2005HEONBA31 rendered on 2006. 3. 30.).\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the contents of the relevant statutes, under the Urban Improvement Act, the project implementer has the authority to prepare the project implementation plan, and the administrative agency merely has the authority to approve it; therefore, the preparation of the project implementation plan by the association, which is the project implementer, is a matter having an autonomous-regulatory element. Since the preparation of the project implementation plan thus has an autonomous-regulatory element, the consent requirements of the owners of land, etc. at the time of the association’s application for approval of project implementation are also matters of autonomous regulation. Accordingly, even if the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act comprehensively delegates the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation to the articles of association of the association, the prohibition against blanket delegation legislation under Article 75 of the Constitution does not apply, and it cannot be said to violate that provision.\\n\\nMoreover, although the consent requirements of the owners of land, etc. at the time of the association’s application for approval of project implementation concern the project implementation plan, which affects the property-related rights and obligations of the owners of land, etc., those consent requirements are merely procedural requirements for prior control by the owners of land, etc. over the application for approval of project implementation and cannot be regarded as basic and essential matters concerning the property-related rights and obligations of the owners of land, etc.; thus, they cannot be said to fall within an area where the principle of statutory reservation or parliamentary reservation must necessarily be observed. Therefore, the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act cannot be said to violate the principle of statutory reservation or parliamentary reservation.\\n\\nThe judgment below on this point, which reached the same conclusion, is proper, and there is no illegality due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of delegated legislation and whether such limits were exceeded, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the lower court determined that the legislative purpose of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act lies in promoting the expeditious implementation of projects by setting in the articles of association the consent requirements of members, etc. in a manner suited to the circumstances of the relevant association in the implementation of redevelopment projects, etc.; therefore, it premised that when setting the consent requirements of members, etc. in the articles of association, if those consent requirements are so unreasonable as not to properly reflect the actual intent of the members, etc., or if they deviate from the legislative purpose of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act and are manifestly unfair, they may be deemed void. On that premise, the lower court determined that the amended articles-of-association provision in this case established by the Intervenor Association based on Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act set the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation as “the consent of landowners holding at least one-half of the area of land and the consent of at least two-thirds of the owners of land, etc.”. While this may be regarded as more lenient than the consent requirements under the former Urban Improvement Act, it does not appear manifestly improper as a consent requirement for determining or confirming the will of the association as a whole in a redevelopment project. The lower court further determined that, although the proviso to Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act requires, where the project implementer is a designated developer, the consent of landowners holding at least 50% of the area of land within the redevelopment zone and the consent of a majority of the owners of land, etc., that does not mean that a project implementer other than a designated developer must necessarily set, in the articles of association, the consent requirement at the time of application for approval of project implementation as requiring the consent of landowners holding at least two-thirds of the area of land.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the inherent limitations of the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 3 of the appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the lower court determined that Article 20(3) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act, in principle, requires that, when an association intends to amend its articles of association, it obtain the consent of a majority of its members and receive approval from the Mayor or County Governor; however, for items 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, and 15 among the matters to be stated in the articles of association under items 1 through 17 of paragraph (1) of the same Article, it requires the consent of at least two-thirds of the members, and for minor matters prescribed by Presidential Decree, the resolution of the general meeting may substitute for the consent of the members. The lower court then found no clear basis for treating matters concerning the consent of members, etc. at the time of application for approval of project implementation as matters requiring a significant amendment to the articles of association such that the consent of at least two-thirds of the members would be required. In light of those considerations, the lower court held that, in amending the articles of association so as to include matters concerning the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of the project implementation plan in a redevelopment project, the consent of at least two-thirds of the members cannot be said to be required, and that since the amendment to the articles of association to establish the amended articles-of-association provision in this case was made with the consent of a majority of the members, there can be no defect in the procedure for amending the articles of association or in the process of granting approval therefor.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the required quorum in the procedure for amending the articles of association with respect to the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. As to Ground 4 of the appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, it can be found that the Intervenor Association is an association that obtained approval for establishment on 2002. 7. 30. pursuant to Articles 12 and 13 of the former Urban Redevelopment Act (prior to its repeal by Act No. 6852 of 2002. 12. 30.) and completed registration of establishment on 2003. 2. 25. Since Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act, which came into force on 2003. 7. 1., provides that “dispositions, procedures, and other acts conducted pursuant to the provisions of the Urban Redevelopment Act, the Temporary Measures Act for Improvement of the Residential Environment of Urban Low-Income Residents, and the housing redevelopment-related provisions of the Housing Construction Promotion Act as of the time this Act enters into force shall be deemed to have been conducted pursuant to the provisions of this Act,” even if the original articles of association of the Intervenor Association did not contain provisions concerning the matters of “the timing and procedures for bearing the costs incurred in the rearrangement project, including construction costs, etc. (Article 20(1), Item 12 of the Urban Improvement Act)” and “the matters to be included in the contract with the contractor and the designer (Article 20(1), Item 15 of the Urban Improvement Act),” the former articles of association do not become void, and there is no basis for concluding that, when amending the articles of association to establish the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, an amendment to establish the matters under Article 20(1), Items 12 and 15 of the Urban Improvement Act must necessarily be made together. Accordingly, even if the Intervenor Association’s articles of association do not contain provisions concerning the matters under Article 20(1), Items 12 and 15 of the Urban Improvement Act, the entire articles of association of the Intervenor Association, including the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, cannot be deemed void.\\n\\nAlthough the reasoning set forth by the lower court on this point is somewhat insufficient, its conclusion is proper, and there is no illegality affecting the outcome of the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the mandatory matters to be stated in the articles of association, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the Plaintiffs’ appeal is all dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Plaintiffs, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Supreme Court Justices."}

Outline of the Case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances may be ascertained.\\n\\nA. Filing and Acceptance of the Plaintiff’s Establishment Report\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff was established on May 28, 1989, when teachers of national, public, and private schools nationwide were allowed to organize trade unions. At the time of establishment, Article 6 of the Plaintiff’s bylaws provided: “Members of this union shall be faculty and staff engaged in kindergartens, elementary schools, middle and high schools, universities, the Ministry of Education, and other educational institutions nationwide, excluding persons working for employers” (paragraph 1), and “Faculty and staff dismissed (dismissal, discharge, removal by authority, etc.) or excluded from appointment by the improper conduct of the Ministry of Education or municipal and provincial offices of education, or a foundation, may also become members” (paragraph 2), thus including not only “incumbent teachers” but also “dismissed teachers” within the qualifications for membership.\\n\\n2) Thereafter, in order to comply with universal international labor standards by guaranteeing the labor fundamental rights of teachers, which had until then been restricted, and, in respect of the plan to guarantee the labor fundamental rights of teachers agreed upon by the Tripartite Commission, to establish the scope of such guarantees and the structure of collective bargaining, Act No. 5727, the Act on the Establishment and Operation of Teachers’ Trade Unions, etc. (hereinafter the “Teachers’ Trade Union Act”) was enacted on January 29, 1999, and came into force on July 1, 1999, thereby permitting the establishment of teachers’ trade unions under positive law. The Teachers’ Trade Union Act provides certain special rules concerning teachers’ trade unions and, as to other matters, refers to the provisions of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (hereinafter the “Trade Union Act”) (Article 14(1)). Since the proviso to Article 2, item 4, of the Trade Union Act provides that, in cases of “allowing persons who are not workers to join [(d)],” the organization shall not be deemed a trade union, membership by “persons who are not teachers,” such as dismissed teachers, was not permitted in teachers’ trade unions [Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act limits the statutory concept of “teacher” to “incumbent teacher” (main text), but provides in its proviso that “a person who has been dismissed and who has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practices with the Labor Relations Commission pursuant to the Trade Union Act shall be deemed a teacher until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission” (proviso). Meanwhile, the main text of Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act was partially amended by Act No. 17430 on June 9, 2020, in accordance with the purport of the Constitutional Court’s incompatible-with-the-Constitution decision (Constitutional Court, Decision of August 30, 2018, 2015HEONGA38, en banc); hereinafter, “Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act” refers to the provision prior to amendment].\\n\\n3) With the enactment and enforcement of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act containing the foregoing content, the Plaintiff convened a national delegates’ convention on June 27, 1999, and resolved to maintain Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws in substance while deleting paragraph 2. On July 1, 1999, the Plaintiff filed an establishment report with the Defendant (who was then the “Minister of Labor” and, following the amendment of the Government Organization Act by Act No. 10339 on June 4, 2010, became the present “Minister of Employment and Labor”) and submitted the amended bylaws as above. Based on the amended bylaws submitted by the Plaintiff, the Defendant determined that there was no defect in the Plaintiff’s establishment requirements under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act and the Trade Union Act, accepted the establishment report on July 2, 1999, and issued the Plaintiff a certificate of report.\\n\\nB. First Corrective Order\\n\\n1) After accepting the establishment report, the Defendant confirmed that the Plaintiff’s bylaws’ supplementary provision Article 5 included the following: “Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws, teachers who have been unfairly dismissed may become members” (paragraph 1), and “Among dismissed teachers who had been qualified for membership under the former bylaws, members who have not been reinstated, and members unfairly dismissed after the effective date of these bylaws, shall maintain their membership notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws” (paragraph 2).\\n\\n2) On February 12, 2010, the Defendant requested the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission to deliberate and decide on a corrective order with respect to matters in the Plaintiff’s bylaws deemed to violate labor-related statutes and regulations, and on March 10, 2010, the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission resolved that Article 9, the supplementary provision Article 5, and the like of the Plaintiff’s bylaws violated Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act (Seoul 2010 Decision No. 6). Accordingly, on March 31, 2010, the Defendant ordered the Plaintiff, pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act and Articles 21(1) and 21(3) of the Trade Union Act, to correct, by May 3, 2010, certain parts of the Plaintiff’s bylaws, including Article 55(4) and the supplementary provision Article 5 (hereinafter the “First Corrective Order”).\\n\\n3) On June 29, 2010, the Plaintiff filed an action seeking revocation of the First Corrective Order, alleging that it was unlawful, but the court rendered a judgment revoking only the part of the First Corrective Order concerning Article 55(4) of the Plaintiff’s bylaws and dismissing the claims regarding the remaining parts, including the supplementary provision Article 5. That judgment became final as rendered because both the Plaintiff’s appeal and appeal on points of law were dismissed (Seoul Administrative Court Judgment of November 5, 2010, 2010GUHAP27110; Seoul High Court Judgment of September 9, 2011, 2010NU43725; and Supreme Court Decision of January 12, 2012, 2011DU24231).\\n\\nC. Second Corrective Order\\n\\n1) On August 14, 2010, the Plaintiff amended its bylaws by deleting paragraph 1 of supplementary provision Article 5 and revising paragraph 2 to read: “A member who has been unfairly dismissed shall maintain membership notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws” (hereinafter, the revised supplementary provision Article 5 shall be referred to as the “Supplementary Provision at Issue”).\\n\\n2) On August 3, 2012, the Defendant requested the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission to deliberate and decide on a corrective order concerning the Plaintiff’s bylaws, and on September 3, 2012, the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission resolved that the portion of the Plaintiff’s bylaws corresponding to the Supplementary Provision at Issue violated Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act (Seoul 2012 Decision No. 7). Accordingly, on September 17, 2012, the Defendant ordered the Plaintiff to correct the Supplementary Provision at Issue by October 18, 2012, for the same reasons as the First Corrective Order (hereinafter the “Second Corrective Order”).\\n\\nD. Notice of Non-Recognition as a Trade Union under the Act\\n\\n1) On September 23, 2013, the Defendant, on the grounds that “despite having twice ordered correction of the bylaws permitting dismissed persons to join as members, the Plaintiff had failed to comply, and dismissed persons were in fact identified as joining and engaging in activities as members,” required, pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 2(4) proviso (d) of the Trade Union Act, Article 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Establishment and Operation of Teachers’ Trade Unions, etc. (hereinafter the “Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act”), and Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (hereinafter the “Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act”), that the Supplementary Provision at Issue be corrected in accordance with Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act by October 23, 2013, and that measures be taken so that dismissed persons who cannot become members do not join or engage in activities (hereinafter the “Request for Correction”). In the written request for correction, the Defendant specifically identified nine dismissed teachers who had joined and were engaging in activities as members of the Plaintiff and stated: “Please note that if the above deadline passes without compliance with the request for correction, notice will be given that the organization shall not be deemed a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act.”\\n\\n2) However, the Plaintiff did not comply with the Request for Correction, and accordingly, on October 24, 2013, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff, pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 2(4) proviso (d) of the Trade Union Act, and Article 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act and Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act, that the Plaintiff “shall not be deemed a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act” (hereinafter, for brevity, a trade union established under the Trade Union Act or the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall be referred to as a “statutory trade union,” and a trade union that is not a statutory trade union shall be referred to as a “non-statutory trade union.” The act of notifying that a trade union shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act or the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall be referred to as a “notice of non-recognition as a trade union,” and the notice of non-recognition as a trade union dated October 24, 2013, issued to the Plaintiff, shall be referred to as the “Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue”).\\n\\n3) On October 25, 2013, the Minister of Education sent each municipal and provincial office of education an official document titled “Request for Cooperation in Implementing Subsequent Measures and Notice of Dissolution of Suspension of Office Due to the ‘Notice that It Is Not a Labor Union’ for the Korean Teachers and Educational Workers Union.” The main content was that, following the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, the Plaintiff had lost the status and authority as a trade union, such as the use of the name “trade union” and the right to collective bargaining, and therefore each municipal and provincial office of education was to implement subsequent measures such as: ① revocation of leave approval for full-time union officials and orders of reinstatement, ② eviction from offices provided to the Plaintiff and a request for return of office support subsidies, ③ loss of effect of previously concluded collective agreements after October 24, 2013, and suspension of ongoing collective bargaining, ④ prohibition on wage withholding for union dues, and ⑤ where members of the Plaintiff had participated as committee members in various committees pursuant to collective agreements, loss of committee qualification due to the lapse of the collective agreements, and to report the results of implementation to the Ministry of Education by December 2, 2013.\\n\\n2. Whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue Was Lawful (Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 2)\\n\\nA. Relevant Statutory Provisions\\n\\n1) Under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, a person who intends to establish a teachers’ trade union must submit an establishment report to the Defendant (Article 4(2)), and matters concerning teachers’ trade unions not provided for in the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall, except as otherwise provided in Article 14(2), follow the Trade Union Act (Article 14(1)).\\n\\n2) Under the Trade Union Act, a trade union means “an organization or federation thereof organized by workers as the principal body, autonomously united for the purpose of maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing the economic and social status of workers” (main text of Article 2(4)); provided, however, that where it “allows persons who are not workers to join [(d)],” it shall not be deemed a trade union (proviso to Article 2(4); hereinafter, the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act, “Provided, however, that if any of the following applies, it shall not be deemed a trade union.” shall be referred to as the “Statutory Provision at Issue,” and the phrase “Provided, however, that if it allows persons who are not workers to join, it shall not be deemed a trade union,” including item (d), shall be referred to as “Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue”). Where a trade union to be established falls under any of the items of the proviso to Article 2(4), the administrative authority shall reject the establishment report (Article 12(3) item 1).\\n\\n3) Article 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act provides that matters concerning teachers’ trade unions not provided for in the Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall, except as otherwise provided in Article 9(2), follow the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act.\\n\\n4) Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act provides: “Where, after a trade union has been issued a certificate of report, a ground for rejection of the establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Trade Union Act arises, the administrative authority shall demand correction by specifying a period of 30 days, and if it is not complied with within that period, shall notify the relevant trade union that it shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act.” (hereinafter the “Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue”).\\n\\nB. The Constitutional Principle of Statutory Reservation and the Limits of Administrative Legislation\\n\\n1) Article 37(2) of the Constitution provides: “The freedoms and rights of citizens may be restricted only by Act when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even when such restriction is imposed, the essential aspect of the freedom or right shall not be violated.” The rule of law under the Constitution takes the principle of statutory reservation as one of its core components, namely, the principle that administrative action requires a basis in formal legislation enacted by the National Assembly. Moreover, the principle of statutory reservation today is understood to include not merely the requirement that administrative action be based on statute, but also the requirement, in areas that have fundamental and important significance for the national community and its members, especially in areas related to the realization of fundamental rights of the people, that such matters not be left to administration but be decided by the legislature itself, i.e., the people’s representative. That is, it includes the principle of parliamentary reservation. Whether a given matter falls within the essential matters that the National Assembly itself must prescribe by formal legislation must be determined individually in concrete cases by considering the importance of the interests or values involved and the degree and method of regulation or infringement. The greater the importance of the regulated subject matter to the fundamental rights of the people, and the greater the need for public debate or reconciliation between conflicting interests, the greater becomes the need for direct regulation by statute enacted by the National Assembly. Therefore, fundamental and essential matters concerning the rights and obligations of the people must be determined by the National Assembly, and when restricting freedoms or rights guaranteed by the Constitution, at least the essential matters of such restrictions must be regulated by the National Assembly itself through legislation (see Supreme Court Decision of October 12, 2007, 2006DU14476; en banc Supreme Court Decision of August 20, 2015, 2012DU23808; and Constitutional Court, en banc decision of February 26, 2009, 2008HEONMA370, etc.).\\n\\n2) Article 75 of the Constitution provides: “The President may issue presidential decrees concerning matters delegated to him or her specifically by Act, and matters necessary to enforce Acts.” Accordingly, the President may issue presidential decrees only concerning matters specifically delegated by Acts and matters necessary for the enforcement of Acts; thus, enforcement decrees may provide only detailed matters delegated by the parent Act or matters necessary for the practical enforcement of the Act within the scope prescribed by the Act. Unless delegated by statute, they may neither alter or supplement the content concerning individual rights and duties prescribed by the Act nor provide new contents not prescribed by the Act (see Supreme Court Decision of September 28, 1990, 89NU2493; en banc Supreme Court Decision of January 24, 1995, 93DA37342, etc.).\\n\\nC. The Unconstitutionality of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a trade union is a grave administrative disposition adverse to rights, depriving a lawfully established trade union of its legal status, and in principle is a matter that must be prescribed by the legislature itself, as the people’s representative, through formal legislation. In order to regulate this by administrative legislation, there must necessarily be an explicit and specific delegation by statute. However, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid in itself because, without statutory delegation, it prescribes a notice of non-recognition as a trade union not provided for by statute and thereby essentially restricts the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) A notice of non-recognition as a trade union should be regarded as a formative administrative disposition that definitively determines that a trade union, although lawfully established and in operation, is no longer a trade union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nThe Trade Union Act establishes a system of establishment report concerning trade unions, and in order to become a statutory trade union, one must not only satisfy the statutory establishment requirements but also complete the establishment report. Accordingly, a trade union under the Trade Union Act comes into existence by submitting an establishment report to the competent administrative authority and receiving a certificate of report from that authority (see Supreme Court Decision of December 11, 1979, 76NU189; Supreme Court Decision of June 28, 1996, 93DO855, etc.). For example, the mere fact that a trade union does not allow persons who are not workers to join does not immediately mean that it acquires the status of a statutory trade union, nor does allowing such persons to join immediately mean that it is not a statutory trade union. The provision in the Statutory Provision at Issue that “it shall not be deemed a trade union” does not itself have legal effect; it merely clarifies the criteria for determining whether it is a trade union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nThe administrative authority rejects the establishment report of an organization that does not satisfy the statutory establishment requirements, and such rejection is a refusal to accept the establishment report, thus constituting an administrative disposition directly affecting the legal status of the organization. In other words, an organization with a disqualifying factor shall not be deemed a trade union pursuant to the Statutory Provision at Issue, but such legal effect is realized only through the rejection of the establishment report as described above.\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a trade union is an administrative disposition by which the administrative authority, through the above procedure, authoritatively determines that a trade union lawfully established and in operation is no longer a trade union under the Trade Union Act. It is not merely a post hoc notice or confirmation that the organization has already become a non-statutory trade union by statute; rather, it is a formative act that causes it to become a non-statutory trade union by virtue of the notice. In other words, if a disqualifying factor arises in a statutory trade union, it does not become a non-statutory trade union immediately by the Statutory Provision at Issue; it becomes a non-statutory trade union only upon issuance of a notice of non-recognition as a trade union on that ground.\\n\\n2) The Trade Union Act provides special protection for trade unions established under the Trade Union Act. That is, a statutory trade union may acquire corporate personality (Article 6), may apply to the Labor Relations Commission for adjustment of labor disputes and relief from unfair labor practices (Article 7(1)), and may be exempt from taxes (Article 8). Above all, only a statutory trade union may use the designation “trade union” (Article 7(3)). Acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report grants it the legal status to enjoy the rights and benefits provided by the Trade Union Act by recognizing a trade union that meets the statutory establishment requirements as a statutory trade union, and a notice of non-recognition as a trade union deprives an already lawfully established trade union of such legal status on the ground that a disqualifying factor has arisen.\\n\\nA trade union that has received a notice of non-recognition can no longer use the designation “trade union,” and even if the employer commits an unfair labor practice, such as refusing collective bargaining, it cannot adequately respond, thereby suffering obstacles in its activities as a trade union. Of course, even if it becomes a non-statutory trade union, it does not lose its status as a trade union itself, so one may say that the general exercise of the three labor rights remains possible (see Supreme Court Decision of February 11, 1997, 96NU2125; Supreme Court Decision of December 27, 2016, 2011DU921; and Constitutional Court, en banc decision of March 29, 2012, 2011HEONBA53, etc.), but even so, practical restrictions and disadvantages cannot be avoided. The three labor rights can be substantively guaranteed only through trade unions, and it is difficult to expect a body that cannot even use the designation “trade union” to effectively exercise the three labor rights. Ultimately, although a notice of non-recognition formally appears merely to remove the special protection under the Trade Union Act, in substance it results in an essential restriction of the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution.\\n\\nArticle 33(1) of the Constitution provides: “Workers shall have the right to independent association, collective bargaining, and collective action for the improvement of working conditions,” thereby guaranteeing the three labor rights as fundamental rights. The three labor rights are not rights that can be realized only through state intervention in the form of legislation, but rather specific rights that may directly operate as legal norms by virtue of the constitutional provision alone, even without legislation. This can also be understood in the same dimension as Article 1 of the Trade Union Act, which provides that “This Act aims to guarantee the rights of workers to association, collective bargaining, and collective action under the Constitution, thereby maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing workers’ economic and social status, and by fairly adjusting labor relations and preventing and resolving labor disputes, contributes to the maintenance of industrial peace and the development of the national economy.” In particular, the right of association among the three labor rights is the concretization of freedom of association in the sphere of labor (see Constitutional Court, en banc decision of March 29, 2012, 2011HEONBA53, etc.), and thus has, historically and conceptually, the nature of a liberty right; therefore, “freedom from the state” rather than “freedom granted by the state” should be emphasized more. Accordingly, when legislating labor-related statutes and regulations, the constitutional meaning and direct normative force of the three labor rights, especially the right of association, must be respected, and in the enforcement and interpretation of such legislation, the essence and value of the right of association must not be impaired.\\n\\nMeanwhile, unlike Article 33(1), Article 33(2) of the Constitution provides that “Workers who are public officials shall have the rights to association, collective bargaining, and collective action only to the extent prescribed by law,” and both teachers at national and public schools, who are educational public officials, and teachers at private schools are restricted in the exercise of the three labor rights (see Article 55 of the Private School Act; Constitutional Court, en banc decision of July 22, 1991, 89HEONGA106, etc.). Accordingly, Article 5 of the Trade Union Act provides in the main text that “Workers are free to organize or join trade unions,” but in its proviso states that “matters concerning public officials and teachers shall be separately prescribed by law.” Ultimately, the three labor rights of teachers are substantively guaranteed only where there are special provisions in the law (see Supreme Court Decision of December 27, 2016, 2011DU921; Constitutional Court, en banc decision of December 26, 2008, 2005HEONMA971, etc.), and the law governing this is precisely the Teachers’ Trade Union Act. Article 1 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act provides: “This Act aims to prescribe matters concerning the establishment of teachers’ trade unions pursuant to the proviso to Article 5 of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act, notwithstanding Article 66(1) of the State Public Officials Act and Article 55 of the Private School Act, and to prescribe special provisions regarding the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act as applied to teachers.” Therefore, notifying a teachers’ trade union that it “shall not be deemed a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act” may not merely deprive it of the status of a “statutory trade union” but may, in substance, deny the very existence of it as a “trade union.”\\n\\n3) As such, whether an organization is recognized as a trade union under the Trade Union Act is an indispensable prerequisite for the substantive exercise of the constitutional three labor rights, and a notice of non-recognition as a trade union issued against a trade union already established through lawful procedure is more adverse to rights than a rejection of an establishment report for an organization not yet a statutory trade union. Therefore, with respect to such a notice of non-recognition that has such a strong connection to fundamental rights, it is consistent with the constitutional principle of statutory reservation to require a clear statutory basis. However, the current Trade Union Act (enacted by Act No. 5310 on March 13, 1997, and last amended by Act No. 17432 on June 9, 2020) directly provides for rejection of an establishment report from the time of its enactment to the present, but contains no provision whatsoever regarding the more rights-restrictive notice of non-recognition as a trade union, nor does it delegate such matter to be prescribed by enforcement decree.\\n\\nOriginally, the former Trade Union Act (enacted by Act No. 280 on March 8, 1953, and repealed by Act No. 5244 on December 31, 1996) provided in Article 32 a system of order for dissolution of a trade union, under which the administrative authority, after issuing an order to revoke or amend the bylaws, could obtain a resolution of the Labor Relations Commission and order dissolution of a trade union that failed to comply therewith (at the time of enactment, the only limiting condition was “a resolution of the Labor Relations Commission,” but an amendment on December 31, 1986 added the limiting condition of “non-compliance with an order to revoke or amend the bylaws”). However, on November 28, 1987, this system was repealed (Act No. 3966) on the ground that allowing the administrative authority to arbitrarily dissolve a trade union that had already been lawfully established and was in operation infringed workers’ right of association and the autonomy of trade unions.\\n\\nYet, only about five months after the repeal of the above dissolution-order system, on April 15, 1988, the notice-of-non-recognition system was newly introduced by Article 8(2) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act (enacted by Presidential Decree No. 782 on April 20, 1953, and repealed by Presidential Decree No. 15321 on March 27, 1997), on the ground that a trade union lacking statutory requirements cannot exist (Presidential Decree No. 12429), and this system has remained unchanged to the present through the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue. However, this notice-of-non-recognition system is, in substance, identical in subject, object, procedure, and effect to the former dissolution-order system, in that it allows the administrative authority to demand correction of bylaws and, if the trade union fails to comply, to notify it of non-recognition and thereby deprive it of the status of a statutory trade union. Indeed, unlike the former law, by omitting the Labor Relations Commission resolution procedure, the possibility of internal administrative control has merely been reduced and the room for arbitrary action by the administrative authority has been expanded.\\n\\nIn other words, the notice-of-non-recognition system is, in essence, a revival by administrative legislation, without statutory basis or delegation, of the trade union dissolution-order system that had originally been prescribed by statute and abolished by the legislative decision of the people’s representative. In determining the unconstitutionality of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, the history of this system must properly be taken into account.\\n\\n4) In short, a notice of non-recognition as a trade union is not a post hoc notice or confirmation of something that has already become a non-statutory trade union by statute; rather, it is a formative administrative disposition that causes it to become a non-statutory trade union by virtue of the notice. Such a notice does not merely eliminate the legal protection for a trade union; it substantially restricts the constitutional three labor rights. Yet the Trade Union Act, while requiring rejection of the establishment report of an organization that does not satisfy the statutory establishment requirements, contains no provision whatsoever regarding a notice of non-recognition as a trade union for a trade union already in operation after establishment, which is even more rights-restrictive, and it contains no express delegation to the enforcement decree either. Moreover, the notice-of-non-recognition system is not materially different from the trade union dissolution-order system that the legislature abolished upon reflective reconsideration. Ultimately, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, concerning a matter not prescribed by statute and without any specific and express delegation, prescribes an essential restriction on the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and thus violates the principle of statutory reservation.\\n\\nD. Illegality of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue\\n\\nThe Defendant issued the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue on the premise that the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue was valid. As noted above, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue violates the constitutional principle of statutory reservation and is therefore invalid in itself. Accordingly, the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, issued on the basis of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, lost its legal basis and must be regarded as unlawful.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below deemed the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue valid and held that the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue was lawful. In such judgment of the court below, there is error affecting the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the constitutional principle of statutory reservation. The ground of appeal pointing out this point has merit.\\n\\n3.
