Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for retrial and a new determination, and judgment is rendered as stated in the order. In this judgment, the opinions of Justices Kim Jaehyung, Ahn Chulsang, Lee Gitaek, and Lee Dongwon were separate opinions and dissenting opinions, and there are supplemental opinions by Justices Park Jeonghwa, Min Yusook, Noh Jeonghee, Kim Sanghwan, and Noh Taeak to the majority opinion.\\n\\n4. Separate Opinion of Justice Kim Jaehyung\\n\\nA. The difficulty of this case lies in the statute itself, not the enforcement decree.\\n\\nThe Trade Union Act provides that where it allows the membership of persons who are not workers, it shall not be deemed a trade union [Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue]. The Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act provides that in such case a notice should be given that it is not a trade union (Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue). The Teachers’ Trade Union Act and its Enforcement Decree apply the foregoing provisions of the Trade Union Act and its Enforcement Decree to teachers’ trade unions as well.\\n\\nAccording to such statutes and enforcement decree, an interpretation that when persons who are not teachers are allowed to join, notice must be given that it is not a teachers’ trade union, appears self-evident [provided, however, that because it is not possible to deny the very existence of a trade union once it has been lawfully established if it later allows persons who are not workers to join, the term “non-statutory trade union” is used in the sense of a trade union not recognized by law]. If the Plaintiff allows dismissed teachers to join as members, the Defendant’s notice of non-recognition to the Plaintiff follows as lawful because the Plaintiff cannot be regarded as a teachers’ trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act. Such a determination may be seen as a legal syllogism applying the statutes and regulations to this case.\\n\\nBut is it justifiable for a statute to deem a lawfully established trade union not to be a trade union if even one dismissed worker is included? In this case, is it proper to deprive the Plaintiff of its status as a teachers’ trade union merely because 9 out of approximately 60,000 members are dismissed teachers? Should the Plaintiff be held not to be a teachers’ trade union merely because it did not exclude, from the union members, persons who lost their status as teachers while serving as members? Should it be considered justified that the Defendant’s measure is proper because the Plaintiff does not merely tolerate membership by dismissed teachers but expressly provides for it in its bylaws? The difficulty of this case lies precisely here. The question is whether the interpretation and application according to the wording of the statute truly lead to a just conclusion.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that the notice-of-non-recognition system, which causes a severe restriction on the constitutional three labor rights, is prescribed in an enforcement decree rather than in a statute, without any special statutory basis or delegation, and thus violates the principle of statutory reservation and is invalid, and therefore the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is unlawful because it has lost its legal basis. However, if a trade union that allows membership by persons who are not workers pursuant to the Trade Union Act is not a lawful trade union but merely a non-statutory trade union, then the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue simply informs of the effect under the above statutory provision and must be regarded as lawful.\\n\\nThe decisive issue in this case is not the propriety of the “notice” of non-recognition as a trade union. If the Plaintiff is a “non-statutory trade union,” notifying that fact is naturally something the Defendant should do and may even be necessary. The core issue is whether the Plaintiff is a trade union under the law, that is, whether it is a non-statutory trade union.\\n\\nShould the Plaintiff be regarded as a non-statutory trade union under Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue? Is allowing a dismissed person to join as a member a matter that determines the essence and fate of a trade union? Is this a matter to be resolved through statutory interpretation, or through a constitutional review by the Constitutional Court or legislation by the National Assembly? The Constitutional Court held that Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, which excludes dismissed teachers from members of teachers’ trade unions, is constitutional (Constitutional Court, en banc decision of May 28, 2015, 2013HEONMA671, etc.). The National Assembly’s legislation allowing dismissed persons to join trade unions has been stagnant for years, and the Government continues to take the position that the Plaintiff is a non-statutory trade union. Even though this matter now awaits only the court’s judgment, should the court be unable to provide relief to the Plaintiff?\\n\\nThis case is, as Ronald Dworkin put it, the so-called “hard case.” A hard case requires deliberation commensurate with its difficulty. For that purpose, this case was reviewed over a long period of time and public arguments were also held. There are cases in which no conclusion can be reached without bypassing the core of the issue. This case is precisely such a case.\\n\\nChanging the section, I will examine the difficulties of interpreting the statutes at issue and present the essence of this case and a proper solution thereto.\\n\\nB. The meaning of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is clear.\\n\\n1) The Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue provides: “Where, after a trade union has been issued a certificate of report, a ground for rejection of the establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Act arises, the administrative authority shall demand correction by specifying a period of 30 days, and if it is not complied with within that period, shall notify the relevant trade union that it shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act.”\\n\\nIts meaning is clear. If a disqualifying factor arises in a trade union that has already completed its establishment report, the administrative authority shall demand correction and, if correction is not made within the deadline, must notify that it “shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act.” In this case, if it is found that a teachers’ trade union that has already completed its establishment report allows persons who are not teachers to join, the administrative authority must demand correction and, if correction is not made within the deadline, notify it as a non-statutory trade union. This is a very natural and obvious provision that requires notice that an “organization that does not satisfy the statutory establishment requirements” is “not a trade union under the Act.” Such notice is nothing more than informing of such circumstances, and has no special formative meaning. Rather, the significance of the notice should be found in clarifying the legal status of the relevant trade union and thereby clarifying the legal relations of the parties and interested persons. It is self-contradictory to say that one cannot notify that something is not a trade union under the Act because it is not a trade union under the Act; for that is no different from saying that it is not a lawful trade union but is a lawful trade union. Therefore, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue should be regarded as lawful and valid because it directly rests on the Statutory Provision at Issue and concretizes the purport and meaning of the statute. In fact, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue can be regarded as a provision that is difficult to assign any substantial independent meaning. Even if no notice of non-recognition as a trade union is given, a trade union that has incurred a statutory disqualifying factor can no longer be regarded as a “trade union under the Act.”\\n\\nThis legal principle does not change simply because the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue makes the notice of non-recognition conditional upon certain corrective procedures and noncompliance therewith. The corrective demand procedure provided by the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is to afford prior notice and an opportunity to submit opinions regarding the notice of non-recognition as a trade union under the general principles of administrative law or the Administrative Procedures Act, thereby giving the trade union that has incurred a violation an opportunity for autonomous correction. Requiring a corrective demand before the notice of non-recognition and making noncompliance a condition for notice only strengthens the justification of the notice of non-recognition.\\n\\n2) The majority opinion states that the notice of non-recognition as a trade union is a formative administrative disposition that makes a trade union with a disqualifying factor become a non-statutory trade union for the first time, and that such a grave adverse disposition must of course have a basis in law or statutory delegation, but the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue independently prescribes notice of non-recognition without such basis or delegation, and therefore it is invalid in violation of the principle of statutory reservation.\\n\\nHowever, as seen above, the notice of non-recognition as a trade union merely informs that it is not a trade union under the Act, and even if viewed as an administrative disposition, it is merely a confirmatory administrative act, not a formative administrative act creating new rights or duties. In other words, once a trade union has become a non-statutory trade union by law, it is a non-statutory trade union even if no notice is necessarily given, and unless the disqualifying factor is removed, even if a notice of non-recognition is issued and later revoked or withdrawn, the fact that the trade union is a non-statutory trade union does not change.\\n\\nThe majority opinion asserts that the part of the Statutory Provision at Issue stating that it “shall not be deemed a trade union” does not itself have legal effect but merely serves as a criterion for determining whether it is a trade union under the Trade Union Act, yet it offers no basis. However, there is no example of interpreting a deeming provision in this manner. A trade union comes into existence under the Trade Union Act only if the establishment report is accepted, but this cannot be a basis for concluding that, if a disqualifying factor arises, it does not become a non-statutory trade union unless there is a notice of non-recognition. The Trade Union Act expressly provides for the establishment report of a trade union, while it contains no provision concerning notice of non-recognition. Therefore, even if the establishment report is viewed as a requirement for the existence of a trade union, it cannot be said that a separate requirement of notice of non-recognition is necessarily needed to deny that status.\\n\\nFor example, if a trade union filed an establishment report by forging documents or deceiving the administrative authority, the administrative authority should be able to take measures to deny the legal status of the trade union. In such a case, it is self-evidently insufficient to say that the administrative authority may only issue a corrective order and, for noncompliance, impose a criminal penalty of a fine not exceeding 5 million won (Articles 93 and 21 of the Trade Union Act) to sanction such a trade union. Even if the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue were invalid or did not exist at all, the administrative authority should still be able to take measures such as a notice of non-recognition as a trade union against a trade union with a statutory disqualifying factor.\\n\\nThe majority opinion does not properly explain, beyond declaring the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue invalid, what the legal status of a trade union with a disqualifying factor is and what the concrete legal relations of this case are. This bypasses the core of the issue and avoids substantive judgment.\\n\\n3) Even if the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid, the question arises whether that fact alone does not immediately render the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue unlawful, but rather makes it unlawful only under the doctrine limiting ex officio revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions.\\n\\nOriginally, the disposing authority that issued an administrative act may revoke it on its own even without a separate legal basis if the disposition is defective, and even if there was no particular defect at the time of disposition and no separate legal basis for withdrawal after disposition, it may withdraw it as a separate administrative act causing it to lose effect if there is a change in circumstances making the original disposition unnecessary to maintain, or if a significant public interest need arises. However, if the original administrative act was beneficial, there is only a certain limitation that the vested rights of the addressee must be considered (see Supreme Court Decision of February 25, 1986, 85NU664; Supreme Court Decision of November 26, 2004, 2003DU10251, 10268, etc.). Acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report is a beneficial administrative disposition that grants the legal status to enjoy special protection under the Trade Union Act by recognizing a trade union that satisfies the statutory establishment requirements as a lawful trade union. Ultimately, a notice of non-recognition as a trade union corresponds to ex officio revocation or withdrawal of such acceptance of the establishment report. Accordingly, the administrative authority may issue a notice of non-recognition as a trade union in the sense of ex officio revocation or withdrawal of the existing acceptance disposition, even without a separate legal basis, subject only to certain limitations in considering the vested rights of the relevant trade union in the process.\\n\\nHowever, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue provides that if the corrective demand is not complied with, a notice of non-recognition must be given. Since the Trade Union Act clearly prescribes the lawful requirements for a trade union, where those requirements are violated, the notice of non-recognition must be given. This should be understood as intending to disallow exceptional limitations on ex officio revocation or withdrawal. Where there is an express provision denying such limitations on ex officio revocation or withdrawal, the general doctrine concerning limitations on ex officio revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions cannot be applied, leaving aside the question whether such provision is unconstitutional or unlawful. And as seen above, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is directly based on the Statutory Provision at Issue and may be seen as intended to give the relevant trade union an opportunity for autonomous correction, so there is no reason to regard it as invalid.\\n\\n4) In short, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue provides that a notice of non-recognition as a trade union shall be made against a trade union with a disqualifying factor. There is no exception. The provision is binding and leaves no room for discretion. Accordingly, under the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, the administrative authority must, after going through the corrective demand procedure, issue a notice of non-recognition as a trade union to a trade union that allows persons who are not workers to join if correction is not made.\\n\\nThe meaning of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is, as above, very clear and should be regarded as constitutional and proper because it concretizes what is provided by the statute. The core issue is not the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, but how the meaning of the Statutory Provision at Issue should be understood.\\n\\nC. How Should the Statutory Provision at Issue Be Interpreted?\\n\\n1) Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue provides: “If it allows persons who are not workers to join, it shall not be deemed a trade union.”\\n\\nThe phrase “shall not be deemed a trade union” should be regarded as a so-called deeming provision and, unlike a presumption provision, should not allow rebuttal (see Supreme Court Decision of February 17, 1995, 94DA52751, etc., concerning Article 28 of the Civil Act). Whether a provision uses the expression “shall be deemed” or “shall not be deemed,” both are deeming provisions, and there is no reason to distinguish between them. Accordingly, if persons who are not workers are allowed to join, it cannot be regarded as a trade union.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that the Statutory Provision at Issue is a criterion for determining a statutory trade union and that a notice of non-recognition is issued according to that criterion, but that even if a disqualifying factor arises, the trade union is not yet a non-statutory trade union unless a notice of non-recognition is given. However, a deeming provision, when its preconditions are satisfied, recognizes the existence or occurrence of the facts or legal effects prescribed by law without exception, even if the actual facts or legal status do not match. Rather, that unconditional legal fiction is the essence of a deeming provision. The meaning and effect of a legal provision do not change depending on where it is placed in a statute, and therefore its meaning and effect do not change merely because a deeming provision appears in the definitional part of the statute. Accordingly, under Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, if persons who are not workers are allowed to join, the trade union is no longer a lawful trade union.\\n\\nThe above situation does not change depending on whether it occurs before or after establishment report. No provision of the Trade Union Act treats the concept of a trade union differently depending on whether establishment report has been made. Article 2 of the Trade Union Act is a definitional provision concerning trade unions, and thus determines the scope of application of the Act; therefore, it should be understood as applying regardless of whether an establishment report has been made.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 2 of the Trade Union Act states, “The definitions of the terms used in this Act are as follows,” and item 1 provides that “the term ‘worker’ means a person who lives on wages, salary, or other income equivalent thereto, regardless of the kind of occupation,” while item (d) of the proviso to item 4 [Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue] provides, “If persons who are not workers are allowed to join. Provided, however, that where a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, he or she shall not be interpreted as a person who is not a worker until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission.” Under these provisions of the Trade Union Act, a dismissed person is a worker “until he or she has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission and there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission,” but after the re-hearing decision, he or she is no longer a worker.\\n\\nUltimately, according to Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, even if a trade union has already completed the establishment report, if it allows dismissed persons to join as members, it can no longer be regarded as a statutory trade union. This is the interpretation according to the wording of the Trade Union Act.\\n\\n2) As seen above, a deeming provision does not permit rebuttal. Accordingly, under Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, which takes the form of a deeming provision, if a lawfully established trade union admits even one dismissed person as a member, the conclusion is reached that such trade union is not a trade union within the meaning of the Trade Union Act. But is this conclusion really valid? The problem begins here.\\n\\nThere is a view that in this case the Plaintiff does not merely tolerate membership by some dismissed persons but expressly permits it through its bylaws, and that this is the problem. However, whether a trade union has provided in its bylaws that dismissed persons may become members is not an essential issue. If a trade union has no bylaw permitting membership by dismissed persons but in fact has dismissed persons as members, is that trade union not a non-statutory trade union? Conversely, what if it has a bylaw permitting membership by dismissed persons but actually has no such members? When determining whether a trade union that allows dismissed persons to join is a non-statutory trade union, whether such permission is stipulated in the bylaws is not decisive. The conclusion may differ depending on how the allowance of dismissed persons’ membership is normatively evaluated.\\n\\nOne may think of resolving this issue from the perspective of the “autonomy” of a trade union. That is, if, at the stage of establishment report, it becomes apparent that dismissed persons are allowed to join as members, the establishment report must be rejected (see Supreme Court Decision of April 10, 2014, 2011DU6998, etc.), but where a lawfully established trade union allows dismissed persons to join, the existence of a disqualifying factor should be determined only if that practice impairs the autonomy of the trade union. However, this approach not only runs counter to the purport of the statute but also lacks practicality. First, the reason the Trade Union Act does not permit persons who are not workers to join without exception should be understood as a preventive measure, considering that if such persons are allowed to join, there is a high risk that the autonomy of the trade union will immediately or at least in the near future be impaired. There is no reason to distinguish a trade union that has completed establishment report from any other. Moreover, it is a very difficult matter for the administrative authority to examine and determine the autonomy of a trade union. Furthermore, the administrative authority competent for establishment reports of trade unions has, after the establishment report stage, no separate investigative authority or special investigative methods for examining autonomy, unlike at the establishment report stage. Requiring the administrative authority to separately examine and determine the autonomy of a trade union for purposes of a notice of non-recognition is not contemplated by the Trade Union Act and does not accord with the reality of labor administration.\\n\\nOne may also consider a stricter interpretation of the “join” element in Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue. Under this view, the provision merely prohibits new membership by persons who are not workers, including dismissed persons, and does not prohibit a person who was already a member from retaining membership after dismissal. This may be consistent with the dictionary meaning of “join” as entering an organization or association. Nor must the conditions for joining and withdrawing from a group necessarily be identical. Under this view, one could easily conclude that the Plaintiff is not a non-statutory trade union because it merely allows dismissed persons to retain membership and does not permit their new membership.\\n\\nHowever, in general, Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue is understood to include not only new membership by persons who are not workers but also cases in which such persons are allowed to retain membership. As seen above, because the proviso to Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue provides that “Provided, however, that where a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, he or she shall not be interpreted as a person who is not a worker until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission,” a dismissed person is considered a worker only until the re-hearing decision of the National Labor Relations Commission if he or she has filed for relief from unfair labor practice, and in other cases cannot be regarded as a worker; therefore, where a dismissed person who is not a worker is a member, the requirements of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue are satisfied. The same applies to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, and the Constitutional Court has based its judgment on the premise that the provision excludes dismissed teachers from membership in teachers’ trade unions (the above Constitutional Court decision, 2013HEONMA671, etc.). In light of these circumstances, it is difficult to adopt an interpretation that limits the word “join” in the main text of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue to new membership, because such interpretation cannot explain the existence and meaning of the proviso.\\n\\n3) Under the conventional view concerning Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, it appears that no other conclusion can be reached by way of interpretation regarding the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue against the Plaintiff. From this perspective, there is a view that the issue of membership by dismissed persons is a matter to be improved by legislation, even if there may be unfair aspects in the current law, rather than a matter that can be resolved by statutory interpretation.\\n\\nWhile the Constitutional Court held constitutional Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, which excludes dismissed teachers from membership in teachers’ trade unions, it stated that the notice of non-recognition against a teachers’ trade union that recognizes dismissed persons as members may be determined at the discretion of the administrative authority and the courts by comprehensively considering matters such as “the number of unqualified members active in the teachers’ trade union, the impact of such members on the activities of the teachers’ trade union, whether the administrative authority took appropriate measures to prohibit or restrict the labor union activities of unqualified members, and whether the relevant trade union is likely to correct this” (the above Constitutional Court decision, 2013HEONMA671, etc.). However, if excluding dismissed persons from membership is constitutional, then a trade union that allows dismissed persons to join as members cannot be said to be a lawful trade union. As seen above, the fact that a notice of non-recognition can be discretionary does not accord with the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, which provides that a trade union allowing dismissed persons to join as members “shall” be notified as a non-statutory trade union. In addition, legislation by the National Assembly allowing dismissed persons to join trade unions has been stagnant for years. The Government itself has submitted to the National Assembly a revised bill allowing dismissed persons to join trade unions, but in this case continues to maintain the position that the Plaintiff is a non-statutory trade union. This issue now awaits only the Supreme Court’s judgment.\\n\\nAs a rule, statutes are to be interpreted faithfully to the wording of the statutory provisions, but there are cases in which exceptions must be recognized. There are cases where, at the time of enactment, the legislature did not envision the matter at all and thus the statute either does not regulate it or regulates it insufficiently; there are also cases where, although an express provision exists in the statute, a gap inevitably emerges between the statute and real life as times and society change. If one insists only on a strict application of the express wording, legal stability may be maintained, but there may arise a problem of diminished adaptability to social change and development. Accordingly, in such cases the court should not be bound by a formal literal interpretation but should ascertain the legislative purpose the statute seeks to realize and give meaning to the statute in a way that realizes that purpose; to the extent necessary for such realization, the court should exercise a substantive law-making function by interpreting the express provision expansively or restrictively. It is necessary to adapt lagging statutes to advancing social phenomena by rational interpretation within limits that do not alter the meaning and essence of the statutory provision, and one must not resign oneself to the idea that, even knowing that the traditional interpretation and application of a lagging statute produce unjust results, one can do nothing until the legislative body amends the statute (see Supreme Court en banc Decision of April 25, 1978, 78DO246; en banc Supreme Court Decision of April 23, 1998, 95DA36466, etc.).\\n\\nLegal norms cannot perfectly regulate every matter arising in reality. Because of their general and abstract nature, laws inevitably contain inherent defects. Accordingly, statutory interpretation does not merely consist of recognizing or discovering existing law. In certain cases, it is necessary to actively shape the law by clarifying its scope of application through analogy or teleological reduction. This is the demand of substantive rule of law. Courts must declare “the law,” not merely “the statute.”\\n\\nIn interpreting and applying the law, one must consider the consequences. If an interpretation yields a highly irrational or unjust conclusion, one should seek a way to exclude such interpretation. Usually, for this purpose, various interpretive methods such as logical, systematic, historical, and teleological interpretation are employed in addition to literal interpretation. If, despite such efforts, irrationality and injustice are not corrected, the court must interpret beyond the wording of the law, and sometimes even contrary to the wording, in a just manner.\\n\\nThis method of interpretation is not entirely new. The Supreme Court interpreted the phrase in Article 55(1) item 6 of the Criminal Act, “When reducing a fine, it shall be one-half of the maximum amount,” to mean “one-half of the amount,” and held that both the upper and lower limits are reduced to one-half (en banc Supreme Court Decision of April 25, 1978, 78DO246). Even though Article 75 item 6 of the Bills of Exchange Act prescribes “date and place of issuance” as requirements of a bill, the Supreme Court interpreted that “even if the place of issuance is not stated on the face of the bill, if, from the other entries on the bill itself, it is recognized that the bill was issued in the country for the purpose of giving rise to effects under the bill, it cannot be regarded as an invalid bill” (en banc Supreme Court Decision of April 23, 1998, 95DA36466).\\n\\nStatutory interpretation must reflect constitutional provisions and their purport. Where multiple interpretations of a statutory provision are possible, the court must first adopt the interpretation that conforms to the Constitution, thereby eliminating unconstitutionality through constitutional-conforming interpretation; furthermore, among constitution-conforming interpretations, the court must adopt the interpretation that best realizes the principles and values of the Constitution, i.e., a constitution-oriented interpretation. If interpreting a statutory provision in light of its wording, structure, and legislative history yields an irrational or unjust conclusion, it can be corrected through such constitution-conscious, constitution-conforming interpretation.\\n\\n4) Then, is this case truly one in which interpretation beyond, or even contrary to, the wording is required in light of the Constitution?\\n\\na) The Constitution, in Article 33(1), provides that “Workers shall have the right to independent association, collective bargaining, and collective action for the improvement of working conditions,” thereby guaranteeing workers’ right of association. For this purpose, Article 1 of the Trade Union Act provides that “This Act aims to guarantee workers’ rights to association, collective bargaining, and collective action under the Constitution, thereby maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing workers’ economic and social status, and by fairly adjusting labor relations and preventing and resolving labor disputes, contributes to the maintenance of industrial peace and the development of the national economy.” And Article 37(2) of the Constitution clearly defines the limits on restriction of fundamental rights by providing: “The freedoms and rights of citizens may be restricted only by Act when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even when such restriction is imposed, the essential aspect of the freedom or right shall not be violated.”\\n\\nThe right of association includes not only the individual right of each worker to organize or join and engage in activities through a trade union or other workers’ organization, but also the collective right of the workers’ organization to exist and function (see Constitutional Court, en banc decision of November 25, 1999, 95HEONMA154, etc.). Accordingly, the right of association of a trade union may be restricted only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even then the essential content of the right of association may not be violated. The legislature, when enacting labor-related statutes such as the Trade Union Act, must respect these constitutional provisions and principles, and the courts likewise must interpret labor-related statutes so that such constitutional provisions and principles are realized to the fullest extent.\\n\\nThe formation and joining of a trade union is the exercise of the right of association itself, and as a trade union is an indispensable foundation for the exercise of labor basic rights, the establishment and continuity of trade unions should be guaranteed to the fullest extent. The Trade Union Act must be interpreted and applied in a way that maximally guarantees the right of association of trade unions, and it must be ensured that the Trade Union Act, enacted to guarantee labor basic rights, does not produce the unjust result of restricting the right of association of trade unions.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in this case, the issue is important not only from the perspective of the right of association but also from the perspective of freedom of association. Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees freedom of association to all citizens in paragraph 1 and provides in paragraph 2 that licensing of associations is not permitted. “Association” here means a group of multiple natural persons or juridical persons that, over a considerable period of time, freely unite for a common purpose and can form an organized will (see Constitutional Court, en banc decision of September 19, 2002, 2000HEONBA84, etc.). Freedom of association is neutral as to the purpose of the organization, so the formation of all organizations is protected regardless of their purpose. Since determining the scope and form of association is itself a matter of freedom, it is not for the state to interfere with how and in what form people form groups. Restrictions based on the purpose, scope, or form of association are possible only within the strict limits on fundamental rights restrictions under Article 37(2) of the Constitution and only to the extent that the essence is not infringed. The right of association among the three labor rights is the concretization of such freedom of association in the sphere of labor (see Constitutional Court, en banc decision of December 26, 2008, 2006HEONMA518, etc.). Accordingly, permission for association by workers cannot be recognized, and its purpose, scope, and form may not be arbitrarily restricted unless they exceed the constitutional limits.\\n\\nThe system of establishment report for trade unions under the Trade Union Act cannot be viewed as a licensing system for associations (see Constitutional Court, en banc decision of March 29, 2012, 2011HEONBA53, etc.). However, Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue ultimately prohibits incumbent workers and dismissed workers from forming a trade union. Prohibiting “incumbent workers and dismissed workers from forming an organization in the form of a trade union for the maintenance and improvement of working conditions and the enhancement of workers’ economic and social status” can constitute an unjust restriction on freedom of association. This is because freedom of association may not, absent special circumstances, be restricted by purpose, scope, or form.\\n\\nOne might think that Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue is not unjust because it only prohibits incumbent workers and dismissed workers from forming a “trade union,” not from forming a “non-trade-union organization.” However, the Constitution’s separate guarantee of the right of association through special provisions such as the three labor rights indicates that workers’ association receives special protection unlike general associations (see the above 2011HEONBA53 decision, etc.). To view an association whose substance must necessarily be “an organization for maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing workers’ economic and social status” as not being protected by the right of association merely because, in addition to incumbent workers, dismissed workers are included as members, and to say it is protected only by freedom of association, contradicts the constitutional purport. Moreover, such an interpretation may render freedom of association meaningless in substance while appearing merely to restrict the right of association. Restricting without exception the association between incumbent workers and dismissed workers is the same as restricting the purpose, scope, and form of association.\\n\\nFreedom of association means that anyone may form a group for any purpose and in a form of his or her own choosing. Individuals must be able to freely form groups and the groups themselves must be able to decide their activities and continuity. Thus the purpose and activities pursued through association are guaranteed. To recognize association but disallow the purpose pursued by that association is the same as not recognizing association at all. If an organization intending to act as a trade union is not recognized as a trade union, the result is ultimately a restriction on freedom of association. Unless it is proven that such restriction is absolutely necessary for “national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare” under Article 37(2) of the Constitution, it is an excessive restriction on freedom of association and threatens its essential content. The Trade Union Act, which exists to faithfully guarantee the constitutional three labor rights, must not, through Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, allow even freedom of association to be infringed.\\n\\nb) In light of the significance of a trade union’s existence, uniformly excluding dismissed persons from trade union membership does not accord with the essence of a trade union. Generally, a dismissed person is only a temporary unemployed person or job seeker and is not an employer. Under the Trade Union Act, “worker” should be judged from the perspective of whether there is a need to guarantee rights such as the right of association among persons supplying labor, and persons temporarily unemployed or seeking employment should be included within that scope to the extent there is a need to guarantee the three labor rights. The Supreme Court interpreted the proviso to Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue (“Provided, however, that where a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, he or she shall not be interpreted as a person who is not a worker until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission.”) restrictively, holding that it does not apply to industrial, occupational, or regional trade unions that are not enterprise-based trade unions, thereby recognizing dismissed persons’ membership in industrial, occupational, or regional trade unions (see Supreme Court Decision of February 27, 2004, 2001DU8568, etc.), which can be understood in this context.\\n\\nIn particular, it is difficult to find justification for making a worker who was originally a member unable to be a member of the trade union merely because he or she has been dismissed. The same is true even if the statute provides certain exceptions in relation to applications for relief from unfair labor practices, etc. Prohibiting dismissed persons from joining a trade union is not derived directly from the Constitution but is merely a legislative policy choice under the Trade Union Act. If there were no Trade Union Act, a trade union allowing dismissed persons to join as members could still be formed as a valid trade union. Yet because the Trade Union Act exists, a trade union allowing dismissed persons to join as members loses its status. This conclusion should not be accepted as is. It fundamentally conflicts with the reason for the existence of the Trade Union Act, which is to guarantee the constitutional three labor rights.\\n\\nEven in light of universal international standards, prohibiting dismissed persons from joining trade unions is unjust. In major countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Germany, and France, dismissed or retired persons are not prohibited or restricted from joining trade unions. Moreover, historically it is difficult to find legislative examples that not only deny membership status of a dismissed person because he or she joined as a member but outright deny the legal status of the trade union itself. Even in Japan, whose system is most similar to ours, matters such as “allowing participation by persons representing the employer’s interests,” “receiving financial assistance from the employer for the expenditure of organizational administration,” “being organized solely for mutual-aid or welfare activities,” and “being organized mainly for political or social movements” are regarded as not constituting a trade union, analogous to items (a), (b), (c), and (e) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act, but item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, namely “allowing persons who are not workers to join,” is not excluded from the concept of a trade union. Thus, recognizing dismissed persons’ membership in trade unions is the standard not only in international labor organizations but also in the domestic law of individual countries.\\n\\nConsidering the above circumstances collectively, Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, namely “allowing persons who are not workers to join,” must be interpreted restrictively as not including “allowing a person who was originally a member to retain membership even if dismissed.”\\n\\nThis interpretation appears to go beyond the wording of the proviso to Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue and Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act. However, here it is necessary to consider the purport of the above Constitutional Court decision, 2013HEONMA671, etc. While that decision held constitutional Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, which excludes dismissed teachers from membership in teachers’ trade unions, it also held that even if dismissed teachers not falling under the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act are members, a notice of non-recognition as a trade union cannot automatically be issued, and that issuing such notice on that ground alone is unconstitutional. This ultimately means that membership by dismissed teachers not falling under the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act may be permitted. Although that decision appears on its face to mean that “even if it is a non-statutory trade union, there are cases in which a notice of non-recognition cannot be issued,” its fundamental purport should be understood as “a trade union should not be treated as non-statutory merely because dismissed persons are members.” For to say that “a notice of non-recognition cannot be issued to a non-statutory trade union” is itself contradictory and plainly unjust. Meanwhile, since the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act is a special provision to Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, the above legal principle applies equally to the interpretation of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue. Therefore, it should be interpreted that a trade union may allow dismissed persons to retain membership. This is an interpretation that excludes unconstitutional results without undermining the foundation of the legal system.\\n\\nc) In the case of general trade unions, a “worker” means a person who lives on wages, salary, or other equivalent income regardless of occupation (Article 2(1) of the Trade Union Act), and where membership by “persons who are not workers” is allowed, it shall not be deemed a trade union (main text of the proviso to Article 2(4)(d) of the Trade Union Act); provided, however, that where a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, he or she shall not be interpreted as a person who is not a worker until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission (proviso to Article 2(4)(d) of the Trade Union Act).\\n\\nIn the case of teachers’ trade unions, a “teacher” means a teacher as provided in Article 19(1) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (main text of Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act); provided, however, that a dismissed person who has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission is deemed a teacher until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission (proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act), and where membership by a “person who is not a teacher” is allowed, it shall not be deemed a teachers’ trade union (Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act; main text of the proviso to Article 2(4)(d) of the Trade Union Act).\\n\\nThese provisions concerning general trade unions and teachers’ trade unions appear similar but are different. In the case of general trade unions, a dismissed person is not excluded from the definition of a worker; rather, he or she is excluded in the process of determining “persons who are not workers.” However, in the case of teachers’ trade unions, a dismissed person is excluded outright from the definition of a teacher. In other words, the Teachers’ Trade Union Act regulates dismissed persons’ membership in trade unions more adversely than the Trade Union Act. In the case of general trade unions, even dismissed persons may, in certain cases, be allowed to join through interpretation (the above Supreme Court Decision of February 27, 2004, 2001DU8568, which recognized membership by dismissed persons in industrial, occupational, or regional trade unions, is an example. Meanwhile, the former Trade Union Act, repealed on December 31, 1996, provided, “Provided, however, that a person contesting the validity of a dismissal shall not be interpreted as a person who is not a worker,” so there was even greater room for diverse interpretations); but in the case of teachers’ trade unions, dismissed persons are deemed persons who are not teachers, so such interpretive possibility is, in principle, blocked.\\n\\nThis discrimination is unjust discrimination without rational basis. Once teachers’ trade unions are recognized, there is no special reason or basis to regulate the membership qualification of dismissed persons differently from general trade unions, except that collective action rights, etc. may be restricted differently in light of the constitutional importance of education and the special status of teachers. It is necessary to seek a method to resolve this problem. The point is not to interpret the difference in wording above as meaning that dismissed workers may join general trade unions but dismissed teachers may not join teachers’ trade unions. Rather, the interpretation that despite such difference in wording, dismissed teachers may also be allowed to join teachers’ trade unions, just as dismissed workers may join general trade unions, is the method of curing unjust discrimination. Teachers’ trade unions may be viewed as corresponding not to enterprise-based unions but to industrial, occupational, or regional unions. Accordingly, similar to the provisions of the Trade Union Act and related case law, an interpretation permitting dismissed teachers to join teachers’ trade unions is required.\\n\\nd) Treating a trade union as a non-statutory trade union is ultimately depriving it of its legal status. However, even if denying the membership status of a dismissed person is justifiable, one should regard that, beyond prohibiting dismissed persons from joining as members or imposing certain sanctions on the relevant trade union, one cannot deprive the trade union of its legal status.\\n\\nGenerally, a juridical person or an unincorporated association becomes the subject of rights and obligations independent of its members and exists as a group itself, regardless of changes due to the admission or withdrawal of members (see Supreme Court Decision of July 10, 1992, 92DA2431; Supreme Court Decision of December 12, 1997, 97NU11027; Supreme Court Decision of July 15, 2005, 2003DU5754, etc.). Under Article 6 of the Trade Union Act, a trade union may acquire corporate personality (the Plaintiff completed registration of establishment on July 7, 1999, and acquired corporate personality), and considering Article 2(4), Articles 10, and 11 of the Trade Union Act together, a trade union that has not acquired corporate personality has the substance of an unincorporated association (in light of the definition of a trade union, matters concerning establishment report, and bylaws, there is no doubt as to the group character and independence of a trade union). Depriving a trade union of its status because of membership by a dismissed person runs contrary to the general legal principles applicable to such juridical persons or unincorporated associations.\\n\\ne) One should once again consider what the meaning is of the Statutory Provision at Issue, which provides that where a disqualifying factor exists, it “shall not be deemed a trade union.” Usually, based on this provision, a workers’ organization with a disqualifying factor is called a “non-statutory trade union” in the sense that it is not a statutory trade union. However, strictly according to the statutory provision, a workers’ organization with a disqualifying factor is not a “trade union,” but is not necessarily a “non-statutory trade union.” The use of the concept and term “non-statutory trade union” is already beyond the wording “shall not be deemed a trade union” in order to prevent the harms resulting from strict application of the Statutory Provision at Issue.\\n\\nf) Making a trade union into a non-statutory trade union on account of the existence of a disqualifying factor is far harsher than imposing criminal punishment under Articles 93 and 21 of the Trade Union Act for noncompliance with a corrective order regarding that disqualifying factor. Therefore, in order to issue a notice of non-recognition as a trade union because of membership by dismissed persons, stricter interpretation is required. One must not treat the irrational and unjust result arising from a literal interpretation of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue as an inevitable conclusion.\\n\\nItem (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue should be understood as not applying where it “allows a worker who was originally a member to retain membership even if dismissed.” Such teleological reduction is a constitution-conforming interpretation that accords with the constitutional provisions and the principles of law and realizes them to the fullest extent. By contrast, interpreting it to mean that where a worker who was originally a member is dismissed, allowing that person to retain membership still constitutes “allowing persons who are not workers to join,” and that the legal status of the trade union may be fundamentally deprived on that basis, not only essentially infringes the right of association of trade unions and unjustly discriminates between general trade unions and teachers’ trade unions, but also runs counter to the general legal principles regarding associations and juridical persons.\\n\\n5) Applying the above legal principles to this case. The Supplementary Provision at Issue provides only: “A member who has been unfairly dismissed shall maintain membership notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws.” The Plaintiff is not generally admitting third parties who are not teachers without restriction as members, nor is it unconditionally allowing membership simply because someone was once a teacher in the past. It merely allows membership to be maintained for a teacher who was originally a member and was unfairly dismissed. Of course, the meaning of “unfair dismissal” is somewhat unclear, and the dismissed teachers at issue are persons who have lost their positions by judicial determination or whose dismissal has been confirmed not to be unfair. However, in light of the above legal principles, the Plaintiff’s maintaining the membership status of the dismissed teachers at issue should not result in depriving the Plaintiff of its status as a trade union. Notwithstanding the Supplementary Provision at Issue and some dismissed teachers being members, the Plaintiff should still be regarded as a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act.\\n\\nD. Conclusion\\n\\nThis case is the so-called “hard case” that raises doubts about the methodology of existing legal interpretation. The difficulty does not lie in the obscure wording or complex structure of the statutes. The core issue is that, when a simple and clear provision is interpreted according to its wording and structure, a result contrary to common sense is produced.\\n\\nStatutory interpretation must also consider the consequences of the interpretation. If a literal interpretation of a statute yields an unjust conclusion, one must question whether that is a just interpretation. The majority opinion, without touching the core of the problem inherent in this case, reaches its conclusion solely on the ground that the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid. However, this avoids a substantive determination of the issue.\\n\\nThe true issue in this case is not the Enforcement Decree prescribing notice of non-recognition as a trade union. The essential problem of this case lies in Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, namely the statutory provision that says “if it allows persons who are not workers to join, it shall not be deemed a trade union,” that is, the statutory provision that provides that even after an organization has already been lawfully established as a trade union, the moment it allows persons who are not workers to join, it is no longer a lawful trade union.\\n\\nThe Constitution guarantees the three labor rights as fundamental rights, and the Trade Union Act exists to realize them to the fullest extent. However, Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue destroys the fundamental foundation for the substantive exercise of the three labor rights and thus runs counter to the raison d’être of the Trade Union Act. In such a case, the court should correct this unjust result through proper interpretation in accordance with constitutional norms and the principles of law.\\n\\nIt is not permissible to allow membership by third parties wholly unrelated to the trade union. Nor may every dismissed person be accepted as a member merely because he or she was once a worker. However, in light of the constitutional three labor rights, especially the meaning and purport of the right of association, the membership status of a worker who was engaged as a member and then dismissed should not be denied, and on that basis the legal status of the relevant trade union should not be deprived.\\n\\nThis case should not be judged by moral standards. This case is not about a social evaluation of the Plaintiff’s overall activities as a teachers’ trade union. The issue is solely what the proper interpretation is, from the perspective of the entire legal order including the Constitution, of the statutory provision that would prevent the Plaintiff from maintaining trade union status.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff does not allow membership by third parties unrelated to teachers, nor does it recognize the membership status of all dismissed teachers without restriction. It merely maintains the membership status of teachers who were engaged as members and then dismissed. The Plaintiff’s conduct should be regarded as not exceeding the scope of rights guaranteed by the Constitution. Interpreting Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue as prohibiting even such conduct is contrary to constitutional norms.\\n\\nIn short, before assessing the propriety of the Plaintiff’s “notice” of non-recognition as a trade union, the very view that the Plaintiff is a “non-statutory trade union” is mistaken, and the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue premised thereon is unlawful. The judgment below, which held otherwise, should be reversed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I express this separate opinion, which agrees with the conclusion of the majority opinion but differs as to the reasoning and grounds.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justice Ahn Chulsang\\n\\nA. Legal Nature of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue\\n\\n1) The gist of the majority opinion is that the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue violates the constitutional principle of statutory reservation and is therefore invalid, and accordingly the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, issued on the basis of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, has lost its legal basis and is unlawful. This stance of the majority appears to evade the issue that has long been a subject of social controversy by invoking general constitutional principles, and thus seems to amount to an “escape into constitutional principles.” In other words, it is difficult to say that the majority opinion provides a fundamental answer to the issue that has long been controversial.\\n\\nThe order of state governance, expressed as the democratic basic order and founded on the principle of separation of powers, presupposes the existence of “rational law made by the representatives of the people through democratic procedures.” It is well established that issuing an administrative disposition restricting the freedoms and rights of the people solely on the basis of a presidential decree, without a statute enacted by the National Assembly, the representative organ of the people, is contrary to the principle of administration by law and is invalid. Based on this general principle, the stance that an administrative disposition restricting the freedoms and rights of the people cannot be made without legal basis is entirely proper, and there is no doubt on that point. However, whether this constitutional principle should be applied to the question of validity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue may be examined in relation to the nature of that provision.\\n\\nIn particular, the majority opinion points to “strong” fundamental-rights relevance and “grave” adverse impact as grounds for unconstitutionality of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue. However, freedoms and rights of the people may be restricted only by law, and any restriction not based on law cannot be permitted, no matter how trivial it may be. In other words, if an enforcement-decree provision violates the constitutional principle of statutory reservation, it should be deemed ineffective regardless of whether its connection to fundamental rights is strong or weak, and regardless of whether its adverse impact is grave or not. The majority opinion treats the issue as one of degree, i.e., the extent of restriction on freedoms and rights, as if it were a matter of whether the constitutional principle of statutory reservation is violated, which is not appropriate. Moreover, even if the disposition at issue were unlawful and revoked according to the majority opinion, unless Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act is unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court en banc decision of May 28, 2015, 2013HEONMA671, etc.), the Plaintiff’s problem of violation of law would remain unresolved.\\n\\n2) Where an establishment report for a trade union is filed, the administrative agency must accept it insofar as it meets the statutory establishment requirements. According to the majority opinion, once a trade union’s establishment report has been accepted, its status as a trade union can never be denied under current law. However, in light of the fact that political parties, whose establishment is free under the Constitution, may also be dissolved when their purpose or activities violate the democratic basic order (Article 8(4) of the Constitution), the rights of trade unions should likewise be understood as guaranteed under the constitutional order such as the democratic basic order. Therefore, it is difficult to accept the position that a trade union’s legal status can never be denied under current law regardless of any violation of law.\\n\\nFor example, if a trade union intentionally deceives the administrative authority and obtains acceptance of its establishment report despite a grave disqualifying factor, should it be said that once the establishment report is accepted, its effect can never be excluded? What if the trade union is evidently unlawful, for example, because it is composed around persons representing the employer’s interests and entirely dependent on financial support from the employer, or because it disregards maintenance and improvement of working conditions and instead pursues only political ideology and devotes itself to party activities and election campaigns? It is not appropriate to say that a status once granted can never be withdrawn, no matter how grave the disqualification. This is the same as it would be inappropriate to say that even if there is only a very trivial disqualifying factor, once there is illegality, the status may absolutely be deprived.\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a trade union is an adverse disposition against a trade union, and this is even more so in the case of the Plaintiff, which has existed as a lawful trade union for more than 10 years. However, a notice of non-recognition is not a sanction for violation of a corrective order or failure to comply with a corrective demand by the administrative authority. It merely returns matters to the state prior to the acceptance of the trade union’s establishment report on the ground that the trade union lacks the statutory requirements. Even if the term “notice of non-recognition as a trade union” is used, its substance corresponds to ex officio revocation or withdrawal of the acceptance of the establishment report for the trade union (since the ground for disposition in this case is that a statutory disqualifying factor arose after acceptance of the establishment report, I will focus hereinafter on withdrawal). Viewed this way, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is not the “basis” for a notice of non-recognition as a trade union, but rather a provision prescribing the “procedure” for withdrawing acceptance of the establishment report. In other words, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue should be regarded as an aggravated procedural provision requiring prior notice and opportunity to state opinions concerning an adverse disposition under the Administrative Procedures Act, by limiting withdrawal of the acceptance of the establishment report for a trade union that could otherwise be effected under the general principles of administrative law, and thereby giving the trade union an opportunity for autonomous correction. Ultimately, whether the disposition at issue is lawful should be viewed as a question not of the validity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, but of the lawfulness of such withdrawal.\\n\\n3) It becomes a question whether an administrative agency may withdraw an administrative act on the ground that a new circumstance has arisen after the act was made that makes it impossible to maintain its effect, especially whether withdrawal is possible even in the absence of an explicit legal basis. Even if the measure is merely to return the status conferred by the original disposition to the original state, arbitrarily withdrawing an existing disposition without any legal basis is, in principle, not permissible. However, although it is desirable that such legal basis be expressly stipulated whenever possible, in the complexity and diversity of modern administrative action, it is not easy to include express provisions in all cases.\\n\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court precedents hold that, even if there was no particular defect at the time the disposition was made and even if there is no separate legal basis for withdrawal after the disposition, the original disposition may be withdrawn as a separate administrative disposition that causes it to lose effect if there is a change in circumstances making it unnecessary to maintain the original disposition or if a significant public interest need arises; however, if the original administrative act is beneficial, since it would infringe the vested rights of the addressee, it may be withdrawn only where, after comparing and balancing the public interest need for withdrawal against the disadvantages to the addressee, such as infringement of vested rights, reliance interests, and stability of legal life, the public interest need is strong enough to justify the disadvantages suffered by the addressee (see Supreme Court Decision of February 25, 1986, 85NU664; Supreme Court Decision of November 26, 2004, 2003DU10251, 10268, etc.).\\n\\nThe majority opinion, emphasizing that the legislature abolished the trade union dissolution-order system upon reflective reconsideration, states that the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid and therefore notice of non-recognition is impossible. In light of the fact that the Constitution guarantees workers’ right of association as a fundamental right, there are aspects of the majority’s stance that seek to deny a notice of non-recognition as a trade union that are understandable.\\n\\nHowever, since acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report cannot be said to have an inviolable absolute effect, even considering the purport of abolishing the dissolution-order system, it does not follow that ex officio revocation or withdrawal of the acceptance of establishment report is impermissible. The doctrine of ex officio revocation or withdrawal of administrative acts presupposes the absence of an express legal basis, and there is no reason to distinguish whether the basis was absent from the beginning or has since disappeared. This is because the doctrine exists not to supplement a “deficiency in legislation” but to secure “legality of administration.” The fact that prior precedents, even where individual statutes expressly provide grounds for revocation or withdrawal, have held that ex officio revocation or withdrawal is possible on grounds of other public interest needs not specified as statutory grounds, can also be understood in this context (see Supreme Court Decision of November 26, 2002, 2001DU2874; Supreme Court Decision of February 8, 2007, 2006DU6505; Supreme Court Decision of July 10, 2014, 2013DU7025, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the majority opinion states that the notice-of-non-recognition system is invalid because it is prescribed by an “enforcement decree” rather than by “statute.” It contends that the statute itself does not prescribe notice of non-recognition and does not delegate it to the enforcement decree.\\n\\nHowever, it is questionable whether all problems are resolved merely if the statute directly prescribes notice of non-recognition as a trade union. Considering the majority opinion’s emphasis on the constitutional principle of statutory reservation and the legislative history of the abolition of the trade union dissolution-order system, it appears that if prescribed by statute, notice of non-recognition under that statute may be possible. On the other hand, given the majority opinion’s emphasis on the grave adverse impact of the notice of non-recognition and its claim that it ultimately essentially restricts the constitutional three labor rights, it also seems that even if prescribed by statute, a notice of non-recognition infringing the right of association may not be permitted.\\n\\nThis is precisely the difficulty of the majority opinion. At first glance, it may seem that the fundamental problem is that notice of non-recognition as a trade union is prescribed by an “enforcement decree” rather than by “statute,” but even if it were directly prescribed by statute, the substantive unconstitutionality of the notice of non-recognition itself would remain intact. Since the Trade Union Act defines the concept of a trade union, prescribes its statutory requirements and disqualifying factors, and provides a system of establishment report, it is not a significant issue whether the direct basis for notice of non-recognition lies in a statute or an enforcement decree. The issue is in what cases notice of non-recognition may be given, and what is clear here is that it cannot be assumed that notice of non-recognition may be uniformly issued without considering the substance and degree of the disqualifying factor, the existence and nature of the public interest pursued, and the vested rights and legal stability of the trade union that are infringed. This is precisely the part emphasized by the doctrine limiting ex officio revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts. Prescribing notice of non-recognition in a statute does not solve the problem. One must determine in what cases notice of non-recognition is permissible. Even if notice of non-recognition were prescribed by statute, if it were drafted so as to require uniform issuance without any limitation merely because a disqualifying factor arose, the majority opinion would presumably regard that statute as unconstitutional.\\n\\nIn short, as long as the law defines the concept of a trade union, clearly prescribes its statutory requirements and disqualifying factors, and provides a system of establishment report to implement them, even if the legislature has abolished the trade union dissolution-order system and has not separately enacted statutory provisions on notice of non-recognition, notice of non-recognition may be issued as ex officio revocation or withdrawal of the acceptance of the establishment report for the trade union, provided that a disqualifying factor has arisen. However, because acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report is a beneficial administrative disposition, certain restrictions apply under the doctrine limiting ex officio revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts. The issue is not the “possibility” of notice, but its “propriety.” In other words, the issue is in what cases notice of non-recognition may be issued.\\n\\n4) Ultimately, regardless of the validity or invalidity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, even if that provision did not exist, notice of non-recognition as a trade union could be issued in the sense of withdrawing acceptance of the trade union’s establishment report, according to current statutory provisions and general principles of administrative law. Therefore, the significance of regarding the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue as invalid, as in the majority opinion, is diminished or lost, and the dispute can be resolved only by substantively determining the legality of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue. From this perspective, it would be appropriate to interpret the nature of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue affirmatively, namely that it prescribes the post hoc withdrawal procedure for the beneficial administrative disposition of accepting a trade union’s establishment report and is therefore not invalid. In other words, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is based on the Statutory Provision at Issue that where a disqualifying factor exists it “shall not be deemed a trade union,” and should be understood as prescribing a procedural aggravating requirement that the administrative authority must go through a corrective demand before notifying non-recognition. Regarding the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue as invalid would only remove the corrective demand procedure and thereby produce a result more unfavorable to the trade union.\\n\\nIf the legal nature of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is viewed as withdrawal of the acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report, the issue in this case shifts from whether the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is valid to whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is lawful when comparing and balancing the public interest sought through notice of non-recognition with the disadvantages borne by the Plaintiff. Such comparison and balancing of public and private interests is expressed by the principle of proportionality, and it is self-evident that the principle of proportionality must be observed even when issuing the adverse disposition of notice of non-recognition at issue. Therefore, it cannot be said that the mere circumstance that the Plaintiff allows dismissed teachers to join as members immediately satisfies the requirements for notice of non-recognition. Ultimately, the lawfulness of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances, including the number of dismissed teachers within the Plaintiff, the influence of those dismissed teachers on the Plaintiff’s activities, whether the Plaintiff’s acceptance of dismissed teachers as members contravenes the constitutional order or impairs the essence of a trade union, the public interest achieved through notice of non-recognition against the Plaintiff, and the disadvantages suffered by the Plaintiff due to such notice.\\n\\nB. Whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue Was Lawful\\n\\n1) The Constitution guarantees freedom of association and, in particular, workers’ right of association. The right of association, collective bargaining, and collective action that compose the three labor rights each have independent significance and operate organically as an integral whole while pursuing the common goal of maintaining and improving working conditions. The formation and operation of a trade union constitute the exercise of this right of association itself and serve as the practical foundation for the substantive guarantee of labor basic rights. Therefore, workers should be free to organize or join trade unions unless special circumstances exist, and the system of establishment report prescribed by the Trade Union Act must be understood and operated within the bounds that do not unduly infringe the constitutional meaning and function of such trade unions.\\n\\nExcessive restriction of the right of association of trade unions turns resistance against that point into the immediate main objective of the organization, brings ideologically faithful and militant people to leadership, and tends to radicalize all policy directions as well. When a powerful obstacle stands in sight, the diverse opinions of members disappear and all efforts are concentrated on removing that obstacle. In order to prevent an organization from being buried in ideology, it is necessary to eliminate the room in which ideological issues may become matters of dispute. Providing a place where rational opinions can stand also helps establish a culture of dialogue and discussion characterized by diversity and flexibility.\\n\\n2) Excluding dismissed persons from trade union membership is contrary to the following universal global standards.\\n\\nAdvanced countries and the international community allow dismissed persons to join trade unions and do not deny the status of the relevant trade union merely because dismissed persons are members. It is not easy to find, other than in our country, a legal system that compels a person who was until then a fellow member to be excluded from a trade union merely because he or she was dismissed by the employer. This directly contravenes the essence and spirit of trade unions. Such universal global standards may be temporarily resisted, but in a healthy society they are standards that will eventually be reached.\\n\\nThe International Labour Organization (ILO), as of June 2020, designates 8 conventions in 4 areas concerning the most fundamental labor rights out of a total of 190 conventions as “Fundamental Conventions” and strongly recommends their ratification and observance by all member states. Among them, the Convention Concerning Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise (Convention No. 87) provides in Article 2: “Workers and employers, without distinction whatsoever and without previous authorization, have the right to establish and, subject only to the rules of the organization concerned, to join organizations of their own choosing.” This establishes as an international labor standard the principle of universal guarantee of the right of association without any discrimination or prior governmental authorization.\\n\\nIn fact, on March 26, 2014, the 320th Governing Body of the International Labour Organization adopted the 371st report of the Committee on Freedom of Association, which contained recommendations concerning the South Korean Government’s violation of freedom of association. There, the Committee stated that “the prohibition on union membership by dismissed persons under item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act [Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue] violates freedom of association.” Furthermore, in its 382nd report of June 17, 2017, the Committee on Freedom of Association, directly in relation to this case, presented the same view and recommended that it “again strongly urges the Korean Government to take the necessary measures to repeal without delay the relevant provisions of law prohibiting dismissed persons from becoming members, and to provide detailed information thereon.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the European Union (EU), based on the Free Trade Agreement between the Republic of Korea and the European Union and its Member States, which entered into force in 2011, has continuously raised issues concerning the South Korean Government’s protection of labor fundamental rights, including by initiating dispute-settlement procedures on the ground that Korea’s efforts to ratify the ILO fundamental conventions are insufficient.
