For a labor union to be established under the Trade Union Act, the establishment report must be accepted, but this cannot be a basis for saying that a labor union becomes a non-statutory union only if there is a notice of non-recognition when a disqualifying ground arises. This is because the Trade Union Act expressly provides for the establishment report of a labor union, but contains no provision whatsoever regarding notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law. Therefore, even if the establishment report of a labor union is viewed as an element of the labor union’s establishment, it cannot be said that a separate requirement of notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law is necessarily required to negate such status.\\n\\nFor example, if a labor union filed an establishment report by forging documents or deceiving the administrative authority, the administrative authority should be able to take measures to deny the union’s legal status. In such a case, it is not to mention insufficient to say that the administrative authority can only issue a corrective order and impose a criminal punishment of up to 5 million won for noncompliance (Articles 93 and 21 of the Trade Union Act). Even if the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue were invalid or did not exist at all, the administrative authority must be able to take measures such as notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law with respect to a labor union that has acquired a statutory disqualifying ground.\\n\\nThe majority opinion does not properly explain, beyond declaring the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue invalid, what the legal status of a labor union with a disqualifying ground is, or how the concrete legal relations in this case are to be understood. This evades the core of the issue and avoids a substantive determination.\\n\\n3) Even if the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue were invalid, the question arises whether that fact alone immediately makes the notice of non-recognition at issue unlawful, or whether it becomes unlawful only under the doctrine limiting ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions.\\n\\nOriginally, the agency that issued an administrative act may, if the act has defects, cancel it on its own even without a separate legal basis, and even if there was no particular defect at the time of the act and no separate legal basis for withdrawing it thereafter, it may withdraw it by a separate administrative act that extinguishes its effect if there is a change in circumstances making it unnecessary to maintain the original act, or if a serious public interest necessity arises. However, if the original administrative act was beneficial, there is only a certain limitation that the vested rights of the addressee of the disposition must be considered (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 85NU664 on 1986. 2. 25., Supreme Court judgments rendered on 2003DU10251 and 10268 on 2004. 11. 26., among others). Since acceptance of a labor union’s establishment report is a beneficial administrative disposition that recognizes a labor union satisfying the statutory establishment requirements as a lawful labor union and thereby grants the legal status to enjoy the special protections under the Trade Union Act, the notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law ultimately corresponds to ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of such acceptance of establishment report. Therefore, the administrative authority may issue a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law in the sense of ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of the existing acceptance disposition even without separate legal basis, subject only to certain limitations that it must consider the vested rights of the relevant labor union in the process.\\n\\nHowever, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue provides that if there is no compliance with a corrective request, a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law must be issued. Since the Trade Union Act clearly sets forth the legal requirements for a labor union, a notice of non-recognition must necessarily be issued where those requirements are violated. This should be understood as meaning that exceptional limitations on ex officio cancellation or withdrawal are not permitted. Where there is an express provision denying such limitations, the general legal principles concerning limitations on ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions cannot be applied, apart from issues of constitutionality or legality of that provision. And, as seen above, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue has a direct basis in the statutory provision at issue and may be regarded as intended to provide the labor union with an opportunity for autonomous correction, so there is no reason to regard it as invalid.\\n\\n4) In short, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue prescribes that a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law shall be given to a labor union with a disqualifying ground. There is no exception. The provision is binding and leaves no room for discretion. Therefore, under the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, the administrative authority must, after going through the corrective request procedure, issue a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law to a labor union that permits membership by a person who is not a worker if correction is not made.\\n\\nThe meaning of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is thus very clear, and it should be regarded as constitutional and proper because it concretizes what the Act provides. The core issue is not the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue but how the meaning of the statutory provision at issue should be understood.\\n\\nC. How should the statutory provision at issue be interpreted?\\n\\n1) Item (d) of the statutory provision at issue provides: “Where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted, it shall not be deemed a labor union.”\\n\\n“Shall not be deemed a labor union” should be understood as a so-called deeming provision, and unlike a presumption provision, it does not allow contrary proof (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 94DA52751 on 1995. 2. 17. concerning Article 28 of the Civil Act, among others). Whether the provision uses the expression “shall be deemed” or the expression “shall not be deemed,” both are deeming provisions, and there is no reason to treat the two differently. Therefore, where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted, it cannot be regarded as a labor union.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that the statutory provision at issue is a criterion for determining a statutory labor union and that, according to that criterion, a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law is issued; but it says that even if a disqualifying ground arises, the labor union is not yet a non-statutory union unless a notice of non-recognition is issued. However, a deeming provision is one that, when certain prerequisite requirements are satisfied, recognizes without exception the existence or occurrence of the facts or effects prescribed by law, even if in reality it does not match the factual or legal state. Rather, this unconditional legal fiction lies at the essence of a deeming provision. Since the meaning and effect of a legal provision do not vary depending on where in the statute it is located, it cannot be said that the meaning and effect differ merely because the deeming provision is located in the definitional part of the legal terms used in the Act. Therefore, under item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted, that labor union is no longer a lawful labor union.\\n\\nThe above situation does not change depending on whether it arises before or after establishment reporting. No provision of the Trade Union Act treats the concept of a labor union differently depending on whether establishment reporting has occurred. Article 2 of the Trade Union Act is a definitional provision concerning labor unions, and accordingly determines the subjects to which the Act applies; it should therefore be understood as applicable regardless of whether establishment reporting has been filed.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 2 of the Trade Union Act states, “The definitions of the terms used in this Act shall be as follows,” and item 1 provides, “The term ‘worker’ means a person who lives by wages, salary, or other equivalent income regardless of the kind of occupation,” while item (d) of the proviso to item 4 [item (d) of the statutory provision at issue] provides, “Where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted. Provided, however, that if a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, such person shall not be construed as a person who is not a worker until the National Labor Relations Commission renders a reexamination award.” According to these provisions of the Trade Union Act, a dismissed person is a worker “until, after filing an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, a reexamination award is rendered by the National Labor Relations Commission,” but after the reexamination award, such person is no longer a worker.\\n\\nIn the end, under item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, even a labor union that has already completed establishment reporting cannot be regarded as a statutory labor union any longer if it permits membership of dismissed persons. This is an interpretation according to the wording of the Trade Union Act.\\n\\n2) As seen above, a deeming provision does not allow contrary proof. Ultimately, under item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, which takes the form of a deeming provision, if a lawfully established labor union accepts even one dismissed person as a member, that union reaches the conclusion that it is not a labor union within the meaning of the Trade Union Act. But is such a conclusion really justified? The problem begins here.\\n\\nThere is a view that, in this case, the issue is that the Plaintiff not only tolerated some dismissed persons as members but also explicitly permitted this through its Articles of Association. However, whether a labor union provides in its Articles of Association that dismissed persons may become members is not the essential issue. If a certain labor union has no provision allowing dismissed persons to join as members but in fact has dismissed persons as members, does that labor union not constitute a non-statutory union? Conversely, what if a labor union has a provision allowing dismissed persons to join as members, but in fact has no dismissed members? When determining whether a labor union permitting membership of dismissed persons is a non-statutory union, whether it is prescribed in the Articles of Association is not decisive. The conclusion may differ depending on how the acceptance of dismissed persons as members is normatively evaluated.\\n\\nOne may consider a solution to this issue from the perspective of the “autonomy” of the labor union. That is, when it is revealed at the establishment-report stage that membership of dismissed persons is permitted, the establishment report should be returned (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2011DU6998 on 2014. 4. 10., among others), but where a labor union has already completed establishment reporting and permits dismissed persons to become members, the existence of a disqualifying ground is determined only if the autonomy of the labor union is thereby impaired. However, such a solution not only contradicts the purpose of the Act, but also lacks realism. First, the fact that the Trade Union Act categorically does not permit membership by persons who are not workers should be understood as a preventive measure in light of the high likelihood that the autonomy of the labor union will be impaired immediately or at least in the near future if membership by persons who are not workers is permitted. There is no reason to view a labor union that has already completed establishment reporting differently. Also, for the administrative authority to examine and determine the autonomy of a labor union is a very difficult issue. Moreover, after establishment reporting, unlike at the establishment-report stage, the administrative authority competent for labor union establishment reporting has no separate investigative authority or special investigative methods for examining autonomy. It is neither contemplated by the Trade Union Act nor consistent with the realities of labor administration to require the administrative authority to separately examine and determine the autonomy of a labor union for purposes of a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law.\\n\\nOne may also consider strictly interpreting the “membership” part in item (d) of the statutory provision at issue. This view would hold that the provision merely prohibits new membership by persons who are not workers, including dismissed persons, and does not prohibit the retention of membership status by persons who were already members and then became dismissed. This would accord with the dictionary meaning of “membership” as entering an organization or group. The requirements for joining a group and the requirements for leaving it need not necessarily be identical. Under this view, because the Plaintiff merely allowed dismissed persons to retain their membership status and did not permit new membership by dismissed persons, it would be easy to conclude that the Plaintiff is not a non-statutory union.\\n\\nHowever, in general, item (d) of the statutory provision at issue is understood as including not only new membership by persons who are not workers but also the case where membership status of persons who are not workers is allowed to continue. As seen above, since the proviso to item (d) of the statutory provision at issue provides that “Provided, however, that if a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, such person shall not be construed as a person who is not a worker until the National Labor Relations Commission renders a reexamination award,” a dismissed person is a worker only until a reexamination award by the National Labor Relations Commission after filing such application; in other cases, such a person cannot be regarded as a worker, and therefore where a dismissed person who is not a worker is a member, the requirements of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue are satisfied. The same applies to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act, and the Constitutional Court has decided on the premise that the provision excludes dismissed teachers from membership in teachers’ labor unions (the above decision in 2013Hun-Ma671 et al.). In light of such circumstances, an interpretation restricting the term “membership” in the main text of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue to new membership cannot be adopted, because it cannot explain the existence and meaning of the proviso to the same item.\\n\\n3) Under the prevailing view concerning item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, there seems to be no room for reaching a different conclusion regarding the notice of non-recognition issued to the Plaintiff by way of interpretation. From this perspective, there is a view that the issue of dismissed persons’ membership status is a matter to be improved through legislation rather than through interpretation of law, even if there are unfair aspects in the current law, and that it cannot be resolved by statutory interpretation.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court, while holding Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act excluding dismissed teachers from membership in teachers’ labor unions to be constitutional, stated that whether to issue a notice of non-recognition as a labor union to a teachers’ labor union that recognizes dismissed persons as members may be determined at the discretion of the administrative authority and the courts, comprehensively considering “the number of unqualified members active in the teachers’ labor union, the influence of such members on the activities of the teachers’ labor union, whether the administrative authorities took appropriate measures to prohibit or restrict the labor union activities of unqualified members, and whether the relevant labor union has the possibility of correcting this” (the above decision in 2013Hun-Ma671 et al.). However, if excluding dismissed persons from membership is constitutional, then a labor union that allows dismissed persons as members cannot be said to be a lawful labor union. The statement that notice of non-recognition may be issued to such a labor union at discretion is inconsistent, as noted above, with the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, which states that a labor union that permits membership of dismissed persons “shall” be notified as not a labor union. Moreover, legislation in the National Assembly allowing membership by dismissed persons has remained stagnant for years. While the Government itself submitted an amendment bill to the National Assembly permitting membership by dismissed persons, it still maintains the position in this case that the Plaintiff is a non-statutory union. This issue now awaits only the Supreme Court’s decision.\\n\\nAs a rule, statutes are to be interpreted faithfully to their wording, but there are cases where an exception must be recognized. There are cases where matters were not regulated by statute, or were insufficiently regulated, because the legislature at the time of enactment could not anticipate them at all; there are also cases where, although an express provision exists, an inevitable gap arises between the statute and actual life as times change and society changes. If one insists on strict application of an express provision, legal stability may be maintained, but problems may arise in terms of reduced adaptability to social change and development; thus, it is necessary to interpret statutes so as to conform to actual life. In such cases, the court must not be bound by a formal literal interpretation, but must discern the legislative purpose that the statute seeks to realize and give meaning to the law in a direction that fulfills that purpose, and, to the extent necessary for that realization, it must exercise a practical law-making function by interpreting the express provision expansively or restrictively. So long as the meaning and essence of the statutory provision are not changed, it is necessary to adapt an outmoded statute to advancing social phenomena by reasonable interpretation, and one must not resign oneself to simply following the traditional interpretation and application of the outdated provision until the legislature amends it (see Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on 78DO246 on 1978. 4. 25., Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on 95DA36466 on 1998. 4. 23., among others).\\n\\nA legal norm cannot perfectly regulate all matters that occur in reality. Because of its general and abstract nature, the law is inherently bound to contain defects. Therefore, statutory interpretation is not limited to merely recognizing or discovering an existing statute. In some cases, it is necessary to actively shape the law by analogy or teleological reduction to clarify the scope of application of the statute. This is the demand of substantive rule of law. The court must declare not merely the “statute” but the “law.”\\n\\nWhen interpreting and applying law, one must consider the result. If, as a result of interpretation, a highly irrational or unjust conclusion is reached, one must seek a way to exclude such an interpretation. Ordinarily, for this purpose, various interpretive methods are employed in addition to literal interpretation, such as logical/systematic interpretation, historical interpretation, and teleological interpretation. If, despite such efforts, irrationality and injustice are not corrected, the court must interpret beyond the wording of the law, and sometimes even adopt a just interpretation contrary to the wording.\\n\\nThis method of interpretation is by no means new. The Supreme Court interpreted the phrase “when reducing a fine, it shall be to one-half of the maximum amount” in Article 55(1) item 6 of the Criminal Act as meaning “one-half of the amount,” and held that both the upper and lower limits were reduced by one-half (Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on 78DO246 on 1978. 4. 25.). Even though Article 75 item 6 of the Bills Act provides “date and place of issuance” as requisites of a bill, the Supreme Court interpreted that “even if the place of issuance is not stated on the face of the bill, if, considering the other entries on the bill, it is recognized that the bill was issued within the country for the purpose of producing bill effects, it cannot be regarded as an invalid bill” (Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on 95DA36466 on 1998. 4. 23.).\\n\\nStatutory interpretation must reflect constitutional provisions and their purpose. Where various interpretations are possible with respect to a statutory provision, first, a constitutional-conforming interpretation should be adopted by choosing the meaning that accords with the Constitution and thereby eliminating unconstitutionality; further, among constitutionally conforming interpretations, a constitutionally oriented interpretation should be adopted that chooses the meaning that best realizes constitutional principles and values. If, as a result of interpreting a statutory provision in light of its wording, structure, and legislative history, an irrational or unjust conclusion is reached, it can be corrected through such a constitutional-conforming interpretation that takes the Constitution into account.\\n\\n4) Then is this case truly one where interpretation beyond, or even contrary to, the wording of the law is necessary in light of the Constitution?\\n\\na) The Constitution provides in Article 33(1) that “Workers shall have the right to independent association, collective bargaining, and collective action in order to improve working conditions,” thereby guaranteeing workers’ right of association. For this purpose, Article 1 of the Trade Union Act provides: “This Act aims, by guaranteeing the worker’s right to association, collective bargaining, and collective action under the Constitution, to promote the maintenance and improvement of working conditions and the economic and social status of workers, and to contribute to the maintenance of industrial peace and the development of the national economy by fairly adjusting labor relations and preventing and resolving labor disputes.” And Article 37(2) of the Constitution clearly defines the limits on the restriction of fundamental rights by providing: “All freedom and rights of citizens may be restricted by Act only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even when they are restricted, the essential aspect of freedom and rights shall not be violated.”\\n\\nThe right of association includes not only the individual right of each worker to organize or join and act in a labor union or other workers’ organization, but also the collective right of workers’ organizations to exist and function (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 95Hun-Ma154 on 1999. 11. 25., among others). Therefore, the right of association of a labor union may be restricted only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even then the essential content of the right of association may not be infringed. The legislature must respect these constitutional provisions and principles when enacting labor-related laws such as the Trade Union Act, and the courts must also ensure, when interpreting labor-related laws, that those constitutional provisions and principles are realized to the fullest extent possible.\\n\\nThe formation and joining of a labor union are exercises of the right of association itself, and because a labor union becomes an indispensable foundation for exercising fundamental labor rights, the establishment and continuation of a labor union must be protected to the fullest extent possible. The Trade Union Act must be interpreted and applied in a way that maximally guarantees the right of association of labor unions, and it must not produce the unjust result that the Trade Union Act, which exists to guarantee fundamental labor rights, instead restricts the right of association of labor unions.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the issue in this case is also an important matter at the level of freedom of association before the above right of association. Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees freedom of association to all citizens in paragraph 1 and provides in paragraph 2 that no permit shall be required for association. Association means a group in which a plurality of natural persons or legal entities freely combine for a common purpose over a reasonable period, with the capacity for organized will formation (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 2000Hun-Ba84 on 2002. 9. 19., among others). Because freedom of association is neutral as to the purpose of the organization, the formation of all organizations is protected regardless of purpose. Since deciding the scope and form of association is itself a matter of freedom, it is not for the state to intervene in how and in what form people will organize. Restrictions based on the purpose, scope, or form of association are possible only within the strict limits on fundamental-right restrictions under Article 37(2) of the Constitution and only so long as the essence is not infringed. The right of association among the three labor rights is the concretization of such freedom of association in the sphere of labor (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 2006Hun-Ma518 on 2008. 12. 26., among others). Therefore, permission for workers’ association cannot be denied, and its purpose, scope, and form also cannot be arbitrarily restricted unless the constitutional limits are exceeded.\\n\\nThe establishment-report system for labor unions under the Trade Union Act cannot be viewed as a licensing system for associations (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 2011Hun-Ba53 on 2012. 3. 29., among others). Yet item (d) of the statutory provision at issue ultimately prohibits incumbent workers and dismissed workers from forming a labor union. Such a prohibition on “incumbent workers and dismissed workers forming an organization in the form of a labor union to maintain and improve working conditions and enhance the economic and social status of workers” may constitute an unjust restriction on freedom of association. This is because freedom of association cannot, absent special circumstances, be restricted based on purpose, scope, or form.\\n\\nOne might think that item (d) of the statutory provision at issue is not unjust because it merely prohibits incumbent workers and dismissed workers from forming a “labor union,” not from forming a “non-labor-union organization.” However, the reason the Constitution separately guarantees the right of association through special provisions such as the three labor rights is precisely to provide special protection to workers’ association, distinct from ordinary associations (see the above decision in 2011Hun-Ba53, among others). To regard an association whose substance can only be “an organization for maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing the economic and social status of workers” as not being protected by the right of association, merely because it includes dismissed workers as members in addition to incumbent workers, and to say that it can be protected only by freedom of association, is contrary to the constitutional purpose described above. Such an interpretation may also render freedom of association meaningless in substance despite its outward appearance of merely restricting the right of association. Restricting association between incumbent workers and dismissed workers without exception is the same as restricting the purpose, scope, or form of association.\\n\\nFreedom of association means that anyone may form an organization for any purpose in a form of their own choosing. Individuals must be able to freely organize, and the organization itself must be able to decide its activities and continuation. In this way, the objectives and activities pursued through association are protected. Recognizing association but disallowing the purpose pursued by that association is equivalent to not recognizing association at all. If an organization that seeks to function as a labor union is not recognized as a labor union, the result is a restriction on freedom of association. Unless it is proven that such a restriction is absolutely necessary for “national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare” under Article 37(2) of the Constitution, it is an excessive restriction on freedom of association and threatens the essential content of freedom of association. The Trade Union Act, which exists to faithfully guarantee the three labor rights under the Constitution, should not allow the result that even freedom of association is infringed through item (d) of the statutory provision at issue.\\n\\nb) In light of the significance of labor unions, a blanket exclusion of dismissed persons from the members of a labor union is not consistent with the essence of a labor union. In general, a dismissed person is merely a temporarily unemployed person or job seeker and does not correspond to an employer. Under the Trade Union Act, “worker” should be determined from the perspective of whether there is a need to guarantee rights such as the right of association among providers of labor, and persons temporarily unemployed or seeking employment should also be included to the extent that there is a need to guarantee their three labor rights. The Supreme Court, by narrowly interpreting the proviso to item (d) of the statutory provision at issue (“Provided, however, that if a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, such person shall not be construed as a person who is not a worker until the National Labor Relations Commission renders a reexamination award.”) as not applying to industrial labor unions, occupational labor unions, or regional labor unions that are not enterprise-based labor unions, recognized membership by dismissed persons in industrial, occupational, and regional labor unions (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2001DU8568 on 2004. 2. 27., among others), which can be understood in this context.\\n\\nIn particular, it is difficult to acknowledge the legitimacy of making an originally member worker unable to become a member of a labor union merely because he or she was dismissed. The same is true even if the law has certain exceptions in relation to applications for relief from unfair labor practices. Disallowing dismissed persons from joining labor unions is not directly derived from the Constitution, but is merely a legislative policy choice under the Trade Union Act. If the Trade Union Act did not exist, a labor union that permits membership by dismissed persons could also be established as a valid labor union. Yet because the Trade Union Act exists, a labor union that permits membership by dismissed persons ends up having its status denied. This conclusion should not be accepted as it stands. It fundamentally contradicts the raison d’être of the Trade Union Act, which exists to guarantee the three labor rights under the Constitution.\\n\\nEven in light of the universal standards of the international community, disallowing dismissed persons from joining labor unions is unjust. In major countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Germany, and France, dismissal or retirement does not bar or restrict membership in a labor union. Moreover, it is historically difficult to find legislative examples that not only deny the membership status of a dismissed person but deny the very legal status of the labor union itself merely because a dismissed person has joined as a member. In Japan, which has a system most similar to ours, items (a), (b), (c), and (e) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act—such as “where participation by a person representing the employer’s interests is permitted,” “where financial assistance from the employer is received for expenses for the operation of the organization,” “where the sole purpose is welfare or mutual aid business,” and “where the main purpose is political or social movements”—are treated as not falling under labor unions, but item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, namely “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted,” is not excluded from the concept of a labor union. Thus, recognizing dismissed persons’ membership in labor unions is the standard not only at the level of international labor organizations, but also at the level of individual states’ positive law.\\n\\nConsidering the above circumstances in combination, item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, namely “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted,” should be construed restrictively as not including “where a person who was originally a member is allowed to retain membership even if dismissed.”\\n\\nThis interpretation appears to go beyond the wording of the proviso to item (d) of the statutory provision at issue and the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act. However, here it is necessary to consider the purport of the above-mentioned Constitutional Court decision in 2013Hun-Ma671 et al. That decision held that Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act excluding dismissed teachers from membership is constitutional, but also stated that a teachers’ labor union cannot automatically be subject to a notice of non-recognition as a labor union merely because a dismissed teacher who does not fall under the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act is a member, and that issuing such a notice for that reason alone would be unconstitutional. This ultimately means that a dismissed teacher who does not fall under the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act may be allowed to join a teachers’ labor union. Although the above decision may outwardly appear to say that there are cases where notice of non-recognition cannot be issued even to a non-statutory union, its fundamental purport should be understood as saying that a union should not be deemed a non-statutory union merely because a dismissed person is a member. This is because saying that notice of non-recognition cannot be issued to a non-statutory union is itself contradictory and plainly unjust. Meanwhile, since the proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act is a special provision relative to item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, the above legal principle can be applied directly to the interpretation of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue as well. Therefore, it should be interpreted that a labor union may allow dismissed persons to retain membership status. This is the interpretation that avoids unconstitutional results without undermining the foundation of the legal system.\\n\\nc) For ordinary labor unions, “worker” means a person who lives by wages, salary, or other equivalent income regardless of occupation (Article 2(1) of the Trade Union Act), and where membership of a “person who is not a worker” is permitted, it shall not be deemed a labor union [main text of item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act]; provided, however, that if a dismissed person has filed an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission, the person shall not be construed as a person who is not a worker until the National Labor Relations Commission renders a reexamination award [proviso to item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act].\\n\\nFor teachers’ labor unions, “teacher” means the teacher provided for in Article 19(1) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (main text of Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act); provided, however, that a dismissed person who has filed an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission is deemed a teacher until a reexamination award by the National Labor Relations Commission is rendered (proviso to Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act), and where membership of a “person who is not a teacher” is permitted, it shall not be deemed a teachers’ labor union [Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act, main text of item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act].\\n\\nThe above provisions regarding ordinary labor unions and teachers’ labor unions appear identical, but there are differences. In the case of an ordinary labor union, a dismissed person is not excluded from the definition of worker, but is excluded in the process of determining a “person who is not a worker.” In the case of a teachers’ labor union, however, a dismissed person is excluded from the definition of teacher itself. In other words, the Teachers’ Labor Union Act regulates dismissed persons’ membership in labor unions more unfavorably than the Trade Union Act. In the case of ordinary labor unions, even if a person is dismissed, there may still be room for labor union membership to be permitted depending on the interpretation in certain cases (the above Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2001DU8568 on 2004. 2. 27., which recognized dismissed persons’ membership in industrial, occupational, and regional labor unions, is an example. Meanwhile, the former Trade Union Act repealed on 1996. 12. 31. provided that “a person challenging the effectiveness of dismissal shall not be construed as a person who is not a worker,” so there was even greater room for diverse interpretation), whereas in the case of teachers’ labor unions, a dismissed person is deemed a person who is not a teacher, so in principle such interpretive possibility is blocked.\\n\\nSuch discrimination is unjust discrimination without rational basis. Once teachers’ labor unions are recognized, apart from the separate issue of whether collective action rights may be restricted differently from ordinary labor unions in view of the constitutional importance of education or the special status of teachers, there is no particular reason or basis to regulate the membership status of dismissed persons differently from ordinary labor unions. It is necessary to seek a way to resolve this issue. It should not be interpreted, by emphasizing the difference in wording described above, that membership in ordinary labor unions by dismissed workers may be allowed while membership in teachers’ labor unions by dismissed teachers may not be allowed. Despite the difference in wording, the interpretive method that can correct the unjust discrimination is to interpret that, just as ordinary labor unions may allow dismissed workers to join, dismissed teachers may also be allowed to join teachers’ labor unions. A teachers’ labor union may be seen as corresponding to industrial, occupational, or regional labor unions rather than enterprise-based labor unions. Therefore, similar to the provisions of the Trade Union Act and the related case law discussed above, an interpretation allowing dismissed teachers to join teachers’ labor unions is necessary.\\n\\nd) Treating a labor union as a non-statutory union ultimately deprives that labor union of its legal status. However, even if denying the membership status of dismissed persons is justified, it should be understood that one cannot go beyond prohibiting membership by dismissed persons or imposing certain sanctions on the relevant labor union and deprive the labor union of its legal status.\\n\\nIn general, a juristic person or an association without legal personality becomes a subject of rights and duties independently of its human members, and exists as the organization itself regardless of changes arising from the joining or withdrawal of members (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 92DA2431 on 1992. 7. 10., on 97NU11027 on 1997. 12. 12., on 2003DU5754 on 2005. 7. 15., among others). Under Article 6 of the Trade Union Act, a labor union may acquire legal personality (the Plaintiff completed registration of establishment and acquired legal personality on 1999. 7. 7.), and when Article 2(4), Article 10, Article 11, and related provisions of the Trade Union Act are considered together, a labor union that has not acquired legal personality has the substance of an association without legal personality (in light of the definition of a labor union, establishment reporting matters, constitution matters, etc., there can be no doubt as to the organizational and independent character of a labor union). To deprive a labor union of its status on the ground that a dismissed person has joined as a member runs counter to these general legal principles concerning juristic persons and associations without legal personality.\\n\\ne) It is necessary once again to consider what the meaning is of the statutory provision at issue stating that where a disqualifying ground exists, it “shall not be deemed a labor union.” Generally, based on this provision, a workers’ organization with a disqualifying ground is called a “non-statutory union” in the sense that it is not a labor union under the law. However, strictly speaking, a workers’ organization with a disqualifying ground is not a “labor union” but not necessarily a non-statutory union. The use of the concept and term “non-statutory union” already goes beyond the wording “shall not be deemed a labor union” in order to prevent the harm resulting from the strict application of the statutory provision at issue.\\n\\nf) Turning a labor union into a non-statutory union on the ground that a disqualifying factor exists is a far harsher infringing disposition than criminal punishment under Articles 93 and 21 of the Trade Union Act for failure to comply with a corrective order concerning that disqualifying factor. Therefore, a stricter interpretation is required to issue a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law on the ground of membership by dismissed persons. The statutory provision at issue should be understood as not applying where “a worker who was originally a member is allowed to retain membership even after dismissal.” Such teleological reduction conforms to constitutional provisions and the principles of law and is a constitutional-conforming interpretation that realizes them to the fullest extent. By contrast, interpreting that “where a worker who was originally a member is allowed to retain membership even after dismissal” also falls under “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted,” and that legal status as a labor union can be deprived ab initio on that ground, not only essentially infringes the right of association of the labor union and unjustly discriminates between ordinary labor unions and teachers’ labor unions, but also conflicts with the general legal principles governing associations and juristic persons.\\n\\n5) In light of the above legal principles, let us examine this case. The supplementary provision at issue merely provides that “a member who has been unfairly dismissed shall retain membership status notwithstanding Article 6(1) of the Articles of Association.” The Plaintiff is not indiscriminately accepting third parties who are not teachers as members, nor is it permitting anyone to join as a member merely because they were formerly teachers. It merely allows retention of membership status only when a teacher who was originally a member is unfairly dismissed. Of course, the meaning of “unfair dismissal” is somewhat unclear, and the dismissed teachers in this case are persons who lost their positions according to judicial determinations or whose dismissal has been finally confirmed not to be unfair dismissal. However, in light of the above legal principles, the Plaintiff’s maintenance of the membership status of the dismissed teachers in this case should not lead to depriving the Plaintiff of its status as a labor union. Despite the supplementary provision at issue and some dismissed teacher members, the Plaintiff should still be regarded as a labor union under the Teachers’ Labor Union Act.\\n\\nD. Conclusion\\n\\nThis case is a so-called “hard case” that calls into question the methodology of existing legal interpretation. The difficulty does not lie in obscure statutory wording or a complex structure. The core issue is that interpreting a simple and clear provision according to its wording and structure leads to a result contrary to common sense.\\n\\nStatutory interpretation must also consider the result of the interpretation. If an unjust conclusion results from interpreting the statute according to its wording, one must question whether that is a just interpretation. The majority opinion reaches its conclusion solely on the basis that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is invalid, without addressing the core issue embedded in this case. However, this evades a substantive determination of the issue.\\n\\nThe true issue in this case is not the enforcement decree prescribing a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law. The essential problem lies in item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, namely, the statutory provision that says a labor union “shall not be deemed a labor union” where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted, that is, the provision that even after a labor union has already been lawfully established, it is no longer a lawful labor union the moment it permits membership by a person who is not a worker.\\n\\nThe Constitution guarantees the three labor rights as fundamental rights, and the Trade Union Act exists to realize them to the fullest extent possible. However, item (d) of the statutory provision at issue undermines the fundamental foundation for the substantive exercise of the three labor rights and is contrary to the raison d’être of the Trade Union Act. In such a case, the court must correct this unjust result through just interpretation in accordance with constitutional norms and the principles of law.\\n\\nIt is not permissible to allow membership by third parties who have no relation to a labor union. Nor can all dismissed persons be accepted as members merely because they were once workers. However, in light of the meaning and purpose of the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution, especially the right of association, the membership status of a worker who was active as a member and then was dismissed should not be denied, and on that basis the legal status of the relevant labor union should not be deprived.\\n\\nOne should not judge this case by a moral yardstick. This case is not about a social evaluation of the Plaintiff’s overall activities as a teachers’ labor union. The only issue is what the just interpretation is, from the standpoint of the Constitution and the legal order as a whole, of the statutory provision that would deprive the Plaintiff of its status as a labor union.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff is not allowing membership by third parties unrelated to teachers, nor is it allowing all dismissed teachers to retain membership without restriction. It merely allows the membership status of teachers who were active as members and then dismissed to be maintained. This conduct of the Plaintiff should be regarded as not exceeding the scope of protection of constitutional fundamental rights. Interpreting item (d) of the statutory provision at issue as prohibiting even such conduct runs counter to constitutional norms.\\n\\nIn short, before judging the propriety of the “notice” of non-recognition as a labor union under the law issued to the Plaintiff, the very act of regarding the Plaintiff as a “non-statutory union” is erroneous, and the notice of non-recognition at issue premised on that view is unlawful. The lower judgment, which held otherwise, must be reversed.\\n\\nAlthough I concur with the majority opinion as to the conclusion, I state this separate opinion because my reasons and grounds differ.\\n\\n5. Separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang\\n\\nA. Legal nature of the notice of non-recognition at issue as a labor union under the law\\n\\n1) The gist of the majority opinion is that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue violates the constitutional principle of statutory reservation and is therefore invalid, and thus the notice of non-recognition at issue based on the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue has lost its legal basis and is unlawful. This attitude of the majority opinion appears to “escape into constitutional principles,” in that it does not directly confront and determine the problem of the notice of non-recognition at issue, which has long been a subject of social controversy, but instead reaches its conclusion by invoking general constitutional principles. In other words, it is difficult to view the majority opinion as having provided a fundamental answer to the problem that has been controversial until now.\\n\\nThe order of state functioning expressed as a democratic constitutional order, based on the principle of separation of powers, presupposes the existence of “rational law enacted by representatives of the people through democratic procedures.” It is a widely known principle that an administrative disposition restricting the freedom and rights of citizens without a basis in an Act enacted by the National Assembly, the representative body of the people, but only through a presidential decree, is contrary to the principle of administration under the rule of law and is invalid. The attitude that administrative dispositions restricting the freedom and rights of citizens cannot be made without legal basis, based on this general principle, is highly appropriate and there is no room for doubt on this point. However, whether such a constitutional principle should be applied to the validity of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is, in my view, a matter that deserves examination in relation to the character of that provision.\\n\\nIn particular, the majority opinion cites “strong” fundamental-right relevance and “significant” infringing nature as grounds for the unconstitutionality of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue. However, freedom and rights of citizens may be restricted only by Act, and a restriction without an Act cannot be permitted however trivial it may be. That is, if an enforcement decree provision violates the principle of statutory reservation under the Constitution, it should be regarded as having no effect, regardless of whether its relevance to fundamental rights is strong or not, or whether its intrusiveness is significant or not. The majority opinion seems to regard as a matter of degree (quantity) the question of the extent of restriction on freedom and rights, and treats it as a question of quality—whether there is a violation of the constitutional principle of statutory reservation—which is not appropriate. Moreover, even if, according to the majority opinion, the disposition in this case is unlawful and revoked, unless Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act is unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 2013Hun-Ma671 et al. on 2015. 5. 28.), the issue of the Plaintiff’s violation of law remains unresolved.\\n\\n2) In the case of a labor union establishment report, the administrative agency must accept it if it meets the statutory establishment requirements. According to the majority opinion, once a labor union establishment report has been accepted, its status as a labor union can no longer be denied under current law in any case. However, in light of the fact that even a political party, whose establishment is free under the Constitution, may be dissolved when its purpose or activities violate the democratic basic order (Article 8(4) of the Constitution), the rights of a labor union should likewise be understood as guaranteed under the constitutional order of the democratic basic order. Therefore, it is difficult to accept the position that, whatever unlawful act a labor union commits, its legal status cannot be denied under current law. For example, if a labor union intentionally deceives the administrative authority and obtains acceptance of the establishment report despite a serious disqualifying ground, should it be said that the effect of the acceptance can never be excluded simply because the report was accepted? What if the labor union is plainly unlawful, such as where it is organized around persons representing the employer’s interests and wholly dependent on the employer’s financial assistance, or where it focuses entirely on political ideology, party activities, and election campaigns while setting aside the maintenance and improvement of working conditions? It is not proper to say that a status once granted can never be withdrawn even if there is a grave disqualifying ground. This is as unreasonable as saying that, even if there is only a very minor disqualifying ground, once there is illegality, the status can absolutely be deprived.\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law is an adverse disposition toward a labor union, and this is even more so in the case of the Plaintiff, which in this case had existed as a lawful labor union for more than 10 years. However, the notice of non-recognition is not a sanction for violation of a corrective order by the administrative agency or failure to comply with a corrective request. It merely returns the situation to what it was before the disposition by which the labor union establishment report was accepted, on the ground that the statutory requirements for a labor union have not been met. Even if the term “notice of non-recognition as a labor union” is used, its substance can be regarded as an ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of the labor union establishment report (since the reason for the disposition in this case is that a statutory disqualifying ground arose after acceptance of the establishment report, hereinafter I focus on withdrawal). If so viewed, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is not a provision forming the “basis” of a notice of non-recognition, but a provision setting forth the “procedure” for withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of the labor union establishment report. In other words, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue should be understood as an enhanced procedural provision that limits withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of a labor union establishment report, which may otherwise be made under general principles of administrative law, and that, through a “corrective request,” affords prior notice and an opportunity to state opinions as required for an adverse disposition under the Administrative Procedures Act, thereby providing the relevant labor union with an opportunity for autonomous correction. In the end, whether the disposition in this case is lawful should be viewed not as a problem of the validity or invalidity of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, but as a problem of the lawfulness of such withdrawal.\\n\\n3) A question arises whether the administrative authority may withdraw an administrative act it has made on the ground that new circumstances have arisen after the fact making continued effect impossible, and especially whether withdrawal is possible even absent an express legal basis. Even if it is a matter of returning the status granted by the original disposition to the original state, arbitrary withdrawal of an existing disposition without any legal basis is, in principle, not permissible. However, although it is desirable to provide such legal basis as expressly as possible, in the complex and diverse administrative actions of the modern state it is not easy to include express provisions in every case.\\n\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court precedent has held that even if there was no particular defect at the time of the disposition and no separate legal basis for withdrawal after the disposition, the original disposition may be withdrawn by a separate administrative disposition extinguishing its effect if there has been a change in circumstances making it unnecessary to maintain the original disposition, or if there is a serious need in the public interest; provided that, if the original administrative act was beneficial, since withdrawing it would infringe the vested rights of the recipient of the disposition, it may be withdrawn only when, after comparing and balancing the serious public-interest necessity for withdrawal with the disadvantages suffered by the recipient, including infringement of vested rights, trust protection, and stability of legal life, the public-interest necessity is strong enough to justify the disadvantages (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 85NU664 on 1986. 2. 25., on 2003DU10251 and 10268 on 2004. 11. 26., among others).\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion emphasizes that the legislature, after reflective consideration, abolished the labor union dissolution order system and says that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is invalid and therefore notice of non-recognition is impossible. In light of the fact that the Constitution guarantees the worker’s right of association as a fundamental right, there is some basis for understanding the majority’s stance against allowing notice of non-recognition.\\n\\nHowever, since the acceptance disposition of a labor union establishment report cannot be said to have an inviolable absolute effect, the fact that the labor union dissolution order system was abolished does not mean that the acceptance disposition of a labor union establishment report can never be ex officio cancelled or withdrawn. The doctrine of ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of administrative acts presupposes the absence of an express legal basis, and there is no reason to distinguish between a case where the basis was absent from the beginning and a case where the original basis later disappeared. This is because the doctrine exists not to supplement a “defect in legislation,” but to secure the “legality of administration.” The fact that prior case law, even where individual statutes expressly provide grounds for cancellation or withdrawal, has recognized the possibility of ex officio cancellation or withdrawal based on other public-interest necessities apart from statutory grounds, can also be understood in this context (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 2001DU2874 on 2002. 11. 26., on 2006DU6505 on 2007. 2. 8., on 2013DU7025 on 2014. 7. 10., among others).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the majority opinion says that the notice of non-recognition system is invalid because it is prescribed in a “presidential decree” rather than in an “Act.” It states that the Act neither prescribes notice of non-recognition nor delegates it to the enforcement decree.\\n\\nHowever, it is questionable whether all problems are solved if the Act directly prescribes notice of non-recognition. Given that the majority opinion emphasizes the constitutional principle of statutory reservation and the history of the abolition of the labor union dissolution order system in the Act, it would appear that if it were prescribed by Act, a corresponding notice of non-recognition might be possible. On the other hand, in light of the majority opinion’s emphasis on the significant intrusiveness of notice of non-recognition and its statement that this ultimately constitutes an essential restriction on the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution, it also seems that even if prescribed by Act, a notice of non-recognition infringing the right of association might not be permissible.\\n\\nThis is precisely where the difficulty of the majority opinion lies. At first glance, the fundamental problem seems to be that the notice of non-recognition is prescribed in an “enforcement decree” rather than in an “Act,” but even if it were directly prescribed by Act, the substantive constitutional problem inherent in the notice of non-recognition itself would remain. Since the Trade Union Act provides an establishment-report system while defining the legal requirements and disqualifying grounds for labor unions, it is not an important question whether the direct basis for notice of non-recognition lies in the Act or in the enforcement decree. The question is in what cases notice of non-recognition may be issued, and it is clear that one cannot conclude that notice of non-recognition may be issued uniformly without considering at all the substance and degree of the disqualifying ground, the existence and nature of the public interest pursued, the vested rights and legal stability of the labor union affected, and so on. Emphasizing precisely this point is the doctrine limiting ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts. The problem is not resolved simply because notice of non-recognition is prescribed by Act. What must be clarified is in what cases notice of non-recognition may be allowed. Even if notice of non-recognition were prescribed by Act, if it were content that mandated notice of non-recognition uniformly and without any limiting conditions merely because a disqualifying ground arose, the majority opinion would probably also view such an Act as unconstitutional.\\n\\nIn short, as long as the law defines the concept of a labor union and clearly sets forth its lawful requirements and disqualifying grounds, while also providing an establishment-report system to enforce those requirements, even if the legislature abolished the labor union dissolution order system and did not separately provide an Act concerning notice of non-recognition, notice of non-recognition as an ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of labor union establishment reporting must be regarded as possible so long as the occurrence of a disqualifying ground is recognized. However, since acceptance of a labor union establishment report is a beneficial administrative disposition, certain limitations apply under the doctrine limiting ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts. The issue is not the “possibility” of notice, but its “appropriateness.” In other words, the question is in what cases notice of non-recognition may be issued.\\n\\n4) Ultimately, regardless of the validity or invalidity of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, even without that provision, notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law can be issued in the sense of withdrawing the acceptance disposition of a labor union establishment report under the current statutory provisions and the general principles of administrative law. Therefore, the meaning of declaring the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue invalid, as in the majority opinion, is diminished or lost, and the dispute can be resolved only if the lawfulness of the notice of non-recognition at issue is substantively determined. From this perspective, I believe it is proper to interpret the nature of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue positively as a provision governing the post-disposition withdrawal procedure of the beneficial administrative disposition of accepting a labor union establishment report, and thus not invalid. In other words, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, based on the statutory provision at issue that where a disqualifying ground exists, the organization “shall not be deemed a labor union,” should be regarded as prescribing an enhanced procedural requirement that the administrative authority must go through a corrective request before notifying that it is a non-statutory union. To regard the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as invalid would only remove the corrective-request procedure and, rather, produce a result more unfavorable to labor unions.\\n\\nIf the legal nature of the notice of non-recognition at issue is viewed as withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of a labor union establishment report, then the issue in this case shifts from whether the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is valid to whether the notice of non-recognition at issue is lawful when comparing and balancing the public-interest need sought to be achieved through the notice of non-recognition with the disadvantages that the Plaintiff would suffer as a result. Such comparison and balancing of public and private interests is expressed as the principle of proportionality, and it is self-evident that the principle of proportionality must also be observed when issuing the notice of non-recognition at issue, which is an adverse disposition. Therefore, it cannot be said that the requirement for notice of non-recognition is immediately satisfied merely because the Plaintiff permits dismissed teachers to join as members. In the end, the lawfulness of the notice of non-recognition at issue must be determined by comprehensively considering the number of dismissed teachers in the Plaintiff, the influence those dismissed teachers have on the Plaintiff’s activities, whether the fact that the Plaintiff accepts dismissed teachers as members violates the constitutional order or impairs the essence of the labor union, the public interest achieved through the notice of non-recognition against the Plaintiff, and the disadvantages the Plaintiff suffers due to the notice of non-recognition, among other circumstances.\\n\\nB. Whether the notice of non-recognition at issue as a labor union under the law is lawful\\n\\n1) The Constitution guarantees freedom of association and, in particular, guarantees workers’ right of association. The right of association, collective bargaining, and collective action, which constitute the three labor rights, each have independent significance and work as an organic unity toward the same goal of maintaining and improving working conditions. Since the formation and operation of a labor union are themselves exercises of such right of association and become a practical foundation for the substantive guarantee of fundamental labor rights, workers should be allowed to freely organize or join a labor union and should not be prohibited or restricted absent special circumstances; and the establishment-report system prescribed by the Trade Union Act must be understood and operated within a scope that does not unjustly infringe the constitutional meaning and function of such labor unions.\\n\\nIf the right of association of a labor union is excessively restricted, resistance to this becomes the principal immediate objective of the organization, ideologically faithful and militant persons take control of the organization, and all policy directions may also become radicalized. When a strong obstacle stands in front of the organization, the various opinions of its members disappear and all effort is focused solely on removing that obstacle. In order for an organization not to be submerged in ideology, it is necessary to eliminate the possibility that ideological issues may become matters of dispute. Providing room for reasonable opinions also helps establish a culture of dialogue and discussion based on diversity and flexibility.\\n\\n2) Excluding dismissed persons from the members of a labor union runs counter to the following universal global standards.\\n\\nAdvanced countries and the international community allow dismissed persons to join labor unions and do not deny the status of the labor union merely because dismissed persons are members. It is not easy to find a legal system outside our country that forces union members who were once colleagues to be excluded from a labor union merely because they were dismissed by the employer. This is directly contrary to the essence and spirit of the labor union. Such universal global standards may be temporarily blocked, but in a healthy society they are eventually reached.\\n\\nAs of 2020. 6., the International Labour Organization (ILO) has designated 8 conventions in 4 fields regarding the most fundamental labor rights out of a total of 190 conventions as “Fundamental Conventions” and strongly recommends ratification and observance by all member states. Among them, the Convention concerning Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise (Convention No. 87) provides in Article 2 that “Workers and employers, without distinction whatsoever, shall have the right to establish and, subject only to the rules of the organization concerned, to join organizations of their own choosing without previous authorization.” This can be said to establish, as an international labor standard, the principle of universal guarantee of the right of association without any discrimination and without prior government authorization.\\n\\nIn fact, on 2014. 3. 26., the 320th Governing Body of the ILO adopted the 371st report of the Committee on Freedom of Association, which contained recommendations regarding the Korean Government’s violation of freedom of association; there, the Committee expressed the position that “the prohibition under item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act [item (d) of the statutory provision at issue] against dismissed persons joining labor unions violates freedom of association.” Furthermore, in its 382nd report on 2017. 6. 17., the Committee on Freedom of Association presented the same purport of opinion directly in relation to this case and recommended that “the Korean Government take the necessary measures to promptly repeal the relevant statutory provisions that prohibit dismissed persons from becoming members, and provide detailed information thereon,” reiterating its strong request.\\n\\nMeanwhile, based on the Free Trade Agreement between the Republic of Korea, the European Union, and its Member States, which entered into force in 2011, the European Union has continuously raised issues with the Korean Government regarding the guarantee of fundamental labor rights, including by initiating dispute-settlement procedures on the ground that Korea’s efforts to ratify the ILO’s fundamental conventions have been inadequate. More recently, on 2019. 7. 4., the European Union formally requested the Korean Government to convene a panel of experts pursuant to Article 14(1) of Chapter 13 (Trade and Sustainable Development) of the Free Trade Agreement, alleging that the Korean Government violated the Free Trade Agreement by infringing fundamental labor rights; here too, it listed as one of the principal violations the point that “the status of the relevant labor union is denied on the ground that dismissed persons joined as members under item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act [item (d) of the statutory provision at issue].”\\n\\nSince joining the ILO in 1991, Korea has ratified conventions step by step in consideration of their relationship with domestic law, but it has not yet ratified the four conventions among the above 8 fundamental conventions concerning freedom of association and the prohibition of forced labor (No. 29, No. 87, No. 98, and No. 105). However, on 2019. 5. 22., the Government (competent authority: Ministry of Employment and Labor) announced that it would begin the ratification process for 3 conventions, including Convention No. 87 among the above 4 conventions, and follow-up work is currently underway. Furthermore, the Government submitted an amendment bill in the 20th National Assembly allowing labor union membership for the unemployed and dismissed persons, and has again submitted the same amendment in the 21st National Assembly.\\n\\n3) Based on the above, the specific circumstances of this case are as follows.\\n\\nMembership of dismissed teachers is a matter that, in light of the established international standards and the constitutional value of the right of association, should be recognized as soon as possible by legislative and policy measures; it is not a matter to be used to dismantle the very existence of a labor union through formal legal application. As related legislative and policy improvements have been delayed, a solution must be sought through judicial determination in this case.\\n\\nThe dismissed teachers at issue in this case are 9 persons, which is a very small portion of approximately 60,000 total members of the Plaintiff, and there is no evidence that these 9 dismissed teachers have affected or are likely to affect the Plaintiff’s activities or autonomy. Rather, according to the record, among these 9 dismissed teachers, there appear to be no members of the Plaintiff’s major decision-making bodies such as the delegates’ general meeting, the central committee, or the central executive committee. Meanwhile, the Plaintiff corresponds not to an enterprise-based labor union but to an industrial, occupational, or regional labor union. In the case of ordinary workers who are not teachers, industrial, occupational, and regional labor unions may have dismissed persons as members (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2001DU8568 on 2004. 2. 27., among others). This is because there is a need to guarantee the right of association in collective labor relations. In light of these circumstances, it is difficult to say that the Plaintiff’s having dismissed teachers as members violates the constitutional order or impairs the essence of the labor union.\\n\\nThe public interest achieved through the notice of non-recognition at issue is also unclear. The Defendant refers to the principle of statutory status of teachers under Article 31(6) of the Constitution and the status of teachers as servants of the entire people, and speaks of the special morality required of teachers and teachers’ labor unions, as well as social trust, in light of the special status of teachers and the importance of their duties. However, one may question whether excluding a union member merely because that member was dismissed actually conforms to those values. On the other hand, the disadvantage caused to the Plaintiff by the notice of non-recognition at issue is very significant. Even if one looks only at the express contents of the Trade Union Act, a labor union that receives a notice of non-recognition can no longer use the designation “labor union” (Article 7(3)), cannot maintain legal personality (Article 6), cannot apply to the Labor Relations Commission for adjustment of labor disputes and relief from unfair labor practices (Article 7(1)), and cannot be exempted from taxes (Article 8). In such a situation, it goes without saying that the Plaintiff cannot properly function as a labor union. The Plaintiff, by the notice of non-recognition at issue, has in fact lost its raison d’être and value as a labor union.\\n\\nMeanwhile, with regard to the legitimacy of the notice of non-recognition at issue, it is a system clearly existing under current statutes, but one must also consider whether the system actually functions and whether it has normative legitimacy. Even according to the Defendant’s assertion, it appears that the only notices of non-recognition issued by the Defendant have been the notice dated 2009. 10. 20. against the Korean Government Employees’ Union and the notice dated 2013. 10. 24. in this case. Yet considering that the notice of non-recognition system was introduced on 1988. 4. 15. on the ground that labor unions lacking statutory requirements should not exist (Presidential Decree No. 12429), the fact that there have been only two notices of non-recognition issued by the Defendant in more than 30 years suggests the obsolescence or arbitrary selective application of this system. There appear to be many labor unions in our industry in which dismissed persons who are not incumbent workers remain members, and thus one cannot help but question whether the notice of non-recognition at issue conforms to the principle of proportionality and equality.\\n\\n4) The Constitution rests on the idea that our people shall form a free and cultural democratic welfare state and contribute to enduring world peace and the common prosperity of humankind. To realize this constitutional ideal, the Framework Act on Education provides in Article 2: “Education aims to enable all citizens to cultivate personality and to possess the qualities necessary as independent persons and democratic citizens, thereby enabling them to lead a humane life and contribute to the development of a democratic nation and the realization of the ideal of common prosperity of humankind.” In particular, Article 6(1) provides: “Education shall be operated so that it fully performs its original function according to its original purpose and shall not be used as a means for propagating political, partisan, or personal bias.”\\n\\nToday, education is centered on organized and institutionalized school education, and since those who carry out school education are teachers, teachers have characteristics different from ordinary workers who are employed by employers, provide labor, and receive wages and other consideration. Accordingly, the Teachers’ Labor Union Act prohibits all strike activities by teachers’ labor unions and their members (Article 8), prohibits all political activities of teachers’ labor unions (Article 3), and elsewhere broadly prohibits teachers’ political acts such as joining political parties and election campaigning under Article 51(1) of the Educational Officials Act, Article 78(1), Article 65, Article 55, and Article 58(1) of the State Public Officials Act, Article 6 of the Political Parties Act, and Article 60(1) of the Public Official Election Act. In light of this current legal framework, the activities of teachers’ labor unions are in fact limited to collective bargaining for the improvement of teachers’ working conditions, and the risk that the politicization of teachers’ labor unions or the resulting impairment of the public nature of education or the people’s right to education would occur is already blocked.\\n\\nIn light of this, the issue of the lawfulness of the notice of non-recognition at issue on the ground that dismissed teachers are members should not be converted into, or judged primarily through, a problem of the importance of education or the special status of teachers. Our legal system is already sufficiently institutionalized so that teachers’ labor unions do not depart from the interests of the entire people, and I believe our society has sufficient resilience to accommodate membership by dismissed teachers in teachers’ labor unions.\\n\\n5) One should not encourage violations of law. As long as positive law exists, it must of course be observed, so sanctions against those who violate it are proper. However, if the sanction exceeds an appropriate level and restricts the organization’s own right of association, that is another matter. Law is always lawful, but that does not make it just in itself. Law cannot be an end in itself and must be tested for its validity. Also, law cannot be eternal.
