There are cases where law is wrong from the beginning, and cases where it becomes wrong as times change; this is something we commonly experience.\\n\\nCitizens have the freedom to express opposition to irrational statutes or systems. While there are methods such as filing a petition for repeal or bringing a lawsuit seeking repeal for such improvement demands, it is not rare for incorrect laws to be corrected in the course of disputing responsibility arising from violations of law during that process.\\n\\nIn this case as well, the Plaintiff can be seen as not correcting the supplementary provision at issue and not excluding the 9 dismissed teachers as a sign of protest against an unfair labor-union legal regime. If the Plaintiff had merely sought to avoid immediate sanctions, it could have formally amended the Articles of Association or temporarily excluded the dismissed teachers. However, the Plaintiff did not do so. Rather, while of course contesting the corrective order in litigation and also in this case, even while suffering severe disadvantages, the Plaintiff is asserting the value of labor unions and improvements to the related legal system. The Plaintiff is asserting “law” rather than “statute.” In such a case, one should not deny the existence of the organization on that ground, but rather correct the situation through an appropriate level of legal sanction against the problematic conduct. Even if radical tendencies or ideological bias in teachers’ organizations are problematic in relation to education, which has a profound effect on the lives of future generations, I believe it is preferable to let them find their proper place through a free marketplace of ideas and on the basis of the sound common sense and sense of balance of the people, rather than through restricting the organization’s right of association. Judicial determination should aim at resolving disputes and conflicts and achieving social integration through legal peace.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law means ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of the acceptance of a labor union establishment report, which is a beneficial administrative disposition; therefore, the lawfulness of the notice of non-recognition at issue must be determined regardless of the validity or invalidity of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue. In other words, it must be examined whether the Plaintiff’s unlawful conduct is truly of a degree sufficient to deprive the Plaintiff of its very status as a labor union. The core issue in this case lies here, and the normative significance of this judgment can also be found here.\\n\\nThe Constitution guarantees workers’ right of association as a fundamental right. Labor unions are the basic foundation for the exercise of the three labor rights, and dismissed persons also need the guarantee of the three labor rights because they cannot leave the status of worker unless they themselves become employers. Globally, even in historical retrospect, it is difficult to find an example of a legal system that excludes dismissed persons from labor unions. Allowing dismissed persons to join labor unions has already become a firm international standard, and Korea is also moving in the same direction. Then the issue in this case is how to evaluate the Plaintiff’s allowing dismissed teachers to retain membership status notwithstanding item (d) of the statutory provision at issue.\\n\\nIn this case, there is also an opinion worth hearing to the effect that issuing a notice of non-recognition to the Plaintiff, which clearly violated the law and even refused the corrective order and corrective request concerning the violation, is lawful, and that it cannot be deemed unlawful merely because notice of non-recognition constitutes withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of labor union establishment reporting. However, as seen above, universal global standards have been established to allow dismissed teachers to join teachers’ labor unions. This shows that, even considering the importance of education and the special status of teachers, there is no inevitable reason to disallow dismissed teachers from joining teachers’ labor unions. Even if the Plaintiff accepts dismissed teachers as members, that fact alone should not deprive the Plaintiff of its legal status as a labor union. The legitimacy of the Plaintiff as a labor union is a matter to be evaluated according to its activities, not a matter to be decided based on whether dismissed teachers are members.\\n\\nIn short, the notice of non-recognition at issue is unlawful not because the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is invalid, but because it is excessive in relation to the Plaintiff’s unlawful conduct. Therefore, the lower court’s holding, based on the contrary premise, that the notice of non-recognition at issue is lawful contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles governing the limitation on withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions. The lower judgment should be reversed.\\n\\nI concur with the majority opinion in concluding that the lower judgment should be reversed, but because the reasons for reversal differ, I state this separate opinion.\\n\\n6. Dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek and Justice Lee Dong-won\\n\\nA. On the legitimacy of the notice of non-recognition at issue as a labor union under the law (Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1 and 2)\\n\\nThe main text of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, which applies to teachers’ labor unions under Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act, provides that where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted, it “shall not be deemed a labor union.” The provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue provides that in such a case the administrative authority shall demand correction, and if the labor union does not comply within the period, it “shall notify that it is not to be regarded as a labor union.”\\n\\nRegarding the above provisions, the majority opinion states that a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law deprives or restricts the legal protection afforded to an already lawfully established labor union, and as a matter of principle should be prescribed by Act; to regulate it by administrative legislation, there must necessarily be an explicit and specific delegation by Act. But the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, without delegation by Act, regulates notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law, which is not even provided for by Act, and is therefore invalid; and the notice of non-recognition at issue, based on that invalid provision, is unlawful.\\n\\nHowever, under the provisions above, even if a labor union has already completed establishment reporting, if it permits membership by a person who is not a worker, it can no longer be regarded as a labor union, and unless this is corrected, the administrative authority must notify that it is not to be regarded as a labor union. There is no room to interpret this clear and unambiguous statute otherwise. In this case, the Plaintiff from the time of its establishment report had, through its Articles of Association, completely permitted membership by dismissed teachers, which falls under the main text of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, and it did not comply with the Defendant’s corrective request regarding this. Therefore, the Defendant’s notice of non-recognition to the Plaintiff pursuant to the above provisions was lawful. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Law is a universal and reasonable norm of society that has the same binding force on an unspecified number of people; therefore, in interpreting it, one must clarify the standard meaning of the law so that it has objective validity and maintain consistency that as many people as possible can accept, thereby avoiding damage to legal stability. Even when employing systematic and logical methods of interpretation that consider the legislative intent and purpose of the statute, its enactment and amendment history, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other statutes and regulations, the principle should be to interpret faithfully, insofar as possible, to the ordinary meaning of the wording used in the law; and if the statutory wording itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, there is in principle no need to use, or only a limited need to use, other interpretive methods (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 2006DA81035 on 2009. 4. 23., and en banc Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2011DA83431 on 2013. 1. 17., among others).\\n\\nArticle 75 of the Constitution provides: “The President may issue presidential decrees with respect to matters specifically delegated by Act and matters necessary to enforce Acts.” The purpose is not that all presidential decrees require delegation by Act, but that the President may enact presidential decrees concerning concrete methods and procedures for enforcement of Acts, except for matters such as restrictions on the basic rights of citizens that the Constitution requires to be regulated only by Act (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2004DU10432 on 2007. 1. 11., among others). And although an enforcement decree or enforcement rule of an Act cannot, absent delegation by that Act, alter or supplement matters concerning individual rights and duties or prescribe new matters not provided for in the Act, if the content of the enforcement decree or enforcement rule merely specifies what is possible by interpretation of the parent Act or is for concretizing the purport of the parent Act based on that purport, after organically and systematically examining the legislative purpose of the parent Act and the entire related provisions, it cannot be regarded as exceeding the scope regulated by the parent Act; therefore, even if the parent Act does not contain a provision directly delegating such matters, it cannot be regarded as invalid (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 2012DU19526 on 2014. 8. 20., and en banc Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2015DO16014 on 2017. 2. 16., among others).\\n\\n2) The main text of Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act defines a “labor union” as “an organization or federation thereof organized by workers independently and voluntarily for the purpose of maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing the economic and social status of workers.” While the Trade Union Act thus expressly states that workers are the subject of a labor union, it separately defines “worker” in Article 2(1) as a person who lives by wages, salary, or other equivalent income regardless of the kind of occupation. Accordingly, a worker under the Trade Union Act means a person who provides labor while being in a dependent relationship with an employer and lives by receiving wages, etc. in return, and so long as there is a dependent relationship with an employer, it does not matter whether the labor-provision contract takes the form of employment, contracting, mandate, or an unnamed contract (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2019DU33712 on 2019. 6. 13., among others), but a person who is not a worker under the Trade Union Act cannot organize a lawful labor union prescribed by the Trade Union Act (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 90NU9438 on 1992. 5. 26., among others).\\n\\nFurthermore, the phrase “organization independently and voluntarily” in the main text of Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act means that, internally, workers organize it by their own will, and externally, interference or intervention by the employer or a third party must be excluded in its operation. In this regard, the statutory provision at issue lists “where participation by an employer or by a person who always acts on behalf of the employer’s interests is permitted [(a)]”, “where the principal part of expenses is assisted by the employer [(b)]”, and “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted [(d), main text],” and provides that organizations falling under these categories shall not be regarded as labor unions under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 5 of the Trade Union Act, while in its main text allowing workers to freely organize and join a labor union, provides in its proviso that public officials and teachers shall be separately determined by Act. Accordingly, the Teachers’ Labor Union Act determines matters concerning the establishment of teachers’ labor unions and provides special provisions regarding the Trade Union Act that apply to teachers, and defines “teacher” in Article 2, which simultaneously determines the scope of teachers to whom the Teachers’ Labor Union Act applies and constitutes a mandatory provision restricting the entity that may establish a teachers’ labor union and the qualifications of its members. Therefore, teachers who can become members of a teachers’ labor union are limited in practice to those who are currently serving as teachers or those who have been dismissed but have filed an application for relief from an unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission and are before the National Labor Relations Commission’s reexamination award (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 2011DU6998 on 2014. 4. 10., and on 2012DO10066 on 2016. 1. 14., among others), and no one else can become a member of a teachers’ labor union. If a teachers’ labor union permits membership by a person who is not qualified as above, it falls under “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted” in the main text of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue. The choice whether to limit “teacher” under the Teachers’ Labor Union Act to incumbent teachers as a matter of principle or to open the door broadly even to teacher-license holders who have not yet been appointed as teachers or to dismissed teachers may ultimately be viewed as a matter of legislative policy, but as seen above, current law clearly takes the position of granting membership qualifications only to “incumbent teachers” who have a direct and substantial interest in the activities of teachers’ labor unions. This is because the purpose is to prevent persons who are not teachers from affecting the working conditions of incumbent teachers by intervening in the decision-making process of teachers’ labor unions and thereby impairing the autonomy of teachers’ labor unions; thus, at least at present, in interpreting and applying this, “dismissed teachers” should be regarded as “third parties” who, if membership is permitted, may instead impair the autonomy of teachers’ labor unions through wrongful interference or intervention.\\n\\n3) The statutory provision at issue provides that if a statutory disqualifying ground exists, it “shall not be deemed a labor union,” and in the main text of item (d) it refers to “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted.” Here, “shall not be deemed a labor union” means that it is to be regarded as not a labor union. And a provision in the law that says “shall be deemed” generally means a deeming that, unlike a presumption, does not permit contrary proof, or at least means that the provision has direct external legal effect. Therefore, a labor union that permits membership by a person who is not a worker can no longer be a labor union under the Trade Union Act, despite the name, and is merely a so-called “non-statutory union.” Even if the administrative authority overlooked this and accepted the establishment report, the legal effect arises and continues that it is to be regarded from the beginning as not a labor union pursuant to the statutory provision at issue, and conversely, if membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted after the establishment report has already been accepted, the effect arises ex post that it is not a labor union, and the status as a labor union under the Trade Union Act should be regarded as lost at that point. This effect rests not on the fact that the statutory provision at issue is a “definition provision,” but on the fact that it is a “deeming provision.” That is, where the requirements set forth in the statutory provision at issue are satisfied, the resulting legal relations are immediately formed, which is the meaning of a deeming provision. The effect of deeming does not change merely because the statutory provision at issue is a definition provision.\\n\\nWhat requires understanding that the statutory provision at issue has direct external legal effect is even more so in light of the fact that the proviso portion is linked with the main text of the same item and is a provision intended effectively to prevent workers from losing the status of subject of a labor union or labor unions from losing autonomy. If a labor union falls under “where participation by an employer or by a person who always acts on behalf of the employer’s interests is permitted [(a)]” or “where the principal part of expenses is assisted by the employer [(b)]”, then that labor union is already seriously deficient in autonomy, which is an essential requirement for becoming a labor union under the Trade Union Act, and it should not be granted the status of a statutory labor union; nor should it be treated differently merely because the labor union’s establishment report has already been accepted by the administrative authority. The interpretation derived in cases falling under item (a) or (b) of the statutory provision at issue should apply equally to the main text of item (d), namely “where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted.” This is because, as seen above, item (d), like items (a) and (b), was enacted to prevent a third party who is not a worker from impairing the autonomy of the labor union through wrongful interference or intervention. The Supreme Court’s holding in judgment rendered on 96NU9829 on 1997. 10. 14., that where the establishment report of an unqualified labor union is accepted, the company in question does not have standing as a plaintiff to directly challenge the acceptance disposition itself in an administrative appeal action, but may directly assert and contest the labor union’s lack of qualification in proceedings in which the labor union specifically participated in a procedure permitted by law, such as filing an application for relief from an unfair labor practice, can also be understood in the same context.\\n\\nMoreover, the Trade Union Act clearly states that protection under this Act is limited to “labor unions established pursuant to the Trade Union Act” (Article 7(1), (3)), and provides that: ① where the administrative authority finds that a labor union establishment report or constitution needs supplementation because required matters are omitted, it shall require supplementation within a period of not more than 20 days as prescribed by Presidential Decree (Article 12(2)); ② it shall cause the administrative authority to return the establishment report of a body having any of the disqualifying grounds listed in the items of Article 2(4) proviso (Article 12(3) item 1); and ③ if a labor union’s constitution violates labor-related statutes, the administrative authority may, upon resolution of the Labor Relations Commission, order correction thereof (Article 21(1)), and a labor union subject to such corrective order must, in principle, comply within 30 days (Article 21(3)), and if it violates this, it shall be punished by a fine not exceeding 5 million won (Article 93 item 2). Thus, under the Trade Union Act, the administrative authority must return the establishment report of an organization with disqualifying grounds and may order correction of a labor union in which a disqualifying ground has arisen. Pursuant to the delegation under Article 12(2) of the Trade Union Act, the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act lists, as one of the grounds requiring supplementation of a labor union establishment report, the case where “the constitution is not attached to the establishment report or there is an omission or false statement among the required matters of the establishment report or constitution” (Article 9(1) item 1). And the portion of Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act, which is the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, stating up to “If, after a labor union has been issued a certificate of report, grounds for return of an establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Act arise, the administrative authority shall demand correction by setting a period of 30 days,” can be viewed as simply repeating or faithfully carrying over the content of Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 21(1), (3) of the Trade Union Act as seen above.\\n\\nTaken together with the content and structure of these related provisions, the Trade Union Act clearly indicates that even in the case of a labor union already established and operating after acceptance of its establishment report, membership by a person who is not a worker is not permitted, just as in the case of a labor union at the establishment stage. Therefore, for a union to become a labor union under the Trade Union Act, it must meet the statutory requirements not only at the time of establishment but also after establishment, and there is no doubt that even a labor union that has already completed establishment reporting ceases to be a lawful labor union from the moment it permits membership by a person who is not a worker. In this case, as in the Supreme Court’s holding in 96NU9829 above, just as the company in question may directly assert that the union is unqualified, the administrative authority must not regard as a labor union an organization that permits membership by a person who is not a worker; rather, treating it as a labor union is unlawful.\\n\\n4) Thus, the effect that a labor union ceases to be regarded as such when membership by a person who is not a worker is permitted is given by the statutory provision at issue itself, namely the provision stating that it “shall not be deemed a labor union.”\\n\\nHowever, while the rule of law in the statute is very clear in this way, it may not always be clear which labor union is currently a non-statutory union or at what time and for what reason it became a non-statutory union, and this may cause unnecessary confusion not only for the labor union itself but also for related interested parties. Accordingly, there arises a need for the administrative authority, which is responsible for no longer treating a labor union with a disqualifying ground as a lawful labor union, to issue a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law in order to clarify the relevant legal relationships, and that is precisely what the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue regulates. In other words, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is a very natural enforcement order that sets forth the concrete methods and procedures for realizing the effect that a union becomes a non-statutory union by operation of the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nHowever, the Trade Union Act and the enforcement decree not only provide for a system of corrective orders for unlawful constitutions, etc., but also require a correction request procedure concerning unlawful constitutions, etc. before notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law. This too can be seen as sound, in that the administrative authority affords a labor union with a disqualifying ground an opportunity for autonomous correction so that it can return to lawful status. Therefore, if, despite having been afforded such an opportunity for correction, the law-violating state continues without correction, the effect under the statutory provision at issue finally arises conclusively, and at that point it is natural that not only interested parties such as the company in question but also the administrative authority may take the position that legal protection under the Trade Union Act is no longer afforded to a labor union with a disqualifying ground. That is, a labor union with a statutory disqualifying ground becomes a non-statutory union pursuant to the provision that it “shall not be deemed a labor union,” but such effect remains abstract and potential while the procedures of corrective order and corrective request remain pending, and only becomes concrete and final when the union fails to comply with the corrective order and corrective request. The administrative authority then issues a notice of non-recognition to the labor union that has become a non-statutory union, stating that it is no longer to be regarded as a labor union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nViewed this way, the part of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue stating that “if such correction is not implemented within that period, it shall notify the relevant labor union that it is not to be regarded as a labor union under this Act” cannot be said to be contrary to the Trade Union Act or invalid, although no specific delegation is made in the parent Act, the Trade Union Act. As noted above, although it is generally true that an enforcement decree of an Act may not, absent delegation by that Act, alter or supplement matters concerning individual rights and duties or prescribe new matters not provided for in the Act, because an enforcement decree may prescribe not only matters specifically delegated by the parent Act but also matters necessary to enforce the parent Act, such a limitation does not apply where the enforcement decree provision does not directly alter or supplement individual rights and duties. Therefore, it is fully permissible to provide matters, guidelines, or standards necessary for implementing or enforcing the parent Act, so long as they do not exceed the scope regulated by the parent Act; moreover, where the content of the enforcement decree merely specifies what is possible by interpretation of the parent Act, after organically and systematically examining the legislative purpose of the parent Act and the related provisions as a whole, or is for concretizing the purport of the parent Act, it cannot be regarded as exceeding the scope of the parent Act.\\n\\nSpecifically, in light of the content and structure of the related provisions discussed in 3) above, it is only a natural measure that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue requires the administrative authority to issue a notice stating that a labor union with a statutory disqualifying ground is not to be regarded as a lawful labor union under the Act if, after a corrective request and similar measures, no correction is made. This is a formal notification that the legal effect of no longer regarding it as a labor union has already arisen pursuant to the statutory provision at issue, and that the administrative authority has also adopted that position. This is necessary not only for efficient organizational adjustment and management by the administrative authority over labor unions, but also desirable from the perspective of protecting and fostering labor unions so that they can remain organizations with autonomy and democracy. If, even where a body that has completed establishment reporting falls under the disqualifying grounds of the items of the statutory provision at issue and thus is contrary to the essence of a labor union or lacks autonomy and democracy as a labor union, one were to deem that the administrative authority could take no measure other than issuing a corrective order or corrective request, then it would be impossible to prevent a proliferation of bodies that are not entitled to legal protection under the Trade Union Act, and should not receive it, yet nonetheless claim to be labor unions. Therefore, even though the Trade Union Act does not contain an express delegation requiring that notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law be prescribed in the enforcement decree, there is no reason to prohibit the administrative authority from informing the union that the legal effect arising under the provision at issue has occurred, so that the effect arising under the provision at issue can be practically enforced. The provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue can be viewed as having been prepared precisely for this purpose.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion says that because the statutory provision at issue is merely a criterion for determining a lawful labor union, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue prescribing notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law newly prescribes a matter not prescribed or delegated by the law and is therefore invalid. But as noted above, the statutory provision at issue provides that when a disqualifying ground exists, the organization is not a lawful labor union, and is itself a complete provision that expressly states both the requirements and the effect. Therefore, notifying a labor union that has become a non-statutory union under such legal provision is not a new matter at all and does not require a special delegation. Nevertheless, the majority opinion presupposes as if there were some defect or incompleteness in the statutory provision at issue and, based thereon, declares the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue to be an entirely new provision lacking legal basis or delegation. This position either overlooks that the statutory provision at issue is itself complete or is merely a convenient interpretation that arbitrarily narrows the meaning of the statutory provision in order to reach the conclusion that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is invalid.\\n\\n5) Meanwhile, under Article 12(1) of the Trade Union Act, when the administrative authority receives an establishment report, it must issue a certificate of report within 3 days except where supplementation is needed because required matters are omitted from the establishment report or constitution, or where the labor union to be established has a disqualifying ground prescribed by law. Accordingly, even if a labor union receives a notice of non-recognition, it may, after correcting the disqualifying ground and filing a new establishment report, regain lawful labor union status within at most 3 days. Generally, in cases such as cancellation of a building permit, a disposition canceling a beneficial administrative act takes effect only upon the cancellation disposition, and because the effect of the disposition is final, the addressee cannot be certain that even if the reason for the disposition is removed, he or she will again receive the same beneficial disposition, thereby causing potentially irreparable harm. However, in the case of notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law, the effect that it is not to be regarded as a labor union has already arisen as a fait accompli pursuant to the statutory provision at issue, and the notice merely informs that it cannot be recognized as a lawful labor union until the union reorganizes its constitution and organization in conformity with law and urges a return to legality. Thus it has characteristics different from ordinary cancellation of beneficial administrative acts, and the same applies to withdrawal. In light of these circumstances, it is not appropriate to be so absorbed by the view that a notice of non-recognition has an infringing character that one should, as far as possible, refrain from issuing it. As noted above, this is also evident when one recalls that if a labor union falls under “where participation by an employer or by a person who always acts on behalf of the employer’s interests is permitted [(a)]” or “where the principal part of expenses is assisted by the employer [(b)]” under the statutory provision at issue, the administrative authority ought to take affirmative measures to notify such a body, which lacks autonomy and democracy as a labor union, that it is a non-statutory union.\\n\\nThe infringing aspect of notice of non-recognition as a non-statutory union under the Trade Union Act stems merely from the contradiction that a body which lacks the requirements prescribed by the Trade Union Act and, despite the administrative authority’s corrective order and corrective request, ultimately refuses to comply, thereby causing the effect that it is not to be regarded as a labor union under the statutory provision at issue, nevertheless seeks to regain lawful labor union status at any time by meeting the requirements prescribed by the Trade Union Act again, even though the path is open. In other words, the issue arises because such a body makes a contradictory demand that it be treated as a labor union under the Trade Union Act as if the statutory provision at issue did not exist, merely to obtain selectively the legal protection under the law, and it is not the type of issue that should be reframed as a question of how to protect citizens from an infringing administrative disposition.\\n\\n6) As seen above, the Plaintiff became a non-statutory union by operation of the statutory provision at issue, not by the notice of non-recognition under the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, and therefore no special significance should be attached to the notice of non-recognition itself; but even if viewed differently, the notice of non-recognition issued by the Defendant to the Plaintiff can be regarded as lawful.\\n\\nAs is well known, the agency that issued an administrative act may, if the act has defects, cancel it on its own even without a separate legal basis, and even if there was no particular defect at the time of the act and there is no separate legal basis for withdrawing it after the fact, it may withdraw it by a separate administrative act that extinguishes its effect if there has been a change in circumstances making it unnecessary to maintain the original act or a serious public-interest necessity has arisen. However, if the original administrative act was beneficial, there may be room in certain cases for the cancellation or withdrawal to be impermissible under the doctrine limiting cancellation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 85NU664 on 1986. 2. 25., on 2003DU10251 and 10268 on 2004. 11. 26., among others).\\n\\nAcceptance of a labor union establishment report broadly corresponds to a beneficial administrative disposition granting legal status that allows a labor union satisfying the establishment requirements set forth in Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act to enjoy the rights and benefits prescribed by the Trade Union Act by recognizing it as a statutory labor union. Therefore, absent a special limiting ground, the Defendant may, even without a separate statutory provision, issue a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law in the sense of retrospectively withdrawing the acceptance of labor union establishment reporting from a teachers’ labor union whose withdrawal ground has arisen. The provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue can be understood as merely a cautious and confirmatory provision stating the administrative authority’s withdrawal power, which naturally follows from the general legal principles of administrative law. This is also consistent with the fact that Article 12(3) item 1 of the Trade Union Act provides that the administrative authority shall examine whether a body submitting an establishment report falls under any item of the statutory provision at issue and return the report if it does. The purpose of that provision is to prevent a proliferation of labor unions that do not satisfy the substantive requirements for labor unions and thereby to guarantee workers’ autonomous and democratic exercise of the right of association. Accordingly, the administrative authority is granted the authority to substantively examine whether the relevant body falls under any item of the statutory provision at issue (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2011DU6998 on 2014. 4. 10., among others; however, under that Supreme Court judgment 2011DU6998, the substantive examination authority at the establishment-report stage is not unlimited but partially restricted). This substantive examination authority remains reserved to the administrative authority even after the labor union’s establishment report has been accepted, as provided in Article 21 of the Trade Union Act, so the administrative authority may take measures through corrective orders, etc. to bring a labor union that has acquired a disqualifying ground under any item of the statutory provision at issue back to lawful status. If, despite this, the union ultimately refuses to return to lawful status, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, which requires the administrative authority to issue notice of non-recognition, merely regulates the real-world implementation of the administrative authority’s authority as described above.\\n\\nThe same is true when normatively comparing and evaluating the situations before and after the administrative authority accepts a labor union establishment report from a body with a disqualifying ground. If, after receiving an establishment report, the administrative authority substantively examines whether the body falls under any item of the statutory provision at issue and discovers a disqualifying ground under one item, and ultimately the supplementation is not completed and the administrative authority returns or refuses the labor union establishment report, such measure is based on Article 12 of the Trade Union Act as noted above and is lawful; therefore, the relevant body whose establishment report was refused would not be given the legal effect of receiving legal protection under the Trade Union Act or the status of a so-called within-law labor union. But if, in the same situation, the administrative authority had overlooked the disqualifying ground and accepted the establishment report, yet then immediately discovered the disqualifying ground and, through the procedure set out in the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, issued a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law, that situation is substantially the same as one in which the disqualifying ground had been discovered before the establishment report was accepted; therefore, it should be viewed as a lawful and proper measure to achieve a balanced result. It is not correct to impose a far stricter judicial review standard simply because the establishment report had already been accepted, as if the entity’s substance had changed and its character had fundamentally differed from the period before acceptance, or as if special legal protection had to be afforded. Even if substantial significance is given to the fact that the administrative authority accepted the establishment report itself and it is deemed necessary to protect the entity’s vested rights or its reliance on acceptance, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue does not allow the administrative authority to issue notice of non-recognition immediately upon finding a disqualifying ground; rather, it provides that the authority must set a period of 30 days and request correction, and only if that is not complied with may notice of non-recognition be issued. Therefore, even if one considers only the measures taken before the notice of non-recognition, the procedural guarantee for protecting the entity’s vested rights or prior reliance should be regarded as sufficiently provided.\\n\\nMoreover, if, in canceling a beneficial administrative disposition, the defect in the disposition is attributable to the party’s concealment of facts or other fraudulent application, the party is deemed to have known that the benefit obtained by the disposition was unlawfully acquired and to have anticipated the possibility of cancellation; thus, the party cannot invoke the benefit of reliance regarding that disposition, and there is no abuse of discretion even if the administrative authority did not consider that factor (see Supreme Court judgments, among others, rendered on 90NU9520 on 1991. 4. 12.). According to the facts found by the lower court, the Plaintiff, at the time of the establishment report, had provisions allowing dismissed teachers to join, yet submitted an untrue constitution to the establishment report with such content deleted, thereby causing the establishment report to be accepted, and thereafter, even when the Defendant confirmed this and issued corrective orders and corrective requests, it failed to comply. The record also shows that the Plaintiff has clearly indicated that it has no intention in the future of satisfying the requirements for a labor union under the Trade Union Act. That is, the Plaintiff never satisfied the requirements of the Trade Union Act from the outset, deliberately deceived the administrative authority to get the establishment report accepted, and, even though that became an issue and it received two corrective orders and one corrective request, refused to correct it and has no intention at all of doing so in the future. In light of such circumstances, the Plaintiff cannot contend that its trust in the administration or legal stability has been impaired on account of the reasons for the notice of non-recognition at issue. Rather, where the original establishment report was from the outset false or obtained by improper means, the administrative authority that discovers this after acceptance must, according to the wording of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, necessarily issue notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law; and even after such notice, the union can at any time recover as a lawful labor union if it merely satisfies the statutory requirements. Thus, there is no room at the outset for discussion of limitations on cancellation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts or of abuse of discretion.\\n\\nThe separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang is worth hearing as a legislative discussion from the perspective that the notice of non-recognition system should not be abused, but it cannot be accepted as an interpretation of current law. The statutory provision at issue does not provide an exception in which a body with a disqualifying ground may still be recognized as a lawful labor union. Accordingly, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue grants an opportunity for correction and provides that, for a labor union that refuses to comply, notice of non-recognition “shall” be given. Notice of non-recognition for a labor union with a disqualifying ground is inevitable unless there is some problem with the corrective order or corrective request that is its premise. In this case, the lawfulness of the First Corrective Order was upheld by final Supreme Court judgments in the administrative litigation disputing it (Seoul Administrative Court judgment rendered on 2010. 11. 5. in Case 2010GuHap27110; Seoul High Court judgment rendered on 2011. 9. 9. in Case 2010Nu43725; Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2011DU24231 on 2012. 1. 12.), and the criminal conviction for noncompliance with the First Corrective Order was also finalized by the Supreme Court (Seoul Southern District Court judgment rendered on 2011. 12. 1. in Case 2011GoDan131; Seoul Southern District Court judgment rendered on 2012. 7. 26. in Case 2011No1798; Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2012DO10066 on 2016. 1. 14.), and in the constitutional complaint case filed immediately after the corrective request at issue, the Constitutional Court upheld the constitutionality of Article 2 of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act, which limits the scope of teachers subject to the Act to teachers currently working in elementary and secondary schools, on the grounds that it does not violate the right of association of the complainant Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union or dismissed teachers (Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 2013Hun-Ma671 et al. on 2015. 5. 28.). That is, the unlawfulness of the Plaintiff’s allowing dismissed teachers to join as members has already been repeatedly confirmed. In such circumstances, allowing the Plaintiff’s claim to vested rights is tantamount to abandoning regulation under current law.\\n\\n7) The reason for the disposition in this case is that the Plaintiff has provisions permitting dismissed teachers to join as members, that 9 dismissed teachers are actually active as members of the Plaintiff, and that, despite the Defendant administrative authority’s request to correct this, the Plaintiff refused.\\n\\nFirst, the fact that 9 dismissed teachers were active as members of the Plaintiff at the time of the notice of non-recognition at issue is an undeniable fact, and the Plaintiff also cannot deny it; thus, this part of the reason for disposition alone is sufficient to recognize the lawfulness of the notice of non-recognition at issue.\\n\\nMoreover, the Plaintiff formalizes such membership by dismissed teachers through the supplementary provision at issue, that is, in its Articles of Association. Articles of Association or constitutions are the most basic and important foundation for the establishment, continuation, and activities of an organization, and are core matters that identify its identity and form and maintain its identity. The Plaintiff is expressly permitting the membership of dismissed teachers in precisely such Articles of Association. This is not merely a past event or a temporary current situation, but an expression of the intention to continue allowing membership by dismissed teachers in the future. It violates the law for a labor union to allow membership by a person who is not a worker and to allow such person to act as a member. If such a situation did not arise temporarily due to a mere clerical mistake but resulted from an explicit decision of the labor union, then such a labor union has voluntarily abandoned being a labor union under the law. It is contradictory, under one and the same law, to say that one will not satisfy the statutory requirements of that law but will enjoy only the effects under that law. This is not only a problem with the Trade Union Act. It is the same under all laws, whether public law or private law, substantive law or procedural law. For example, one cannot accept a claim that one will not possess the essential facilities prescribed by the Medical Service Act, but that one should still be granted the status of a hospital under the Medical Service Act. A legal order that permits such contradictory positions cannot exist in the first place.\\n\\nAgain, in this case, the Plaintiff did not merely passively tolerate the membership of dismissed teachers. Nor did a dismissed teacher temporarily become a member contrary to the Plaintiff’s true intention. By means of its official Articles of Association, the Plaintiff expressly permitted membership by persons who are not teachers, thereby directly violating the establishment requirements of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act; despite repeated corrective orders by the Defendant and final court judgments upholding the lawfulness of those corrective orders, the Plaintiff argued that retaining unlawful Articles of Association was justified, and it clearly indicated that it has no intention whatsoever of correcting the issue of membership by persons who are not teachers in the future. Yet the Plaintiff is demanding status and protection as a labor union under the Teachers’ Labor Union Act. Such self-contradictory claims have always been rejected and must continue to be rejected. One cannot recognize, under the law that the organization rejects, the organization as lawful under that law despite its failure to satisfy the requirements prescribed by law.\\n\\nThe separate opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyung may be valid as a general theory, but it is difficult to regard it as appropriate as an interpretive theory for this case. The Trade Union Act and its Enforcement Decree explicitly deny worker status under the Trade Union Act to dismissed persons, while recognizing certain exceptions related to unfair dismissal and, in order to prevent unexpected unjust results, provide a corrective-order system and a corrective-request procedure, thereby affording even a post hoc opportunity for correction. The situation arising despite such clear legislative intent and consideration is not, as the separate opinion assumes, an “unreasonable result contrary to common sense.” It is merely “a situation in which legal protection of the right of association is insufficient,” not “a situation in which a labor union does not comply with current law.” In this case, no interpretation different from the wording is needed. Even if one assumed that a different interpretation is needed in this case, one could reach the same conclusion as the above separate opinion by interpreting the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as involving “discretion” rather than “binding force,” moderating the effect of “deeming” under the statutory provision at issue, judging the main text of item (d) of the statutory provision at issue based on whether the labor union’s “autonomy” is impaired, or limiting the “membership” of persons who are not workers to new membership only. Nevertheless, the above separate opinion rejects all such possibilities of interpretation as being contrary to the clear wording, while singling out the retention of membership status by dismissed members as requiring an interpretation different from the wording. Such an approach is difficult to avoid the criticism that it presupposes the conclusion and then arbitrarily and selectively interprets the law to fit it.\\n\\n8) The majority opinion criticizes the current notice of non-recognition system as reviving, by presidential decree, the former labor union dissolution order system under the old law.\\n\\nHowever, the law in force when the labor union dissolution order system existed defined labor unions and provided that, in cases of disqualifying grounds such as permitting membership by persons who are not workers, “the foregoing shall not apply in any of the following cases.” This is substantially different from the current law’s provision that “where any of the following applies, it shall not be deemed a labor union.” “The foregoing shall not apply” is more of a negative expression, and whether positive legal effect arises therefrom is unclear; whereas “it shall not be deemed a labor union” should be regarded as inherently conferring positive legal effect.\\n\\nMoreover, while the grounds for a labor union dissolution order were “where the labor-related statutes and regulations were violated or where there was concern that the public interest would be harmed” [Article 32 of the former Trade Union Act (before amendment by Act No. 3966 on 1987. 11. 28.)], the grounds for notice of non-recognition are, as prescribed by the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, “where grounds for return of an establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Act arise,” that is, “where any of the items of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Act applies,” which ultimately means “where a disqualifying ground arises such that it shall not be deemed a labor union” (Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act, Article 12(3) item 1, Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act). Thus, the labor union dissolution order system allowed dissolution even for any violation of law regardless of its nature or severity, or even merely on the ground that there was concern about harm to the public interest; whereas the notice of non-recognition system strictly limits the grounds for notice to cases where, under the definitional provisions of the Trade Union Act, the organization cannot be recognized as a labor union, that is, where it cannot be a subject of the Act from the outset.\\n\\nAdding to this, as noted above, notice of non-recognition does not newly make the organization a non-statutory union by the notice itself, but merely retroactively informs that it has already become a non-statutory union under the Trade Union Act. Thus, whereas under the former labor union dissolution order system there was a risk that the administrative authority would arbitrarily and unjustly deprive or infringe the status of a lawful labor union, under the current notice of non-recognition system the administrative authority simply informs, through the prescribed procedure, a body that no longer falls within the labor union under the Trade Union Act that the legal effect has already arisen by law, and there is absolutely no room for unjust arbitrariness to intervene.\\n\\nThe legislature’s purpose in abolishing the labor union dissolution order system was to prevent unjust infringement of the labor union’s right of association, not to guarantee the perpetual survival of unlawful labor unions. There is no reason to think that, because the labor union dissolution order system was abolished, notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law for labor unions lacking statutory requirements is also prohibited.\\n\\nTaking these circumstances together, the current notice of non-recognition system is an essential mechanism for securing the effectiveness of the definitional provisions concerning labor unions and is already inherent in the Trade Union Act. It cannot be placed on the same plane as the former labor union dissolution order system or dismissed as a system arbitrarily revived by the executive branch after legislative abolition.\\n\\n9) As examined thus far, if an organization satisfies the requirements prescribed by the Trade Union Act, it becomes a lawful labor union; if it does not satisfy those requirements, it becomes a non-statutory union; and this is a legal effect directly given by the statutory provision at issue itself. The administrative authority must return the establishment report of a body that does not meet the requirements prescribed by law, and if such circumstances are revealed after the establishment report has been accepted, the authority must, through corrective orders and criminal punishment for noncompliance, induce correction, and if correction still is not made, it must issue a notice of non-recognition through the corrective-request procedure.\\n\\nThis is different from a situation where the law imposes a certain duty but is silent on how to deal with violation of that duty. The Trade Union Act and its Enforcement Decree clearly provide for the effect of violation by stating that where the organization does not meet the requirements for being a labor union, it “shall not be deemed a labor union,” and furthermore ensure realization of that legal effect by prescribing return of the establishment report and notice of non-recognition.\\n\\nThus, there is no defect whatsoever in this part of the legal system. On the contrary, viewed strictly as a body of statutes and regulations, it is a perfect set of provisions without any problem. Nevertheless, the majority opinion starts its interpretation from the basic premise that there is a defect in this perfectly complete legal system. But this case is not a constitutional review of statutes, nor is it a matter of legislative theory. In this case, only judicial adjudication is at issue. The court need only interpret and apply the completed legal system as it is and confer legal effect when the requirements are satisfied. The majority opinion unnecessarily complicates the issue. If one believes the law lacks legitimacy, one should request a constitutional review from the Constitutional Court or petition the National Assembly for amendment.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the majority opinion is also difficult to accept from the standpoint of legal method. Resolution of this case must begin with the interpretation of the statutory provision at issue, namely, the provision that it “shall not be deemed a labor union.” Yet that provision is extremely clear: if the disqualifying grounds prescribed by the Trade Union Act are satisfied, it is no longer a lawful labor union. In other words, if the “requirement” that the body falls under the disqualifying grounds prescribed by the Trade Union Act is met, the “effect” that it is no longer a lawful labor union arises. There can be no room for further interpretation of such a self-sufficient and complete provision. To see it otherwise exceeds the limits of legal interpretation. Nevertheless, the majority opinion deliberately ignores this clear textual meaning and avoids a definite interpretation by saying the provision is merely a criterion for determining a lawful labor union, while discussing the validity or invalidity of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue. Where there are the Constitution, an Act, and a presidential decree on a given matter, if the validity of the presidential decree is in issue, one must first determine whether the decree violates the Act, and if not, then determine whether the decree violates the Constitution, or whether the Act itself is unconstitutional. Moreover, the notice of non-recognition at issue (Exhibit A No. 5) clearly cites, as the basis statutes, not only the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue (Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act) but also item (d) of the statutory provision at issue [item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act]. Therefore, the question of validity of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue should fundamentally be derived through interpretation of the statutory provision at issue. One cannot assess the validity of a presidential decree concerning a parent Act without first determining the meaning of the parent Act.\\n\\nThe majority opinion is also problematic because, if a disqualifying ground arises after establishment reporting, it ultimately renders the statutory provision at issue meaningless. If a disqualifying ground is discovered at the establishment-report stage, the organization cannot be recognized as a statutory labor union under the provision that it “shall not be deemed a labor union,” and the administrative authority must return its establishment report; there the provision has a clear meaning. This is not much different even if, like the majority opinion, one simply views the provision as a criterion for determining a lawful labor union. However, if a disqualifying ground arises after the establishment report has been accepted, then, under the majority opinion, the provision loses all meaning. As seen above, under the general principles of administrative law, the administrative authority may ex officio cancel or withdraw a prior administrative act, and this also applies to acceptance of a labor union’s establishment report. That is, even without the provision that it “shall not be deemed a labor union,” the administrative authority may ex officio cancel or withdraw the existing acceptance disposition of establishment reporting from a labor union with a disqualifying ground. The majority opinion, even if it opposes cancellation or withdrawal in this case, would not deny the general principles concerning cancellation or withdrawal of administrative acts or the Supreme Court’s established precedent based thereon. If, like the majority opinion, one denies the independent meaning of the above provision and says it is merely a criterion for determining a lawful labor union, this ultimately amounts to repeating the obvious—that when a labor union acquires a disqualifying ground, the existing acceptance disposition of establishment reporting may be canceled or withdrawn ex officio—and thus the above provision ends up having no substantive meaning. Interpreting the law contrary to the wording is unjust, but so too is an interpretation that renders an existing law meaningless.\\n\\nIn order to realize the constitutional principle of rule of law, finding the ideal legal order in a concrete case is the court’s most important mission. But this is not the court’s alone. It is shared with the National Assembly, the Government, and the Constitutional Court under the constitutional order. Therefore, one must move toward a more ideal legal order in harmony with legislative action by the National Assembly, law enforcement and administrative legislation by the President and the executive branch, and constitutional review by the Constitutional Court. If the National Assembly has not amended the law, the President and the executive branch have not suspended enforcement or improved administrative legislation, and the Constitutional Court has recognized the constitutionality of such statutes and systems, that situation should naturally be respected. It is by no means desirable, even if the interpretation is ultimately in the right direction, for the court unilaterally to overturn in one stroke the existing legal state formed and maintained by such statutes and systems based on its own judgment. This is all the more true if it is done by disregarding the clear wording of statutes and the structure of a complete system. For the court to ignore the order established by constitutional statutes and systems, unilaterally declare its own justice, and force other state organs to follow it goes far beyond the limits of adjudication and is closer to legislation. The majority opinion does not interpret the law; it creates law itself. Even if the majority opinion ultimately points to where our society should go, at least at present I find it difficult to accept its reasons and conclusion.\\n\\n10) In short, because law is a universal and reasonable norm of society, it should in principle be interpreted according to its wording so as to maintain objective validity and consistency. The Trade Union Act defines labor unions as organizations composed of workers, and the Teachers’ Labor Union Act, which is a special act to the Trade Union Act, defines the “teachers” who may become members of teachers’ labor unions, expressly excluding dismissed teachers. Furthermore, the statutory provision at issue provides that where membership of a person who is not a worker is permitted, it “shall not be deemed a labor union,” and this should apply both to labor unions in the process of establishment and to labor unions after establishment. Therefore, even a labor union that has already completed establishment reporting gives rise, by that provision itself, to the legal effect that it is no longer deemed a lawful labor union if it permits membership by a person who is not a worker. In this regard, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue provides that, for the enforcement of the statutory provision at issue, the administrative authority shall demand correction from the labor union and, if it does not comply, “shall notify that it is not to be regarded as a labor union.” Therefore, if a labor union already established and operating is found to have permitted membership by a person who is not a worker and does not comply with the administrative authority’s corrective request, the administrative authority must notify that it is a non-statutory union without any room for discretion, and if it fails to do so, it is instead abandoning its duty to ensure workers’ autonomous and democratic exercise of the right of association and is therefore unlawful. There is no room to interpret this clear and complete statutory scheme differently, and if there are parts of the current regulatory framework or content with which one cannot agree, that is a matter to be resolved through legislation. The majority opinion, while laboring to ignore a perfect legal system, blurs the boundary between legislation and adjudication and denies the legitimacy of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue while avoiding a clear interpretation of the statutory provision at issue. Meanwhile, under the general principles of administrative law, the administrative authority may ex post cancel or withdraw the acceptance of a labor union establishment report from a labor union with disqualifying grounds even without an express statutory basis, and the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, which cautiously and confirmatively states this, should be regarded as lawful and valid even without a specific delegation from the parent Trade Union Act. Moreover, the Plaintiff expressly permits membership by dismissed teachers through its Articles of Association, obtained acceptance by deceiving the administrative authority while concealing the existence of such provision at the time of establishment reporting, and refused to comply even with the Defendant’s repeated corrective orders and corrective requests pointing this out; thus, the Plaintiff had no vested rights or trust capable of legal protection from the outset. A legal system in which one need not comply with legal requirements but may still demand only the legal status and protection granted when those requirements are satisfied has never existed and should never exist in a modern civilized society based on the rule of law. The Defendant’s notice of non-recognition to the Plaintiff was justified. That is the proper demand of law and justice derived from the wording of the relevant statutes and their constitutional interpretation.\\n\\nB. On the remaining grounds of appeal (Grounds of Appeal Nos. 3 to 7)\\n\\nThe lower court held, for reasons stated in its judgment, that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue does not violate the principle of nulla poena sine lege, that the Plaintiff’s granting of membership status to dismissed teachers through the supplementary provision at issue falls under item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, and that because the Plaintiff was afforded advance notice and a sufficient opportunity to present its views before receiving the notice of non-recognition at issue from the Defendant, there were no substantive or procedural defects in the notice of non-recognition at issue, and that, in light of the circumstances found, the notice of non-recognition at issue cannot be regarded as violating the principle of proportionality, the principle of protection of trust, or the doctrine of estoppel.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles and related legal principles discussed above, there is no error in the lower court’s above determination affecting the judgment, with respect to the principle of nulla poena sine lege, the negative establishment requirements of labor unions, prior notice and hearing under the Administrative Procedures Act, the principle of proportionality, the principle of protection of trust, and the doctrine of estoppel.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, it is proper that the lower court affirmed the first-instance judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim for the above reasons. The Plaintiff’s final appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I express my dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplementary opinion of Justices Park Jung-hwa, Min Yoo-sook, No Jeong-hee, Kim Sang-hwan, and No Tae-ak to the majority opinion\\n\\nArticle 107(2) of the Constitution provides: “Where the constitutionality or legality of a command, rule, or disposition becomes the premise of a trial, the Supreme Court shall have the final authority to review it.” The majority opinion found, on the basis of Article 107(2) of the Constitution, that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is unconstitutional and therefore invalid. This is a conclusion reached by focusing on the fact that the constitutionality of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is a preliminary and important constitutional issue in this case, and by faithfully performing one of the fundamental roles assigned to the Supreme Court by the Constitution, namely control of administrative legislation. Below, while listening to the issues raised and arguments made in the separate opinions and dissenting opinions, I wish to supplement the purport and meaning of the majority opinion.\\n\\nA. Importance of constitutional adjudication by the courts\\n\\n1) For a judge who adjudicates bound by law, determining whether the law is unconstitutional or invalid is a very difficult task. The fact that Article 107(2) of the Constitution grants courts the authority to review the constitutionality and legality of legal norms enacted by the executive branch such as presidential decrees, prime ministerial decrees, and ministerial decrees (hereinafter referred to as “administrative legislation”) means, on the other hand, that courts are entrusted with a very difficult but important constitutional task.\\n\\n2) In order to properly perform the above authority and task entrusted to the courts, it is necessary for the courts to understand and follow the constitutional significance and function of judicial control over administrative legislation.\\n\\na) The Constitution provides that all state action—legislative, executive, and judicial—operates within the framework of the separation of powers established by the Constitution. For example, the principle of statutory reservation is a control principle over administrative action, requiring administrative action to have a basis in an Act enacted by the National Assembly, the representative of the people, through democratic procedures. In the case of administrative legislation, the Constitution similarly provides that it may issue only with respect to matters specifically delegated by Act and matters necessary to enforce the Act (Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution). In this way, the Constitution establishes the superiority of National Assembly legislation (Acts) over administrative legislation by making the Constitution the supreme norm.\\n\\nb) Ultimately, the reason Article 107(2) of the Constitution empowers courts to declare administrative legislation void and exclude it from the legal order when it contradicts the Constitution or Acts is: ① to maintain the supreme normative force of the Constitution and preserve the relation among legal norms by the principle of superiority of higher law, thereby enhancing the unity and coherence of the law; ② to restore the relationship between the National Assembly and the executive branch to the constitutional system of checks and balances by eliminating situations in which legislative power of the National Assembly is infringed through administrative legislation; and ③ ultimately to ensure that constitutionally permissible restrictions on the freedom and rights of citizens are determined by the National Assembly, the democratic legislature, through deliberation and debate, thereby preventing arbitrary administrative action and providing a firm foundation for the protection of fundamental rights.\\n\\nIt is precisely for these reasons that judicial control over administrative legislation, that is, normative control, is described as a kind of objective litigation emphasizing the protection of the objective legal order.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the constitutional significance of judicial control over administrative legislation is even more emphasized in modern states, where the role and function of administration are expanding and, accordingly, the legislative function of the executive branch is also being strengthened, because the executive branch is more likely to disguise its actions as administration under the rule of law (administration based on law) while in reality violating the normative order envisioned by the Constitution.\\n\\nc) The following point deserves special attention. The process by which courts exercise control over administrative legislation is a highly meaningful institutional space where citizens themselves, whose legal status is affected by administrative legislation, can directly voice their views in an open courtroom regarding the constitutional legitimacy of administrative legislation and hear the answer from the neutral adjudicatory body, the court. As sovereigns, the source of all state power, citizens naturally have political opportunities to participate in the legislative process concerning laws and administrative legislation related to their fundamental rights, and through the court proceedings described above they gain normative opportunities to contest the constitutional legitimacy of administrative legislation more concretely, which is of no small practical significance.\\n\\nIf the court listens to the significant arguments raised by the litigants and further identifies problems with administrative legislation based on the proper interpretation of the Constitution and Acts and excludes its effect, then the court’s judgment ultimately conveys valid opinions of the people to the state organs, thereby allowing the norms affecting the people to be changed in a direction more consistent with constitutional values.\\n\\n3) But on what does the court rely and what does it emphasize when adjudicating to control administrative legislation? In order for the adjudication to be faithful to the constitutional significance and function of judicial control over administrative legislation, the court must above all emphasize the people’s fundamental rights and fundamental-right values guaranteed by the Constitution and fully perform its role as “guardian of fundamental rights.”\\n\\nArticle 10 of the Constitution provides: “All citizens shall be assured of human dignity and worth and shall have the right to pursue happiness. It shall be the duty of the State to confirm and guarantee the inviolable basic human rights of individuals.” There can be no doubt that a court, entrusted with judicial power under Article 101 of the Constitution, has the duty under Article 10 of the Constitution to confirm and guarantee the fundamental rights of the people. Article 103 of the Constitution also provides that “Judges shall adjudicate independently according to their conscience and in accordance with the Constitution and law,” thereby requiring the court to take the Constitution as its foremost standard when adjudicating. Since the Constitution guarantees, as core components of the Constitution, the liberty and rights of members of the community by setting out numerous fundamental rights, notably under Chapter II entitled “The Rights and Duties of Citizens,” the court must ultimately make “serious attention and evaluation of fundamental rights and fundamental-right values, which legislation and administration are prone to overlook,” a major part of its authority and duty.\\n\\nB. The preliminary constitutional issue in this case\\n\\n1) Since the notice of non-recognition at issue as a labor union under the law was issued on 2013. 10. 24., the main portion of the legal conflict between the parties up to the present has concerned the fundamental problems inherent in the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue itself.\\n\\n2) Whether an administrative legislation is truly based on the higher norm, namely an Act, whether it rests on a proper understanding of the authorizing Act, and whether its content itself conforms to the purport of the Constitution and the Act, may be evaluated differently depending on different perspectives and understandings. In this case as well, the Plaintiff consistently argued that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue was enacted without delegation by Act and without properly considering fundamental-right values such as the right of association of labor unions, and that the Defendant’s measures based on such a provision lacked constitutional legitimacy, while the Defendant raised various counterarguments.\\n\\n3) Apart from the question whether item (d) of the statutory provision at issue itself, presented as one of the legal bases for the disposition in this case from the perspective of normative control, is unconstitutional, the question whether the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is unconstitutional is a significant constitutional issue that the court must consider and determine, and it is also a preliminary issue that decides the lawfulness of the disposition in this case. Therefore, the court must, pursuant to Article 107(2) of the Constitution, review the issue that forms the premise of this trial, namely the constitutionality of the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue.\\n\\n4) Of course, there may be room to criticize the Plaintiff, from the standpoint of “strict compliance with the law,” for retaining as members of the labor union persons who lost their teacher status due to dismissal, contrary to the wording of the statutory provision at issue. However, as the dissenting opinions point out, the Plaintiff’s raising of such a problem on the basis of the Constitution and law cannot be evaluated as self-contradictory or inconsistent; the court need only calmly and objectively determine the merits of the Plaintiff’s arguments. This is even more so when one remembers that judicial control over administrative legislation by the courts has the characteristic of a kind of objective litigation that emphasizes the protection of the objective legal order.\\n\\nC. Supplementary reasons for viewing the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as unconstitutional\\n\\n1) The majority opinion explained in detail why the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue violates the principle of statutory reservation. Below, I wish to repeat or add, by way of emphasis, several circumstances that should be specially considered in reaching that determination.\\n\\n2) First, I wish to emphasize the significance of the constitutionally guaranteed right of association.\\n\\na) Article 33(1) of the Constitution provides that “Workers shall have the right to independent association, collective bargaining, and collective action in order to improve working conditions,” thereby setting forth workers’ three labor rights. Among these three labor rights, the right of association is the priority right that must necessarily be presupposed for the realization of the other labor fundamental rights, and it has the strongest character of a liberty right. And Article 33(1) should be understood as guaranteeing not only the individual right of association of workers, but also the right of association of the organization itself. If only the individual right of association of workers is guaranteed and the right of association of organized groups is not recognized, then the guarantee of individual right of association may become meaningless.\\n\\nThat is, because the right of association in Article 33(1) of the Constitution is also a right of organized groups, that provision should be understood as protecting the continuation, maintenance, development, and expansion of workers’ organizations from unjust interference or intervention by state power (the right to continue existence), guaranteeing autonomous determination in the form of articles of association with respect to the organization and will-formation procedures of workers’ organizations (the right to organizational autonomy), and protecting the activities of workers’ organizations for the maintenance and improvement of working conditions, namely collective bargaining, conclusion of collective agreements, collective action, propaganda by the organization, and solicitation of membership (the right to collective activity) (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 95Hun-Ma154 on 1999. 11. 25., among others).\\n\\nb) In this way, the Constitution clearly guarantees the right of association, which is a liberty right in the special form of freedom of association, as a fundamental right, and makes clear that the State must not unjustly interfere or intervene through laws or enforcement decrees not only in the formation of labor unions, which are workers’ organizations, but also in their continuation, and that the
